entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need DFA runs, contradiction, and quantifier discipline. > [!question] Does failing to find a DFA prove that no DFA exists? > [!success]- Check your answer > No. It reports a failed search, not a proof covering every possible finite automaton. > Source: Lecture 3, PDF pp.24–30.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Can any DFA recognize exactly $$L=\{0^n1^n\mid n\ge0\}?$$ A proposed checker may have as many states as its designer wants, but the number is fixed before the input arrives. Testing many strings or rejecting one candidate machine does not settle the question. Success requires a proof applying to every finite automaton. | Challenge | Needed idea | |---|---| | Cover every possible state count | Use an arbitrary pumping length p | | Force a loop into the zero block | Choose 0^p1^p and use |xy|≤p | | Cover every legal split | Write y=0^b with 1≤b≤p | | Break equality | Pump to change zeros while ones remain fixed |

entries.title: Why a long run contains a loop
entries.text: Assume DFA M has p=|Q|≥1 states and accepts a word w of length at least p. During the first p transitions it visits positions r0,r1,…,rp: p+1 visits but only p possible state identities. Therefore ra=rb for some 0≤a<b≤p.[^l3pump] Let x be the first a input symbols, y the next b-a, and z the rest. Then $$w=xyz,\qquad |y|=b-a\ge1,\qquad |xy|=b\le p.$$ Reading y returns to the same state. Replacing that loop by zero, one, two, or any finite number of traversals leaves the machine at the same state before z; the unchanged suffix still reaches acceptance. flowchart LR S["start"] -->|x| R["repeated state r"] R -->|y, nonempty loop| R R -->|z| F["accept"] Figure 1 — The suffix cannot detect how often the loop ran Read it: x reaches state r; each copy of y returns to r; z therefore begins from the same state. Key takeaway: Pumping changes the string without changing the state from which the accepted suffix runs. Provenance: Pedagogical Mermaid derived from Lecture 3, PDF pp.26–34. > [!note] Regular pumping lemma > If L is regular, some integer p≥1 exists such that every w∈L with |w|≥p has a split w=xyz satisfying |y|≥1, |xy|≤p, and xy^iz∈L for every integer i≥0.[^l3pump]

entries.title: Read the quantifiers as a proof protocol
entries.text: $$\exists p\;\forall w\;\exists(x,y,z)\;\forall i.$$ The split is also constrained by the three conditions above. For contradiction, negate the operational order: 1. Assume regularity and accept an arbitrary promised p. 2. Choose a long w∈L, allowed to depend on p. 3. Consider an arbitrary legal split, not your favourite split. 4. Choose an i that may depend on that split. 5. Prove the pumped word is outside L. flowchart TD A["Assumption supplies p"] --> W["You choose long w in L"] W --> D["Lemma may choose any legal split"] D --> I["You choose a failing i"] I --> C["Contradiction: pumped word not in L"] Figure 2 — Who controls each choice Read it: Alternate between the assumption/lemma and the contradiction proof. Key takeaway: A proof that selects one convenient split skips the lemma's existential choice. Provenance: Pedagogical quantifier diagram derived from Lecture 3, PDF pp.35–40. > [!warning] Source shorthand > “For any i” on Lecture 3 p.35 should be read through the exact quantifiers: for each legal split, finding one failing exponent is enough. “One example” on p.40 means a witness family depending on arbitrary p, with every legal split covered.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Assume L={0^n1^n} is regular and let p be a pumping length. Choose w=0^p1^p, which belongs to L and has length 2p≥p. For an arbitrary legal split, x and y lie within the first p symbols, all zeros. Therefore $$x=0^a,\quad y=0^b,\quad z=0^{p-a-b}1^p$$ for integers a≥0, b≥1, a+b≤p. The residual zeros in z matter: the lemma does not require a+b=p. Pump with i=2: $$xy^2z=0^a0^{2b}0^{p-a-b}1^p=0^{p+b}1^p.$$ Because b≥1, zeros outnumber ones. The pumped word is not in L. This defeats every legal split, contradicting the lemma. Thus L is not regular, so no DFA, NFA, or classical regex recognizes it. > [!warning] Source proof repair > Lecture 3 pp.36–37 display only splits with a+b=p. Including 0^(p-a-b) in z covers all permitted splits while preserving the same contradiction.

entries.title: Worked transfer: square lengths
entries.text: Let S={0^(n^2) | n≥0}. Assume regularity, take pumping length p, and choose 0^(p^2). Every legal loop has length b with 1≤b≤p. Pumping twice produces length p^2+b. Now establish both sides: $$p^2<p^2+b\le p^2+p<(p+1)^2.$$ No integer square lies strictly between consecutive squares, so the pumped word leaves S. The lower bound alone is insufficient: a larger number might be another square. The upper bound is the decisive missing step in Lecture 3 p.39.[^l3pump] > [!question] Explain it yourself > Why does i=1 never help produce a contradiction? > [!success]- Check your explanation > xy^1z=xyz=w, the original chosen member of the language. > Source: Pumping-lemma definition, Lecture 3 p.32.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source | |---|---|---|---| | State visit | Distinct state | A run position versus a state identity; visits may repeat | L3 pp.33–34 | | Pumping length | Word length | Fixed language-dependent bound versus size of one chosen input | L3 p.32 | | One legal split | All legal splits | Example versus the coverage required for contradiction | L3 pp.35–40 | | Necessary condition | Sufficient condition | Required of regular languages versus enough to prove regularity | L3 pp.24–32, 41 | | Regular pumping lemma | Context-free pumping lemma | Different theorem and split structure; only the former is supplied here | L3 pp.25–41 |

entries.text: Full Understanding Use the complete reasoning above and the ordinary reference for the full source-repair record.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - p+1 visits among p states force a repeated state. - The loop y is nonempty and ends within the first p symbols. - To disprove regularity: arbitrary p, chosen w, arbitrary legal split, chosen failing i. - Equal-count proof changes only the initial zero block. - Square-length proof traps the new length between consecutive squares. - Passing one pumping attempt never proves regularity.

entries.title: 60-Second Recall
entries.text: p+1 visits · w=xyz · |y|≥1 · |xy|≤p · every i≥0 · arbitrary split · 0^p1^p · square gap [^l3pump]: Lecture 3 Regular Expression and Pumping Lemma.pdf, PDF pp.25–41.

entries.title: Current-source extension — Quantifiers inside language membership
entries.text: Problem first: Tutorial 3 P6 asks why “at least k” gives a regular language B while “at most k” gives nonregular C, for words $1^kw$ with existential k≥1. Here B={1^k w : k≥1 and w contains at least k ones} and C={1^k w : k≥1 and w contains at most k ones}, with binary suffix w and existential k chosen separately for each word. A language member may have several prefix/suffix representations; our proof cannot ignore that freedom. For B, replace any witness k by 1: its first 1 remains the prefix and a later 1 remains in the suffix. Conversely, starting with 1 and having a later 1 is enough with k=1. The regex is $1(0\cup1)^*1(0\cup1)^*$. This does not count an unbounded k; it eliminates that existential search. For C, put a separator into the witness $1^p01^p$. When a nonempty initial segment y is pumped down, the initial run shrinks to p−t but the later p ones do not. Any new prefix choice k' must fit into the shortened run, hence k'≤p−t p” should be “k≥p”; either is incompatible with the shortened bound, but the corrected inequality follows exactly from “at most k”. A fixed global k would make both languages regular; the source solution establishes the existential-per-word interpretation. The 6 October lecturer confirmation supports arbitrary valid splits. Current L3 cites the lemma on p.33, equal counts on pp.37–38 and squares on pp.39–40; earlier references here identify the preserved 42-page original. P1.4–5 · P4 · B · P6 all lead to original tasks with complete local help. Tutorial occurrence is not exam-paper occurrence.

entries.title: The Pumping Lemma
entries.text:
The Pumping Lemma Course index · Exercises Opening case — Can finite memory compare unbounded counts? Synthetic checker scenario using the lecture's language. A checker reads a block of zeros followed by a block of ones. It should accept exactly $L=\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}$: the two blocks have equal length, including the empty input. A proposed design may use any finite number of states, but that number is fixed independently of input length. Decide whether any DFA, NFA or classical regular expression can recognize exactly this language. If the answer is no, provide a proof covering every possible finite-state design. Finite testing or failure to draw a machine does not meet the success criterion. What We Need to Learn | Question | Concepts | |---|---| | Why does any sufficiently long run repeat a state? | State visits, finite memory, pigeonhole reasoning | | What does a repeated state allow? | A nonempty loop and pumping | | Who chooses the long word and its split? | Quantifier order | | How can the loop violate equal counts? | Bound the split, then pump | | Why is one lucky sample insufficient? | Necessary condition versus a regularity proof | Prerequisites: DFA run traces, the equivalence of DFA/NFA/regex, and contradiction proofs. Source scope: Lecture 3, PDF pp. 25–41. 1. Failure to find a machine is not impossibility A construction proves regularity when it recognizes all and only the desired strings. If we cannot find one, we have only learned about our search, not all possible machines. We need a necessary property of every regular language and then a contradiction. This is the motivation on Lecture 3 pp. 24–30. The useful intuition is finite memory: a long enough run revisits some state. Once it reaches the same state again, its later behavior has no record of how many times that intervening path was followed. The argument below makes this precise without treating “cannot count” as a proof. 2. Derive the pumping lemma from a run Suppose $L$ is recognized by a DFA with $p=|Q|\geq1$ states. Take any $w\in L$ with $|w|\geq p$. During its first $p$ transitions it visits $p+1$ state positions $r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_p$. Since there are only $p$ state identities, two positions have the same state: $r_a=r_b$ for some $0\leq a<b\leq p$. Split the input into $x$, the first $a$ symbols; $y$, symbols $a+1$ through $b$; and $z$, everything after position $b$. Then: $$w=xyz,\qquad |y|=b-a\geq1,\qquad |xy|=b\leq p.$$ The path for $y$ returns from $r_a$ to itself. Omitting it or repeating it any number of times still leaves the machine at $r_a$ before reading $z$. The original suffix path therefore still reaches the final state. Sources: Lecture 3, PDF pp. 26–34. pumping-loop.svg Figure 1 — A loop that can be repeated without changing the suffix run Read it: Follow x to state r. Reading y returns to r; z then follows the same route to a final state. Key takeaway: Pumping changes the input length but preserves the state at which the final suffix begins. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. > [!note] Regular pumping lemma > If $L$ is regular, there is an integer $p\geq1$ such that every $w\in L$ with $|w|\geq p$ has some split $w=xyz$ satisfying $|y|\geq1$, $|xy|\leq p$, and $xy^iz\in L$ for every integer $i\geq0$. Here $p$ is a pumping length, $x,y,z$ are strings and $i$ counts copies of $y$. All lengths are symbol counts; no rounding or physical units apply. Source: Lecture 3, PDF p. 32. The bound is $|w|\geq p$, not strictly greater. There are $p+1$ visits, not necessarily $p+1$ distinct states. The word need not end just after the repeated state; $z$ can be long or empty. Different DFAs can give different valid pumping lengths, and the proof never needs the smallest one. Worked positive example. For the regular language of binary strings ending in 1, use its two-state DFA, so $p=2$ is valid. For 001, choose $x=\varepsilon$, $y=0$, $z=01$. Then $xy^iz=0^{i+1}1$ ends in 1 for every $i\geq0$. This is an illustration of a valid split; it is not a proof that checking one word establishes regularity. 3. Quantifiers determine the proof strategy The lemma says: $$\exists p\geq1\; orall w\in L	ext{ with }|w|\geq p\;\exists x,y,z\; orall i\geq0.$$ The split in this shorthand must satisfy the three displayed structural conditions. To contradict the lemma, the nonregularity argument must defeat every candidate pumping length: | Stage | Proof obligation | |---|---| | Assume regularity | Receive an unknown $p\geq1$ promised by the lemma | | Choose $w$ | It may depend on $p$; prove $w\in L$ and $\vert w\vert \geq p$ | | Consider the split | Cover all $xyz$ with $\vert y\vert \geq1$ and $\vert xy\vert \leq p$ | | Choose $i$ | It may depend on the split; show $xy^iz
otin L$ | | Conclude | No promised split works, contradicting regularity | You control the witness $w$ and pumping exponent $i$, but you do not get to choose just the easiest split. A symbolic description of all legal splits often makes the proof short. One exponent such as $i=0$ or $i=2$ may defeat them all; the proof needs one failing exponent for each split, not every exponent failing. In fact $i=1$ always restores the original $w\in L$. > [!warning] Qualifying the lecture shorthand > Page 35's “for any i” should be read through the lemma's quantifiers: find an exponent that breaks each permitted split. Page 40's “only needs one example” means one witness family depending on arbitrary p, with all legal splits covered. One fixed word or one chosen split does not prove nonregularity. 4. Bound the movable part before changing it For a block-structured word, $|xy|\leq p$ locates $y$ in the first $p$ symbols. If those symbols are all 0, every valid $y$ consists only of 0s, even though you do not know its exact length. This is how a local loop changes one block's count without changing the other. pumping-split.svg Figure 2 — All legal splits of the equal-count witness Read it: The first p positions are zeros. Both x and y lie inside that region; z includes the remaining zeros and all the ones. Key takeaway: Do not assume x and y consume every zero. The condition is a + b ≤ p, not a + b = p. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. Counterexample to a proof shortcut. If a proposed proof examines only $x=\varepsilon,y=0$, it may show that this particular split fails but leave all other splits untouched. The lemma needs only one successful split; a contradiction must rule out every permitted one. Using a variable $b$ with $1\leq b\leq p$ handles all loop lengths at once. Solve the opening case Decision. No DFA, NFA or ordinary regular expression recognizes $L=\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}$. Justification. Assume, for contradiction, that $L$ is regular. Let $p\geq1$ be a pumping length. Choose $w=0^p1^p$. It belongs to $L$ and has length $2p\geq p$. Operation — characterize every split. For any permitted $w=xyz$, the first $p$ symbols are zeros and $|xy|\leq p$. Write $$x=0^a,\quad y=0^b,\quad z=0^{p-a-b}1^p,$$ where $a\geq0$, $b\geq1$ and $a+b\leq p$. The nonnegative exponent $p-a-b$ accounts for any zeros remaining in $z$. Intermediate result — pump twice. Choose $i=2$. Then $$xy^2z=0^a0^{2b}0^{p-a-b}1^p=0^{p+b}1^p.$$ There are $p+b$ zeros but only $p$ ones. Since $b\geq1$, the counts differ, so $xy^2z
otin L$. Interpretation and conclusion. This argument applies to every valid split. No split promised by the lemma can survive all pumping exponents, contradicting regularity. Therefore $L$ is not regular. Unit 03's equivalence means NFAs and classical regexes cannot evade this limitation. The proof allows any fixed finite state count; it does not merely refute one candidate design. It says nothing here about more powerful computational models. > [!warning] Source proof repair > Lecture 3 pp. 36–37 display $z=1^p$ and $a+b=p$, covering splits at the end of the zero block. The lemma also permits $a+b<p$. The extra factor $0^{p-a-b}$ above covers those omitted splits, while giving the same contradiction $p+b
e p$. 5. Transfer — Unary strings of square length The second lecture example is $S=\{0^{n^2}\mid n\geq0\}$ (PDF pp. 38–39). Equal-block counts are no longer available, but the increasing gap between squares can trap the pumped length. Assume regularity and let $p\geq1$ be a pumping length. Choose $w=0^{p^2}$, which is in $S$ and has length $p^2\geq p$. For every legal split, $y=0^b$ for an integer $1\leq b\leq p$. Pump with $i=2$; the new length is $p^2+b$. Now derive both bounds: $$p^2<p^2+b\leq p^2+p<p^2+2p+1=(p+1)^2.$$ The strict first inequality uses $b\geq1$; the weak inequality uses $b\leq p$; the final strict inequality uses $p+1>0$. No integer square lies strictly between the consecutive squares $p^2$ and $(p+1)^2$. Thus the pumped word is not in $S$, for every permitted split, contradicting regularity. square-gap.svg Figure 3 — Trap the new length between consecutive squares Read it: The pumped length increases by b, but b is at most p. The next square is 2p + 1 beyond p². Key takeaway: Being larger than one square is insufficient; the upper bound rules out reaching the next square. Provenance: Original teaching diagram derived from the cited concepts. For a numerical illustration only, take $p=3$. The original length is 9 and possible added lengths are 1, 2 or 3, producing 10, 11 or 12; the next square is 16. The symbolic inequalities establish the result for arbitrary $p$, including $p=1$, where the new length is 2 between 1 and 4. > [!warning] Source proof repair > Page 39 states that $p^2+b>p^2$ makes the pumped word leave the square-length language. That lower bound alone is insufficient: a larger number can be another square. The necessary upper bound is $p^2+b<(p+1)^2$, proved above from $b\leq p$. Exam-style answer and reusable method “Assume regularity with pumping length $p$. Choose a member $w$ of length at least $p$. For an arbitrary legal split, use $|xy|\leq p$ and $|y|\geq1$ to constrain the pumped segment. Choose an exponent and derive a violation of membership. Since every legal split fails, the lemma is contradicted.” This is a method for proving nonregularity when a suitable witness can be found. It is not an algorithm guaranteed to find a proof for every language, and failing to find a contradiction does not prove regularity. To prove regularity, construct a machine or expression with a correctness argument. Misconceptions and quick review - Long input guarantees a repeated state, not a repeated input symbol sufficient for pumping by itself. - The repetition is found within the first $p$ transitions, explaining $|xy|\leq p$. - A finite regular language may have no words as long as a chosen pumping length; the lemma then holds vacuously for those lengths. - Pumping a chosen long word successfully does not establish regularity of the whole language. - $0^n1^n$ with a shared unbounded variable is language-description notation, not an ordinary regex for all equal-count words. For a fixed specified $n$, the single word can of course be written using concatenation. > [!summary] Retrieval targets > State the lemma with its quantifiers. Derive it from $p+1$ visits among $p$ states. Reconstruct both source proofs with all legal splits and both square-gap bounds. Explain exactly what your chosen witness and exponent depend on. Current Tutorial 3 — Prove against every permitted choice Current source locators: the 43-page Lecture 3 has the lemma on p.33, state visits on p.35, equal counts on pp.37–38, square lengths on pp.39–40 and Q&A on p.42. Earlier citations here remain references to the preserved 42-page original. The additional explicit elimination slide precedes this material. The captured 6 October lecturer reply explicitly confirms handling every valid split. The displayed lecture shorthand $a+b=p$ must not replace the theorem's $a+b\le p$. Residual zeros belong in z. This is now lecturer-supported clarification, not merely an unconfirmed interpretation of the older slide. Similar language descriptions can hide different quantifiers Original motivating task: current Tutorial 3 P6, pp.4–5, asks for a regex for B and a nonregularity proof for C: $B=\{1^kw: k\ge1,\ w\in\{0,1\}^*,\ \#_1(w)\ge k\}$, $C=\{1^kw: k\ge1,\ w\in\{0,1\}^*,\ \#_1(w)\le k\}$. The phrase “for some k” is interpreted existentially per word, as in the supplied solution. It does not declare one globally fixed k. Success requires respecting all possible representations of a pumped word. For B, any representation with k≥1 gives a first 1 and at least one later 1; conversely, any word beginning with 1 and containing a later 1 works with k=1. Therefore B is described by $1(0\cup1)^*1(0\cup1)^*$. Larger possible k adds no words beyond the k=1 case. For C, choose $s=1^p01^p$. Its initial block supports k=p and its remaining suffix contains exactly p ones. Every permitted y is $1^t$ with $1\le t\le p$. Pumping down leaves $1^{p-t}01^p$. A different representation cannot save it: its prefix parameter must satisfy $k'\le p-t$, since the next symbol after that initial run is 0. Its suffix still contains the p trailing ones, so $\#_1(w')\ge p>k'$. If p=t, the word starts with 0 and has no admissible positive k'. Thus every split fails. Source qualification: P6's supplied solution says membership would need k>p. The actual condition “at most k” would require k≥p, already impossible because k≤p−t is unnecessary and imprecise; the contradiction and conclusion survive. No instructor erratum is claimed. If k were one fixed integer, both languages would be regular: a finite prefix and a fixed lower/upper bound on the later count can be tracked by finite states. This explains why the existential interpretation matters. We preserve the source wording, expose the interpretation and do not silently prove a different fixed-k task. Complete original P6 · Original optional Tock check for B

entries.title: Exercises
In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A grammar is a finite recipe for generating words. Variables mark unfinished work; terminals make up finished words. Recursion can express matched counts or nesting that a finite automaton cannot track without bound. A derivation lists replacements, whereas a parse tree records their structure. Different grammars may generate the same language, yet disagree on grouping. After this unit, derive a word, justify a CFG's exact language, combine grammars and encode precedence/association rather than assuming that rule order gives them.[^l4] The connected ideas are ==generation==, ==terminal yield==, ==recursive invariant==, ==structural ambiguity== and ==precedence levels==. You will use Unit 01's set reasoning and Unit 02's DFA semantics; Unit 04 supplies the equal-count/nonregular contrast.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: > [!note] Concept — A reusable production > Plain-language meaning: A variable can be replaced by a finite RHS wherever it occurs; its neighbours are not a condition. > Why it matters: One rule may be reused to create an unbounded family of finite words. > Connects to: recursion, base cases and CFG tuples. > Source: Lecture 4 PDF pp.5–8. > [!note] Concept — Generated language > Plain-language meaning: Collect only terminal words obtainable from the designated start, not unfinished forms. > Why it matters: A correct rule set with a different start may generate a different language. > Connects to: membership witnesses and both-direction proofs. > Source: Lecture 4 p.11; Tutorial 4 pp.1–2, P1–P2. > [!note] Concept — Ordered parse tree > Plain-language meaning: The tree records nested choices; reading leaves left to right gives the word. > Why it matters: Replacement schedules can differ without changing the tree. > Connects to: leftmost/rightmost derivations and ambiguity. > Source: Lecture 4 pp.22–24; Tutorial 4 pp.3–4, P5. > [!note] Concept — Grammar composition > Plain-language meaning: A new start selects one grammar, joins two, or repeatedly chooses a factor. > Why it matters: It proves CFL closure under union, concatenation and star. > Connects to: disjoint variable names and finite concatenations. > Source: Lecture 4 pp.14–19. > [!note] Concept — Expression structure > Plain-language meaning: Separate variables give precedence levels; recursion direction gives association. > Why it matters: Equal terminal strings may hide different grouping. > Connects to: grammar versus language ambiguity. > Source: Lecture 4 pp.20–24; Tutorial 4 pp.4–7, P6–P7.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Recall string concatenation and the difference between “produce one example” and “prove two sets equal”. > [!question] Does exhibiting a grammar derivation of 0011 prove its entire language is exactly $\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}$? > [!success]- Check your answer > No. It proves one membership witness. We must show every completed derivation has the required form and every target word has a derivation. > Source: L4 pp.5–11; pedagogical interpretation of the grammar construction.

entries.title: A motivating question — A generator and a parser
entries.text: Synthetic case grounded in T4. A processor needs (a) exactly a^n b^n including epsilon and (b) a unique intended structure for a+a+a and a↑b↑c. Can a finite grammar do both? Success requires a general language argument and a structural argument; matching one output is not enough. | Question | What you need | |---|---| | Why do counts match? | recursive invariant and base rule | | Why does order match? | insertion around the remaining variable | | Do two schedules mean ambiguity? | tree versus chronology | | Which operator groups first? | precedence and association |

entries.title: Let the unfinished middle carry the dependency
entries.text: Start with $S\to aSb\mid\varepsilon$. Intuitively, every unfinished middle receives one new a on its left and b on its right. Formally, after n recursive steps the form is $a^nSb^n$; that is the invariant. Choosing epsilon removes the only variable and leaves $a^nb^n$. For aaabbb, keep the unfinished S visible: $S\Rightarrow aSb\Rightarrow aaSbb\Rightarrow aaaSbbb\Rightarrow aaabbb$. Before the last step we have a sentential form, not a word in the language, because S is not a terminal. “⇒*” allows zero or more replacement steps, whereas “→” declares a rule. These arrows answer different questions.[^t4] Why is the language exact? No derivation can insert b to the left of a, and every recursive application adds the same count. Conversely, any desired n can be achieved by n recursive choices and one terminating choice. Both inclusions matter. Therefore aabbb and abab fail for different reasons: unequal counts versus incorrect order. This grammar is unambiguous: the target length fixes the number of recursive layers and each layer has only one S to expand. That does not mean all recursive grammars are unambiguous. > [!question] Explain it yourself > Why does S→0S11 generate two ones per zero without storing a numerical counter? > [!success]- Check your explanation > Each recursive layer adds one 0 before the remaining variable and two 1s after it. After n layers the invariant is $0^nS1^{2n}$; termination removes S. > Source: Tutorial 4 PDF p.3, P4.

entries.title: See a tree rather than just a sequence
entries.text: For S→00S1|ε, the word 000011 requires two recursive layers. The ordered children at each layer are 0,0,S,1, not merely a set of symbols. parse-tree.svg Figure 1 — Structure fixes the terminal yield Read it: descend through the middle S nodes, then read all terminal leaves from left to right, omitting epsilon. Key takeaway: the yield is 000011; the leftmost and rightmost derivations coincide because one variable remains at each step. Provenance: technical redraw of Tutorial 4 P5, pp.3–4; tutor-local copy avoids ordinary-output aliasing. Contrast the pedagogical grammar S→AB, A→a, B→b. S⇒AB⇒aB⇒ab and S⇒AB⇒Ab⇒ab apply choices in different orders, but both trees have S above ordered children A and B. This is not ambiguity. To prove ambiguity, exhibit two structures or two distinct leftmost derivations, not a leftmost and a rightmost schedule for one structure.

entries.title: Compose whole languages by composing starts
entries.text: Let renamed CFGs generate A and B. Introduce fresh X. X→S_A|S_B selects one whole derivation for union. X→S_A S_B puts two independent derivations next to each other for concatenation. X→S_A X|ε chooses a finite sequence of A-words for star. Old rules remain available; renaming variables prevents cross-expansion.[^l4closure] The star construction handles zero factors explicitly through X→ε. It also handles epsilon in A: extra empty factors may yield another description, not another distinct terminal word. Construction correctness is about the generated set, not necessarily uniqueness. Every DFA can also become a CFG: assign A_q to each state, add A_q→aA_r for each q— a→r transition and A_f→ε for accepting f. The variable records the state reached after the generated prefix. Epsilon termination is possible exactly at an accepting state. Thus regular ⇒ context-free, not conversely. Equal-count words supply the counterexample to the converse.[^l4regular]

entries.title: Why grouping cannot be guessed from the printed word
entries.text: For S→S+S|a, a+a+a has trees (a+a)+a and a+(a+a). One expands the left subtree at the top split; the other the right. Both can be written as different leftmost derivations, so this is genuine grammar ambiguity. A left-recursive replacement S→S+a|a has the same terminal language $a(+a)^n$ but fixes left grouping.[^t4ambiguity] A second problem before its solution: the reference E/T/F grammar handles + and *, but how can ↑ bind tighter and group rightward? Adding ↑ at E's level would not enforce stronger precedence. Insert P between T and F: E→E+T|T; T→T*P|P; P→F↑P|F; F→(E)|a|b|c. Reading from the top: E combines complete products, T complete powers, P complete factors. Deeper structure is grouped inside an outer operand, so a*b↑c means a*(b↑c). The expandable P is to the right of ↑, so a↑b↑c means a↑(b↑c). This says nothing about the direction in which a parser must expand variables during derivation. The reference F lacks c; the supplied P7 solution explicitly adds it to support its example words.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Generator: S→aSb|ε generates all and only $a^nb^n$ by the invariant/converse argument. Epsilon is included through the base; terminal order is maintained through wrapping. Parser: S→S+a|a removes the two possible + groupings while preserving the word set. For a↑b↑c, the P-level right recursion determines a↑(b↑c). The same production hierarchy gives multiplication higher precedence than addition. Neither a unique tree for one tested word nor one successful tool run proves unambiguity for every unrelated grammar.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Pair | Decisive distinction | Source | |---|---|---| | Variable / terminal | unfinished placeholder / finished-word symbol | L4 pp.6–8 | | Production / derivation | allowed rewrite / actual application | L4 p.11 | | Sentential form / language member | may contain variables / terminal word from start | T4 pp.1–2 | | CFG / CFL | finite description / generated set | L4 p.11 | | Two schedules / two trees | chronology can differ / structural alternatives | T4 P1.3, P6 | | Ambiguous grammar / inherently ambiguous language | this description has ambiguity / every CFG description has it | T4 p.8 | | Precedence / association | relative operator levels / grouping among same-level operators | T4 P7 |

entries.title: Source traps to keep visible
entries.text: The forum request for 01010101 under S→RR, R→0R1|ε has no derivation: only two balanced 0^n1^n blocks are available. The student question had no visible lecturer answer at capture. T4 P1's non-CFL subset is a stated source counterexample, not a result proved by regular pumping here. The source establishes CFL union/concatenation/star closure but not a new intersection/complement proof. These are limits, not an invitation to guess missing course material.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Return to the mechanisms above, then the full reference for exact closure and language arguments.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: A CFG is (V,Σ,R,S), with one variable per rule's left side. Define an invariant for recursive generation and prove both inclusions. Parse trees preserve RHS order; derivation schedules do not by themselves establish ambiguity. Translate DFA states into variables, with epsilon only at accepting states. Rename variables before combining starts. To prove ambiguity, find one word with two trees; to encode expressions, separate precedence levels and place recursion on the association side.

entries.text: - Four CFG components - Production versus derivation arrows - Terminal membership condition - Recursive invariant and base case - Tree versus schedule - Fresh-start closure rules - DFA-to-grammar termination - Precedence versus association [^l4]: Lecture 4 Context-Free Languages.pdf, PDF pp.5–26. entries.title: Context-Free Grammars and Languages
entries.text: Context-Free Grammars and Languages Course index · Exercises · Lab Roadmap and objectives Languages → production rules → derivations → parse trees → closure constructions → ambiguity → expression structure. Prerequisites are Unit 01's strings/set equality and Unit 02's DFA transitions. Unit 04 explains why equal-count languages are not regular; it does not prevent grammars from generating them. After study, construct and justify a CFG, derive a word, distinguish terminals from unfinished sentential forms, translate a DFA into a grammar, combine grammars and exhibit structural ambiguity. Sources: Lecture 4 PDF pp.5–26; current Tutorial 4 PDF pp.1–8. This unit does not infer PDA, normal-form or context-free pumping chapters from the handbook roadmap. Opening case — Two jobs for a small language processor Synthetic teaching case grounded in L4/T4. A processor must generate exactly $0^n1^n$ for n≥0 and parse expressions built from a, b, c, +, *, ↑ and parentheses. Multiplication binds more tightly than addition; exponentiation binds most tightly and associates rightward. Can finite production rules enforce equal counts? Can they determine whether a+b*c means a+(b*c), and whether a↑b↑c means a↑(b↑c)? Success means exact generated membership and a unique intended structure—not merely one convenient example. | Question | Knowledge needed | |---|---| | Generate matched blocks | recursive and terminating rules | | Explain membership | derivation invariant and converse construction | | Explain structure | ordered parse trees | | Enforce precedence and association | separate variables and recursion direction | 1. Generate a word instead of remembering every count A finite automaton recognizes a word presented to it. A grammar generates a word by replacing variables. For equal counts, start with S, repeatedly surround its unfinished middle with 0 and 1, then terminate: $S\to0S1\mid\varepsilon$. One finite rule can be reused any finite number of times. S is a placeholder, not an input symbol. Terminals 0 and 1 survive in the finished word.[^l4basic] A context-free grammar is $G=(V,\Sigma,R,S)$: finite variables V, finite terminals Σ, finite production rules R and a designated start variable S∈V. Distinguish variable names from terminal symbols. Each production has form $A\to\alpha$, with one variable A on its left and $\alpha\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*$ on its right. Empty RHS is permitted. A rule does not inspect the neighbours of A, which is what “context-free” means. The example $0S\to0S1$ is not a CFG rule because its left side has two symbols; this unit does not develop context-sensitive grammar theory. 2. Rules, steps, sentential forms and terminal words The production arrow → declares an allowed replacement. The derivation arrow ⇒ records one actual application: $uAv\Rightarrow u\alpha v$ when $A\to\alpha$ is a production. The surrounding strings u,v are unchanged. The relation ⇒* allows zero or more steps.[^l4derive] For example, $S\Rightarrow0S1\Rightarrow00S11\Rightarrow000S111\Rightarrow000111$. The first three results still contain S and are sentential forms, not members of the generated language. Only terminal strings derived from the designated start count: $$L(G)=\{w\in\Sigma^*:S\Rightarrow^*w\}.$$ Choosing S→ε directly gives epsilon. Terminating is a production choice, not deletion of an inconvenient variable. Both-direction proof: after n uses of S→0S1, the form is $0^nS1^n$; S→ε produces exactly $0^n1^n$. Thus no generated terminal word has unequal counts or a 1 preceding a later 0. Conversely, for every n≥0, use the recursive rule n times and terminate. Hence the grammar generates all, and only, the target words. “It generates 0011” alone would prove much less. Independent variables are independent choices L4 p.9 uses $S\to RR,\ R\to0R1\mid\varepsilon$. Each R generates an independent $0^n1^n$ block. The language is $\{0^i1^i0^j1^j:i,j\ge0\}$, not “any number of balanced blocks.” For 010011: $S\Rightarrow RR\Rightarrow0R1R\Rightarrow01R\Rightarrow010R1\Rightarrow0100R11\Rightarrow010011$. The first R used its recursive rule once; the second twice. The forum's requested 01010101 cannot be derived: a nonempty factor $0^n1^n$ has exactly one 0→1 block pair and no internal 1→0. Two factors cannot form four alternating 01 blocks. Even 010101 is excluded, as L4 p.9 states. The unanswered student question is not proof that a derivation exists.[^forum] Balanced parentheses need nesting and concatenation L4 p.10 gives $S\to(S)\mid SS\mid\varepsilon$. The wrap rule nests a balanced word, the concatenation rule joins two, and epsilon supplies the base. For ()(): $S\Rightarrow SS\Rightarrow(S)S\Rightarrow()S\Rightarrow()(S)\Rightarrow()()$. For (()), use wrapping twice and then epsilon. Soundness follows by induction on a parse tree: empty, wrapping and joining all preserve balance. For completeness, a nonempty balanced word splits at the closing parenthesis matching its first opening one into (u)v, where u and v are balanced; recursively derive both with wrap and concatenation. This gives a general construction rather than an example-only claim. This grammar need not be unambiguous: epsilon-producing branches can create different trees for the same word. Language correctness and uniqueness of structure are different goals. 3. Read a parse tree in two directions An ordered parse tree records production choices. Its root is the start variable; each variable node's ordered children spell its chosen RHS; leaves read left to right give the terminal word, ignoring epsilon. Horizontal order matters. Leftmost derivation expands the leftmost remaining variable; rightmost derivation expands the rightmost.[^l4trees] Open Figure 1 parse-tree.svg Figure 1 — Two recursive expansions and one terminating expansion Read it: each S→00S1 node has children 0, 0, S, 1. The deepest S produces epsilon. Read leaves to obtain 000011. Key takeaway: the tree specifies two matched recursive layers; it is not a time-line of symbol consumption. Provenance: technical redraw of Tutorial 4 P5, PDF pp.3–4; the source's text-tree connectors are replaced by readable edges. Different derivation orders need not imply ambiguity. For the pedagogical grammar $S\to AB,\ A\to a,\ B\to b$, leftmost steps are $S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow aB\Rightarrow ab$; rightmost steps are $S\Rightarrow AB\Rightarrow Ab\Rightarrow ab$. Both traverse the same tree. In a grammar with only one variable at every stage, such as S→00S1|ε, these orders coincide. 4. Every regular language has a CFG For a DFA $M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$, introduce a variable $A_q$ for each state q. Add $A_q\to aA_{\delta(q,a)}$ for each transition and $A_f\to\varepsilon$ for each accepting state f; start at $A_{q_0}$.[^l4regular] Invariant: after generating prefix u, the remaining variable is $A_{\delta^*(q_0,u)}$. Epsilon termination exists exactly when that state is accepting. Thus the grammar generates precisely L(M). L4 pp.12–13's displayed DFA recognizes binary words ending in 1. Its grammar is $A_0\to0A_0\mid1A_1$, $A_1\to0A_0\mid1A_1\mid\varepsilon$. For 101: $A_0\Rightarrow1A_1\Rightarrow10A_0\Rightarrow101A_1\Rightarrow101$. It cannot terminate for 10 because A0 has no epsilon rule. The slide's informal $\delta(q_0,q_0)=0$ reverses the standard argument/result roles; the graph means $\delta(q_0,0)=q_0$. Therefore all regular languages are context-free. The converse fails: $0^n1^n$ has the grammar above and is nonregular by Unit 04. Having a CFG is not a proof of regularity. 5. Combine grammars without mixing their variables Before combining two CFGs, rename their variables to disjoint sets and choose a fresh start X. Otherwise one grammar's rules could accidentally expand another's variables. This is a technical condition for implementing L4 pp.14–19 faithfully.[^l4closure] | Target | Additional start rules | Why the terminal words are exactly right | |---|---|---| | A∪B | X→S_A or S_B | choose one original grammar | | AB | X→S_A S_B | independently derive an A-word then a B-word | | A* | X→S_A X or ε | choose finitely many A-words, then stop | Keep all old rules. Soundness: each start construction produces only the stated combinations. Completeness: choose the appropriate branch, pair of witnesses or finite list of star factors and derive each. For A*, zero factors generate epsilon; if epsilon∈A, multiple descriptions of the same terminal word are harmless for language membership but may affect ambiguity. The source establishes closure under union, concatenation and star. Its concatenation tuple slide retains a union label; use its actual rule X→S_A S_B and the concatenation theorem. The unanswered forum question about intersection/complement supplies no demonstrated closure theorem; no missing later proof is silently imported here. 6. Ambiguity is structural, not just a choice of schedule A grammar is ambiguous when some terminal word has two distinct ordered parse trees, equivalently two distinct leftmost derivations. The existence of any two differently ordered derivations is insufficient. A language can have an ambiguous grammar and another unambiguous grammar. “Inherently ambiguous” means every CFG for that language is ambiguous; the example here does not establish that property.[^t4ambiguity] For $S\to S+S\mid a$, a+a+a can have structure (a+a)+a or a+(a+a). Both yield the same terminal string. To force left grouping while keeping the same language, use $S\to S+a\mid a$; right grouping uses $S\to a+S\mid a$. All describe $a(+a)^n$ for n≥0. Equal generated sets do not imply equal trees. Lecture 4 pp.20–24 similarly compares a layered E/T/F expression grammar with $E\to E+E\mid E\times E\mid(E)\mid a$. The layered grammar fixes precedence; the single-variable grammar allows both top-level + and × structures for a+a×a. Rule-list order alone does not impose precedence. Solve the opening case Matched blocks: $S\to0S1\mid\varepsilon$ generates exactly $0^n1^n$ by the invariant/converse argument. The base handles n=0; recursion maintains order and equal counts. It does not claim a finite automaton can recognize the same language. Expression structure: following T4 P7, use $$ \begin{aligned} E&\to E+T\mid T,\\ T&\to T*P\mid P,\\ P&\to F\uparrow P\mid F,\\ F&\to(E)\mid a\mid b\mid c. \end{aligned} $$ E adds whole T operands, so multiplication/exponentiation are completed inside them. T adds whole P operands; P puts a recursively expandable P on the right of ↑. Therefore a+b*c groups as a+(b*c), a*b↑c as a*(b↑c), and a↑b↑c as a↑(b↑c). Left recursion at E/T gives left association for +/*. Parentheses return to E and allow explicit overrides.[^t4precedence] The source's reference F lists only a,b but its requested words use c; the supplied solution extends F to include c. This minimal source-supported extension is explicit rather than pretending the original two-terminal grammar derives c. Exam-style answer and reusable method A CFG has one variable on each rule's left side. Define the target language, choose a base case and invariant-preserving recursive step, then prove both inclusions. For parsing, construct a tree or leftmost derivation; prove ambiguity with one word and two distinct trees. For expression structure, separate precedence levels and place recursion on the association side. This is source-based answer practice, not an official marking scheme or predicted exam question. Native Obsidian/PDF checks for this new unit remain pending. Misconceptions and quick review - S→ε does not put the epsilon symbol into the alphabet. - Equal counts alone do not permit interleaving; grammar order matters. - A sentential form with variables is not a member of L(G). - Two grammars with identical rules can differ when their starts differ. - Arbitrary subsets of a CFL need not be CFLs: Tutorial 4 P1 supplies a non-CFL counterexample. Its non-context-freeness is a stated source fact; a later proof tool is not in this unit. - “I found one parse” does not prove unambiguity; “I found two derivation schedules” does not prove ambiguity. - The grammar for exactly two blocks cannot generate four alternating blocks. [^l4derive]: Same lecture, PDF pp.9–11; Tutorial 4 - Context-Free Grammars.pdf, PDF pp.1–3, definitions and P2. [^l4trees]: Lecture 4 PDF pp.22–24; Tutorial 4 PDF pp.3–4, P5. [^l4regular]: Lecture 4 PDF pp.12–13, DFA diagram and grammar translation; figure and accepting state visually checked. entries.title: Exercises
entries.text: Exercises Notes · Lab Every T4 task below is an ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE. Source is the current solution PDF (7 October); student PDF (6 October) and both notebooks retain the corresponding statements. Try the statement, then reveal its own hint and complete solution. One-based PDF positions are used. T4 P1 — Concepts and counterexamples Source: Tutorial 4 solution PDF pp.1–2, P1.1–4; student PDF pp.1–2; solution notebook cell 4. Answer and justify: 1. Same variables, terminals and rules but different start variables: must languages agree? 2. If L is context-free and L'⊆L, must L' be context-free? 3. Can an unambiguous grammar have different leftmost/rightmost derivations of one word? 4. Does every terminal/variable sequence appearing during a derivation belong to L(G)? > [!tip]- Hint > The tuple includes its start. Distinguish subset, terminal yield and tree structure from replacement order. > [!success]- Solution > 1. No. With rules S→0A, A→1 and variables {S,A}, start S generates {01}; start A generates {1}. Rules alone do not determine the language. > > 2. No. The source counterexample takes context-free $\{0,1\}^*$ and its subset $\{0^n1^n0^n:n\ge0\}$, stated to be non-context-free. That non-CFL fact is supplied here without a proof: a later context-free pumping argument is outside the provided Lecture 4. It is not proved merely by regular pumping. Arbitrary-subset closure does not follow from the three closure operations established in L4. > > 3. Yes. For S→AB, A→a, B→b, leftmost is S⇒AB⇒aB⇒ab, rightmost S⇒AB⇒Ab⇒ab. Only one tree exists: the schedules differ, not the structure. > > 4. No. For S→aSb|ε, aSb is a sentential form, not a terminal word. L(G) includes only words in Σ* derived from the designated start. T4 P2 — Language and derivation Source: solution PDF p.2, P2.1–4; student p.2; solution notebook cell 5. For $S\to aSb\mid\varepsilon$: (1) derive aaabbb; (2) describe L(G); (3) explain exclusion of aabbb, abab and ba; (4) decide ambiguity. > [!tip]- Hint > Describe the form after n recursive applications, and count the remaining variables. > [!success]- Solution > 1. $S\Rightarrow aSb\Rightarrow aaSbb\Rightarrow aaaSbbb\Rightarrow aaabbb$. > > 2. After n recursive steps the form is $a^nSb^n$. Terminating produces $a^nb^n$, and every n≥0 is realizable. Thus $L(G)=\{a^nb^n:n\ge0\}$. > > 3. aabbb has unequal counts; abab violates all-a-before-all-b order; ba reverses that order. Neither production can create any of those patterns. > > 4. Unambiguous: for a terminal word of length 2n, exactly n recursive rules and one epsilon rule must be used. There is only one variable at every stage, so its expansion tree is uniquely determined. T4 P3 — Construct the requested grammar Source: solution PDF pp.2–3, P3; student p.2; solution notebook cell 6. Give a CFG for binary-letter strings over {a,b} ending in a. Derive a, ba and abba. Explain why epsilon and abb cannot be generated. > [!tip]- Hint > Generate an arbitrary prefix recursively, but reserve the final production for the required last symbol. > [!success]- Solution > Use $S\to aS\mid bS\mid a$. > > $S\Rightarrow a$; $S\Rightarrow bS\Rightarrow ba$; $S\Rightarrow aS\Rightarrow abS\Rightarrow abbS\Rightarrow abba$. > > Every completed derivation terminates with S→a, so its last symbol is a and it is nonempty. Conversely, generate each symbol of any desired prefix using aS/bS, then terminate with a. Hence the language is exactly the target. No epsilon rule exists and no terminal derivation ends in b, excluding epsilon and abb. T4 P4 — One count and twice that count Source: solution PDF p.3, P4; student p.2; solution notebook cell 7. Construct a CFG for $\{0^n1^{2n}:n\ge0\}$, derive 001111 and justify terminal order. > [!tip]- Hint > Each recursive step must add one 0 and two 1s around the remaining variable. > [!success]- Solution > Use $S\to0S11\mid\varepsilon$. Then $S\Rightarrow0S11\Rightarrow00S1111\Rightarrow001111$. > > After n recursive steps, the form is $0^nS1^{2n}$. Terminating produces the required word; for every n, that derivation exists. Added zeros occur to the left of S and pairs of ones to its right, so all zeros precede all ones. The base n=0 produces epsilon. T4 P5 — Parse tree and derivation Source: solution PDF pp.3–4, P5.1–3; student p.2; solution notebook cell 8. For $S\to00S1\mid\varepsilon$, (1) draw a parse tree for 000011; (2) write its leftmost derivation; (3) describe L(G). > [!tip]- Hint > Use two recursive layers. At every layer keep all four children, in RHS order. > [!success]- Solution > 1. The exact ordered tree is shown below: outer children 0,0,S,1; inner S children 0,0,S,1; deepest S child epsilon. Its terminal yield is 000011. > > parse-tree.svg > > 2. $S\Rightarrow00S1\Rightarrow0000S11\Rightarrow000011$. One variable remains at each stage, so leftmost and rightmost orders coincide. > > 3. After n recursive uses, $0^{2n}S1^n$ terminates to $0^{2n}1^n$. Every n≥0 is possible and no other terminal form is possible. Hence $L(G)=\{0^{2n}1^n:n\ge0\}$. T4 P6 — Detect and remove ambiguity Source: solution PDF pp.4–6, P6.1–3; student p.3; solution notebook cell 9. For $G_1:S\to S+S\mid a$, with terminal +, give two distinct leftmost derivations of a+a+a, identify their groupings and give an unambiguous grammar for the same language. > [!tip]- Hint > Expand the left child first in one structure and the right subtree in the other. Preserve the replacement order as leftmost in both derivations. > [!success]- Solution > First: $S\Rightarrow S+S\Rightarrow S+S+S\Rightarrow a+S+S\Rightarrow a+a+S\Rightarrow a+a+a$. In its second step the left S expands, giving (a+a)+a. > > Second: $S\Rightarrow S+S\Rightarrow a+S\Rightarrow a+S+S\Rightarrow a+a+S\Rightarrow a+a+a$. It gives a+(a+a). The distinct leftmost histories represent two distinct trees; equal terminal yields establish ambiguity. > > Replacement grammar: $G_2:S\to S+a\mid a$ fixes left association. Both languages are $\{a(+a)^n:n\ge0\}$: binary branching adds one + and one additional eventual a; its terminal order is alternating a,+,a. Conversely any such sequence can be generated by repeated left expansion. G2 also generates every such sequence via n recursive rules followed by S→a; its fixed-length word has exactly one tree. > > This equality is about generated words, not matching trees. The source's informal S⇒S(+S)^n is not a compulsory intermediate stage of every derivation; its terminal-language characterization is justified by structural induction. T4 P7 — Add exponentiation Source: solution PDF pp.6–7, P7; student p.3; solution notebook cell 10. Start with E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→(E)|a|b. Add ↑ with precedence above * and right associativity. Explain a*b↑c and a↑b↑c. > [!tip]- Hint > Insert a power level between product and factor, and put its recursive variable on the right of ↑. Address the source's c explicitly. > [!success]- Solution > $E\to E+T\mid T$; $T\to T*P\mid P$; $P\to F\uparrow P\mid F$; $F\to(E)\mid a\mid b\mid c$. > > The added c is required by the example strings and is explicitly present in the supplied solution, though absent from the reference grammar. > > For a*b↑c, $E\Rightarrow T\Rightarrow T*P\Rightarrow P*P\Rightarrow F*P\Rightarrow a*P\Rightarrow a*F\uparrow P\Rightarrow a*b\uparrow P\Rightarrow a*b\uparrow F\Rightarrow a*b\uparrow c$. The product's right P expands to the whole b↑c, so the grouping is a*(b↑c). > > For a↑b↑c, $E\Rightarrow T\Rightarrow P\Rightarrow F\uparrow P\Rightarrow a\uparrow P\Rightarrow a\uparrow F\uparrow P\Rightarrow a\uparrow b\uparrow P\Rightarrow a\uparrow b\uparrow F\Rightarrow a\uparrow b\uparrow c$. The nested P is on the right, so a↑(b↑c). Left-recursive E/T preserve left association of +/*; separate levels preserve precedence. L4 example — Two independent blocks ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE: Lecture 4 PDF p.9; original question asks which words the rules describe. For $S\to RR,\ R\to0R1\mid\varepsilon$, describe the language, derive 0101 and 010011, and explain exclusion of 010101. The extra forum request 01010101 is a student question, not a new official exercise. > [!tip]- Hint > Name separate repeat counts for the two copies of R. > [!success]- Solution > The language is $\{0^i1^i0^j1^j:i,j\ge0\}$. > > $S\Rightarrow RR\Rightarrow0R1R\Rightarrow01R\Rightarrow010R1\Rightarrow0101$. > > $S\Rightarrow RR\Rightarrow0R1R\Rightarrow01R\Rightarrow010R1\Rightarrow0100R11\Rightarrow010011$. > > Every nonempty R yields one contiguous zero block then one equal-sized one block. At most two such factors cannot create three alternating 01 blocks, so 010101 is excluded. Four blocks in 01010101 are excluded for the same reason. L4 example — Balanced parentheses ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE: Lecture 4 PDF p.10 asks for a CFG for all balanced parentheses. > [!tip]- Hint > Empty word, wrapping and concatenation cover the two ways a balanced word grows. > [!success]- Solution > $S\to(S)\mid SS\mid\varepsilon$. Empty, wrapping and concatenation preserve balance. Conversely, any nonempty balanced word is (u)v, where its first opening parenthesis matches the displayed close and u,v are balanced. Recursively derive u and v, with S⇒SS⇒(S)S, then substitute their derivations. Thus all and only balanced words are generated. Ambiguity of this grammar does not refute its language correctness. L4 Q&A navigation Lecture 4 PDF p.26 questions 1–3 are the same conceptual tasks as T4 P1.1–3; their complete statements, counterexamples and solutions are at T4 P1. They are separate source occurrences in the map, not extra exam-paper occurrences.

entries.title: Compare generated words with structural parses
entries.text: Compare generated words with structural parses Notes · Exercises Source: Tutorial 4 solution PDF p.7, §4.4, notebook cells 12–13; student PDF pp.3–4, cells 11–12. Open the unchanged student notebook; solution notebook is available after your attempt. Motivation and environment A parser may return one tree for a word even when a second exists. Compare membership exploration with ambiguity exploration before accepting a tool's output as a proof. The source uses Tock's Grammar.from_lines, any_parse and all_parses. It writes & for epsilon and names the + terminal plus. The package version is UNCONFIRMED. Install/run only in a separate environment if desired; source files remain unchanged. This run inspected these cells but did not install or execute Tock. Original experiment — Predict the trees The source creates S→aS|bS|a and S→0S11|ε. Explain the expected results for a, ba, aba under the first grammar, and epsilon, 011, 001111 under the second. Then predict all_parses for a plus a plus a under S→S plus S|a. > [!tip]- Hint > Separate one membership witness from the set of different trees. Count binary groupings of exactly three operands, not all possible schedules. > [!success]- Solution > All six listed membership samples should have parses. First grammar: a; S⇒bS⇒ba; S⇒aS⇒abS⇒aba. Second grammar: direct epsilon; one recursive step then epsilon gives 011; two give 001111. > > The ambiguous expression grammar has exactly two ordered binary trees for three a leaves: (a+a)+a and a+(a+a). The notebook expects len(parses)==2 and asserts it. This is a source-provided expected result, not an observed Tock execution. > > any_parse returning one tree establishes one derivation for that word, not global unambiguity. Enumerating two distinct trees establishes ambiguity for the grammar; failing to find a second in a bounded search does not prove none exists. Controlled comparison Replace the exploratory grammar in a separate copy with S→S plus a|a, predict one tree for the same word, then compare the trees if you run the activity. Both grammars generate the same word set, but only the replacement forces left association. Do not equate generated-language equality with structural equality. Record and interpret Record package version, input tokens, production lines, returned trees and errors if you actually execute. Any future observation must be distinguished from the predictions here. This finite experiment does not prove grammar unambiguity for every word, inherent ambiguity of the language, or an official marking rule.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A CFG generates a language; Chomsky normal form (CNF) reorganises its rules without changing that language. A sufficiently tall binary parse tree repeats a variable on a single root-to-leaf path. Reusing that nested derivation pumps two string pieces together. The CFL pumping lemma gives a necessary condition: break it for every permitted decomposition to prove that a language is not context-free. Closure arguments can then transfer that impossibility to another language. This Week 6 edition uses Lecture 6 (34 pages) and Tutorial 6 (7 pages, dated 19 October 2026), acquired on 20 October. Prerequisites: Unit 05's CFG derivations and Unit 04's pumping quantifiers. Lecture 5/PDA materials remain pending import; the PDA recap on Lecture 6 pp.2–3 is context, not a substitute for that lesson. No test questions or new exam-frequency claims are included. The original hashed exam PDF is unavailable; historical assessment coverage has not been reverified.

entries.title: Recognise Chomsky Normal Form
entries.text: Every rule has the form $A\to BC$ or $A\to a$: one variable expands to two variables or to one terminal. If the language contains $\varepsilon$, a fresh start variable may additionally have $S_0\to\varepsilon$ and must never occur on a right-hand side. A unit rule $A\to B$, a mixed rule $A\to aB$, and a three-variable rule $A\to BCD$ are not CNF. $A\to BB$ is allowed: the two children need not have different variable names. A binary parse tree with a long terminal yield needs a long path. Since there are only finitely many variables, a long enough path repeats one. Two equal variables on separate branches do not give the nested derivation needed for pumping. Source: Lecture 6 pp.8–13, 21–23; Tutorial 6 p.1 and Problem 1. The slide's informal explanation of the short window is not a proof of its bound; use the lemma's stated conditions.

entries.title: Convert a CFG Without Changing Its Language
entries.text: Use this order, keeping track of the original start and nullable variables: 1. Introduce a fresh start $S_0\to S$ that never occurs on a right-hand side. 2. Compute all nullable variables. For each RHS, add the alternatives formed by omitting nullable occurrences; remove epsilon rules except the permitted fresh-start rule. Preserve the empty word when it belongs to the original language. 3. Remove unit rules by copying reachable non-unit productions through unit chains. 4. Replace terminals in RHSs of length at least two by fresh variables such as $U_a\to a$. 5. Split RHSs of length at least three into binary rules using fresh variables. A two-variable RHS already has the required form. For Tutorial 6 Problem 1, $S\to ABC$, $A\to01$, $B\to\varepsilon$, $C\to11$ generates only 0111. Since B contributes only epsilon, the useful RHS is AC. One CNF is $S_0\to AC$, $A\to U_0U_1$, $C\to U_1U_1$, $U_0\to0$, $U_1\to1$. Verify $S_0\Rightarrow AC\Rightarrow U_0U_1U_1U_1\Rightarrow^*0111$. Deleting a nullable variable outright is valid in this particular grammar because B generates nothing else; in general, preserve both omitted and non-omitted alternatives. Source: Lecture 6 pp.14–20; Tutorial 6 p.2, Problem 1. The precise handling of nullable alternatives and unit chains makes the conversion procedure explicit.

entries.title: Read the Two-Piece Pumping Protocol
entries.text: If L is context-free, there exists $p\ge1$ such that every $s\in L$ with $|s|\ge p$ has a decomposition $s=uvxyz$ satisfying $$|vy|>0,\qquad |vxy|\le p,\qquad uv^ixy^iz\in L\quad\text{for every }i\ge0.$$ The middle x stays once. The pieces v and y use the same exponent; either one may be empty, but not both. The window bound covers v, x and y together, not just the deleted pieces. To refute context-freeness, assume L is a CFL; accept the lemma's p; choose a witness depending on p; consider an arbitrary valid decomposition; choose an exponent that breaks it. Your argument must cover every valid decomposition. A single successful decomposition does not prove L is context-free, and one bad decomposition does not refute it. If even one decomposition pumps for every exponent, that witness cannot support a contradiction. One pumping success at one exponent proves even less. Source: Lecture 6 pp.22–23; Tutorial 6 pp.1–3, Problem 2. Tutorial 6's final wording in Problem 2 is misleading if read as a fully successful decomposition: such a decomposition defeats that witness, while a single successful exponent does not.

entries.title: Prove Three Equal Blocks Are Not Context-Free
entries.text: Let $L=\{a^nb^nc^n:n\ge0\}$. Assume L is a CFL with pumping length p and choose $s=a^pb^pc^p$. For every valid split, $|vxy|\le p$ prevents the window from meeting both the a and c blocks: it would have to contain all p b's and at least one symbol on each side, requiring at least p+2 symbols. Thus v and y affect at most two adjacent blocks. Pump down with i=0. Because $|vy|>0$, some count decreases, while at least one of the three counts stays p. Deletion preserves the a-then-b-then-c order, but destroys equal counts. Hence $uxz\notin L$ for every valid split, contradicting the lemma. This proves non-context-freeness, and therefore also nonregularity. Merely proving nonregularity would not have proved non-context-freeness. Source: Lecture 6 pp.24–26 (0/1/2 notation); Tutorial 6 p.3, Problem 3 (a/b/c notation).

entries.title: Use Closure With the Correct Language Class
entries.text: | Operation | Regular languages | Context-free languages | |---|---|---| | Union, concatenation, star | Closed | Closed | | Arbitrary intersection | Closed | Not closed in general | | Complement relative to a fixed alphabet | Closed | Not closed in general | | Intersection with a regular language | Closed | Closed | | Homomorphism | Closed | Closed | For $A=\{a^mb^nc^n:m,n\ge0\}$ use $S\to DE$, $D\to aD\mid\varepsilon$, $E\to bEc\mid\varepsilon$. For $C=\{a^nb^nc^m:m,n\ge0\}$ use $S\to FG$, $F\to aFb\mid\varepsilon$, $G\to cG\mid\varepsilon$. Their intersection forces all three counts equal, giving the non-CFL above. Therefore CFLs are not closed under arbitrary intersection. If CFLs were closed under complement, union closure and De Morgan's law would make $A\cap C=\overline{\overline A\cup\overline C}$ context-free, a contradiction. All complements must use the same alphabet. “Not closed” means a counterexample exists; it does not mean every intersection or complement is non-CFL. Source: Lecture 6 pp.27–30; Tutorial 6 pp.2–4, Problem 4. Local clarification: the supplied Problem 4 solution refers to a grammar for C without actually supplying it there; the explicit C construction above fills that omission and is independently checked by its derivation invariant.

entries.title: Filter the Copy Language
entries.text: Tutorial 6 Problem 5 uses $D=\{ww:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}$ and the regular filter $R=0^*1^*0^*1^*$. Their intersection is $H=\{0^m1^n0^m1^n:m,n\ge0\}$. When w contains both symbols, a repeated w matching R must start with 0, end with 1 and have no internal 1-to-0 transition; otherwise ww has too many runs or the wrong endpoints. Thus w is $0^m1^n$. Unary and empty w give the cases m=0 or n=0. Assume H is context-free and choose $s=0^p1^p0^p1^p$. A window of length at most p meets at most two adjacent blocks, so it cannot touch both members of either matched pair (blocks 1/3 or 2/4). Pump down. If all blocks survive, a changed block has an unchanged partner, breaking equality. If a full block disappears, it uses all p permitted deletions; all other blocks remain. The possible results are $1^p0^p1^p$, $0^{2p}1^p$, $0^p1^{2p}$ or $0^p1^p0^p$. Each contains both symbols but fewer than four maximal blocks, unlike any member of H containing both symbols. Every split fails, so H is not context-free. If D were context-free, closure under intersection with regular R would make H context-free. Therefore D is not context-free. This uses intersection with a regular language, not the false general intersection closure. Source: Tutorial 6 pp.4–6, Problem 5. The run-count argument above expands the supplied filter explanation.

entries.title: Check Your Reasoning and Source Limits
entries.text: Before moving on, explain why $A\to BB$ is CNF, why both pumped pieces share an exponent, why the short window cannot reach three length-p blocks, and why a regular filter preserves context-freeness under the contradiction assumption. Then attempt all five tutorial problems before opening help. Tutorial 6 pp.6–7 also provides optional Tock examples. Their comments contain stale references: the displayed CNF code concerns equal 0/1 counts rather than Problem 1's fixed word 0111, and the second grammar generates equal a/b counts followed by arbitrary c's. These are illustrations, not proofs or locally executed results. No package installation or notebook execution is claimed. Coverage: Lecture 6 pp.4–30 supplies the new theory; pp.1–3 and 31–34 are title, recap, review, lecturer/contact and closing context. Tutorial 6 Problems 1–5 and reference card are mapped here and in practice. The notebook download is unverified. Study status remains untested; no official marks, predictions or current test answers are inferred.

entries.title: What is an alphabet?
entries.text: A nonempty finite set of symbols.

entries.title: What is Σ*?
entries.text: The set of all finite strings over Σ, including ε.

entries.title: Distinguish ε and ∅.
entries.text: ε is a length-zero string; ∅ is a language containing no strings.

entries.title: Why is ε∈L* for every language L?
entries.text: Star permits k=0; the empty product is ε.

entries.title: What witnesses that v is a substring of w?
entries.text: Strings x,z satisfying w=xvz.

entries.title: What proves a universal assertion false?
entries.text: One valid counterexample within its stated domain.

entries.title: What must a set-equality proof contain?
entries.text: Both inclusions: every left member is right, and every right member is left.

entries.title: What is a cofinite language?
entries.text: A language whose complement relative to the fixed Σ* is finite.

entries.title: Does an infinite language require infinite strings?
entries.text: No. It may contain infinitely many distinct finite strings.

entries.title: For a language A, why can $|A|^k$ exceed the number of distinct strings in $A^k$?
entries.text: Different ordered factor tuples can concatenate to the same string.

entries.title: What makes a DFA deterministic?
entries.text: Every state-symbol pair has exactly one defined next state.

entries.title: When does a DFA accept ε?
entries.text: Exactly when its start state is accepting.

entries.title: What does a missing NFA transition do?
entries.text: It kills that branch; it does not keep the state unchanged.

entries.title: What is NFA acceptance?
entries.text: Some path consumes all input and finishes in an accepting state.

entries.title: What does an epsilon transition consume?
entries.text: Nothing; the next unread input symbol remains unchanged.

entries.title: What is epsilon closure?
entries.text: States reachable from a set using zero or more epsilon moves.

entries.title: When is a subset-construction state accepting?
entries.text: When the subset contains at least one old accepting state.

entries.title: When must the empty subset appear in a reachable-state DFA construction from an NFA?
entries.text: If reachable, it represents that no NFA path survives the consumed prefix. Every symbol keeps it empty, so it is a rejecting sink. An unreachable empty subset need not be drawn.

entries.title: How does a DFA product recognize intersection?
entries.text: Track both states and accept only pairs where both components accept.

entries.title: Why can an NFA's finals not simply be flipped?
entries.text: Existential acceptance may retain a formerly rejecting branch even when an accepting branch exists.

entries.title: How do you construct an NFA for $A^*$ from an arbitrary NFA for A, including acceptance of ε?
entries.text: Add a fresh accepting start r and an epsilon edge r→q0. Keep all old transitions and accepting states, and add an epsilon edge from each old accepting state back to r. Staying at r accepts zero factors; repeated complete old runs accept more factors.

entries.title: What does atomic regex a denote?
entries.text: The one-word language {a}.

entries.title: What does regex ε denote?
entries.text: The language {ε}, containing one empty string.

entries.title: What does regex ∅ denote?
entries.text: The empty language, containing no strings.

entries.title: What does regex union express?
entries.text: A word may come from either operand language.

entries.title: What does concatenation require?
entries.text: A split into a first-language word followed by a second-language word.

entries.title: Why is a regex not normally an input word?
entries.text: It is syntax denoting a set of base-alphabet words.

entries.title: Why add a fresh start and a fresh sole accepting state before GNFA state elimination?
entries.text: To obtain one start with no incoming and one final with no outgoing edges.

entries.title: When eliminating GNFA state k, what label replaces the edge from i to j, and what does each term mean?
entries.text: $R_{ij} \cup R_{ik}(R_{kk})^*R_{kj}$. Keep the direct route i→j, or enter k, traverse its loop zero or more times, then exit to j. Omitting the direct term can lose accepted words.

entries.title: What does an absent GNFA edge mean?
entries.text: Its label is ∅, permitting no traversal.

entries.title: Does elimination order change the language?
entries.text: No, but it can change expression syntax and size.

entries.title: In the three-state NFA for binary strings ending in 01, what property of accepting q2 requires the match to end at input end?
entries.text: The accepting state has no outgoing transitions, so a successful path cannot consume a later suffix.

entries.title: Why can elimination orders yield different-looking regexes?
entries.text: They create different intermediate syntax while preserving the same recognized language.

entries.title: Why must a DFA with p states repeat a state within the first p transitions of a sufficiently long run?
entries.text: p+1 visits among only p state identities.

entries.title: In the pumping lemma for regular languages, why must the loop substring y be nonempty?
entries.text: The repeated visits occur at different input positions, so b-a≥1.

entries.title: Which pumping-lemma bound ensures that the loop substring y ends within the first p symbols?
entries.text: The condition |xy|≤p.

entries.title: Who chooses the pumping length?
entries.text: The assumed regularity claim supplies some valid p.

entries.title: In a nonregularity proof using the pumping lemma, who chooses the witness word, and when?
entries.text: The contradiction proof, after seeing p.

entries.title: Must a contradiction cover every legal split?
entries.text: Yes; the lemma needs only one surviving split.

entries.title: In a pumping-lemma contradiction, may the failing exponent i depend on the chosen legal split?
entries.text: Yes; each split needs at least one failing exponent.

entries.title: What does i=0 do?
entries.text: It removes the loop substring y.

entries.title: Does successful pumping prove regularity?
entries.text: No. The lemma supplies a necessary condition, not a converse proof here.

entries.title: For $L=\{0^{n^2}:n\ge0\}$, why is $p^2+b>p^2$ alone insufficient when pumping a loop with $1\le b\le p$?
entries.text: An upper bound below (p+1)^2, not merely a length above p^2.

entries.title: For C={1^k w : k≥1 and binary w has at most k ones}, is k one global fixed parameter or a membership witness chosen for each word?
entries.text: Existentially for each word, not as one fixed parameter for the whole language.

entries.title: What must be ruled out after pumping a word with existential membership witnesses?
entries.text: Every possible new membership witness, not just the original one.

entries.title: What makes a production context-free?
entries.text: Its left side is one variable; replacement does not require a particular surrounding context.

entries.title: What are the four components of a CFG?
entries.text: Finite variables V, finite terminals Σ, finite rules R and a designated start variable S∈V.

entries.title: What does the production arrow declare?
entries.text: An allowed replacement rule, rather than an actual derivation step.

entries.title: What does the starred derivation relation permit?
entries.text: Zero or more derivation steps.

entries.title: When is a derived form a language member?
entries.text: When it contains only terminals and is derived from the designated start variable.

entries.title: What form appears after n recursive uses of S→aSb?
entries.text: The sentential form aⁿSbⁿ.

entries.title: What is read from the leaves of an ordered parse tree?
entries.text: The terminal word in left-to-right order, ignoring epsilon leaves.

entries.title: What must a leftmost derivation expand next?
entries.text: The leftmost remaining variable.

entries.title: What demonstrates grammar ambiguity?
entries.text: One terminal word with two distinct parse trees, equivalently two distinct leftmost derivations.

entries.title: Why rename variables when combining CFGs?
entries.text: To prevent rules of one grammar from expanding variables of the other.

entries.title: Where do epsilon termination rules occur in a DFA-derived grammar?
entries.text: At variables corresponding to accepting DFA states.

entries.title: Which side recursively expands for right-associative exponentiation?
entries.text: The right operand: P→F↑P.

entries.title: Which rules are CNF?
entries.text: $A\to BC$ and $A\to a$; optionally fresh $S_0\to\varepsilon$ when needed, with S0 absent from all RHSs.

entries.title: May a CNF rule use the same child variable twice?
entries.text: Yes: $A\to BB$ is valid. It still has two variable occurrences.

entries.title: What is the CNF conversion order?
entries.text: Fresh start; nullable alternatives and epsilon removal; unit-rule elimination; terminal isolation; binary RHS splitting.

entries.title: What are the CFL pumping conditions?
entries.text: $s=uvxyz$, $|vy|>0$, $|vxy|\le p$, and $uv^ixy^iz\in L$ for every $i\ge0$.

entries.title: Who chooses the pumping decomposition?
entries.text: An adversary may choose any valid split; the non-CFL proof must defeat all of them.

entries.title: Can just one pumped piece be empty?
entries.text: Yes. v or y may be empty, but not both; both use the same exponent.

entries.title: Why does the three-block witness work?
entries.text: A length-p window cannot touch both a and c in $a^pb^pc^p$. Pumping down changes at least one count and leaves another at p.

entries.title: Which intersection closure can a CFL proof use?
entries.text: Intersection with a regular language preserves context-freeness; intersection with an arbitrary CFL need not.

entries.title: How does complement closure imply intersection closure?
entries.text: With union closure, De Morgan gives $A\cap C=\overline{\overline A\cup\overline C}$.

entries.title: Do finite Tock checks prove a language is CFL or non-CFL?
entries.text: No. Finite runs illustrate examples; use a correct grammar/PDA construction or a general pumping/closure argument.

entries.text: Closure Properties of Languages: Formal Goal: Show finite automata equivalent to regular expressions We need some tools for analyzing a set of languages. Closure of Binary Operation Closure of Unary Operation - Set 𝐶 is closed under ⨁: 𝐶 x 𝐶-> 𝐶, - Set 𝐶 is closed under ⨁: 𝐶 -> 𝐶, if ∀𝐴, 𝐵 ∈ 𝐶, A⨁𝐵 ∈ 𝐶 if ∀𝐴 ∈ 𝐶, ⨁𝐴 ∈ 𝐶 • Regular language is a set of languages, regular operations can be examined for their closure property on regular language. 32

entries.title: Lecture 1 Intro and Regular Language.pdf · p. 33
entries.text: Closure Properties of Regular Language • Say 𝐴 = {𝑤|𝑤 𝑒𝑛𝑑𝑠 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ 0}, 𝐵 = 𝑤 𝑤 𝑒𝑛𝑑𝑠 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ 1 , and 𝐶 = {𝑤|𝑤 𝑒𝑛𝑑𝑠 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ 0 𝑜𝑟 1}. • Based on the description, we can easily observe that 𝐶 is the union set of 𝐴 and 𝐵, as it contains all the strings in 𝐴 and 𝐵. Other operations on languages • From sets: union, intersection, complement, difference • Unique on languages: concatenation, star, reverse, … (string as element) 33

entries.text: Regular Language is Closed under Union: Example if 𝐴 and 𝐵 are both regular languages, so is 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵. entries.text: Regular Language is Closed under Union: Formal Theorem: if 𝐴 and 𝐵 are both regular languages, so is 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵. Equivalently, regular languages are closed under union. Proof: Components of 𝑀: Let 𝑀1 = (𝑄1 , Σ, 𝛿1 , 𝑞1 , 𝐹1 ) recognize 𝐴 𝑀2 = (𝑄2 , Σ, 𝛿2 , 𝑞2 , 𝐹2 ) recognize B 𝑄 = 𝑄1 × 𝑄2 We want a 𝑀 = (𝑄 , Σ , 𝛿 , 𝑞0, 𝐹 ) = 𝑞1 , 𝑞2 𝑞1 ∈ 𝑄1 and 𝑞2 ∈ 𝑄2 } that recognize 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 accept 𝑤. 𝑞0 = (𝑞1 , 𝑞2 ) 𝛿 𝑞, 𝑟 , 𝑎 = 𝛿1 𝑞, 𝑎 , 𝛿2 𝑟, 𝑎 𝐹 = 𝐹1 × 𝑄2 ∪ 𝑄1 × 𝐹2 M simulates M1 and M2 in a product space, and accept in the union of acceptance states in production space. 35

entries.text: Review of Today • A string is a sequence of characters; A language is a set of strings; • A finite automaton 𝑀 is a 5-tuple vector (𝑄, Σ, 𝑞0 , 𝐹, 𝛿): • 𝑀 accepts 𝑤 , if 𝑀 reads ALL characters in 𝑤 and ends in an accept state • M recognize L if M accepts all w in L, and rejects all w not in L. • A language is regular if some finite automaton recognizes it. • Regular operations on languages are union ∪, concatenation ∘, and star ∗. • Regular expressions, are built from Σ, ∅, 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝜀 and regular operations ∪,∘,∗. • Language closure properties are defined over a set of languages. • Regular languages are closed under Union.
