entries.text: Operation Regular languages Context-free languages Union, concatenation, star yes yes Complement yes no Intersection yes no Intersection with a regular language yes yes Homomorphism yes yes 3 Part A — CNF and the CFL pumping lemma 3.1 Problem 1 — Convert a grammar to CNF Check the following CFG 𝑆 → 𝐴𝐵𝐶, 𝐴 → 01, 𝐵 → 𝜀, 𝐶 → 11 Convert it to Chomsky normal form. Solution — click to expand Introduce a new start variable 𝑆0 and let it generate the original start variable 𝑆0 → 𝑆 Variable 𝐵 generate 𝜀, which doesn’t affect the generated strings, so directly disgard this rule, so 𝑆 → 𝐴𝐶. Considering unit rules, we have 𝑆0 → 𝑆, so copy the rule of S, i.e., 𝑆 → 𝐴𝐶, and we have 𝑆0 → 𝐴𝐶. Since now 𝑆 doesn’t appear at the RHS of the rules concerning 𝑆0 , we could get rid of 𝑆. Introduce terminal variables 𝑈0 → 0, 𝑈1 → 1. so 𝐴 → 01 and 𝐶 → 11 can be changed to 𝐴 → 𝑈0 𝑈1 and 𝐶 → 𝑈1 𝑈1 . To sum up, the CNF form of the given CFG is: 𝑆0 → 𝐴𝐶, 𝐴 → 𝑈 0 𝑈1 , 𝐶 → 𝑈 1 𝑈1 , 𝑈0 → 0, 𝑈1 → 1. 3.2 Problem 2 — Quantifiers and the two pumped pieces Answer the following. 1. Put the choices in order: pumping length 𝑝, witness 𝑠, decomposition 𝑢𝑣𝑥𝑦𝑧, exponent 𝑖. 2. Who controls each choice in a proof by contradiction? 2

entries.title: Tutorial 6 - CNF, CFL Pumping, and Closure Properties.pdf · p. 3
entries.text: 3. Can we pump 𝑣 twice while leaving 𝑦 unchanged? 4. What does |𝑣𝑥𝑦| ≤ 𝑝 tell us geometrically about a block-structured witness? 5. Why does finding one decomposition that pumps successfully fail to refute a non-CFL proof? Solution — click to expand 1. Assume 𝐿 is context-free; the lemma supplies 𝑝. The prover chooses 𝑠 ∈ 𝐿 with |𝑠| ≥ 𝑝. An adversary chooses any valid decomposition. The prover then chooses 𝑖. 2. A correct non-CFL proof must handle every valid decomposition and find an exponent that breaks each one. 3. No. Pumping produces 𝑢𝑣𝑖 𝑥𝑦𝑖 𝑧, so both pieces use the same exponent. 4. The entire window containing 𝑣, 𝑥, and 𝑦 is short. In a witness built from blocks of length 𝑝, this often prevents the window from reaching three separated blocks. 5. The lemma promises the existence of some good decomposition for each suﬀiciently long string. Showing that one selected decomposition works says nothing about the others. 3.3 Problem 3 — Prove {𝑎𝑛 𝑏𝑛 𝑐𝑛 } is not context-free Use the CFL pumping lemma to prove that 𝐵 = {𝑎𝑛 𝑏𝑛 𝑐𝑛 ∣ 𝑛 ≥ 0} is not context-free. Your case analysis should explain why 𝑣𝑥𝑦 cannot touch all three blocks. Solution — click to expand Assume that 𝐵 is context-free and let 𝑝 be its pumping length. Choose 𝑠 = 𝑎𝑝 𝑏 𝑝 𝑐 𝑝 . For any valid decomposition 𝑠 = 𝑢𝑣𝑥𝑦𝑧, we have |𝑣𝑥𝑦| ≤ 𝑝. Therefore the window 𝑣𝑥𝑦 cannot contain both an a and a c: reaching from the a block to the c block would require crossing all 𝑝 copies of b and would make the window longer than 𝑝. Thus 𝑣 and 𝑦 together affect symbols from at most two adjacent blocks. Since |𝑣𝑦| > 0, pumping down with 𝑖 = 0 removes at least one symbol from one or two blocks while leaving the third block unchanged. If removal crosses a boundary in a way that disturbs the order 𝑎∗ 𝑏∗ 𝑐∗ , the result is already outside 𝐵; otherwise the three symbol counts are no longer equal. Hence 𝑢𝑥𝑧 ∉ 𝐵. This contradicts the pumping lemma, so 𝐵 is not context-free. 4 Part B — Closure-based proofs 4.1 Problem 4 — CFLs are not closed under intersection or complement Let 3

entries.title: Tutorial 6 - CNF, CFL Pumping, and Closure Properties.pdf · p. 4
entries.text: 𝐴 = {𝑎𝑚 𝑏𝑛 𝑐𝑛 ∣ 𝑚, 𝑛 ≥ 0}, 𝐶 = {𝑎𝑛 𝑏𝑛 𝑐𝑚 ∣ 𝑚, 𝑛 ≥ 0}. 1. Give a CFG, or a short CFG construction, showing that each language is context-free. 2. Compute 𝐴 ∩ 𝐶. 3. Use Problem 3 to prove that CFLs are not closed under intersection. 4. Use De Morgan’s law and the fact that CFLs are closed under union to prove that CFLs are not closed under complement. Solution — click to expand For 𝐴, use 𝑆 → 𝐷𝐸, 𝐷 → 𝑎𝐷 ∣ 𝜀, and 𝐸 → 𝑏𝐸𝑐 ∣ 𝜀. The grammar in Problem 4 generates 𝐶. Both languages are context-free. A string in both languages must satisfy the equalities between the a and b counts and between the b and c counts. Therefore 𝐴 ∩ 𝐶 = {𝑎𝑛 𝑏𝑛 𝑐𝑛 ∣ 𝑛 ≥ 0}, which is not context-free by Problem 3. Hence CFLs are not closed under intersection. Now suppose CFLs were closed under complement. Since they are closed under union, De Morgan’s law would give 𝐴 ∩ 𝐶 = 𝐴 ∪ 𝐶, and the right-hand side would be context-free. This contradicts the result above. Therefore CFLs are not closed under complement. 4.2 Problem 5 — Filter the copy language Let 𝐷 = {𝑤𝑤 ∣ 𝑤 ∈ {0, 1}∗ } and let the regular language 𝑅 = 0∗ 1∗ 0∗ 1∗ . 1. Compute 𝐷 ∩ 𝑅. 2. Prove that the resulting language is not context-free using the witness 0𝑝 1𝑝 0𝑝 1𝑝 . 3. Conclude that 𝐷 is not context-free. Solution — click to expand The regular filter forces each half of a copied string to consist of a 0 block followed by a 1 block. Thus 𝐻 = 𝐷 ∩ 𝑅 = {0𝑚 1𝑛 0𝑚 1𝑛 ∣ 𝑚, 𝑛 ≥ 0}. 4

entries.title: Tutorial 6 - CNF, CFL Pumping, and Closure Properties.pdf · p. 5
entries.text: Pumping-lemma proof that 𝐻 is not context-free. Assume, for a contradiction, that 𝐻 is context-free. Let 𝑝 ≥ 1 be the pumping length promised by the CFL pumping lemma. Choose 𝑠 = 0𝑝 1𝑝 0𝑝 1𝑝 ∈ 𝐻, |𝑠| = 4𝑝 ≥ 𝑝. We consider the string as a concatenation of 4 blocks, i.e., 0𝑝 , 1𝑝 , 0𝑝 , and 1𝑝 . Consider an arbitrary decomposition 𝑠 = 𝑢𝑣𝑥𝑦𝑧 satisfying |𝑣𝑥𝑦| ≤ 𝑝, |𝑣𝑦| > 0. We will show that pumping down, with exponent 𝑖 = 0, gives 𝑢𝑣0 𝑥𝑦0 𝑧 = 𝑢𝑥𝑧 ∉ 𝐻 for every such decomposition. Number the four blocks of 𝑠 from left to right. The window 𝑣𝑥𝑦 can meet at most two adjacent blocks: meeting three would require it to contain the entire intervening block of length 𝑝 and at least one symbol on each side, giving length at least 𝑝 + 2. In particular, it cannot meet both blocks 1 and 3, or both blocks 2 and 4. For 𝑗 = 1, 2, 3, 4, let 𝑑𝑗 be the number of symbols pumped down from block 𝑗 when 𝑣 and 𝑦 are pumped down. Then 1 ≤ 𝑑1 + 𝑑2 + 𝑑3 + 𝑑4 = |𝑣| + |𝑦| ≤ 𝑝, and the pumped-down string is 𝑢𝑥𝑧 = 0𝑝−𝑑1 1𝑝−𝑑2 0𝑝−𝑑3 1𝑝−𝑑4 . There are two cases. Case 1: no block is completely deleted. All four displayed exponents are positive, so these are exactly the four maximal blocks of 𝑢𝑥𝑧. At least one 𝑑𝑗 is positive. Its corresponding block (1 paired with 3, or 2 paired with 4) is outside the window and loses no symbols. Thus one block has length strictly less than 𝑝 while its corresponding block still has length 𝑝. This violates the equalities required in 0𝑚 1𝑛 0𝑚 1𝑛 , so 𝑢𝑥𝑧 ∉ 𝐻. Case 2: a block is completely deleted. Then 𝑑𝑗 = 𝑝 for that block. Since the total deletion is at most 𝑝, all other 𝑑ℓ are zero. Depending on which block is deleted, the result is one of 1𝑝 0𝑝 1𝑝 , 02𝑝 1𝑝 , 0𝑝 12𝑝 , 0 𝑝 1𝑝 0𝑝 . Each string contains both symbols but has fewer than four maximal blocks. Every string in 𝐻 containing both symbols has 𝑚, 𝑛 > 0 and therefore exactly four maximal blocks: 0𝑚 , 1𝑛 , 0𝑚 , 1𝑛 . Hence none of these pumped-down strings belongs to 𝐻. In every valid decomposition, exponent 𝑖 = 0 produces a string outside 𝐻. This contradicts the pumping lemma, which requires the existence of a valid decomposition for which 𝑢𝑣𝑖 𝑥𝑦𝑖 𝑧 ∈ 𝐻 for every 𝑖 ≥ 0. Therefore 𝐻 is not context-free. 5

Since 𝐻 is not context-free, 𝐷 is not context-free. 4.3 Optional Tock checks Tock can construct and parse CFGs directly, so no local CYK or PDA simulator is needed. These finite runs support the examples; they do not replace the general pumping and closure proofs above. entries.text: except ValueError: print(f"{word!r:18} reject") else: print(f"{word!r:18} accept") display(tree) 4.4 What to take away • CNF separates terminals from binary variable combinations and removes unit rules. • The CFL pumping lemma pumps two pieces together. The short window 𝑣𝑥𝑦 makes block- based case analysis possible. • A grammar or PDA is often easier than pumping when the language is context-free. • CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star, intersection with regular languages, and homomorphism. • CFLs are not closed under unrestricted intersection or complement. • Regular filters and homomorphisms can expose a known non-context-free core inside a more complicated language. 7

Its byte-preserved originals are in Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Sources/; the external download copies remain untouched. | Official item | Released scope | Status | |---|---|---| | Task 1.1 | Set up the environment; understand and test JDBC.java on a basic JDBC query | Released and mapped; remote runtime not performed during ingestion | | Task 1.2 | Understand and test JDBCandIndex.java on a basic JDBC query with an index | Released and mapped; remote runtime not performed during ingestion | | Task 2 | Print the time for the Task 1 query without and with an index; time only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); | Released, implemented, compiled, and locally executed | Lab-specific configuration is MySQL with MySQL Connector/J. The PDF states Connector/J 9.4.0 as current on PDF p. 10, but gives no MySQL server/JDK/storage-engine version. The supplied Java uses com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver, searchKey = "num", and searchKeyValue = "7". Lab 02 discrepancies and import cautions - Server host: PDF p. 6 gives 10.7.1.127; PDF p. 11 gives 10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME]; both supplied Java files use 10.7.1.127/[DATABASE NAME]. A 24 September 2026 reachability probe connected to 10.7.1.127:3306, while .36:3306 did not respond within three seconds; no university authentication or SQL was attempted. - Java filename: PDF p. 11 names JDBCIndex.java, while the supplied official files are JDBC.java and JDBCandIndex.java. - SQL width: yeast_prosite.sql declares mmatch varchar(12), but static inspection finds 771 supplied non-NULL values longer than 12 characters, with a maximum of 89. The original is preserved; import errors/warnings depend on the actual server mode and must be inspected. - SQL bootstrap: the dataset begins with unconditional drop table Orf_Motif;, which can report a missing-table error in a fresh schema. - Date mapping wording: PDF p. 24 says java.Date; the mapping table on p. 25 specifies java.sql.Date. The lab note preserves the discrepancy and uses the fully qualified JDBC type shown in the table. - Performance: the two official Task 1 Java files do not time the query or inspect a plan. The separate Task 2 solution times only executeQuery, compares logical results, and verifies key=numIndex; its one local timing pair is not a universal speedup, I/O, or physical B+ tree claim. The two official Java files compile together with JDK 17 without Connector/J on the compile classpath. A separate reference solution was compiled with JDK 17.0.18 and Connector/J 9.4.0 and executed against isolated local MySQL instances. Tasks 1.1 and 1.2 returned the same 607 final rows, and the indexed plan named numIndex. The released Task 2 run then measured 8.723 ms without the index and 2.083 ms with it, again returned the same 607 logical rows, and confirmed EXPLAIN key=numIndex. This did not authenticate to or execute SQL on the university server. The SQL contains one table definition with columns orf, acc_num, num, pos, len, and mmatch; 285 inserts use NULL for both pos and mmatch. Static parsing finds 614 INSERT statements with num=7, while later deletions produced 607 final matches in that controlled local import. > [!note]- SOE201 Presentation Standard > Use Unit 01 as the approved presentation reference. The current production request authorised all remaining supplied lecture units; do not rewrite Unit 01. > > - Structure: Unit NN - Topic/ contains 01 Notes.md, 02 Exercises.md, an optional useful 03 Lab.md, and Attachments/. Keep operational evidence in the archive. > - Hierarchy: begin with a compact roadmap and observable abilities; use short contextual openers, concept headings, named formula sections, and occasional checkpoints. Finish with a checklist, a 60-second recap, and practice links. > - Callouts: abstract = roadmap; info = key idea or interpretation; note = definition; example = worked example; tip = study/exam guidance; warning = misconception or implementation-specific caveat; question = retrieval; summary = takeaway; success = hidden solution/check. Use them selectively. > - Exercises: organise A–E as Quick Retrieval, Guided Problems, Independent Problems, Error Diagnosis, and Exam-Style Problems. Every question is immediately followed by [!tip]- Hint and [!success]- Solution; both are collapsed. Keep solutions local, with no duplicate answer appendix. Use difficulty labels mainly for reasoning problems. > - Figures: retain consistent SVG typography, spacing, teal/blue/amber roles, and arrowheads; use Mermaid for clear relationships and sequences. Number educational figures consistently and place a bold caption, Read it, and Key takeaway beneath each. A compact navigation roadmap is separate from figure numbering. > - Calculations: introduce the model before the formula; explain symbols once nearby. Worked examples show Given, Find, Method, Calculation/Answer, and Interpretation where useful. Preserve validated assumptions, formulas, source quotations, and results. > - Navigation: use vault-relative wiki links and descriptive aliases. Link Notes ↔ Exercises ↔ Lab, resolve heading targets and attachment embeds, and show only Notes, Exercises, and Lab in the course index. Keep SQL and original source filenames unchanged. > - Readability: use ==highlight== sparingly for method-changing assumptions, selected inputs, key distinctions, and final outputs. Keep mathematical expressions, source quotations, and identifiers intact. Separate dense exercise inputs into Key Data and tasks into What You Need to Find only when helpful; use short bullet hints and stepwise solutions ending in a key idea. Keep short recall questions compact. Newly completed lecture coverage | Unit | Primary course source | Coverage and practice | |---|---|---| | 02 — B+ Tree Indexing | Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf, PDF pp. 2–37 | Structure, lookup, capacity, insertion, deletion; all original lookup/construction/update tasks and their intermediate states | | 03 — Hash Indexing | Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 2–43 | Static hashing, extendable hashing, lookup, splitting, overflow, coalescing and workload choice; all embedded worked tasks including the two-split Taiyuan case | | 04 — Advanced Indexing | Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 2–22 | LSM/buffer, bitmap/Bloom, spatial and temporal mechanisms; original bitmap outputs and temporal table, plus explicitly supplementary exercises and a Python lab | Each lecture's cover, learning outcomes and final reading page are accounted for as context. Lecture 2a's pp. 3–4 provide retrieval motivation and illustrative indexes, pp. 5–18 are already in the approved Unit 01 boundary, and p. 19 is a reading reference: no additional unfinished unit is implied by this file. The original Tutorial 1 Q1–Q6 remain in their approved Unit 01 locations; they were not re-audited or relocated in this run. Textbook availability does not extend the production scope to every textbook chapter or exercise. During the Units 02–04 production run, the earlier 12 PDFs were rechecked unchanged, and the same two duplicate pairs yielded 10 distinct documents. Lab 2 was ingested afterward as an additional official PDF plus Java/SQL sources; all 26 PDF pages were inspected visually as well as through extracted text. Conventions and clarifications for Units 02–04 - B+ tree order: maximum internal child pointers; leaf capacity is one fewer key. Lecture 2b p. 4's leaf-root “children” wording is clarified as key entries. The root has its own minimum-occupancy exception. - B+ tree deletion: follow the source's merge-first rule. Retained internal separators may be absent from leaves while still defining valid ranges (Lecture 2b pp. 9, 27, 32–33). The source does not prescribe a universal sibling preference when both are valid. - Height calculation: the million-key, order-100 example has at most four visited index nodes under the course occupancy model. The displayed logarithm on Lecture 2b p. 11 is rounded; the chapter derives the bound and separates edges, node visits, cache effects and data-page reads. - Hash bit direction: Lecture 3a reads high-order bits from the left; preserve leading zeros in fixed-width hashes. Directory size is $2^i$ pointers and physical buckets number at most $2^i$ (p. 13 uses a strict inequality that excludes the equality case). - Failed hash splits: retain the course's rollback-before-overflow convention. The city case permits exactly two unsuccessful splits (pp. 32–40). Its initial Taiyuan is a real existing record; the new Taiyuan is another record with the same city name. - Hash-source ambiguities: p. 5 repeats G in the J position and gives X as 25; punctuation/spacing encoding is unspecified. Page 11 shows index ID 33456 but a Gold row labelled 33465. Preserve source-local IDs; do not silently equate them. The department overflow example supplies no numeric hash or exact trial limit, so only its supported duplicate-key overflow result is claimed. - Vendor correction: Lecture 3a p. 42's PostgreSQL statement is contradicted by [PostgreSQL 18's official on-disk hash-index documentation]( The correction is supplementary; it does not identify the course DBMS. Other vendor mentions remain lecture context, not a verified current support matrix. - LSM deletion: the slide's matching deletion/record removal is a simplified merge model. The new chapter explains why older unmerged versions must not be resurrected by prematurely discarding a tombstone. - Bloom estimates: Lecture 3b p. 12's 10% and 1% are rounded estimates; the chapter derives approximately 9.52% and 0.819% under its stated model. The tiny lab deliberately uses different, correlated functions and reports its actual finite-domain result. - Time endpoints: the slides do not fully specify interval inclusion. Unit 04 declares half-open intervals [start,end) for its worked queries; this remains an instructor-convention uncertainty rather than an asserted source rule. Lecture 3b p. 6 names BigTable, Cassandra, MongoDB, SQLite4, LevelDB and MyRocks in its discussion of LSM-related systems. Those names are preserved here as source examples only; the supplied material does not establish a specific installed engine, version, or configuration. The new material teaches the depicted abstract mechanism rather than inferring identical current behaviour across those products. Validation and learning status Units 02–04 passed technical/pedagogical review, source/task mapping, deterministic calculation or invariant checks, and Markdown/YAML/link/SVG checks. All 41 new SVGs and 231 MathJax expressions were rendered in a standalone Chromium harness. Its dark and narrow layouts and expanded-help A4 PDFs were inspected; these are standalone checks, not native Obsidian tests. Some standalone page breaks separate captions or callout titles from their following content, so native pagination still needs review; no approved CSS was changed to impose a different print policy. The new Python 3.14.6 lab executed 98 bitmap predicate comparisons and 4356 spatial rectangle comparisons against direct predicates. Its observed output and limits are recorded with the unchanged script hash in staging. It makes no DBMS, disk-I/O or latency claim. Native Obsidian Reading View/Live Preview and native PDF export for all new units remain pending, including whether the selected exporter includes expanded or collapsed help. Unit 01's user-reported approval does not transfer to the new units. All new material has study_status: untested. No study completion is inferred. No remaining supplied lecture supports another new theory unit. Lab 2 is a course-level practical rather than “Unit 2”; its released Tasks 1.1, 1.2, and 2 are now covered. Announced later topics still need their own released original material, so the entire SOE201 course is not declared complete.

entries.title: SOE201 Tutor Mode
entries.text: SOE201 Tutor Mode This is a guided companion to the ordinary SOE201 reference edition. It covers every unit currently supported by supplied teaching materials: physical storage/index foundations, B+ trees, hash indexing, advanced indexes and the released JDBC/index lab. How to use it 1. Orient: read a unit's *In 60 Seconds* and Concept Preview. 2. Learn: work through the motivating problem, explanation, visual and worked example. 3. Retrieve: close references and answer the atomic cards. 4. Practise: attempt a question before opening its collapsed hint. 5. Compare: open the complete solution and compare method, assumptions and intermediate steps. 6. Record real gaps: only an actual attempt can establish a learning weakness. 7. Transfer: finish with a changed surface problem that requires choosing the method. Preview cards support recognition; recall cards require retrieval. Reading does not establish mastery, and the time labels are navigation aids rather than measured learning guarantees. Tutor units | Tutor route | Ordinary reference | Main capability | |---|---|---| | Unit 01 · Tutor Notes · Practice | Notes · Exercises · Lab | calculate storage/index blocks and justify access paths | | Unit 02 · Tutor Notes · Practice | Notes · Exercises | trace and validate lookup, insertion and deletion | | Unit 03 · Tutor Notes · Practice | Notes · Exercises | route fixed-width hashes and manage split/overflow states | | Unit 04 · Tutor Notes · Practice | Notes · Exercises · Lab | choose and reason about write, set, membership, spatial and temporal indexes | | Lab 02 · Tutor Notes · Practice | Reference Lab 02 | distinguish JDBC execution, index creation, plan evidence and performance evidence | Assessment evidence The supplied image-only pack contains four distinct official logical papers: 2023/24 Final and Resit, and 2024/25 Final and Resit. Every rendered question page was inspected. Each paper's cover/administrative page 1 is absent, but its complete question pages are present. See Past-paper intelligence. This is a study-priority guide based on the supplied historical assessment sample, not a forecast of the next exam. No official marking schemes were supplied. If You Are Short on Time Prerequisites come first: Unit 01's packing/index language supports the later index units. Priority 1 — High Exam Relevance - Unit 01 record/block packing and introductory index sizing/selection — observed in 4/4 papers, 20 known marks. Study whole-record capacity and attempt Tutorial Q3 practice. - B+ tree deletion/repair — observed in 3/4 papers, 6 known marks. Study deletion repair and attempt independent deletion. - Spatial-index identification/selection — observed in 3/4 papers, 6 known marks. Study spatial distinctions and attempt selection practice. Priority 2 — Medium Exam Relevance - Hash-index trade-offs — observed in 2/4 papers, 4 known marks: comparative explanation. - B+ lookup trace — observed in 1/4 papers, 2 known marks: guided lookup. Priority 3 — Remaining Source-Supported Material Do not omit source-supported topics merely because they were not observed in four papers: - HDD timing, variable records, slotted pages and file maintenance; - B+ insertion, capacity/height and range access; - hash calculations, directory aliases, coalescing and full-hash overflow; - LSM/buffer trees, bitmaps, Bloom filters and temporal indexing; - released JDBC Tasks 1.1–1.2 and their evidence limits. Later exam topics such as query optimisation and transactions are repeatedly visible in the papers but their teaching lectures are NOT IN MATERIALS. Tutor Mode does not invent those missing units. If You Have Only 30 Minutes Suggested schedule—not a measured guarantee: 1. 8 minutes: Unit 01 floor→ceiling packing method and dense/sparse/primary/secondary distinctions. 2. 8 minutes: B+ lookup plus merge-first deletion decision. 3. 5 minutes: k-d versus quadtree versus R-tree selection. 4. 4 minutes: static versus extendable hashing trade-offs. 5. 5 minutes: attempt one Unit 01 packing problem without notes, then compare the solution. Sacrificed coverage: detailed HDD modelling, B+ insertion sequences, extendable-hash multi-split traces, LSM/bitmap/Bloom/temporal mechanisms and JDBC practice. This is not full course coverage and does not make the omitted topics unimportant or non-examinable. Optional interactive conventions /teach, /quiz, /grade, /weak, and /cram can be used in conversation. They are not native commands. Document answers are collapsed locally; chat quiz answers remain withheld until an attempt or explicit reveal request. Status and limitations - All generated material has study_status: untested. - Structural and standalone-render checks are recorded separately from native Obsidian and native PDF checks. - Tutor Mode does not modify or replace ordinary SOE201 material.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: This unit explains how logical rows become physical records, how whole records fit into fixed-size blocks, and how file order and index density change the route to a record. The central ideas are: 1. a query ultimately needs pages, not isolated bytes; 2. unspanned capacity uses floor(block size / item size) before counting blocks; 3. clustered groups must be packed as groups when the question says they stay together; 4. a primary index follows physical file order, while dense/sparse describes coverage; 5. an index is useful only if its entries can lead to every required match. After study, you should be able to calculate record and index blocks, trace a disk-read model, and justify an access path without inventing overhead or performance results.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: > [!note] Page and buffer > Plain-language meaning: the DBMS transfers a page/block and then reads records from the in-memory copy. A buffer hit avoids that data-page fetch. > > Why it matters: row count alone does not determine physical I/O. > > Connects to: record packing, file organisation and indexes. > > Source: Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf, PDF pp. 3–10. > [!note] Blocking factor > Plain-language meaning: the maximum number of whole, unspanned records that fit in one block. > > Why it matters: rounding in the wrong order changes every later result. > > Connects to: dense and sparse index sizing. > > Source: Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf, PDF pp. 16–18; Tutorial Q3–Q6. > [!note] File organisation > Plain-language meaning: the physical rule used to place records—heap, sequential, hashed or clustered. > > Why it matters: the same logical table can support very different access and maintenance costs. > > Connects to: primary indexes and range access. > > Source: Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf, PDF pp. 24–29. > [!note] Dense and sparse indexes > Plain-language meaning: dense coverage normally has an entry for every search-key occurrence/record; sparse coverage samples ordered data blocks. > > Why it matters: a sparse entry is safe only when the file order lets the search continue to every match. > > Connects to: primary versus secondary access paths. > > Source: Lecture2a - Indexing Techniques (1).pdf, PDF pp. 5–18.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need integer division, ceilings and the distinction between a logical tuple and a physical record. > [!question] Prerequisite check > A 4096-byte block stores unspanned 350-byte records. Which operation determines records per block: floor or ceiling? > [!success]- Check your answer > Floor: $\lfloor4096/350\rfloor=11$. A twelfth record would cross the block boundary. > > Source: Tutorial Q3, Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf, PDF p. 4.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Synthetic case using Tutorial Q3's physical model. A registry has 25,000 fixed 350-byte records in 4096-byte blocks. Records are ordered by a 10-byte student_ID. A sparse primary-index entry is the 10-byte key plus a 10-byte pointer. 1. How many data blocks are required? 2. How many sparse entries and index blocks are required? 3. Why is the index sparse only because the file is ordered on the same search key? Success criteria: keep records and entries unspanned, show both floor and ceiling steps, and explain the access invariant rather than reporting numbers alone. | Question | Knowledge needed | |---|---| | Data blocks | blocking factor, ceiling of record demand | | Index blocks | one sparse entry per data block, entry capacity | | Correctness | physical order and candidate-block selection |

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: From tuple to page fetch A tuple is a logical row. Its encoded record lives inside a page/block. The buffer holds page copies in memory. On a buffer miss, the page is fetched; on a hit, the record can be read from the resident page. Index pages and data pages are separate costs unless a problem explicitly combines them. flowchart LR Q["Row predicate"] --> A["Choose access path"] A --> I["Read index page(s), if used"] I --> D["Locate data block"] A --> D D --> B{"Data block buffered?"} B -->|no| F["Fetch block"] B -->|yes| R["Read record"] F --> R Figure 1 — A logical lookup becomes page work Read it: follow either the index route or direct file route; both converge on a data block. Key takeaway: a short index does not prove a query is cheap when qualifying records occupy many scattered data pages. Provenance: teaching construction from Lecture1b, PDF pp. 3–10, and Lecture2a, PDF pp. 5–18. Whole-record capacity For block size $B$, record size $R$, and $N$ records: $$bfr=\left\lfloor\frac{B}{R}\right\rfloor, \qquad b=\left\lceil\frac{N}{bfr}\right\rceil.$$ bfr is the blocking factor. Floor first because only whole records fit; ceiling second because a partially filled final block still occupies a block. > [!warning] Pedagogical trap — dividing total bytes directly > $\lceil NR/B\rceil$ permits unused bytes from one block to combine with another. That contradicts the unspanned-record condition whenever the remainder cannot hold another complete record. Groups that must stay together Tutorial Q4 requires one 300-byte student and five 200-byte module records in the same block. The indivisible group is $$G=300+5(200)=1300\text{ bytes}.$$ Then $\lfloor4096/1300\rfloor=3$ groups fit per block and $\lceil1000/3\rceil=334$ blocks are needed. Pooling all student and module bytes would violate the clustering constraint. Dense, sparse, primary and secondary are different axes | Term | Decisive question | |---|---| | Primary index | Is the data file physically ordered by this search key? | | Secondary index | Is the index on a different order from the data file? | | Dense index | Is every search-key value represented, with a route to all records having that value? | | Sparse index | Can representative entries select a block/range because the file order completes the search? | A logical primary key need not be the primary index key. In Tutorial Q6 the file is ordered by the non-key name; an index following that physical order is primary in the lecture terminology. Index capacity For key length $K$, pointer length $P$, and $E$ entries: $$e=K+P,\qquad bfr_I=\left\lfloor\frac{B}{e}\right\rfloor,\qquad b_I=\left\lceil\frac{E}{bfr_I}\right\rceil.$$ For a sparse primary index in this course, $E$ is normally the number of data blocks. For a dense index, read the question: Tutorial Q4 explicitly requires one entry per student tuple. HDD read phases The source model separates seek, rotational waiting and transfer: $$T_{read}=T_{seek}+T_{rotation}+T_{transfer}.$$ Minimum, maximum and average cases choose different seek/rotation assumptions. Tutorial Q2 averages seek as half the stated maximum and rotation as half a revolution, while retaining the full transfer time. This is the course approximation, not a universal disk benchmark. > [!question] Explain it yourself > Why can a sparse index on unordered IDs miss a matching record even if every index entry is correct? > [!success]- Check your explanation > Sampling blocks works only when file order makes the selected block/range contain every possible match. Unordered IDs can occur outside that range. > > Source: Lecture2a - Indexing Techniques (1).pdf, PDF pp. 8–18; Tutorial Q6.

entries.title: Worked example — solve the motivating question
entries.text: Step 1 — Data records per block $$bfr=\lfloor4096/350\rfloor=11.$$ Step 2 — Data blocks $$b=\lceil25000/11\rceil=\lceil2272.727\ldots\rceil=2273.$$ Step 3 — Sparse entries One entry per data block gives $E=2273$ entries. Each entry is $10+10=20$ bytes. Step 4 — Index entries per block and index blocks $$bfr_I=\lfloor4096/20\rfloor=204,$$ $$b_I=\lceil2273/204\rceil=\lceil11.142\ldots\rceil=12.$$ Interpretation: the sparse index occupies 12 blocks and selects among 2273 ordered data blocks. A lookup still needs its index traversal and at least the candidate data block; cache state is unspecified. Source: Tutorial Q3, Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf, PDF p. 4; supplied answer, Lab1-Tutorial_Answers.pdf, PDF p. 8.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The answers are 2273 data blocks, 2273 sparse entries, and 12 index blocks. The sparse design is correct because data blocks are sequentially ordered by student_ID; an entry representing a block identifies the candidate range, and the search continues within that block. Remove the order assumption and the same sampling no longer guarantees complete lookup.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source | |---|---|---|---| | Tuple | Record | logical row versus encoded physical representation | Lecture1b, pp. 3–4 | | Page/block | Record | transfer/container unit versus one stored item | Lecture1b, pp. 7–10 | | Primary key | Search key | logical uniqueness constraint versus lookup attribute(s) that may repeat | Lecture2a, pp. 5–7 | | Dense index | Sparse index | direct complete coverage versus representative coverage relying on order | Lecture2a, pp. 8–18 | | Primary index | Secondary index | follows physical file order versus indexes another order | Lecture2a, pp. 8–18 |

entries.title: Common confusions
entries.text: - Ceiling too early: records per block uses floor; required blocks uses ceiling. - Invented overhead: add page headers or slots only when supplied. - Logical key = physical order: not necessarily. - Fewer index blocks = faster: retrieval may still touch many data blocks. - Sparse = one entry per arbitrary block: only safe with an ordering/routing invariant.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Return to #Learn the mechanism and #Worked example — solve the motivating question.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: 1. Identify the indivisible item: record, clustered group or index entry. 2. Compute whole items per block with floor. 3. Compute blocks with ceiling. 4. Decide entry count from dense/sparse coverage. 5. Verify that physical order makes the access path complete. 6. Keep index-node, data-page and buffer assumptions separate.

entries.title: 60-Second Recall
entries.text: - tuple → record → page → file - buffer hit versus miss - floor(B/R) then ceil(N/bfr) - clustered group as indivisible item - primary versus secondary - dense versus sparse - key bytes + pointer bytes - seek + rotation + transfer

entries.title: Physical Storage & File Organisation
entries.text: Physical Storage & File Organisation SOE201 · Unit 01 From logical rows to physical pages—and the cost of finding them. Course home · Practise · Try the lab Unit Roadmap flowchart TD A["Pages and buffers"] --> B["Storage and I/O"] B --> C["Record layouts"] C --> D["Page updates"] D --> E["File organisation"] E --> F["Index access"] classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; > [!abstract] What You Will Be Able to Do > - Explain when a logical lookup causes a physical page fetch. > - Separate seek, rotational wait, and transfer costs. > - Calculate space for whole records, related groups, and index entries. > - Trace deletion, insertion, and compaction while preserving valid references. > - Justify file organisation and index coverage for a stated workload. > - Interpret the SQLite lab's results without inferring unmeasured performance. Topic overview A database stores records in pages, arranges those pages into files, and uses access structures to find the right data. This unit connects the layout of bytes with space, reads, insertions, and deletions. | Learn to… | Start here | |---|---| | Explain where a lookup's cost comes from | #From rows to pages and the buffer · #HDD geometry and read phases | | Calculate storage without losing whole-record constraints | #Fixed-length records and blocking factor | | Trace records as they grow, move, or disappear | #Variable-length records · #Slotted pages and stable references | | Choose an organisation for a workload | #File organisations | | Size an index and explain how it finds a record | #Introductory indexes | | Revise the tutorial calculations | #Worked examples · #Exam-style summary | Scope: Lecture1b, PDF pp. 2–29; introductory indexing from Lecture2a, PDF pp. 5–18; Tutorial 1, Q1–Q6. B+ tree balancing and hashing algorithms are outside this unit. You need rows, attributes, keys, basic SQL, and integer division. > [!info] Key Idea — Keep the model explicit > Tutorial records and index entries are ==unspanned==, with maximum packing and no invented overhead. Count overhead when a question explicitly supplies it. The HDD question transfers ==16 384 bytes== per block; the file-sizing questions use ==4096-byte blocks==. These are separate cases. > > The course DBMS and dialect are unconfirmed. The optional SQLite lab demonstrates logical behaviour; it does not reproduce the tutorial's physical layout. Why this matters Imagine a university registry during registration week. Staff need quick student lookups, address updates, ordered reports, and student-plus-module information. Each task favours different properties: | Task | Storage question | |---|---| | Find one student | How many pages must be located and fetched? | | Store new registrations | Where can new records fit, and what must be maintained? | | Change a long address | Can the record grow without invalidating references? | | Read a student and five modules | Would keeping related records together save data-page fetches? | | Produce an ordered report | Does logical order also provide physical locality? | A good design explains space, access, and maintenance together. Fewer index pages alone do not prove faster queries. Key concepts Follow the storage path from a logical row to its page, then examine how records and access structures change. From rows to pages and the buffer A query asks for rows; storage retrieves the pages that contain them. A schema defines attributes and constraints; a tuple is a logical row. A physical record contains the encoded fields, and a ==page/block== holds records. A file groups pages. Databases also need metadata, statistics, indexes, and logs, which are outside a tutorial count of data blocks.[^logical][^architecture] | Aspect | Logical view | Physical view | |---|---|---| | Unit of data | Tuple and attribute | Record and encoded field | | Grouping | Relation | File and pages | | Lookup | A requested row | An access path plus buffer state | A ==primary key== is a logical unique, non-null identifier; a search key is an attribute set used for lookup and may repeat. A foreign key connects a child value to a referenced key. DDL declares structures; DML reads or changes their contents. > [!note] Definition > A ==buffer== holds page copies in memory. A hit uses a resident page; a miss requires fetching it. A dirty page has changes not yet reflected in its persistent copy.[^buffer] flowchart TD A["Locate required page"] --> B{"In buffer?"} B -->|"Hit"| C["Read record in memory"] B -->|"Miss"| D["Fetch page into a frame"] D --> C C --> E{"Changed?"} E -->|"Yes"| F["Mark dirty; later writeback"] E -->|"No"| G["Read complete"] classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 1 — A logical request meets the buffer Read it: choose the hit or miss branch before reading the record. Key takeaway: two row requests can require only one data-page fetch if both rows share a retained page; eviction can change that. Index and metadata fetches need separate accounting. A memory write alone does not establish durability. Storage hierarchy and units Before comparing costs, identify both the storage layer and the unit being transferred. | Layer in the course model | Examples | Role | |---|---|---| | Primary | Cache, main memory | Fast working copies; volatile in this model | | Secondary | Flash, magnetic disk | Persistent database storage | | Tertiary | Optical storage, tape | Archival storage | The course hierarchy describes roles, not current hardware prices or a rule covering every memory technology.[^media] 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KiB = 1024 bytes. Thus 4096 bytes = 4 KiB, while four 4096-byte sectors = 16 KiB. A disk transfer block, a DBMS page, a NAND page, and a NAND erase block are different objects.[^blocks] Larger pages may reduce transfer counts but also bring unwanted data into memory or waste space. Keep the ==unit and storage layer== explicit. HDD geometry and read phases Reaching the right track and reaching the right sector are separate operations. A platter is a disk with recording surfaces. Each surface has circular tracks, divided into sectors. A ==cylinder== groups tracks of equal radius across surfaces.[^hdd] figure-02-hdd-geometry.svg Figure 2 — Platter, track, sector, cylinder Read it: follow the highlighted ring; the highlighted arcs across the stack share its radius. Key takeaway: moving to a track is radial positioning; reaching a sector also depends on angular position. The geometry is schematic. | Phase | What happens | Symbol | |---|---|---| | ==Seek time== | Move the head to the required track | $T_s$ | | ==Rotational wait== (latency) | Wait for the starting sector | $T_w$ | | ==Transfer time== | Read all requested sectors | $T_t$ | Formula — Read time For $r$ revolutions/minute, $S$ sectors/track, and $q$ contiguous sectors/block: $$ T_r=\frac{60\,000}{r}\text{ ms},\qquad T_t=\frac{q}{S}T_r,\qquad T_{\text{read}}=T_s+T_w+T_t. $$ | Symbol | Meaning | Unit | |---|---|---| | $T_r$ | Time for one revolution | ms | | $T_s$, $T_w$, $T_t$ | Seek, rotational wait, transfer | ms | > [!info] Interpretation > Transfer occupies the fraction $q/S$ of one revolution. Faster rotation reduces the rotation and transfer terms in this model; seek remains a separate input. figure-03-read-phases.svg Figure 3 — Position first, then transfer the complete block Read it: compare the worst-case and course-average bars; transfer has the same duration. Key takeaway: averaging the positioning costs does not halve the number of sectors read. Segment widths are schematic; the labels give the times. We use total read time, including transfer. The textbook's “access time” ends when transfer begins; the lecture also allows a definition including transfer.[^timing] Uniform angular arrival gives half a revolution on average. The tutorial additionally approximates average seek as ==half the maximum==; that is a course convention, not a universal probability law.[^q2-answers] > [!info]- Optional depth — why an average needs a model > For independent continuous uniform positions $X,Y$ across a span of $L$ tracks, > $$\mathbb{E}|X-Y|=\frac{2}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^x(x-y)\,dy\,dx=\frac{L}{3}.$$ > A positive-distance seek model $1+d/1000$ ms would then give approximately $1+L/3000$ ms. This alternative is not substituted for the tutorial's half-maximum convention. Elevator scheduling. The lecture's policy serves pending requests in one direction, then reverses when none remain in that direction.[^elevator] Starting at 40, moving upwards: | Current head | Next request | Movement | Pending after service | |---:|---:|---:|---| | 40 | 45 | 5 tracks | 10, 20, 70 | | 45 | 70 | 25 tracks | 10, 20 | | 70 | 20 | 50 tracks | 10 | | 20 | 10 | 10 tracks | None | The path is 40 → 45 → 70 → 20 → 10, totalling 90 tracks. Under $1+d/1000$ ms per positive seek, its seek component is $4+90/1000=4.09$ ms. Rotation and transfer are additional. Some scheduling variants travel to the physical disk end before reversing; they require a different trace. Sequential reads can exploit proximity, but this is not a measured timing guarantee.[^sequential-book] SSDs, mirroring, and striping Different mechanisms change access costs, placement, and protection against failure. NAND flash has no mechanical seek or rotation. It still has read, program, transfer, controller, and reclamation costs. Programming and erasing operate at different granularities: pages are programmed, while groups of pages form ==erase blocks==. A translation layer may remap logical addresses.[^ssd][^flash-book] flowchart TD A["Logical page L maps to X"] --> B["Program new content into erased Y"] B --> C["Remap L to Y; X becomes obsolete"] C --> D["Later: move live pages, erase old block"] classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 4 — A logical overwrite can change physical location Read it: L keeps its logical identity while X and Y are physical locations. Key takeaway: deleting a row need not immediately erase a NAND page. This diagram does not prescribe crash-safe ordering. figure-05-mirroring-striping.svg Figure 5 — Copies versus distribution Read it: identical page labels denote copies; different labels denote different data. Key takeaway: a mirror can retain data after one device fails under the shown assumptions; striping alone cannot.[^raid] | Mechanism | What it provides | Limit to remember | |---|---|---| | Striping | Independent devices may work concurrently | No exact speedup is guaranteed | | Mirroring | Redundancy against some failures | A mistaken deletion can propagate to every mirror; no exact speedup is guaranteed | Key distinction: ==redundancy== is not historical recovery or backup. > [!question] Before continuing > Can two row requests cause just one data-page fetch? Would replacing the HDD with an SSD make every remaining access cost disappear? > [!success]- Check > Yes, if both rows share a page that remains buffered. An SSD removes mechanical seek and rotation, but electronic access, controller work, transfer, and possible reclamation remain. Fixed-length records and blocking factor The first question is how many complete records fit in one page. In ==fixed-length== storage, every record in the model occupies $R$ bytes. Unspanned means each record stays within one page; spanned storage permits a record to continue across pages and needs an appropriate continuation representation.[^records] | Aspect | ==Unspanned== | ==Spanned== | |---|---|---| | Page boundary | A record stays within one page | A record may continue across pages | | Leftover tail | Cannot complete a record on another page | May hold a fragment under the chosen representation | | Model used here | Tutorial capacity calculations | Contrast only; continuation overhead is unspecified | figure-06-blocking-and-spanning.svg Figure 6 — Why leftover bytes do not combine across unspanned pages Read it: the twelfth record needs 350 bytes but the tail has only 246. Key takeaway: calculate whole records per page before counting pages. The spanned alternative illustrates a different model; its continuation overhead is not specified. Formula — Whole-record capacity Let $N$ be records, $B$ bytes/page, $H$ fixed overhead/page, and $U=B-H$ usable bytes: $$ \boxed{f=\left\lfloor\frac{U}{R}\right\rfloor} \qquad \boxed{b=\left\lceil\frac{N}{f}\right\rceil} \qquad w=U-fR. $$ > [!info] Interpretation > Capacity changes in whole-record steps. More usable space helps only when another complete record fits; any remaining records still need another page. - $f$: ==blocking factor== — whole records/page, because $fR\leq U$. - $b$: required data pages, because $bf\geq N$. - $w$: residual bytes in a maximally packed page. Check the model before calculating: - Use $H=0$ for the tutorial unless overhead is supplied. Do not count a record header twice if already included in $R$. - The formula assumes $N\geq0$ and $0<R\leq U$. - If $R>U$, the unspanned representation cannot store even one record; do not divide by $f=0$. - Zero records imply zero data pages in this model, not a zero-byte database. > [!tip] Exam Tip — Round according to the constraint > ==Floor== capacity; ==ceiling== demand. First find how many complete objects fit. Then allocate enough complete pages for all objects. The object might be a record, a whole related group, or an index entry. Deletion and free lists Deleting a record is useful only if its space can be found and reused. A ==free list== links reusable fixed-size record positions from a header pointer. Each free position stores the next link.[^free-list] In this teaching example, deletion adds a slot at the front. figure-07-free-list.svg Figure 7 — Delete slot 3, then reuse it Read it: follow the header through free slots; occupied slots are outside the chain. Key takeaway: ==save a free slot's successor== before overwriting its bytes. Other occupied records need not move. A deleted flag marks a hole but does not efficiently locate it. A free list helps discover space; it does not preserve a sequential file's key order or guarantee that a variable-length record fits. Affected indexes still need maintenance. The sequence shown is a logical trace, not a concurrent or crash-recovery protocol. Variable-length records When a field grows, the record must still describe where its fields begin and end. > [!note] Definition > If field lengths vary, a fixed prefix can store ==(offset, length)== pairs. A field offset is relative to the record start. A ==null bitmap== distinguishes a missing value from a present empty string.[^variable][^variable-book] | Aspect | Fixed-length records | ==Variable-length records== | |---|---|---| | Size in the model | Every record occupies $R$ bytes | Field values can change the record length | | Finding fields | Predetermined boundaries | Offset/length descriptors in the illustrated layout | | Growth | Must fit the chosen representation | May require new space and updated offsets | | Question | Metadata to consult | |---|---| | Where are the field's bytes, and how long are they? | The field's (offset, length) descriptor | | Is the value missing rather than a present empty string? | The null bitmap | figure-08-record-layouts.svg Figure 8 — Fixed fields and variable-field descriptors Read it: follow each descriptor to its bytes. Key takeaway: an unchanged offset can still need a new length; growth must also fit in the containing page. Widths are schematic; the variable example assumes a 16-byte prefix and one byte per character. In the example, Ana occupies bytes 16–18. Changing Hall to Hall-B changes the address pair from (19,4) to (19,6) and the total record length from 23 to 25 bytes. If the *name* instead grows by two bytes, the following address begins at 21. Character count is not generally byte count. The lecture's instructor example uses three 4-byte pairs at bytes 0–11: ID (21,5), name (26,10), and department (36,10). salary uses bytes 12–19, and the null bitmap is at 20. The last field ends at byte 45, so the total is 46 bytes. These are that figure's encoding assumptions, not a universal format.[^variable][^variable-book] Slotted pages and stable references A small directory lets record bytes move without rewriting every surviving reference. > [!note] Definition > A ==slotted page== has a header, a directory of record locations and lengths, free space, and record bytes. Referencing a record through (page, slot) lets its bytes move *within the page* while its slot stays stable.[^slotted][^slotted-book] Formula — Page free space For $n$ allocated slots of $s$ bytes each—including ==retained deleted slots==—the free space after compaction is: $$ F=B-H-ns-\sum_{i\in\mathrm{live}}R_i. $$ > [!info] Interpretation > Both live records and allocated slots consume page space. Deleting a record releases its payload bytes; retaining its slot keeps the directory cost. | Insertion situation | Free bytes required | |---|---:| | Allocate a new slot | $R_{\mathrm{new}}+s$ | | Reuse a retained slot | $R_{\mathrm{new}}$ | figure-09-slotted-page.svg Figure 9 — Delete, compact, reuse Read it: left-to-right bars show byte order; track record C and slot 2 through compaction. Key takeaway: contiguous free space grows when C moves, while updating slot 2 keeps surviving references valid. Intervals are half-open: [start,end) has length end − start; directory widths are enlarged for readability. > [!warning] Common Mistake — Counting only record bytes > Wrong: If the page has enough free bytes for the record, insertion must fit. > > Why it fails: Total free bytes may be fragmented; contiguous free bytes may be smaller. A new slot also consumes space, and a retained deleted slot still occupies directory bytes. > > Correct idea: Check a ==usable extent== and include any directory growth. Reference limits: - Compaction does not preserve the identity of a deleted record when its slot is reused. - Moving a record to another page needs additional reference handling. - A raw byte pointer becomes stale when its record moves. Immediate compaction is the course's explanatory model, not every DBMS's deletion policy. > [!question] Before continuing > When C moves during compaction, what must change so that (page, slot 2) still finds it? Why does a deleted-but-retained slot still count toward page occupancy? > [!success]- Check > Update slot 2 to C's new offset. The directory entry remains allocated even when its record is deleted, so its bytes remain part of the page's occupied space. File organisations Choose what should stay together: free space, nearby keys, or related records. | Organisation | Layout and access | Update cost or trade-off | |---|---|---| | ==Heap== | No record ordering; use free space where available | Easy placement; searches need a scan or suitable complete index | | ==Sequential / ordered== | Records follow a search-key order | Good ordered locality; insertion may need movement or overflow | | ==Multitable clustering== | Related records from different relations share pages | Helps grouped access; single-relation scans fetch other relation bytes | | B+ tree / hashing | Named alternatives in the lecture taxonomy | Their algorithms are deferred beyond this unit | These are the course's layout concepts.[^file-organisations] Choose using query frequency, ranges, joins, insertions, memory, and maintenance—not a universal ranking. Heap free-space map A map advertises approximate available space per page; a higher level can summarise groups with their maximum.[^heap] With illustrative buckets [1,4,0,2], a group maximum of 4 directs a request needing 3/8 of a page toward the page with bucket 4. The actual page must still be checked. For the teaching rule $v=\min(7,\lfloor8F/B\rfloor)$, a 4096-byte page with 2100 free bytes has bucket 4. Inserting 1536 bytes, including any slot cost, leaves 564 bytes and bucket 1; the group maximum becomes 2. Stale maps or fragmentation may require retrying or compaction. This rounding rule is illustrative, not a specified course implementation. figure-10-file-organisations.svg Figure 10 — Three ways to organise records Read it: distinguish physical boxes from the logical chain in the ordered example. Key takeaway: order, free-space discovery, and locality solve different problems. The small page capacities are teaching assumptions. Sequential insertion and reorganisation Into full pages [10,14,19] and [23,28,35], insert 16 by allocating an overflow record, setting its successor to 19, then redirecting 14 to 16. The logical sequence is now 10 → 14 → 16 → 19 → 23 → 28 → 35. An ordered scan must include ==overflow==.[^sequential] Reorganisation rewrites the sequence into [10,14,16], [19,23,28], [35], with affected references and indexes repaired. It restores locality at the cost of reads and writes. On a separate branch from the post-insertion state, delete 19 by saving successor 23, redirecting 16.next to 23, and reclaiming 19 under the free-space policy. Do not mix this branch with the seven-record reorganisation result. Multitable clustering Keep one student(sID, ...) record with its five related module(sID, ...) records. module.sID references the student's key; the module record's own key is unspecified. Tutorial Q4 requires all six records in the same block, so pack ==whole groups==.[^clustering][^q4] Formula — Whole-group capacity $G$ is bytes/group, $R_s$ and $R_m$ are bytes/student and bytes/module, $m$ is modules/student, and $N_s$ is the number of student groups. $$ G=R_s+mR_m,\qquad f_G=\lfloor B/G\rfloor,\qquad b_G=\lceil N_s/f_G\rceil. $$ > [!info] Interpretation > More child records make each group larger. The packing unit is the entire related group, so leftover bytes cannot be pooled across pages to complete it. With variable child counts, group lengths vary even if each record type has fixed length. A student with 25 modules would need $300+25(200)=5300$ bytes, violating a 4096-byte one-page requirement. Per-relation pointer chains can skip module records logically during a student-only scan, but fetched pages still contain their bytes. Introductory indexes An index must provide a complete route from the requested value to every matching record. An ==index entry== stores a search-key value and a pointer. Ordered indexes sort search values; hash indexes map them to buckets without preserving key order.[^index-key][^ordered-hash] | File-order category | Meaning in this course | Distinction | |---|---|---| | ==Primary index== | Index on the file's ordering key | Different from the relational primary-key constraint | | Secondary index | Index on a different key | Sorting its directory does not make unordered data suitable for simple sparse lookup | | Aspect | ==Dense index== | ==Sparse index== | |---|---|---| | Coverage | Every search-key value; all matching records must be reachable | Selected representatives; default here is one per data block | | Entry count | Depends on the duplicate representation | Depends on the representative rule | | Absence reasoning | No matching entry can establish absence when coverage is complete | No matching representative does not establish absence from the data | The slides also use clustering/clustered and non-clustering/non-clustered as aliases for primary and secondary. Product terminology can differ. Multitable clustering is a related-record layout, not the same definition.[^index-types] figure-11-index-coverage.svg Figure 11 — When sparse lookup works, and when sampling fails Read it: for target 28 choose the largest block minimum ≤ 28; compare the missing route to ID 20 below. Key takeaway: sparse lookup needs a valid continuation rule in the underlying file, not merely sorted sampled index entries.[^sparse] For ==unique keys== and block-minimum representatives, choose the largest representative ≤ K and inspect that block. With representatives 10, 23, 40: | Target | Candidate and result | |---:|---| | 23 | Choose D1 directly; equality matters | | 9 | Below the first minimum: absent | | 39 | Search D1; absent before next minimum 40 | | 99 | Search D2 to its end; absent | The slide uses < K followed by a forward scan. That can work with proper first-key handling; it is not universally wrong. Our ≤ K rule directly chooses the target block under the stated assumptions. Duplicate runs spanning pages need adaptation. Duplicate values and complete coverage Name-ordered [Ana,id7] [Ana,id2] [Bo,id9] can use one value entry for Ana pointing to its first occurrence, then scan its contiguous run. On an ID-ordered file, a secondary name index can instead use Ana → {id2 location, id7 location}. Count any pointer-bucket storage separately.[^dense] Q4 explicitly requires one dense entry ==per student tuple==; that local rule controls its calculation. A complete dense index can establish absence when no entry matches. A sparse directory cannot: 28 is absent from the directory but present in D1. Formula — Index capacity For $K_b$ key bytes, $P_b$ pointer bytes, and $n_I$ entries, with no extra overhead: $$ E=K_b+P_b,\qquad f_I=\lfloor B/E\rfloor,\qquad b_I=\lceil n_I/f_I\rceil. $$ > [!info] Interpretation > Decide what one entry represents before counting entries. A sparse directory may use fewer entries, but that space saving is useful only if the access path remains complete. Index maintenance - Changed indexed value: remove its old entry/pointer and add its new one consistently with the data change. - Insertion or deletion: index entries and page allocation can change. - Deleted block minimum: its sparse representative can change; deleting a non-minimum may leave it unchanged. - Empty page: remove or redirect its entry. - Unindexed field update without record movement: an index may remain unchanged.[^index-metrics] Multilevel directories A small outer index can describe the pages of an inner ordered index.[^multilevel] flowchart TD A["Outer index: 1 page, 12 entries"] -->|"Choose one inner page"| B["Inner sparse index: 12 pages"] B -->|"Choose one data page"| C["Registry: 2273 data pages"] classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 12 — A directory over a directory Read it: follow one selected page at each level. Key takeaway: a cold lookup on this path uses three fetches; with the outer page resident it needs two more. This extension has 13 index pages, while Q3's requested single-level index has 12. A secondary-index scan may jump among scattered data pages while a primary-index scan follows nearby ones. This locality argument depends on the access pattern and buffer; neither index size nor correct results alone establishes a speedup. The supplementary lab demonstrates index maintenance and result preservation without claiming a physical footprint or timing result. > [!question] Before continuing > Why can a value be absent from a sparse directory but present in the file? What makes its candidate page discoverable? > [!success]- Check > Sparse entries represent selected values. Compatible file order and a valid representative/continuation rule lead to the candidate data page; sorting samples alone cannot create that property. Worked examples The cases below are separate tutorial datasets, not a single shared schema. All use unspanned, maximally packed records and entries. The page-update example is a labelled teaching construction. Example 1 — Registry storage and its index · Q3 > [!example] Worked Example — Registry storage and its index · Q3 > Given > > - student(student_ID, address, ...): 25 000 records, 350 bytes each. > - Ordered by unique 10-byte student_ID; 4096-byte blocks, 10-byte pointers. > - The 50-byte address is already included in 350 bytes.[^q3] > > Find · Calculate data pages, sparse and dense index alternatives, and packing slack. > > Method · Records → records/block → data blocks → index entries → index blocks. > > Calculation and answer > > | Step | Calculation | Result | > |---|---|---:| > | Records/block | $\lfloor4096/350\rfloor$ | 11 | > | Data blocks | $\lceil25\,000/11\rceil$ | 2273 | > | Last block | $25\,000-2272(11)$ | 8 records | > | Index entry | $10+10$ | 20 bytes | > | Entries/block | $\lfloor4096/20\rfloor$ | 204 | > | Sparse index | $\lceil2273/204\rceil$ | 12 blocks | > | Dense unique-ID alternative | $\lceil25\,000/204\rceil$ | 123 blocks | > > Interpretation > The requested single-level sparse design uses ==2273 data + 12 index = 2285 blocks==.[^q3-answer] Its last index block holds $2273-11(204)=29$ entries. > > A full data block leaves $4096-11(350)=246$ bytes. Payload is 8 750 000 bytes; allocated data space is 9 310 208 bytes; slack is 560 208 bytes. Check it independently: $2272(246)+1296=560\,208$. > > Pooling all row bytes gives 2137 blocks, but that answer illegally combines tails across unspanned pages. Example 2 — HDD timing · Q1–Q2 > [!example] Worked Example — HDD timing · Q1–Q2 > Given > > - 16 384 tracks/surface; 128 sectors/track; 4096 bytes/sector. > - 7200 rpm; four contiguous sectors per transfer block; no gaps. > - For positive distance $d$, seek time is $1+d/1000$ ms; no movement costs zero seek time in the best case.[^q1][^q2] > > Find · Calculate the seek cases and the best, approximate worst, and course-average read times. > > Method · Keep seek, rotational wait, and full-block transfer separate; state the distance convention. > > Calculation and answer > > One-track seek: $1+1/1000=1.001$ ms. The answer sheet uses 16 384 as the end-to-end distance, yielding 17.384 ms. Literally, 16 384 track centres have 16 383 gaps, yielding 17.383 ms. State which convention you use.[^q1-answer] > > $$ > T_r=60\,000/7200=8.333333\ldots\text{ ms},\qquad > T_t=(4/128)T_r=0.2604167\text{ ms}. > $$ > > | Read case | Seek + wait + full transfer | Total | > |---|---|---:| > | Best | $0+0+0.2604167$ | 0.2604 ms | > | Approximate worst | $17.384+8.3333333+0.2604167$ | 25.9778 ms | > | Course average | $17.384/2+8.3333333/2+0.2604167$ | ==13.1191 ms== | > > A near-full revolution is the worst rotational bound. The published answer rounds intermediate values to 17.38, 8.33, and 0.2603, producing about 25.9703 and 13.1153 ms. Retaining precision until the end explains the difference; it does not change the model.[^q2-answers] Example 3 — Page insertion and compaction > [!example] Worked Example — Page insertion and compaction > Given — teaching assumptions > > - 4096-byte page; 64-byte header; three 8-byte slots. > - Records: A = 600 bytes, B = 800, C = 1000. > - Records are packed from the end downwards. > > Find · Decide what fits, then track deletion, compaction, and slot reuse. > > Method · Account for the header, all allocated slots, live records, and free bytes on each independent branch. > > Calculation and answer > > $$F=4096-64-3(8)-(600+800+1000)=1608\text{ bytes}.$$ > > A new 1600-byte record plus an 8-byte slot fits exactly; 1601 bytes plus its slot does not. These are ==independent tests== from the original page. > > Now restart from that original page, delete B, compact, and insert D = 1600 using B's retained slot: > > | State | Slot 0 → A | Slot 1 | Slot 2 → C | Free space | > |---|---|---|---|---| > | Initial | (3496,600) | B (2696,800) | (1696,1000) | 1608 contiguous bytes | > | Delete B | Unchanged | Retained, marked free | Unchanged | 2408 total, split into two gaps | > | Compact | Unchanged | Still free | (2496,1000) | 2408 contiguous bytes | > | Insert D | Unchanged | D (896,1600) | (2496,1000) | ==808 contiguous bytes== | > > The final check is $64+24+600+1600+1000+808=4096$. Slot count remains three; surviving C is still reachable through slot 2 after its offset changes. Use Figure 9 to connect the arithmetic with the byte movement. Example 4 — Student and module groups · Q4 > [!example] Worked Example — Student and module groups · Q4 > Given > > - 1000 student records, 300 bytes each; 5000 module records, 200 bytes each. > - Exactly five modules per student; each whole group must share a 4096-byte block. > - Groups are ordered by 20-byte sID. > - A 10-byte pointer contains an 8-byte block ID and a 2-byte offset.[^q4] > > Find · Calculate combined data blocks and the two alternative index sizes. > > Method · Pack a whole student-plus-five-module group before counting data blocks; count each index alternative separately. > > Calculation and answer > > $$G=300+5(200)=1300,\qquad f_G=\lfloor4096/1300\rfloor=3,\qquad > b_G=\lceil1000/3\rceil=\mathbf{334}.$$ > > Three groups leave 196 bytes per full block. The last block holds one group. Entries are $20+10=30$ bytes, so each index block holds $\lfloor4096/30\rfloor=136$ entries. > > | Index alternative | What one entry represents | Required index blocks | > |---|---|---:| > | Dense, as Q4 defines it | One student tuple: 1000 entries | 8 | > | Sparse primary | One combined data block: 334 entries | 3 | > > These are alternatives, not two indexes to add together by default.[^q4-answer] After locating a group, one data block contains all six records; locating it may still require index reads. > > Separate files would use $\lceil1000/13\rceil=77$ student blocks and $\lceil5000/20\rceil=250$ module blocks: 327 total. Clustering spends ==7 extra blocks== for guaranteed group locality. A student-only scan must fetch pages containing module bytes. Example 5 — Product file · Q5 > [!example] Worked Example — Product file · Q5 > Given > > - 10 000 product records, 50 bytes each. > - Ordered by unique 2-byte productID. > - 4096-byte blocks; 10-byte pointers; sparse primary index.[^q5] > > Find · Calculate data blocks and a single-level sparse primary index. > > Method · Find whole-record capacity, then count one sparse entry per data block. > > Calculation and answer > > $$ > f=\lfloor4096/50\rfloor=81,\quad b=\lceil10\,000/81\rceil=124, > \quad E=2+10=12,\quad f_I=341,\quad b_I=\lceil124/341\rceil=1. > $$ > > Answer: ==124 data blocks + 1 index block==. The last data block contains $10\,000-123(81)=37$ products. There are 124 sparse entries, not 10 000.[^q5-answer] Example 6 — A file ordered by a non-key name · Q6 > [!example] Worked Example — A file ordered by a non-key name · Q6 > Given > > - 30 000 students records, 30 bytes each; ordered by non-key name (4 bytes). > - studentID is the 2-byte primary key. > - Blocks are 4096 bytes; index pointers are 6 bytes.[^q6] > > Find · Identify the primary-index key, calculate its maximum compact dense size, and assess ID sampling. > > Method · Use the file ordering to classify the index, then state how dense entries cover duplicates. > > Calculation and answer > > The primary-index key is name, because it determines file order. > > $$ > f=\lfloor4096/30\rfloor=136,\quad b=\lceil30\,000/136\rceil=221, > \quad E=4+6=10,\quad f_I=409. > $$ > > The last data block holds 80 records. If $D$ is the number of distinct names, a compact dense-by-value directory has $D\leq30\,000$ entries, giving a maximum of $\lceil30\,000/409\rceil=74$ index blocks. Non-key status permits duplicates; it does not require them in every dataset. Unspecified duplicate buckets, headers, and spare space are excluded. A one-entry-per-tuple format also yields 74, so that total alone does not establish the representation. > > A simple sparse secondary index on unordered studentID cannot locate all omitted IDs (Figure 11). A dense secondary ID index would provide complete coverage while preserving name order.
