Quick Review You Should Now Be Able To Use these actions to check your understanding before moving to practice. - [ ] Explain page hits, misses, and dirty pages. - [ ] Identify track, sector, cylinder, and the three read phases. - [ ] Derive floor/ceiling formulas from whole-object constraints. - [ ] Trace deletion and reuse without losing the free-list successor. - [ ] Count new slots and retained deleted slots correctly. - [ ] Explain which references survive compaction. - [ ] Follow overflow records in an ordered scan. - [ ] Pack related groups before counting blocks. - [ ] Distinguish primary keys, primary indexes, and dense coverage. - [ ] Separate a correctness observation from a performance measurement. 60-Second Review > [!summary] Takeaway > Physical layout determines what fits and what must be fetched. Buffers may avoid a fetch. HDD positioning and transfer have distinct costs. Fixed records favour simple packing; variable records need descriptors and indirection. Heap, sequential, and clustered layouts serve different workloads. An index helps only if its coverage and continuation rules can find all required records, and every update must preserve that property. Practice Next - 02 Exercises — attempt a question, then open its local hint or solution. - 03 Lab — connect index maintenance with observed logical results. Reading: Course sources and scope. Footnotes retain the reviewed source locations; textbook passages provide the identified buffer, NAND, and slot-indirection clarifications.

entries.title: Unit 1 Exercises
entries.text: Unit 1 Exercises Notes · Lab > [!abstract] Practice Map > A · Retrieve → B · Build the method → C · Apply it → D · Repair reasoning → E · Integrate Work with the notes closed. Show units, state assumptions, and explain every rounding decision. All datasets in these exercises are teaching constructions. Use ==unspanned records and entries==, maximum packing, and only the overhead explicitly stated. Attempt → reveal a hint if needed → check your solution. Both help panels sit directly below their question and stay collapsed until opened. Difficulty labels describe the amount of reasoning required, not predicted exam difficulty. A. Quick Retrieval Explain each distinction in a few sentences before revealing help. Exercise A1 — Explain an access path Draw fields → record → page → file, and show where memory enters a lookup. Why can two row requests cause ==one data-page fetch==? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Separate row requests from page fetches. > - Check whether the same page remains in the buffer for the second request. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Follow the storage hierarchy > > Fields form records, records occupy pages, and pages form a file. A requested page is fetched into a buffer on a miss. > > Step 2 — Apply buffer state > > If it remains resident and contains both rows, the second request hits that same buffer page. Index and metadata access require separate accounting. > > Key idea: A ==buffer hit== can satisfy a second row request without another data-page fetch. Exercise A2 — Derive rather than memorise Why does records-per-block use ==floor== while required block count uses ==ceiling==? What happens if one record is larger than the usable block? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Ask how many complete records can fit inside one block. > - Then ask how many complete blocks are needed for all records. > - Check whether even one record fits before dividing. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Enforce whole-record capacity > > Only whole unspanned records fit, so fractional capacity is discarded. > > Step 2 — Allocate enough blocks > > Any remaining records still need a whole additional block. > > Step 3 — Check the domain > > If a record exceeds usable capacity, the assumed unspanned layout is impossible; a zero blocking factor cannot be used as a divisor. > > Key idea: ==Whole objects== determine both rounding decisions. Exercise A3 — Predict a boundary lookup > [!info] Key Data > > - The file is ==ordered by a unique key==. > - Pages: D0 [10,14,19]; D1 [23,28,35]; D2 [40,47]. > - Index representatives are the ==block minima==: 10, 23, and 40. For a lookup of key 23: - Which block should be chosen? - What extra rule is needed if the implementation uses a strict predecessor? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Test equality with a block minimum. > - For a strict predecessor, identify what must happen after reading the preceding block. > - Consider the first representative as a boundary case. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Choose the direct candidate > > Choose D1 through representative 23. > > Step 2 — Handle a strict predecessor > > A strict-predecessor rule chooses the preceding representative and must explicitly continue forward and handle the first-key boundary. It cannot simply inspect only the predecessor block and stop. > > Key idea: The ==equality boundary== and continuation rule determine whether lookup is complete. Exercise A4 — Interpret a diagram During ==compaction==, C moves from offset 1696 to 2496. - Which pointer remains useful? - What must be changed? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Compare a raw byte offset with a reference through a slot. > - Identify which directory value must follow the moved record. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Maintain indirection > > (page, slot 2) remains useful if slot 2's directory offset is changed to ==2496==. > > Step 2 — State the limit > > A raw pointer to offset 1696 does not follow C. Slot identity is not a guarantee for deleted records or movement between pages. > > Key idea: Stable slots protect surviving ==within-page references== under the stated model. Exercise A5 — Compare mechanisms > [!info] Key Data > > - The students file is ==ordered by name==; its logical primary key is studentID. > - A separate advising layout groups students with module records. Distinguish primary key, primary index, and multitable clustering using these two cases. > [!tip]- Hint > > - Identify the logical row identifier. > - Identify the actual file-ordering attribute. > - For advising, ask which related records occupy the same page. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Identify the logical key > > studentID is a logical unique identifier in the legacy relation. > > Step 2 — Identify file order > > Its primary index follows the actual ordering attribute name. > > Step 3 — Identify co-location > > Advising multitable clustering instead co-locates a student's record with five records from another relation. These answer different questions. > > Key idea: Logical identity, file order, and co-location are ==different properties==. Exercise A6 — Explain a timing model Which HDD terms disappear as ==mechanical mechanisms== on an SSD? Does that leave exactly the old transfer time? > [!tip]- Hint > > - First identify the delays that require moving parts. > - Then list the work still needed to deliver the data. > [!success]- Solution > > - ==Arm seek and rotational waiting== disappear. > - Electronic access, controller processing, data transfer, and possible reclamation remain; the HDD transfer formula does not specify those costs. > > Key idea: Removing moving parts does not remove every access cost. Exercise A7 — Reason about SQL and NULL A table has ==250 missing addresses==. Why do address = NULL and address IS NULL produce different counts? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Determine the truth value of equality with NULL. > - Recall which truth value WHERE retains. > - Compare that with an explicit missing-value test. > [!success]- Solution > > - Equality with NULL is unknown, which WHERE does not retain; IS NULL directly tests missingness. > - The counts are ==0 and 250== respectively. > - This is not evidence of an index losing the missing-address rows. > > Key idea: ==Missingness== is not tested by ordinary equality. Exercise A8 — Compare reliability claims Why does ==mirroring== not provide the same protection as restoring an ==older backup== after an accidental deletion? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Follow the same logical deletion on both live copies. > - Ask whether either copy still retains the earlier state. > [!success]- Solution > > - A mirror can preserve service after some device failures while also applying the same logical deletion to every current copy. > - Recovering a former state requires suitable historical recovery or backup facilities. > > Key idea: Device redundancy does not by itself preserve an earlier logical state. Exercise A9 — Interpret dense duplicates > [!info] Key Data > > - name has ==5000 distinct values==. > - The file contains 30 000 rows. Must every dense index have exactly 30 000 search-value entries? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Count distinct values separately from rows. > - Explain how a lookup reaches the second and later matches. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Count value entries > > No. A dense-by-value representation can have ==5000 value entries== plus a way to reach all matching records, such as contiguous runs or pointer buckets. > > Step 2 — Compare the tuple representation > > One-entry-per-tuple representations have ==30 000 entries==. State the representation and include additional storage before counting physical blocks. > > Key idea: State the ==duplicate representation== before counting blocks. Exercise A10 — Transfer beyond the model What additional evidence is needed to replace the registry's academic block count with a ==real DBMS file-size estimate==? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Separate record/page format details from additional storage. > - Identify what the ideal packing model omits. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Specify the implementation > > Confirm the engine/version, page and record formats, headers, alignment, variable representations, compression, indexes and their levels, free-space policy, overflow, metadata, and any other files being counted. > > Step 2 — Obtain implementation evidence > > Inspect or measure that implementation; do not label the tutorial's ideal packing as a real footprint. > > Key idea: An ideal packing count is not an implementation measurement. B. Guided Problems Use the supplied structure; justify the rounding and the timing model. Exercise B1 — Complete the missing steps Difficulty: ★★☆ > [!info] Key Data > > - Records: 12 000 records; ==180 bytes== per record. > - Block size: ==4096 bytes==; no extra header. > - Organisation: ==ordered by a unique key==; records are unspanned. > - Index fields: key 8 bytes; pointer 8 bytes. Complete the missing steps and justify each rounding decision. > [!question] What You Need to Find > > - Records/block: $f=\lfloor4096/180\rfloor=\square$. > - Data blocks: $b=\lceil12\,000/f\rceil=\square$. The last block holds $\square$ records. > - A full block leaves $4096-f(180)=\square$ bytes. > - Index entry length is $8+8=16$ bytes; capacity is $\square$ entries/block. > - ==Sparse== entries = $\square$, hence sparse index blocks = $\square$. > - ==Dense== entries = $\square$, hence dense index blocks = $\square$. > - Which quantity changes between the indexes, and what property makes the sparse index valid? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Find whole-record capacity with ==floor==, then required blocks with ==ceiling==. > - Do not size the index until you know what one entry represents. > - For the last data block, subtract the records in all preceding full blocks. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Pack the data file > > $f=22$; $b=546$. The first 545 blocks hold $545(22)=11\,990$ records, leaving ==10==. A full block leaves $4096-22(180)=136$ bytes. > > Step 2 — Size one index block > > Entries occupy 16 bytes, so $f_I=256$. > > Step 3 — Count the two alternatives > > Sparse: 546 entries and $\lceil546/256\rceil=3$ blocks. Dense: 12 000 entries and $\lceil12\,000/256\rceil=47$ blocks. > > Step 4 — Explain the rounding and coverage > > The entry count changes, not entry length. Sparse representatives work because the data are ==ordered by the represented unique key==. Floor prevents partial records/entries; ceiling reserves space for remainders. > > Answer: ==546 data blocks==; 3 sparse or 47 dense index blocks. > > Key idea: The ==entry count== changes; the ==entry length== does not. Exercise B2 — Transfer the timing model Difficulty: ★★☆ > [!info] Key Data > > - Rotation: ==6000 rpm==. > - Track: 200 sectors. > - Transfer block: ==five contiguous sectors==. > - Maximum seek time: 12 ms. > [!question] What You Need to Find > > - Revolution time and transfer time. > - Best, approximate worst, and ==course-average read time==. > - Why the average is not half the worst total. > [!tip]- Hint > > - Convert minutes to milliseconds once. > - Use the fraction of a revolution occupied by the block. > - Apply the course's half-maximum approximation to seek and rotational wait only. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Separate revolution and transfer > > Revolution: $60\,000/6000=10$ ms. Transfer: $(5/200)(10)=0.25$ ms. > > Step 2 — Combine the three costs > > Best: ==0.25 ms==. Approximate worst: $12+10+0.25=\mathbf{22.25}$ ms. Course average: $12/2+10/2+0.25=\mathbf{11.25}$ ms. > > Step 3 — Interpret the average > > Half of the worst total, 11.125 ms, incorrectly halves the transfer. All calculations assume no queue or controller overhead and contiguous sectors without gaps. > > Answer: best 0.25 ms; worst 22.25 ms; course average ==11.25 ms==. > > Key idea: The average still includes the ==full transfer==. C. Independent Problems Choose the method yourself and state the assumptions that make it valid. Exercise C1 — Calculate a new case Difficulty: ★★☆ > [!info] Key Data > > - Records: 18 000; ==150 bytes== each. > - Block size: ==4096 bytes==. > - Ordering key: unique; 6 bytes. > - Pointer: 10 bytes. > [!question] What You Need to Find > > - Data blocks and ==sparse-index blocks==. > - The number of records in the last data block. > [!tip]- Hint > > - Determine the object stored in one data page. > - Determine what one sparse entry represents. > - Use the last-block remainder as a separate check. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Pack and check the data file > > $f=27$, $b=667$; 666 blocks hold 17 982 records, leaving 18. > > Step 2 — Count the sparse index > > Index entries are 16 bytes, capacity 256; one entry per data block gives 667 entries and ==3 index blocks==. > > Answer: ==667 data blocks== and 3 sparse index blocks; last data block 18 records. > > Key idea: A ==sparse entry== represents a data block in this model. Exercise C2 — Transfer to a changed workload Difficulty: ★★☆ Compare advising clustering under two workloads: - Why might it help a ==join== but hurt a ==student-only scan==? - What happens if a group grows beyond one page? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Compare the bytes needed by a grouped lookup with those needed by a student-only scan. > - Test whether one whole group still fits in a page. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Compare the workloads > > Related records share one page for the group lookup, but a student-only scan reads pages full of module bytes. > > Step 2 — Check the group-size limit > > If a group exceeds usable page capacity, the one-page requirement becomes impossible; change the layout or the constraint rather than applying the same floor formula blindly. > > Key idea: A one-page group is a constraint, not an automatic guarantee. D. Error Diagnosis Identify the first faulty assumption, then repair the reasoning. Exercise D1 — Diagnose a wrong solution Difficulty: ★★☆ The file is ==ordered by surname==; personID is its primary key. A classmate writes: > “The primary key is personID, so a primary index must use personID. Store only the first ID in each block, sort those IDs in the index, and use the greatest stored ID no greater than the query. Every record will then be found.” > [!question] What You Need to Find > > - Identify the first incorrect assumption and the later error. > - Give a concrete failure. > - Propose a correction that ==preserves the current file order==. > [!tip]- Hint > > - Try surname-ordered pages containing IDs 90, 20 and then 70, 10. > - Identify the sampled IDs. > - Ask how the proposed access path would find an omitted ID. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Find the two assumptions > > The first error equates the relational primary key with the course's file-order primary index. Here the primary index follows surname. The second error assumes sorting sampled personID values creates ordering in the underlying records. > > Step 2 — Construct a failure > > Counterexample: surname-ordered block A contains (Adams,90),(Brown,20) and block B contains (Clark,70),(Davis,10). Sampling 90 and 70 gives no complete path for ID 20. Sorting the two entries still cannot reveal the omitted identifier's location. > > Step 3 — Repair the proposal > > Retain surname order and use a ==dense secondary index== with a reference for every personID. Reordering the entire file by personID could enable a sparse primary alternative, but would change the stated condition. > > Key idea: Sorting sampled values does not sort the underlying file. Exercise D2 — Debug a free-list update Difficulty: ★☆☆ An insertion overwrites the head slot ==before reading== its next field. What information can be lost? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Locate the free slot's successor pointer. > - Identify which write destroys that value. > [!success]- Solution > > - The pointer to the remainder of the free list. > - Save that pointer first, update the header, and only then overwrite the slot's bytes, within the assumed single-operation model. > > Key idea: ==Save the successor== before overwriting the free slot. Exercise D3 — Predict an overflow scan Difficulty: ★☆☆ > [!info] Key Data > > - The ==ordered file== has full pages D0 [10,14,19] and D1 [23,28,35]. > - Record 16 is inserted into an ==overflow page== linked between 14 and 19. > - The later scan reads only D0 and D1. What is wrong with the scan's result? > [!tip]- Hint > > - List the physical pages the scan visits. > - Compare them with the full live logical sequence. > [!success]- Solution > > - It omits the overflow record 16. > - Until reorganisation or another complete access method incorporates it, traversal must follow the structure containing the overflow record. > > Key idea: A complete scan must include ==overflow==. Exercise D4 — Diagnose an unjustified measurement claim Difficulty: ★★☆ A report says “2273 blocks means 2273 physical reads at 13 ms each.” Give ==at least three missing assumptions==. > [!tip]- Hint > > - Separate file capacity from the pages visited by this query. > - Check buffer state, access pattern, and the device model. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Identify missing access assumptions > > The query may not scan all blocks; some may be buffered; reads may be sequential or prefetched; index pages may add work; the actual device and transfer block size may differ; contention may matter. > > Step 2 — Interpret the timing claim > > The 13 ms figure is an approximate tutorial model, not a measured latency for this file. > > Key idea: ==Stored blocks== and ==physical reads== are different quantities. Exercise D5 — Debug an index experiment Difficulty: ★★☆ The row sequence changed after CREATE INDEX, but the query had ==no ORDER BY==. > [!question] What You Need to Find > > - What should you compare? > - Which claim remains unsupported? > [!tip]- Hint > > - Separate row membership from requested output order. > - Ask what evidence establishes correctness, index use, or speed. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Make the results comparable > > Compare the same multiset of rows, or add a deterministic ordering before comparing sequences. > > Step 2 — State what the evidence proves > > Equivalent results establish correctness for those tests. Unforced comparisons do not establish that the optimiser used the new index or that execution became faster. The lab’s separately required index probes verify a named access path, not its unforced selection or speed. > > Key idea: ==Correctness==, index selection, and speed require different evidence. E. Exam-Style Problems Combine calculation, interpretation, and limitations in one defensible answer. Exercise E1 — Choose and justify a file organisation Difficulty: ★★★ > [!info] Key Data > > - Workload: many new registrations; frequent ==unique-identifier lookups==; occasional name-ordered reports. > - Records: 18 000, each 150 bytes; blocks contain 4096 bytes. > - Index fields: identifier 6 bytes; pointer 10 bytes. > - Storage contract: ==unspanned records and entries==; ignore other overhead. > - You may choose the file organisation. > [!question] What You Need to Find > > - Propose a layout and access structure; justify them against the workload. > - Calculate ==data and index blocks== under your chosen model. > - State what evidence could reverse your decision. > - Compare a file ordered by the identifier, using one representative per block. > [!tip]- Hint > > - Start with the frequent operations. > - Explain how the chosen access structure finds every identifier. > - Compare the cost of maintaining order with the saving in index entries; fewer entries alone do not settle the choice. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Choose a complete access structure > > A defensible provisional choice is a ==heap with a dense secondary index== on the unique identifier. It avoids maintaining a name-ordered sequential layout for frequent arrivals and gives complete identifier coverage; name reports can sort explicitly. > > Step 2 — Size the data file > > With maximal packing, $f=\lfloor4096/150\rfloor=27$, $b=\lceil18\,000/27\rceil=667$. The first 666 blocks hold 17 982 records, leaving 18. > > Step 3 — Size the dense index > > Entry length is $6+10=16$ bytes, so 256 entries/block. Dense entries = 18 000, requiring $\lceil18\,000/256\rceil=71$ blocks. This includes no spare capacity or extra index levels. > > Step 4 — Compare an ordered alternative > > If identifier order were maintained, a sparse primary index would have 667 entries and need $\lceil667/256\rceil=3$ blocks. > > Step 5 — Revisit the workload > > That saving must be weighed against maintaining order and the actual search path. High report/range frequency, expensive sorting, or different insertion patterns could change the decision. Frequencies, memory, actual implementation, and measurements are needed for a performance conclusion; a justified alternative can be correct. > > Answer under the stated models: 667 data blocks; ==71 dense index blocks== for the heap choice, or 3 sparse index blocks if identifier order is maintained. > > Key idea: Choose ==complete coverage== first, then compare space and maintenance costs. Exercise E2 — Track page capacity through two branches Difficulty: ★★★ > [!info] Key Data > > - Page size: ==4096 bytes==. > - Overhead: 96-byte header plus three 8-byte slots. > - Existing records: 500, 900, and 700 bytes. > - Initially, the free region is ==contiguous== and no slot is reusable. > [!question] What You Need to Find > > - Branch A: find the ==largest new record== that fits. > - Branch B: restart from the initial state; delete the 900-byte record, compact, retain and reuse its slot, and find the largest replacement. > - State the reference guarantee. > [!tip]- Hint > > - Treat the two branches independently. > - Branch A needs a new directory slot. > - Branch B reuses a retained slot; deleting payload bytes does not delete the slot entry. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Account for initial occupancy > > Initial occupancy is $96+3(8)+500+900+700=2220$ bytes, leaving 1876. > > Step 2 — Branch A: allocate a new slot > > A new slot costs 8, so the maximum new record is ==1868 bytes==. > > Step 3 — Branch B: restart and reuse > > On the restarted deletion branch, free bytes become $1876+900=2776$. After compaction and slot reuse, a ==2776-byte replacement== fits because no new slot is needed. > > Step 4 — State the reference guarantee > > Both branches exactly fill 4096 bytes. Surviving records can retain (page, slot) references if their directory offsets are updated; the deleted record's identity is not preserved, and movement between pages needs additional mechanisms. > > Key idea: A ==new slot== costs bytes; a ==reused slot== is already counted. Choose Your Next Review | If you missed… | Revisit in Notes | |---|---| | Capacity or remainders | Blocking factor | | Page growth or surviving references | Slotted pages | | Lookup completeness or key terminology | Indexes | | Timing units or averages | Read costs | | Claims about plans or speed | Lab interpretation | - [ ] I attempted the questions before opening solutions. - [ ] I corrected the reasoning behind each error. - [ ] I can solve a changed-number version without copying the method.

entries.title: What changes when we add an index?
entries.text: What changes when we add an index? Notes · Exercises Purpose See how an additional index preserves logical query results and remains consistent when records change. The lab connects the unit's index-maintenance ideas to an executable example using ==synthetic student data==. > [!info] General database concept > Adding a non-unique index changes an access structure. It should preserve the tested answers, including duplicate addresses and NULL values. Updates and deletions must remain visible through that index. > [!warning] SQLite-specific behaviour > This is a supplementary SQLite experiment. It does not reproduce 350-byte physical records, measure query speed, or identify the course DBMS. Environment used The existing recorded run used SQLite 3.53.1, through Python's standard-library sqlite3 module, on 20 September 2026 at 12:42:10 UTC. It used one connection and an isolated temporary on-disk database, configured with PRAGMA page_size = 4096 before table creation. No server or additional Python packages are needed. Your Python installation may bundle a different SQLite version. The runner prints its actual version and flags a difference from the recorded environment. The previous observed results are summarised below; this presentation refactor did not rerun the experiment.[^sqlite-release][^sqlite-pragma] Files and how to run All six executable source files are in this unit's Attachments folder, with their original filenames and contents. | File | What to inspect | |---|---| | schema.sql | Table, explicit NOT NULL, primary key, length constraint | | seed.sql | Deterministic generation of 25 000 rows | | queries.sql | Fourteen named queries, including duplicates, NULLs, ranges, and ordered results | | indexes.sql | Non-unique idx_student_address | | experiment.sql | Address update and record deletion | | run_lab.py | Controlled sequence, comparisons, and reversible edge cases | Open a terminal in the SOE201 course folder and run: python3 "Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/run_lab.py" The runner creates a temporary database beside the scripts, closes and removes it afterwards, and prints a concise result. It needs no report option for studying. A failed assertion stops the run instead of reporting success. The scripts use their own folder to locate one another, so relocating them together preserves how they work. Follow the experiment Track the baseline, the changed state, and the restored state as separate observations. flowchart TD A["Create schema and synthetic rows"] --> B["Record baseline answers"] B --> C["Add idx_student_address; compare answers"] C --> D["Savepoint: update ID 1, delete ID 2"] D --> E["Check counts and required-index ID sets"] E --> F["Roll back; baseline returns"] F --> G["Reversible branches: constraints, empty table, BLOB ID"] G --> H["Drop added index; compare again; clean up"] classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px; Figure 13 — Change one part, compare with a known state Read it: each reversible branch returns to the baseline before continuing. Key takeaway: these comparisons test correctness and index consistency; they do not measure an unforced optimiser plan or latency. 1. Understand the schema. student_ID TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY supplies explicit uniqueness and non-nullness. name is non-null; address permits NULL. CHECK(length(student_ID) = 10) tests reported length, not a complete ==ten-digit text domain==.[^sqlite-table] 2. Read the seed. WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) generates 1–25 000; UNION ALL keeps those generated rows. printf('%010d', n) makes padded IDs. n % 100 produces 100 names; multiples of 100 get NULL addresses, while other rows get hall values.[^sqlite-with][^sqlite-functions] 3. Predict the baseline. Multiples of 100 give 250 missing addresses. Hall-01 and Hall-02 each contain 2500 rows. The padded text-ID range 100–110 contains 11 rows because BETWEEN includes both ends.[^sqlite-expr][^sqlite-aggregate] 4. Add the address index. The table already has SQLite's primary-key support. “Before the index” means before the ==additional address index==, not before all indexes. Duplicate addresses remain allowed.[^sqlite-index] 5. Change data under a savepoint. ID 0000000001 moves from Hall-01 to Hall-02; ID 0000000002 is then deleted. ROLLBACK TO restores the saved state; RELEASE closes the savepoint. The runner checks complete expected ID sets using separate INDEXED BY diagnostics.[^sqlite-savepoint][^sqlite-indexedby] 6. Inspect edge cases. Duplicate, NULL, and wrong-length IDs are rejected. Separate branches empty the table and probe a ten-byte BLOB ID; each is rolled back. Finally, drop only idx_student_address and compare the original queries again. Observed results summary > [!summary] Takeaway > These values come from the existing recorded execution, which passed 45 of 45 checks. Adding the address index preserved all 14 tested query results; the update and deletion changed the expected memberships, and rollback restored the ==baseline==. | Stage | Observed result | Interpretation | |---|---|---| | Baseline | 25 000 rows; 250 NULL addresses; 100 distinct names | Seed matches its construction | | Duplicate name | N001 matches 250 rows | A search value need not be unique | | Address queries | Hall-01 2500; Hall-02 2500; Hall-00 2250 | The NULL rule removes 250 would-be Hall-00 values | | NULL comparison | IS NULL → 250; = NULL → 0 | Equality with NULL is unknown, so WHERE does not retain it | | Point / range / missing key | ID 1 returns its row; range 100–110 returns 11; absent ID returns none | Lookup boundaries agree with expectations | | Add index | All 14 query results unchanged | The additional index preserves tested answers | | Update ID 1 | Hall-01 2499; Hall-02 2501; total 25 000 | Both the record and indexed memberships reflect the change | | Delete ID 2 | Hall-02 2500; total 24 999 | Deleted membership disappears | | Rollback | Baseline restored | The reversible branch returns to its starting state | | Invalid values | Duplicate / NULL / short IDs, NULL name, and short-ID update rejected | Explicit constraints take effect for these cases | | Empty-table branch | Count 0; no point or indexed results | Empty-state behaviour is consistent | | Ten-byte BLOB ID | Accepted; reported storage class blob, length 10 | The ordinary non-STRICT table does not enforce a text-only ID domain | | Drop index / integrity | Baseline answers unchanged; integrity check ok | Removing the added structure preserves tested data | General ideas and SQLite-specific details Use the distinction below when transferring the lesson to another database engine. | General idea illustrated | SQLite detail used here | |---|---| | Indexes must preserve logical answers | CREATE INDEX idx_student_address ON student(address) | | Results need a requested order for sequence comparison | ORDER BY student_ID in full-result queries | | Missing values differ from ordinary values | IS NULL versus = NULL | | Changes must maintain access structures | Diagnostic INDEXED BY idx_student_address requires that named index | | A reversible experiment needs a known earlier state | SAVEPOINT, ROLLBACK TO, RELEASE | | Declared types and constraints need precise interpretation | Explicit text-key NOT NULL; ordinary SQLite affinity can still accept BLOBs | | Storage configuration belongs to an implementation | PRAGMA page_size, sqlite_master, sqlite_source_id(), and integrity checks | Explicit ORDER BY defines output order; a changed sequence without it is not by itself an incorrect result.[^sqlite-select] For seeded text without embedded NUL characters, SQLite's length counts Unicode code points; for BLOB values, it counts bytes. Ten ASCII digits happen to be ten UTF-8 bytes, but that does not make the full stored record ten bytes or reproduce the tutorial's fixed-size layout. printf, recursive seed syntax, transaction interfaces, and typing behaviour should not be assumed portable to an unidentified course engine. > [!warning] SQLite-specific behaviour — Required-index probes > ==Equal results== do not prove that an unforced query used the new index or became faster. The separate INDEXED BY probes require the named index for those probes; they are not an optimiser hint or a benchmark. No full plans, timings, concurrency conflicts, or crash-recovery behaviour were measured. The detailed execution tables, source identity, fingerprints, and earlier review evidence remain in the unchanged _AI Staging archive. They are not required for this study workflow. entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A B+ tree is a balanced ordered index. Internal nodes route by separator ranges; leaves hold the searchable key entries and are linked for range scans. In this course, order $n$ means at most $n$ child pointers in an internal node and therefore at most $n-1$ leaf keys. Lookup follows boundaries to a leaf. Insertion splits overflowing nodes. Deletion repairs underflow using the lecture's merge-first, otherwise redistribute rule. The root has special occupancy rules. After study, you should be able to trace lookup/range access, apply insertion and deletion one state at a time, and validate occupancy, order, routing, leaf links and equal depth.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: > [!note] Separator boundary > Plain-language meaning: an internal key divides child ranges; it is not itself proof that a record exists. > > Why it matters: membership is confirmed only at a leaf. > > Connects to: lookup and separator maintenance. > > Source: Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf, PDF pp. 4–9. > [!note] Occupancy > Plain-language meaning: non-root nodes have minimum and maximum capacities; the root is allowed to be smaller. > > Why it matters: overflow triggers splitting and underflow triggers repair. > > Connects to: insertion, deletion and height. > > Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–6, 12–27. > [!note] Copy versus promote > Plain-language meaning: a leaf split copies a boundary upward while retaining data keys in leaves; an internal split promotes a separator. > > Why it matters: treating both splits identically loses a searchable leaf key or duplicates routing incorrectly. > > Connects to: cascading splits. > > Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 12–18. > [!note] Merge-first deletion > Plain-language meaning: when a node underflows, the supplied algorithm first merges with an eligible sibling if the combined content fits; otherwise it redistributes. > > Why it matters: it determines the exact intermediate tree expected by the source examples. > > Connects to: parent deletion and root contraction. > > Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Recall ordered keys, pointers and the distinction between an index block and a data block. > [!question] Prerequisite check > If an internal node has separators [10, 20], how many child ranges does it have? > [!success]- Check your answer > Three: values below 10, values from 10 to below 20, and values at least 20. > > Source principle: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–9.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Use the exact order-4 initial tree from Lecture2b, PDF p. 34: [7 | 13 | 19] / | | \ [4,5] [7,9] [13,17] [19,25,31] Apply insert 33, insert 11, delete 25 in that order. How can the tree remain balanced while only local nodes change? What evidence proves the final tree is valid? | Question | Knowledge needed | |---|---| | Insert 33 and 11 | leaf overflow, split, copied separator, parent capacity | | Delete 25 | underflow test, merge-first repair, parent/root repair | | Validate | sorted leaves, range boundaries, occupancy, equal depth |

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: Course order and occupancy For order $n$: | Node | Minimum | Maximum | |---|---:|---:| | non-root internal | $\lceil n/2\rceil$ child pointers | $n$ pointers | | non-root leaf | $\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ keys | $n-1$ keys | | internal root | 2 child pointers | $n$ pointers | | root that is a leaf | 0 keys | $n-1$ keys | For order 4, non-root leaves hold 2–3 keys and non-root internal nodes have 2–4 children. Count child pointers, not separator labels, when checking an internal node. Lookup is interval routing At separator equality, route right into the range beginning at that boundary. Continue until a leaf, then compare actual leaf keys. An internal separator may remain as a valid boundary after the equal leaf key has been deleted; it need not be duplicated in a leaf under the lecture's retained-boundary examples. flowchart TD R["root: 13"] -->|"x < 13"| L["left subtree"] R -->|"x ≥ 13"| G["right subtree"] G --> C{"leaf contains x?"} C -->|yes| P["follow record pointer"] C -->|no| N["not present"] Figure 1 — A separator chooses a range, not membership Read it: equality takes the right branch; only the leaf decides presence. Key takeaway: routing correctness is about ranges, not whether every separator is currently stored as a leaf key. Provenance: teaching construction from Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–9. Range scans use linked leaves Descend once to the first leaf that can contain the lower bound, then scan right through leaf links until the upper bound is exceeded. The index preserves order; a hash index does not provide this route. Insertion: copy at leaves, promote internally 1. Route to the target leaf. 2. Insert in sorted order if capacity remains. 3. On leaf overflow, split the ordered entries. Keep all data keys in leaves and copy the first key of the new right leaf into the parent. 4. If the parent overflows, split the internal node and promote its middle separator; that separator leaves the split internal children. 5. If the root splits, create a new root. All leaves remain at the same depth. > [!warning] Common confusion > A leaf split and an internal split are not interchangeable. Leaf entries represent searchable keys, so the boundary is copied. Internal separators route only, so the middle separator is promoted. Deletion: remove, test, repair upward 1. Route to the leaf and remove the key if present. 2. If occupancy remains valid, update a separator only when its routing range requires it. 3. If the node underflows, apply the lecture's rule: merge with an eligible sibling when combined content fits; otherwise redistribute and adjust the parent boundary. 4. A merge deletes one parent child pointer and its separator. This may make the parent underflow, so repair can propagate upward. 5. If the root has one remaining child, replace the root with that child; height decreases by one. Sibling choice is not universally fixed when both sides satisfy the rule. State and use a consistent supported choice rather than claiming the source prescribes one. > [!question] Explain it yourself > Why can deleting one leaf key cause a root contraction even though most of the tree is unchanged? > [!success]- Check your explanation > Leaf underflow can cause a merge; deleting the corresponding parent pointer can propagate underflow upward until the root has only one child. > > Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27. Height and access cost If $h$ counts edges from root to leaf, an uncached equality lookup visits $h+1$ index nodes. Fetching the data record can require another data-page read. Cache residency can reduce physical reads, so height is a structural bound under a stated cache model, not a measured latency.

entries.title: Worked example — the opening update sequence
entries.text: Initial leaves: [4,5], [7,9], [13,17], [19,25,31]; root [7,13,19]. Insert 33 The rightmost leaf becomes [19,25,31,33] and overflows. Split it into [19,25] and [31,33]; copy boundary 31 upward. The root would have five children, so it also overflows. Promote 19 into a new root, producing two internal children whose leaf ranges remain ordered. Insert 11 Route through the left internal subtree to leaf [7,9]. Insert to obtain [7,9,11]; this is within leaf capacity, so no split occurs. Delete 25 Route to [19,25]; deletion leaves [19], below the minimum of two. Under the lecture's merge-first rule, merge it with eligible sibling [31,33] to form [19,31,33], then delete the redundant parent pointer/boundary. The right internal node now has only one child, below the minimum of two. Merge it with the left internal sibling: their 3 + 1 children fit order 4. Move the old root separator 19 down between the merged ranges. The old root then has one child, so contract it. The new root is [7,13,19] with four leaf children. The final leaves are [4,5] → [7,9,11] → [13,17] → [19,31,33]. Validation: every surviving key appears once; leaf order and links are correct; all leaves share a depth; each non-root leaf has 2–3 keys; internal ranges contain their leaf keys; the final root has four children, every leaf is one edge below it, and the temporary extra level has disappeared. Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 34–37; full illustrated sequence in reference notes.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The tree stays balanced because each overflow or underflow is repaired locally and the repair propagates only when its parent violates capacity. The proof is invariant-based: sorted keys, correct ranges, valid occupancy, linked leaves and equal depth—not resemblance to one drawing.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source | |---|---|---|---| | separator | leaf key | routing boundary versus searchable key entry | Lecture2b, pp. 4–9 | | leaf split | internal split | copy right-leaf minimum versus promote middle separator | Lecture2b, pp. 12–18 | | merge | redistribution | combine nodes and remove a parent pointer versus move entries while keeping both nodes | Lecture2b, pp. 19–27 | | height edge count | node visits | a path of $h$ edges visits $h+1$ index nodes | Lecture2b, pp. 10–11 |

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - route by ranges and confirm at a leaf; - leaves are ordered and linked; - order controls maximum pointers/keys; - leaf split copies; internal split promotes; - deletion uses merge-first, otherwise redistribute; - repair may propagate and contract the root; - validate invariants after every operation.

entries.title: 60-Second Recall
entries.text: - order = max internal pointers - leaf max = order − 1 - root exception - equality routes right - membership at leaf - copy vs promote - merge vs redistribute - root contraction - linked-leaf range scan

entries.title: B+ tree indexing
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises · Course Lab 02 — JDBC and Index B+ tree indexing Opening case — keep a changing registry searchable Synthetic teaching case using the exact tree and update sequence of Lecture 2b, PDF p. 34. A registry stores unique numerical search keys. Its index has ==order 4==: at most four child pointers in an internal node and three key entries in a leaf. Each index node occupies one block; data records are stored separately. The initial tree appears below. Treat this as a logical block model, with no DBMS selected. case-initial.svg Figure 1 — The opening registry index Read it: Start at the root; each downward arrow selects an interval. Horizontal arrows link leaves. Key takeaway: The root has four children; each leaf holds actual search keys. Given: the four leaves are [4,5], [7,9], [13,17], [19,25,31]. Internal separators are 7,13,19. All leaves have the same depth and are linked in that order. Questions 1. How do equality lookup for 17 and the inclusive range 9–25 reach their records? 2. What happens after inserting 33, then 11, then deleting 25, in that exact order? 3. What invariants prove the final tree is valid? How many index blocks does one uncached equality lookup read before and after the complete sequence? Constraints and success criteria: retain all undeleted keys exactly once in leaves; use the lecturer's leaf and internal split rules; ==merge before redistribution== when an eligible sibling pair fits; keep all leaves at one depth. Explain every separator change and distinguish index reads from data-record reads. | Question | Concepts needed | |---|---| | Find 17 and 9–25 | Separators, equality routing, leaf links | | Apply the update sequence | Occupancy, split propagation, merge and root contraction | | Defend the result | Invariants, height and block-I/O model | Prerequisite: Unit 1's records, blocks, pointers, sparse and dense indexes. This chapter covers Lecture 2b, PDF pp. 2–37. All page locators below are PDF pages, which also match the displayed slide numbers in this lecture. Why an index must reorganise locally A static multilevel index can locate a block quickly, but growth can accumulate overflow blocks and require expensive reorganisation. A B+ tree changes a small number of nodes around the affected search path. Its extra space and update work buy bounded depth and continued ordered access.[^motivation] Intuitively, an internal node is a directory of key intervals; a leaf is the searchable catalogue entry. A large block can hold many directory pointers, so each step narrows the search by a large factor. This is why the tree is “short and fat”. Logical neighbours need not occupy physically adjacent disk blocks: pointers encode the relationships.[^structure] > [!note] Definition and order convention > A ==B+ tree== is an ordered, height-balanced index: every path from the root to a leaf has the same length. In this course, order $n$ is the maximum number of child pointers per internal node, so an internal node has at most $n-1$ separator keys. Leaf entries contain a search-key value and a record pointer or pointer to a duplicate-record bucket; a leaf also has a next-leaf pointer.[^structure] Occupancy and the root exception | Node | Minimum | Maximum | |---|---:|---:| | Non-root internal node | $\lceil n/2\rceil$ child pointers | $n$ child pointers | | Non-root leaf | $\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ key entries | $n-1$ key entries | | Root with internal children or leaf children | 2 child pointers | $n$ child pointers | | Root that is itself a leaf | 0 key entries | $n-1$ key entries | Ceilings mean rounding upward to the next integer. For $n=4$, internal nodes need at least two children; non-root leaves need at least two keys. For $n=3$, the respective minima are two children and one key. For $n=6$, they are three children and three keys; leaves hold at most five keys, as in the source's name index on p. 6. Source wording clarification: p. 4 calls the contents of a leaf-root “children”; a leaf has no child subtrees. Here the 0 to $n-1$ bound is stated correctly in key entries. The root exception also takes precedence over the slide's blanket minimum for non-leaf nodes. These are terminology clarifications, not a change to the supplied exercises. A separator is a routing boundary For ordered separators $K_1<\cdots<K_m$ and child pointers $P_1,\ldots,P_{m+1}$: - $P_1$ covers values below $K_1$. - $P_j$ covers $K_{j-1}\le V<K_j$ for middle children. - $P_{m+1}$ covers values at least $K_m$. A separator may be copied from the smallest key in its right subtree when created. After deletion it may remain a valid boundary even when that key no longer exists. The invariant is that every left-side key is smaller than the separator and every right-side key is at least the separator. Membership is established at a leaf. The source deliberately illustrates absent separators 33 and 11.[^lookup][^delete-examples] lookup.svg Figure 2 — The lecture lookup tree Read it: Compare target 33 with the root, then 44; inspect the reached leaf. Key takeaway: Routing boundaries can be absent from the data; source PDF pp. 5, 8–9. Worked counterexample: in Figure 2, 33 routes right at the root and left at separator 44, reaching [37,41]; it is absent. Seeing 33 at the root is insufficient. This also explains why “every internal key must currently occur in a leaf” is too strong for the lecturer's retained-boundary convention. > [!question] Check your understanding > In an order-4 non-root internal node, do two separator keys mean the node is underfull? Explain using three child pointers. Lookup and ordered range access Equality lookup 1. Start at the root. At each internal node, choose the interval containing the target $V$; ==equality goes right== of the matching separator. 2. Follow that child pointer. Repeat until reaching a leaf. 3. Search the leaf for $V$. If present, follow its record or bucket pointer. Otherwise report absence. 4. If multiple records share $V$, retrieve every record referenced by its bucket. Search keys remain distinct in the course node model; duplicate records do not require repeated separator values.[^lookup][^insert] For the source tree in Figure 2, search 29 visits root [33], internal [11,22], then leaf [29]. It takes three index-node reads with an empty cache. Retrieving the actual record is additional work, not a fourth tree level. Range lookup Pedagogical extension of the ordered leaves shown in the source: descend once to the first leaf that can contain the lower bound, scan entries from that bound, then follow next-leaf pointers until exceeding the upper bound. A leaf skipped by equality routing may still be needed for the next range value. The linked leaves avoid restarting at the root for each result. For the opening tree and range $9\le V\le25$, read root [7,13,19], reach leaf [7,9], emit 9, follow to [13,17], emit both, and follow to [19,25,31], emit 19 and 25, then stop before 31. There are four index-node reads in this example: one root and three leaves. Five qualifying records do not imply five data-block reads; their physical placement is unspecified. Limitation: an unclustered index may point to scattered data pages. Fast index traversal does not guarantee cheap retrieval of a large fraction of a table. Why height controls search cost Let $h$ count edges from root to leaf, $K$ count distinct leaf search keys, $m=\lceil n/2\rceil$ be minimum internal fan-out, and $\ell=\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ be minimum keys per non-root leaf. These counts are dimensionless. For $h\ge1$: $$K\ge 2m^{h-1}\ell.$$ Derivation: the root has at least two children. Each of the next $h-1$ internal branching stages multiplies the minimum leaf count by $m$. Each resulting leaf has at least $\ell$ keys. A proposed height is impossible if the available $K$ cannot fill those leaves. The root-as-leaf case $h=0$ is handled separately. For one million distinct keys and $n=100$, $m=50$ and $\ell=50$: | Proposed edge height | Minimum keys | |---|---:| | $h=3$ | $2\times50^2\times50=250,000$ | | $h=4$ | $2\times50^3\times50=12,500,000$ | One million is too small for height 4. Therefore at most three edges and four index nodes are visited. This derives the slide's four-node result while stating root and leaf occupancy explicitly.[^height] > [!warning] Logarithms, rounding, and measurements > PDF p. 11 writes $\log_{50}(1{,}000{,}000)=4$. The logarithm is approximately 3.532, whose ceiling is 4. Page 10's compact logarithmic bound leaves the height convention implicit; use the occupancy argument above when precision matters. A four-node bound is not a measured latency and excludes data pages. Cached nodes reduce physical reads, not logical tree depth. The source's approximately 100 pointers per 4 KB node is an illustrative scale, not a universal node format. For a synthetic internal layout with a 4096-byte block, a 16-byte header, 8-byte pointers, and 32-byte separator keys, capacity obeys $$16+8n+32(n-1)\le4096.$$ Combine terms: $40n-16\le4096$, so $n\le102.8$. Since pointers come in whole units, choose $n=102$. Check: 4064 bytes fit; $n=103$ would need 4104 bytes. Actual DBMS overhead and leaf layouts can differ. Insertion — copy at a leaf, promote internally Why split? An overflowing node cannot remain inside the block capacity, while relocating the whole tree would defeat local maintenance. Splitting creates two valid nodes and one new routing boundary.[^insert] 1. Descend to the target leaf. If the key exists, add the new record pointer to its bucket where appropriate. 2. Otherwise insert the key-pointer entry in order. If the leaf still has at most $n-1$ entries, stop. 3. On leaf overflow there are $n$ entries in a temporary memory area. Keep the first $\lceil n/2\rceil$ entries in the original leaf and put the remainder in a new right leaf. 4. Repair the leaf chain: old leaf → new leaf → old successor. Copy the new right leaf's minimum key into the parent together with the new pointer. The key remains in the leaf. 5. If the parent overflows, it contains $n$ separators and $n+1$ children. Set $c=\lceil(n+1)/2\rceil$. Keep pointers $P_1\ldots P_c$ and keys $K_1\ldots K_{c-1}$ on the left; move $K_c$ to the parent; put pointers $P_{c+1}\ldots P_{n+1}$ and keys $K_{c+1}\ldots K_n$ on the right. 6. Continue upward. Splitting a root creates a new root with two children and increases every root-to-leaf path by one edge. split-rules.svg Figure 3 — Two different split rules Read it: Read each column downward; compare where the promoted or copied key remains. Key takeaway: Leaf entries survive in leaves; an internal promoted separator leaves both children. Synthetic leaf example, source internal mechanism pp. 13–16. Worked internal split: with $n=4$, an overflowing internal node has separators [7,13,19,31] and five children. $c=\lceil5/2\rceil=3$. Promote the third separator, 19. The left node has [7,13] and three children; the right has [31] and two children. Neither internal child retains 19. Limitation: a leaf split need not increase height. It does so only if propagation reaches an overflowing root. Different valid splitting policies exist; source exercises use the precise distribution above. Deletion — repair occupancy without losing ranges Deleting one record is different from deleting an entire search-key entry. If a duplicate bucket still contains records, keep its leaf entry. Remove the key entry only when its bucket is empty, or when the indexed key itself is to be deleted.[^delete] For an underfull node, consider an adjacent sibling with the same parent. The course checks merging first: merge if the pair fits in one node; otherwise redistribute. It does not prescribe a universal left-versus-right preference when both choices are valid. State the sibling chosen. | Repair | What moves | Parent action | |---|---|---| | Merge leaves | Combine leaf entries; reconnect leaf chain | Remove separating key and redundant child pointer | | Redistribute leaves | Move enough boundary entries to satisfy both minima | Replace separator by the new right-leaf lower boundary | | Merge internal nodes | Combine children and pull down the parent separator | Remove that separator and redundant pointer | | Redistribute internal nodes | Move boundary child pointer; rotate keys through parent | Old parent separator moves down; donor boundary key moves up | Leaf worked example, order 4: after a deletion, [10,20,30] and [40] contain four keys together. Maximum leaf capacity is three, so merging is impossible. Move 30 from the left leaf to the right: [10,20], [30,40]; replace parent separator 40 by 30. Both leaves now contain the required two keys. internal-redistribute.svg Figure 4 — Internal redistribution Read it: A–D denote ordered child subtrees. Follow C from left to right and the boundary keys through the parent. Key takeaway: Pointers and routing boundaries move together. Synthetic example of PDF p. 24. Internal worked example, order 3: the left internal node in Figure 4 has three children; the underfull right node has one. Four children exceed the three-child capacity of a merged internal node. Move left's last child C to the right. Separator 50 descends to separate C from D, while 35 rises to separate the two internal nodes. Both finish with two children. Moving only a key without its child pointer would disconnect an entire subtree. After a merge, the parent can itself become underfull; repeat at that level. If the root is left with a single child, make that child the new root and decrease the height by one. A final empty leaf-root is valid. This is local reorganisation along a search path, not a full rebuild.[^delete] Solve the opening case 1 — Lookup and range For 17, choose the root interval $13\le17<19$ and find 17 in [13,17]: two index blocks, followed by the record pointer. For range 9–25, the earlier leaf-chain trace returns 9,13,17,19,25, reading the root and three leaves. Both answer the original predicates completely. 2 — Insert 33, then 11, then delete 25 Insert 33. The leaf [19,25,31] is full. Its temporary entries are [19,25,31,33]. Keep the first $\lceil4/2\rceil=2$ entries and create [31,33]. Copy 31 upward. The old root becomes [7,13,19,31] with five child pointers, so promote 19 as derived above. The tree now has three node levels. case-insert33.svg Figure 5 — After inserting 33 Read it: 19 becomes the new root; the leaves remain linked and at equal depth. Key takeaway: The root split adds one level; source PDF p. 35. Insert 11. At root 19 go left; at [7,13] choose the middle child. [7,9] becomes [7,9,11]. Three entries fit; no separator or height change is needed. case-insert11.svg Figure 6 — After inserting 11 Read it: Find 11 in the second leaf; compare the upper nodes with Figure 5. Key takeaway: Insertion can be entirely local; source PDF p. 36. Delete 25. Route right at 19 and left at 31. [19,25] becomes [19], below the two-key leaf minimum. Its sibling [31,33] allows a three-key merge, yielding [19,31,33]. Remove separator 31 and one pointer from their parent. That internal node now has only one child. Merge it with the left internal sibling: their $3+1=4$ children fit order 4, and parent separator 19 moves down between them. The former root now has one child, so contract it. case-delete25.svg Figure 7 — After deleting 25 Read it: The rightmost leaf now contains 19,31,33; its parent became the root. Key takeaway: Merge propagation can undo the earlier height increase; source PDF p. 37. 3 — Validate and interpret The final root has three separators and four children. Its leaves contain 2, 3, 2, and 3 keys, each within 2–3. Every leaf is one edge below the root. The leaf sequence is [4,5,7,9,11,13,17,19,31,33]: both inserted keys survive and only 25 is removed. Intervals remain correct at 7, 13, and 19. Equality lookup again reads two index nodes with no cache; it temporarily required three after the root split. This completes all opening success criteria. Exam-style answer and reusable method > [!summary] A defensible short answer > Order 4 permits at most three leaf entries. Inserting 33 splits the rightmost leaf and then the full root; promote 19. Inserting 11 fits its leaf. Deleting 25 causes a leaf merge, an internal merge, and root contraction. The final root is [7,13,19] with leaves [4,5], [7,9,11], [13,17], [19,31,33]. Occupancy, routing, key preservation, and equal leaf depth all hold. For an unfamiliar problem: write the order and minima first; preserve the supplied starting tree; trace the target; make the local change; test overflow/underflow; propagate only when necessary; finally check all leaves and every child range. Count child pointers for internal occupancy and keys for leaf occupancy. This method assumes the course model and its merge-first policy, not a confirmed commercial implementation. Misconceptions and quick review | Tempting claim | Correct reasoning | |---|---| | A separator proves a record exists | Only a matching leaf entry establishes membership | | Order 4 means four keys per leaf | It means up to four internal child pointers; three leaf keys | | A leaf merge pulls down the parent key | Only an internal merge needs that separator as an internal boundary | | Any two neighbouring leaves are eligible siblings | Local repair uses siblings with the same parent | | Every insert changes the root | Most fit locally; only root overflow increases height | | One matching key means one record | A duplicate bucket can reference multiple records | Before looking at a solution, be able to draw a leaf split, rotate an internal child through its parent, explain an absent separator, and derive the four-node million-key example. Then attempt the original lecture tasks in Exercises. Study status remains untested. entries.title: B+ tree exercises
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises B+ tree exercises Attempt each task before opening its hint. Every original lecture task and worked update appears below; A–E headings indicate retrieval, guided, independent, diagnosis, and exam practice. Original tasks retain their data. Brackets denote keys within one node, never an unordered bag of whole-tree keys. All original page references are to Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf. A1 — Read the order correctly Supplementary practice · Difficulty: ★☆☆ For orders 3, 4, and 6, give minimum and maximum non-root internal child counts and leaf key counts. Explain the root exception. > [!tip]- Hint > Keep pointers and keys separate. > [!success]- Solution > Internal child ranges are 2–3, 2–4, and 3–6. Leaf key ranges are 1–2, 2–3, and 3–5. These follow from ceilings of $n/2$ and $(n-1)/2$, respectively. An internal root requires only two children; a leaf-root may contain zero through $n-1$ keys. Two children imply one separator, not two. B1 — Find 29, 31, and 33 Original course worked lookup and questions · PDF pp. 8–9 · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Using the source tree below, trace lookup for 29, 31, and 33. State whether each exists and where the decision is made. lookup.svg Figure E1 — Original lookup starting tree Read it: Use the key intervals at each internal node. Key takeaway: An internal match is a routing instruction, not a final answer. > [!tip]- Hint > At separator equality choose the right child. Always finish in a leaf. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Route 29. At 33 go left, then at [11,22] take the rightmost pointer. Leaf [29] contains 29. Follow its record pointer. > > Step 2 — Route 31. Take the same path as 29. Leaf [29] contains no 31, so the search is unsuccessful. > > Step 3 — Route 33. Equality at root 33 selects the right child. In [44], 33 is smaller than 44, so visit [37,41]. No 33 exists there. > > Each search examines three index nodes in the empty-cache model. ==33 is absent== despite appearing as an internal separator. These paths match the algorithm on PDF p. 7. B2 — Insert Adams, then follow the name deletions Original course worked updates · PDF pp. 17–18 and 25–27 · Difficulty: ★★★ The source tree has ==order 4==, visible from its node capacities. Use the tree below; names are search keys ordered lexicographically. Apply these operations sequentially, drawing each state: 1. Insert Adams. 2. Delete Srinivasan. 3. Delete Singh, then Wu, showing both intermediate results. 4. Delete Gold. names-0.svg Figure E2 — Initial name index Read it: The root separates names at Mozart; each lower internal node points to its own leaves. Key takeaway: Only same-parent adjacent nodes are eligible for the immediate local repair. > [!tip]- Hint > Leaves hold 2–3 keys; non-root internal nodes need 2–4 children. Try merging first. Internal merging must count child pointers. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Insert Adams. [Brandt,Califieri,Crick] overflows into [Adams,Brandt,Califieri,Crick]. Split 2+2 and copy Califieri into the left internal parent. That parent now has four children and fits. > > names-1.svg > > Figure E3 — After Adams > > Read it: The new boundary is Califieri. > > Key takeaway: The root remains Mozart. > > Step 2 — Delete Srinivasan. The rightmost leaf becomes [Wu], under the two-key minimum. Merge it with [Mozart,Singh] into [Mozart,Singh,Wu]. The right internal node is left with one child. Merging the internal siblings would require $4+1=5$ child pointers, exceeding order 4, so redistribute instead: move leaf [Gold,Katz,Kim] from the left internal node to the right. The root separator changes from Mozart to Gold; old root boundary Mozart moves down into the right internal node. > > names-2.svg > > Figure E4 — After Srinivasan > > Read it: Gold rises; Mozart moves down. > > Key takeaway: A leaf merge can trigger internal redistribution. > > Step 3a — Delete Singh. [Mozart,Singh,Wu] becomes [Mozart,Wu]; two entries remain, so stop. > > names-3.svg > > Figure E5 — After Singh > > Read it: Only one leaf changes. > > Key takeaway: Minimum occupancy is still satisfied. > > Step 3b — Delete Wu. The leaf becomes [Mozart]. With sibling [Gold,Katz,Kim], the total is four keys, so a three-key leaf merge cannot fit. Move Kim right and update their parent boundary from Mozart to Kim. The leaves become [Gold,Katz] and [Kim,Mozart]. > > names-4.svg > > Figure E6 — After Wu > > Read it: Kim becomes the new right-leaf minimum. > > Key takeaway: Redistribution preserves two leaves. > > Step 4 — Delete Gold. [Gold,Katz] becomes [Katz]; merge with [Kim,Mozart] into [Katz,Kim,Mozart]. The right internal node has one child. Its sibling has three children, so an internal merge fits four pointers. Pull down the root separator Gold, then remove the redundant root level. > > names-5.svg > > Figure E7 — After Gold > > Read it: The new root is Califieri, Einstein, Gold. > > Key takeaway: Gold remains a valid boundary even though its data entry was deleted. > > Interpretation: the final leaves contain exactly the original names plus Adams, minus Srinivasan, Singh, Wu, and Gold. Gold in the root separates El Said on the left from Katz on the right; it need not be a current leaf key. This matches the source's retained-boundary convention. C1 — Construct the order-3 tree Original course exercise · PDF p. 28; source stages pp. 29–30 · Difficulty: ★★☆ Start with an empty B+ tree of ==order 3==. Insert (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17) in that exact order. Draw the tree after each insertion. > [!tip]- Hint > A leaf copies its new right minimum upward; an internal split removes the promoted key from its children. > [!success]- Solution > Leaves hold at most two keys. On overflow, keep $\lceil3/2\rceil=2$ keys in the left leaf and put one in the right. An overflowing internal node has three separators and four children; promote separator $\lceil(3+1)/2\rceil=2$. > > Step 1. Insert 2 into the leaf-root. > > construct-1.svg > > Figure E8 — Construction stage 1 > > Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. > > Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. > > Step 2. Insert 3 into the same leaf; it now reaches capacity. > > construct-2.svg > > Figure E9 — Construction stage 2 > > Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. > > Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. > > Step 3. Insert 5: split [2,3,5] into [2,3] and [5]; copy 5 to a new root. > > construct-3.svg > > Figure E10 — Construction stage 3 > > Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. > > Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. > > Step 4. Insert 7: the right leaf becomes [5,7]. > > construct-4.svg > > Figure E11 — Construction stage 4 > > Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. > > Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. > > Step 5. Insert 11: split [5,7,11] into [5,7] and [11]; root becomes [5,11]. > > construct-5.svg > > Figure E12 — Construction stage 5 > > Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. > > Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. > > Step 6. Insert 13: the final leaf becomes [11,13]. > > construct-6.svg > > Figure E13 — Construction stage 6 > > Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. > > Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. > > Step 7. Insert 17: split the final leaf into [11,13] and [17]. The root temporarily has [5,11,17] and four children; promote 11 to a new root, leaving internal children [5] and [17]. > > construct-7.svg > > Figure E14 — Construction stage 7 > > Read it: Read the tree from root to leaves. > > Key takeaway: The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far. > > The final tree has two edges to every leaf; each internal non-root node has two pointers, and every non-root leaf contains one or two keys. Sorting the input first is unnecessary here because it is already sorted, but changing the stipulated insertion order in another problem can change the shape. C2 — Two deletion paths from the same initial tree Original course exercise · PDF p. 31, parts (1)–(2); solutions pp. 32–33 · Difficulty: ★★★ Use the ==order-3== tree below. It is not the final tree of C1. 1. Delete 5, then delete 11. Draw both states. 2. Restart from the original tree below and delete 11 only. Draw the result. delete-initial.svg Figure E15 — Original deletion starting tree Read it: The left internal node has three children; the right has two. Key takeaway: The reset in part 2 is essential. > [!tip]- Hint > For part 1, state which sibling you choose for the empty [5] leaf. After any leaf merge, inspect the parent child count. > [!success]- Solution > Part 1, delete 5. Its leaf becomes empty. Choose the left sibling [2,3]; combining two keys fits the maximum of two. Remove the old separator 5 and redundant pointer. The left internal node becomes [7] with two children. Choosing the right sibling is also a permitted source alternative, but this solution follows the displayed result on p. 32. > > delete5.svg > > Figure E16 — After deleting 5 > > Read it: Left internal separator is 7. > > Key takeaway: No height change is needed yet. > > Part 1, then delete 11. Its leaf becomes empty. Merge with [13,17]. The right internal node is left with one child. Merge it with the left internal sibling, which has two children: $2+1=3$ fits order 3. Bring down root separator 11 and contract the old root. The new root is [7,11], with leaves [2,3], [7], [13,17]. > > delete5-11.svg > > Figure E17 — Then delete 11 > > Read it: The tree is one level shorter. > > Key takeaway: Separator 11 still partitions 7 from 13 correctly. > > Part 2, restart and delete 11. The same leaf merge leaves the right internal node with one child. This time its left internal sibling still has three children. $3+1=4$ exceeds order 3, so merge-first now fails at the internal level. Redistribute the rightmost left child [7] to the right internal node. Root separator 11 moves down; left boundary 7 moves up. Final root [7]; left internal [5] over [2,3], [5]; right internal [11] over [7], [13,17]. > > delete11.svg > > Figure E18 — Restart, then delete 11 only > > Read it: Compare the still-present leaf [5] with part 1. > > Key takeaway: Different prior operations change which repair fits. > > Both final trees satisfy the capacity and routing invariants. The source notes that leaf redistribution can also solve the original deletion, but requests merging first (p. 33); that is the policy used here. D1 — Diagnose three incorrect explanations Supplementary practice · Difficulty: ★★☆ A student says: (a) “The root contains 33, so record 33 exists”; (b) “An internal merge joins the two key lists but ignores the parent separator”; (c) “Deleting one record always removes its search key.” Correct each claim with a counterexample. > [!tip]- Hint > Use B1, the internal merge rule, and a bucket containing two record pointers. > [!success]- Solution > (a) B1 reaches leaf [37,41] and proves 33 absent; the root value is only a boundary. (b) If the left subtree covers values below 11 and the right begins above it, pulling 11 down preserves the boundary between their child-pointer groups; omitting it leaves one fewer separator than required for the combined children. (c) A leaf entry Physics → [r1,r2] remains after deleting r1 because r2 is still indexed. Remove the entry only after its bucket becomes empty. E1 — The sequential order-4 update exercise Original course exercise · PDF p. 34, operations (1)–(3); answers pp. 35–37 · Difficulty: ★★★ Draw the trees after (1) insert 33, (2) insert 11, (3) delete 25. Each operation uses the preceding result. The source starting tree is reproduced here so that you can attempt this without returning to Notes. case-initial.svg Figure E19 — Original order-4 starting tree Read it: Use all four leaves and the supplied separators. Key takeaway: Do not rebuild a different valid tree from the same data. > [!tip]- Hint > For insertion 33, test both the leaf and the root. After deletion 25, count the parent pointers again. > [!success]- Solution > 1 — Insert 33. The rightmost leaf overflows to [19,25,31,33]; split 2+2, copy 31 upward. The root overflows to [7,13,19,31] with five children. Promote 19, leaving internal [7,13] and [31]. > > case-insert33.svg > > Figure E20 — After operation 1 > > Read it: All leaves move one level farther from the new root. > > Key takeaway: A split cascade reaches the root. > > 2 — Insert 11. Descend left of 19, then between 7 and 13. Leaf [7,9] becomes [7,9,11], which fits. > > case-insert11.svg > > Figure E21 — After operation 2 > > Read it: Only the second leaf changes. > > Key takeaway: No split is needed. > > 3 — Delete 25. Leaf [19,25] becomes [19]; merge with [31,33] to get [19,31,33]. Remove parent separator 31. Its parent now has one child, so merge with the three-child left sibling, bringing separator 19 down. Contract the root. Final root [7,13,19] over [4,5], [7,9,11], [13,17], [19,31,33]. > > case-delete25.svg > > Figure E22 — After operation 3 > > Read it: The final root again points directly to leaves. > > Key takeaway: Every non-root leaf has two or three entries, and all survivors appear once. E2 — Capacity and a search bound Supplementary transfer problem · Difficulty: ★★☆ An internal-node block has 4096 bytes, a 16-byte header, 8-byte child pointers, and 32-byte separator keys. Find its maximum order. Separately, for order 100 and one million distinct leaf keys, prove a bound on uncached index-node reads. Do not assume that the computed byte-layout order and the stipulated order 100 are identical. > [!tip]- Hint > With n pointers there are n−1 keys. For height, count minimum leaves and keys at a proposed depth. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Capacity. $16+8n+32(n-1)\le4096$ gives $40n\le4112$ and $n\le102.8$. Floor to ==102 pointers==. At 102, bytes used are $16+816+3232=4064$; 103 would use 4104 and fail. > > Step 2 — Order-100 occupancy. Minimum internal fan-out and leaf occupancy are both 50. A tree with four root-to-leaf edges would require at least $2\times50^3\times50=12,500,000$ keys. One million cannot fill it; at most three edges and ==four index-node reads== are possible. Data-record retrieval and caching are separate. The argument is about an academic structural model, not measured performance.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Hashing computes a bucket address from a search key. A collision means several keys share a bucket, so lookup still compares actual keys. Static hashing keeps a fixed main address set and uses overflow chains when buckets fill. Extendable hashing adds a directory: global depth says how many high-order hash bits the directory reads; each bucket's local depth says how many bits distinguish that bucket. A full bucket may split with or without directory doubling. Some collisions cannot be separated by more bits, so overflow can still be necessary. You should be able to trace fixed-width hashes, split/alias states, deletion/coalescing and workload choice without assuming hash order or constant worst-case lookup.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: > [!note] Collision > Plain-language meaning: different search keys can map to the same bucket address. > > Why it matters: the hash gives a candidate bucket, not guaranteed equality. > > Connects to: overflow chains and failed lookup. > > Source: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 2–12. > [!note] Global depth > Plain-language meaning: the number of high-order hash bits currently used by the directory. > > Why it matters: the directory has $2^i$ pointer entries. > > Connects to: directory doubling. > > Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–18. > [!note] Local depth > Plain-language meaning: the number of prefix bits that uniquely identify one physical bucket. > > Why it matters: it determines alias count and whether a split needs directory growth. > > Connects to: $2^{i-i_j}$ shared directory pointers. > > Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–21. > [!note] Full-hash collision > Plain-language meaning: keys share every available hash bit, so another split cannot separate them. > > Why it matters: overflow is then necessary under the supplied model. > > Connects to: the Taiyuan rollback case. > > Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 32–40.
