entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need modulo arithmetic, fixed-width binary and the distinction between a directory pointer and a physical bucket. > [!question] Prerequisite check > Write $1$ as a three-bit value. > [!success]- Check your answer > 001. Leading zeros determine high-order prefix routing. > > Source principle: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–18.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Use the source's numeric state on Lecture3a, PDF p. 23. Bucket capacity is three; $h(x)=x\bmod8$ is written in exactly three bits. Global depth is 1. One bucket holds [9]; the other holds [4,5,7]. Insert 13, then explain: 1. why the directory must double; 2. which old entries move after splitting; 3. why a later insertion may still require overflow even after several splits.

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: Static hashing With a fixed set of $B$ buckets, a function such as $h(v)=(av+b)\bmod B$ chooses a main bucket. If it is full, add an overflow page. Lookup reads the main bucket and follows its chain until finding the key or exhausting candidates. flowchart LR K["search key"] --> H["hash function"] H --> B["main bucket"] B -->|"full/collision"| O1["overflow page"] O1 --> O2["next overflow page"] Figure 1 — Static hash lookup follows one address and its chain Read it: the hash selects the chain; actual key comparisons decide the result. Key takeaway: growth concentrated at one address lengthens that chain even when other buckets are empty. Provenance: teaching construction from Lecture3a, PDF pp. 7–12. Static hashing is simple, but fixed capacity creates a trade-off: too few buckets create overflow; too many waste space. If all keys collide, worst-case lookup grows with the chain. Hashing gives no sorted next-key route for range queries. Extendable hashing: directory versus buckets Let $i$ be global depth and $i_j$ a bucket's local depth. | Quantity | Meaning | |---|---| | $2^i$ | directory pointer entries | | $i_j\le i$ | bits distinguishing bucket $j$ | | $2^{i-i_j}$ | directory aliases pointing to bucket $j$ | Physical buckets are at most $2^i$; equality is possible. The strict inequality printed on lecture p. 13 excludes the valid case where every directory entry reaches a distinct bucket, so Tutor Mode records the corrected bound and preserves the source discrepancy. Insertion decision 1. Compute the fixed-width hash. 2. Read the first $i$ high-order bits and follow that directory entry. 3. Insert if the bucket has room. 4. If full and $i_j<i$, split the bucket using the next bit; the directory already has enough detail. 5. If full and $i_j=i<b$, double the directory, increment $i$, then split. 6. Redistribute old and new entries; recheck capacity. 7. If available bits or the source's split limit cannot separate the entries, use overflow under the lecture's rollback convention. > [!warning] Common confusion > Doubling the directory does not duplicate data buckets. It duplicates pointers first; only the overflowing bucket is split. Deletion and coalescing Remove the key from its bucket/overflow chain. Two buddy buckets can coalesce only when they share the same local depth, differ in the relevant last prefix bit, and their combined entries fit one bucket. The survivor's local depth decreases. If no bucket now needs the current global depth, the directory can contract. Hash versus ordered index | Workload | Hash index | B+ tree | |---|---|---| | exact equality | direct candidate bucket, collision check | root-to-leaf route | | ordered range | no adjacent-key path | linked leaves support scan | | skew/collisions | chains or repeated splits | depends on balanced occupancy | | growth | overflow or directory/bucket changes | splits/merges along a path | This is a mechanism comparison, not a universal benchmark. > [!question] Explain it yourself > At global depth 3, why can a local-depth-1 bucket have four directory aliases? > [!success]- Check your explanation > One prefix bit is fixed and two directory bits remain free, giving $2^{3-1}=4$ combinations. > > Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 13–18.

entries.title: Worked example — insert 13
entries.text: $h(13)=13\bmod8=5=101_2$. At global depth 1, prefix 1 routes to full bucket [4,5,7]. Its local depth equals global depth, so double the directory from 2 to 4 pointers and increase global depth to 2. Split by the first two bits: - 4 hashes to 100, prefix 10; - 5 hashes to 101, prefix 10; - 7 hashes to 111, prefix 11; - 13 hashes to 101, prefix 10. The resulting buckets are 10 → [4,5,13] and 11 → [7], each with local depth 2. The old [9] bucket has hash 001 and local depth 1, so both directory entries 00 and 01 still alias it. Source: Lecture3a, PDF pp. 23–28.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The directory doubled because the overflowing bucket already used all directory bits. Only that bucket split; the [9] bucket remained shared. Redistribution used fixed-width high-order prefixes. More splitting cannot solve keys that share every available hash bit, so the supplied algorithm eventually rolls back the failed split and uses overflow.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source | |---|---|---|---| | hash address | search key | candidate location versus actual value compared in the bucket | Lecture3a, pp. 2–12 | | directory entry | physical bucket | pointer slot versus storage container | Lecture3a, pp. 13–18 | | global depth | local depth | bits read by directory versus bits distinguishing one bucket | Lecture3a, pp. 13–21 | | directory doubling | bucket split | duplicate pointer table versus redistribute one bucket | Lecture3a, pp. 19–31 | | collision | duplicate key | same address versus same search-key value | Lecture3a, pp. 2–12 |

entries.text: Full Understanding Return to #Learn the mechanism and #Worked example — insert 13.

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - hash to a candidate bucket, then compare keys; - static hashing uses fixed main buckets and overflow; - directory size is $2^i$; - bucket aliases are $2^{i-i_j}$; - keep leading zeros and read high-order bits from the left; - split without doubling when $i_j<i$; - double then split when $i_j=i$ and bits remain; - coalesce only valid buddies that fit; - range workloads favour ordered indexes.

entries.title: 60-Second Recall
entries.text: - collision ≠ equality - main bucket + overflow - fixed-width hash - high-order prefix - global depth - local depth - alias formula - double versus split - buddy coalescing - equality versus range

entries.title: Hash indexing
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises Hash indexing Opening case — an equality index that must grow Synthetic teaching case. A service repeatedly finds records by numerical ID. Start with the exact numeric structure used in Lecture 3a, PDF p. 23: one bucket holds [9], the other [4,5,7]. Each bucket holds at most ==three entries==. The hash is $h(x)=x\bmod8$, represented in exactly three bits. The directory currently reads its first bit, from the left. Records are stored separately; entries contain IDs and record pointers. 692 Figure 1 — Opening directory Read it: Two directory entries select two buckets; both local depths are 1. Key takeaway: Read fixed-width hash prefixes from the left; source initial state p. 23. Questions 1. Insert 13, then 21. Draw the directory, bucket contents, global depth, and every local depth after each operation. 2. Insert 29. The hash-width limit is ==three bits==; when that limit prevents useful splitting, use overflow. Explain why more bucket allocation alone cannot separate some entries. 3. Find 21 and the absent key 37. How does overflow affect the lookup? Would this layout also be an efficient ordered range index for IDs 4–21? Success criteria: every entry has a valid route from its hash prefix; all main buckets respect capacity; directory aliases are correct; overflow preserves every entry; failed searches inspect all candidate entries. The first insertion is source-derived; the subsequent operations are explicitly additional teaching practice. | Case question | Concepts needed | |---|---| | Insert 13 and 21 | Hash representation, global/local depth, splitting and directory doubling | | Insert 29 | Full-hash collision, split limit, overflow | | Find 21, reject 37, assess a range | Candidate buckets, equality comparison, query workload | Prerequisites: block and pointer concepts from Unit 1, and the ordered-index comparison from Unit 2. The chapter covers Lecture 3a, PDF pp. 2–43; p. 44 is its reading reference. The course DBMS, version, and dialect remain unconfirmed. Hashing replaces an ordered route with a computed address A bucket is a storage unit, typically a disk block, containing multiple entries. A hash function maps a search key into a finite address space. In hash file organisation, buckets hold the data records. In a hash index, buckets hold search keys with record pointers. The source calls the latter secondary indexing: its terminology for a primary index requires sequential file order on that key.[^basics] > [!note] Collision and lookup > A ==collision== occurs when different search-key values map to the same bucket. The hash identifies a candidate bucket, not a unique matching record. Search the bucket and its overflow chain, comparing actual keys. Equal hashes do not imply equal keys. What makes a useful hash function? A useful function spreads keys across addresses with little dependence on troublesome patterns in the actual dataset. “Random” here describes distribution quality; lookup must still reproduce the same address for the same key. An adversarial or skewed distribution can overload one bucket while others remain empty.[^basics] The source gives $h(v)=(av+b)\bmod N$, where $v$ is a numerical key, $a,b$ are chosen constants, and $N$ is the number of static buckets. Remainders are addresses 0 through $N-1$. The formula alone does not guarantee uniformity: with $a=2,b=0,N=8$, integer inputs reach only even residues. With $h(v)=v\bmod8$, keys 5,13,21,29 all collide. Constants and key distribution matter. Source worked calculation: on p. 5, the teaching character encoding assigns M=13, U=21, S=19, I=9, C=3, so Music hashes as $(13+21+19+9+3)\bmod8=65\bmod8=1$. This is the slide's alphabet-position example, not a specified Unicode or ASCII algorithm. The alphabet row repeats G where J would normally occur and prints X as 25; spacing and punctuation handling for department names are unspecified. Preserve the supplied Music result and the depicted department placement; do not invent missing encoding rules. Static hashing and overflow chains Static hashing fixes the main bucket address set. Insertions target the same bucket as lookup. If that bucket is full, attach an overflow page and continue the chain as necessary. Deletion first finds the matching entry; the main hash route remains the same. Overflow pages are additional storage attached to an existing address, not new values in the hash function's range.[^static] 810 Figure 2 — Static collision and overflow Read it: Trace the digit-sum calculation to bucket 5, then its linked overflow page. Key takeaway: The source bucket contents on p. 11 require key comparisons. Source worked example: the ID index on PDF p. 11 uses sum-of-digits modulo 8. For 15151, the digit sum is $1+5+1+5+1=13$ and the bucket is 5. The source's bucket 5 also contains 33456, with 58583 and 98345 in overflow. For 98345, the sum is $9+8+3+4+5=29$, and $29\bmod8=5$. A lookup may require both pages before following a record pointer. The slide's data-row label for Gold is 33465 while the index entry is 33456; both digit sums are 21, but they are different IDs. No exercise silently equates them. Cost and the growth trade-off Let $r$ be number of stored entries, $B$ main buckets, and $c$ entries per bucket. The synthetic occupancy ratio is $\alpha=r/(Bc)$; it is dimensionless and measures average main-bucket demand, not a guarantee against local overflow. With 8 buckets of capacity 2 and 12 entries, $\alpha=12/16=0.75$. A chain can still occur because four entries hash to one bucket. If a target bucket spans $q$ pages including overflow, an unsuccessful lookup scans those $q$ candidate pages in the source model. Add directory and data-record reads separately where relevant. This explains both extremes: too few buckets cause long chains as a file grows, while preallocating many buckets wastes space before growth or after shrinkage. Rehashing all entries can repair the layout but disrupts normal access.[^static] Counterexample to a universal performance promise: no hash index guarantees constant worst-case lookup. If all keys collide, a bucket chain can grow in proportion to the file. Extendable hashing — two depths, one routing invariant The lecture's spelling is extendable hashing, also commonly called extendible hashing. A fixed-width hash provides $b$ bits; the directory uses only its first $i$ high-order bits. Here $i$ is the ==global depth==. A bucket $j$ stores its ==local depth== $i_j$, the number of hash-prefix bits needed to identify that bucket.[^depth] | Quantity | Meaning | Constraint | |---|---|---| | $b$ | Full hash width in bits | Fixed for the chosen function/representation | | $i$ | Global depth in bits | $0\le i\le b$ | | $i_j$ | Local depth of bucket $j$ | $0\le i_j\le i$ | | $2^i$ | Directory pointer entries | Count, not number of physical buckets | | $2^{i-i_j}$ | Directory aliases for bucket $j$ | All aliases share its $i_j$-bit prefix | Derive the alias count: once the first $i_j$ bits are fixed, each of the remaining $i-i_j$ bits has two choices. Multiplying those choices gives $2^{i-i_j}$. At global depth 3, a bucket with local depth 1 has $2^{3-1}=4$ directory pointers. A local-depth-3 bucket has one. Source correction: PDF p. 13 says the number of physical buckets is less than $2^i$. Equality is possible when every local depth equals $i$; the precise relation is at most $2^i$. Do not confuse directory duplication with creation of new physical buckets. Fixed-width binary representation matters For the opening hash, $h(9)=1$ must be written 001, not just 1. At global depth 1, its high-order bit is 0. By contrast, $h(5)=5=101_2$, whose high-order bit is 1. Omitting leading zeros routes 9 incorrectly. At global depth 2, 5 uses prefix 10. The lecture query on p. 18 follows directory entry 10 to bucket [4,5], then compares keys to find 5. Entries 00 and 01 share bucket [9] with local depth 1; 11 points to [7] with local depth 2.[^query] > [!question] Check your understanding > A directory has 16 pointers and one bucket's local depth is 2. How many pointers reach that bucket? Identify global depth before calculating. Insertion — separate directory growth from bucket splitting Why do two operations exist? The directory may already distinguish the next bit even when a particular bucket ignores it. Only when the directory is too shallow must it grow.[^insertion] 1. Compute the full-width hash and follow its $i$-bit prefix to bucket $j$. 2. If there is room, insert the entry and stop. 3. If full and $i_j<i$, allocate a sibling bucket. Increase both resulting local depths to $i_j+1$. Split the old directory aliases according to the next hash bit: the 0 subgroup stays with one bucket; the 1 subgroup goes to the other. 4. Redistribute the old entries and retry the new one. Only the affected bucket's entries move; unrelated buckets remain unchanged. 5. If full and $i_j=i$, first test the hash-width and stipulated split limits. If growth is allowed, increase global depth to $i+1$ and double the directory. Each old prefix gains suffixes 0 and 1 that initially point to the same old bucket. Then perform step 3. 6. Recheck capacity. A split may move no records away from the target prefix, so more than one split may be needed. At the specified stopping limit, use the source's rollback-and-overflow rule. A directory doubling alone changes no bucket contents or local depths. A bucket split changes two local-depth labels and some pointers. Keeping those changes separate makes both diagrams and code easier to verify. The source's first split For insertion of 13 into the opening structure, $13\bmod8=5=101_2$, so the full bucket with prefix 1 is targeted. Its local depth equals global depth 1. Double the directory to four pointers, then split prefix 1 into 10 and 11. Redistribute 4 (100) and 5 (101) into 10; move 7 (111) into 11; insert 13 into 10.[^numeric] 854 Figure 3 — Insertion 13 Read it: 00 and 01 both reach bucket 0; 10 and 11 reach the split buckets. Key takeaway: Directory doubling and bucket splitting are different actions; source pp. 23–28. The untouched [9] bucket stays at local depth 1 and has two aliases (00,01). The two split buckets have local depth 2 and one alias each. There are four directory entries but only three buckets. When splitting cannot solve the problem A new bit helps only if it differs among competing entries. Exact duplicate search keys have the same complete hash, and different keys may share the complete hash too. Adding more directory bits cannot separate them beyond the function's full width. The course instructs: after the allowed number of unsuccessful splits, ==restore the index to before the first split== and add overflow. This is an exercise algorithm convention, not a universal implementation policy. The city case sets the limit to two splits; the department example shows why another Comp.Sci. record still needs overflow.[^limits] Deletion, coalescing, and directory contraction Find and remove the record or entry from its candidate bucket/chain. Do not remove the route while matching records remain. Bucket merging, also called coalescing, requires buddies with equal local depth $d$ that share their first $d-1$ bits and differ only in bit $d$. Their combined contents must fit the chosen bucket capacity; matching prefixes alone do not guarantee enough room.[^deletion] Synthetic worked example: at global depth 2, delete 13 from Figure 3's bucket 10. It now holds [4,5]; buddy 11 holds [7]. Both have local depth 2 and their three entries fit. Merge into prefix 1 with local depth 1, and redirect 10 and 11 to it. The other bucket has prefix 0 and local depth 1. Every adjacent directory pair now has the same pointer, so remove the final directory bit and return to global depth 1 with buckets [9] and [4,5,7]. Limitation: one empty bucket does not automatically justify halving the entire directory. All pointer pairs must remain representable after removing the last prefix bit. The lecture cautions that resizing is expensive; a system may defer it. Core lookup correctness and an aggressive space-reclamation policy are different decisions. Solve the opening case 1 — Insert 13 and then 21 Insertion 13 is Figure 3 above: global depth 2, buckets 0:[9] (depth 1), 10:[4,5,13] (depth 2), and 11:[7] (depth 2). Now $h(21)=21\bmod8=5=101_2$. The 10 bucket is full and its local depth 2 equals global depth 2. Grow the directory from four to eight entries. Split 10 into 100 and 101: 4 goes to 100, while 5 and 13 go to 101. Insert 21 there. 844 Figure 4 — Insertion 21 Read it: Four directory arrows share bucket 0 and two share bucket 11. Key takeaway: Alias counts depend on the difference between global and local depth; synthetic continuation. The unchanged 0 bucket has $2^{3-1}=4$ aliases; unchanged 11 has $2^{3-2}=2$. Each depth-3 bucket has one. Check: $4+2+1+1=8$ directory entries, matching $2^3$. 2 — Insert 29 $h(29)=5=101_2$. The target [5,13,21] is full, and both its local depth and global depth equal the full hash width 3. No unused hash bit exists. Retain the current index and attach overflow containing 29. All other buckets and depth labels remain unchanged. 819 Figure 5 — Full-width collision Read it: Follow 101 to its main bucket, then the overflow page. Key takeaway: The three-bit limit prevents further useful refinement; synthetic continuation. 3 — Find 21, reject 37, and assess the range query For 21, follow prefix 101; compare against [5,13,21] and find it in the main bucket. For 37, $37\bmod8=5=101_2$, so inspect the same main bucket and overflow [29]. No entry equals 37; only after both candidate pages are checked is absence established. If the directory is in memory, this absent lookup needs two bucket-page reads, excluding any unrelated data record fetch. Without a memory-resident directory, account for its access too. A hash route does not preserve numerical order: 9 is in prefix 0, whereas 4 is in 100. To find IDs 4–21 efficiently as an ordered interval, prefer an ordered index such as a B+ tree. Enumerating every possible key in a small integer interval is a special case, not the general hash range-search mechanism. A full scan here would return 4,5,7,9,13,21, and would not obtain them in order from the directory alone. Ordered versus hashed access: choose from the workload | Workload or constraint | Consequence | |---|---| | Mostly equality queries with well-distributed keys | Hashing can give a direct candidate-bucket route | | Range queries, ordered traversal | B+ tree leaves preserve order | | Many repeated values | Hash overflow can persist despite splitting | | Rapid growth/shrinkage | Dynamic allocation helps, but directory resizing and overflow still cost work | | Large directory | May need disk access or another structure to locate its pages | The source describes benefits of growth without full-file rehashing, but also extra indirection, potentially large directories, and expensive resizing. These are trade-offs, not universal guarantees of minimal space or constant response time.[^comparison] > [!warning] Supplementary technical correction — PostgreSQL > Lecture 3a, PDF p. 42 says PostgreSQL does not support hashing on disk. PostgreSQL 18's official documentation explicitly describes persistent, crash-recoverable on-disk hash indexes and equality-only support. The source claim is therefore not correct for that documented version. This correction does not establish PostgreSQL as the SOE201 course DBMS.[^postgres] Exam-style answer and reusable method > [!summary] A defensible answer to the opening case > Fixed-width hashes route 13,21,29 to 101. Inserting 13 doubles global depth to 2 and splits bucket 1. Inserting 21 doubles it to 3 and splits bucket 10. Inserting 29 reaches the three-bit limit and adds overflow. The final directory has eight pointers to four main buckets; duplicate prefixes share buckets according to their local depths. Lookup must compare actual keys and inspect overflow before declaring absence. For any new task: write the fixed hash width, capacity, bit direction, current global depth, local depths, and split limit; compute the target hash; distinguish alias updates from entry movement; retry insertion; enforce rollback if required; check all routes and entry counts. Do not transfer a suffix-bit algorithm into these prefix-bit exercises without explicitly changing the convention. Misconceptions and quick review - “Two directory entries imply two buckets.” They may be aliases of one bucket. - “Low average occupancy prevents overflow.” Skew concentrates local demand. - “Different IDs separate after enough splits.” They can share a complete finite hash. - “Doubling changes every local depth.” Only buckets actually split change local depth. - “The first bucket proves absence.” Overflow belongs to the same candidate route. Explain the two depths without looking, draw insertion 13, and then solve the city rollback exercise with its original data. Personal learning remains untested. [^basics]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 3–6, 9–10. Encoding and identifier ambiguities are explicitly retained. [^static]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 7–12. Occupancy ratio and cost examples are labelled teaching calculations. [^depth]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 13–16; alias formula is visible on p. 15. [^query]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 17–18. [^insertion]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 19–21. [^numeric]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 23–28. [^limits]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 29–40; two-split limit specified on p. 32. [^deletion]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF p. 22; capacity and directory-pair reasoning are explanatory consequences of the depicted structure. [^comparison]: Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 41–43. Vendor statements on p. 42 are source context rather than confirmed course configuration. [^postgres]: Supplementary official clarification: [PostgreSQL 18 — Hash Indexes]( section 65.6.1, checked 2026-09-20. Supports the persistent on-disk hash-index correction only; no PostgreSQL execution was performed.

entries.title: Hash-index exercises
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises Hash-index exercises All original page references below identify Lecture3a - Hash Indexing.pdf; its (1) copy is byte-identical. Try each question before opening the adjacent hint or solution. The supplementary exercises are labelled explicitly. A1 — Directory entries and physical buckets Source-derived worked relationship · PDF pp. 15–16; supplementary numerical check · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Explain why a bucket of local depth $i_j$ receives $2^{i-i_j}$ directory pointers. For the source example $i=2$, $i_1=1$, $i_2=i_3=2$, give every bucket's pointer count. Then find the alias count for a local-depth-2 bucket when global depth is 4. > [!tip]- Hint > Fix the local prefix; count the remaining free directory bits. > [!success]- Solution > Derivation: each of the $i-i_j$ remaining bits has two choices, giving $2^{i-i_j}$ aliases. In the source example, the counts are $2^{2-1}=2$, $2^{2-2}=1$, and 1: four pointers to three physical buckets. In the supplementary case, $2^{4-2}=4$ aliases reach that bucket. Counting pointers as separate buckets would overcount storage. B1 — Reproduce the supplied hash calculations Original course worked examples · PDF pp. 5 and 11 · Difficulty: ★☆☆ 1. Using the source's letter values M=13, U=21, S=19, I=9, C=3, compute the bucket for Music with sum modulo 8. 2. Using digit-sum modulo 8, compute the bucket for ID 15151. The source diagram shows bucket 5 with entries 15151,33456 and overflow 58583,98345; explain why collisions require full-key comparison. Do not replace the supplied character values with ASCII codes. The slide's inconsistent alphabet cells and Gold data-row ID are documented in Notes; they are not silently corrected inputs here. > [!tip]- Hint > Sum first, then take the remainder on division by 8. > [!success]- Solution > 1. $13+21+19+9+3=65=8\times8+1$, so Music maps to ==bucket 1==. > > 2. $1+5+1+5+1=13=8+5$, so ID 15151 maps to ==bucket 5==. IDs 33456, 58583, and 98345 have digit sums 21,29,29, all remainder 5. The hash narrows the candidate set; compare actual IDs to distinguish them. A search for 98345 must continue into the overflow page. The bucket entry 33456 is retained exactly; the source row elsewhere labelled 33465 is not treated as the same identifier. B2 — Follow the source lookup for 5 Original course worked lookup · PDF p. 18 · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Use $h(x)=x\bmod8$, three-bit hashes, global depth 2. Directory 00,01 points to [9] of local depth 1; 10 points to [4,5] of local depth 2; 11 points to [7] of local depth 2. Trace the source lookup for 5. > [!tip]- Hint > Use the first two bits of 101, then compare entries. > [!success]- Solution > $h(5)=5=101_2$. Its two-bit prefix is 10, so follow that directory entry to [4,5]. Compare the full key and find 5. The directory does not return a record merely because the prefix matches: 4 is in the same bucket. If the directory is cached, the candidate-bucket read is one block in this simplified model; fetching a separate record is additional. C1 — Insert 13 into the original two-bucket index Original course exercise · PDF p. 23; source solution pp. 24–28 · Difficulty: ★★☆ The hash is $h(x)=x\bmod8$, stored as three bits. A bucket holds ==three records==. The initial index below has global depth 1. Draw the index after inserting a record with search key 13; show directory growth, bucket redistribution, and local depths. 575 Figure E1 — Original numeric starting index Read it: Both buckets have local depth 1. Key takeaway: Insert into the route determined by the high-order bit. > [!tip]- Hint > The target is full and its local depth equals global depth. Double the directory before splitting. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Locate. $13\bmod8=5=101_2$; prefix 1 selects [4,5,7], already full. > > Step 2 — Double. Increase global depth from 1 to 2. Before redistribution, 00,01 both point to [9] and 10,11 both point to [4,5,7]. Local depths remain 1 at this intermediate step. > > Step 3 — Split. Split the latter bucket into prefixes 10 and 11, each with local depth 2. Existing hashes are 4→100, 5→101, 7→111; therefore redistribute as [4,5] and [7]. > > Step 4 — Insert. Put 13 into the 10 bucket, producing [4,5,13]. The [9] bucket remains local depth 1 and retains two aliases. > > insert13.svg > > Figure E2 — Original insertion result > > Read it: Four directory entries point to three physical buckets. > > Key takeaway: All buckets fit capacity 3, and all original records are retained. > > This matches the final source figure on PDF p. 28. The algorithm changes neither the numerical hash function nor unrelated bucket contents. C2 — Another Comp.Sci. record Original course worked insertion · PDF pp. 29–30 · Difficulty: ★★☆ The source uses an index on Department, global depth 3, and two-record buckets. Its displayed buckets are: Music (local depth 1) containing (15151, Mozart, Music, 40000); Physics (depth 3) containing Einstein and Gold; Finance (depth 3) containing Wu; History (depth 3) containing El Said; and Comp.Sci. (depth 3) containing (10101, Srinivasan, Comp.Sci., 65000) and (45565, Katz, Comp.Sci., 75000). Insert the exact new record (83821, Brandt, Comp.Sci., 92000). Explain the overflow result shown on p. 30. A numerical hash function and exact trial limit are not supplied for this example; do not invent them. > [!tip]- Hint > Hashing depends on Department. Ask whether another bit can distinguish equal Department values. > [!success]- Solution > All three Comp.Sci. records have the same search-key value and therefore the same complete hash. The existing two-record bucket is full. Splitting on more bits cannot separate identical values. Under the source's stated limit/fallback rule, retain or restore the original directory and chain an overflow bucket containing (83821, Brandt, Comp.Sci., 92000) to the existing Comp.Sci. bucket. The other four buckets stay unchanged. Equality lookup for Comp.Sci. must return all three records across the chain. We cannot reconstruct a numerical split trial without the missing hash/limit inputs; the source demonstrates the final overflow outcome directly. E1 — Taiyuan and the two-split rollback rule Original course case study · PDF pp. 32–34; supplied solution pp. 35–40 · Difficulty: ★★★ A block holds up to ==three records==. Begin with the original city-name index below. It already contains one Taiyuan record. The task is to insert a new record with Taiyuan, retaining the existing record. If insertion is still unsuccessful after ==two splits==, revert to the original index and use overflow. | City name | Supplied 32-bit hash | |---|---| | Lianyungang | 1101 0111 1011 0101 1110 0101 1110 1111 | | Nottingham | 0010 0110 1101 0101 0111 0010 1100 0101 | | Cambridge | 0110 1001 1000 0011 1100 0010 0101 0000 | | Venice | 0011 0001 0011 0100 1101 1101 0111 0101 | | Kuala Lumpur | 1000 0001 1100 0000 1010 0001 1100 1110 | | Taiyuan | 0010 1001 1000 0011 1100 0010 0101 0000 | | Java Island | 0111 1001 1000 0011 0110 1001 1000 0011 | | Valencia | 1110 1001 1000 0011 1100 0010 0101 0000 | | Florence | 0010 1001 1000 0011 0110 1001 1000 0011 | | Chiang Mai | 0010 1110 0001 0001 0101 0111 1100 1100 | The full table is retained from PDF p. 33. Only the stated Taiyuan insertion is required; the other city names are not extra unstated insertion tasks. 607 Figure E3 — Original city starting index Read it: Global depth is 2; prefixes 10 and 11 share the local-depth-1 bucket. Key takeaway: A duplicate city name denotes another record, not an instruction to discard it. > [!tip]- Hint > Taiyuan, Florence, and Nottingham share prefix 0010. Show both failed split states before the required rollback. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Locate the full bucket. The new Taiyuan hash begins 00, so its candidate bucket already holds Taiyuan, Florence, Nottingham. Four records do not fit three slots. > > Step 2 — First attempt. Local depth 2 equals global depth 2, so double the directory to global depth 3. Split 00 into 000 and 001, both local depth 3. All three existing records and the new one begin 001; 000 remains empty and the new record still cannot fit. > > city-split1.svg > > Figure E4 — First failed split > > Read it: The main bucket at 001 still contains only the three old records. > > Key takeaway: The pending new Taiyuan record is not silently stored beyond capacity. > > Step 3 — Second attempt. Increase global depth to 4 and split 001 into 0010 and 0011, both local depth 4. Taiyuan, Florence, and Nottingham all begin 0010; the new Taiyuan does too. The split again leaves the target full and an empty sibling. > > city-split2.svg > > Figure E5 — Second failed split > > Read it: 0000 and 0001 share the earlier empty local-depth-3 bucket. All sixteen directory entries are shown. > > Key takeaway: Both allowed splits have failed; continuing to bit 5 would violate this exercise. > > Step 4 — Roll back, then overflow. Restore global depth 2 and the original three main buckets with local depths 2,2,1. Remove the temporary buckets and redirect directory aliases exactly as before the first attempt. Attach an overflow page to prefix 00 containing the new Taiyuan record. > > city-overflow.svg > > Figure E6 — Required final city index > > Read it: The main bucket retains the old Taiyuan; overflow holds the new record. > > Key takeaway: Rollback restores the original directory, not the deepest failed state. > > Check: the initial six records plus one new record give seven records: three in bucket 00, one in its overflow, one in 01, and two in prefix 1. The final directory has four pointers to three main buckets. This reproduces PDF p. 40 without treating the duplicate city name as a typo. D1 — Find the routing error Supplementary error diagnosis · Difficulty: ★★☆ A student uses $h(x)=x\bmod8$ but writes $h(9)=1$ and follows directory prefix 1 at global depth 1. They then claim every physical bucket doubles when the directory doubles. Correct both errors. > [!tip]- Hint > The hash representation has a fixed width; pointers can alias a bucket. > [!success]- Solution > Write $h(9)=001_2$. Its first bit is 0, so the correct route is prefix 0. Directory doubling creates twice as many pointer entries, initially copying routes. Existing physical buckets and local depths do not double. Only an actual split creates one additional main bucket and increases the two resulting local depths by one. E2 — Merge buddies, then assess query type Supplementary transfer problem · Difficulty: ★★☆ Start from C1's final index. Delete 13. Decide whether buckets 10 and 11 can merge and whether the directory can shrink. Then explain why this index does not provide an ordered range traversal. > [!tip]- Hint > Check local depths, common prefix, combined occupancy, and all directory pairs. > [!success]- Solution > After deletion, 10 holds [4,5] and 11 holds [7]. They are buddies of local depth 2, share prefix 1, and their three entries fit one bucket. Merge them into local-depth-1 prefix 1, then redirect both aliases. Prefix 0 already covers 00,01; every adjacent directory pair now aliases one bucket. Shrink global depth from 2 to 1. Final buckets are 0:[9], 1:[4,5,7]. > > Numerical order is not directory order: 9 precedes bucket entries 4,5,7 in the directory. A B+ tree's ordered leaves support range traversal; this hash organisation would generally need to examine multiple buckets and filter actual keys.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Different predicates need different structures. LSM and buffer trees batch updates; bitmap indexes compute exact sets; Bloom filters cheaply reject definite non-members but may return false positives; k-d trees, quadtrees and R-trees prune spatial regions; temporal indexes locate versions by valid interval. The right question is not “which index is fastest?” but “which mechanism preserves the predicate and workload we need?” After study, you should be able to select a mechanism, trace its intermediate state, distinguish exact results from candidates, and explain its trade-offs without turning vendor examples into universal behaviour.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: > [!note] LSM tree > Plain-language meaning: accumulate newer entries in memory and merge sorted batches into larger disk levels. > > Why it matters: converts scattered writes into batched sequential work but adds merges and multi-level reads. > > Source: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 4–6. > [!note] Bitmap index > Plain-language meaning: one aligned bit vector represents which record positions have a value. > > Why it matters: Boolean operations return exact candidate positions quickly for suitable low-cardinality attributes. > > Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 8–10. > [!note] Bloom filter > Plain-language meaning: a compact probabilistic membership filter with no false negatives under its model, but possible false positives. > > Why it matters: it can avoid expensive lookups when any required bit is zero. > > Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 11–12. > [!note] Spatial pruning > Plain-language meaning: partition or bound regions so a query examines only plausible objects. > > Why it matters: a bounding-region hit may still need an exact geometry predicate. > > Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 13–20. > [!note] Temporal interval > Plain-language meaning: a version is valid over a time interval, possibly with an open end. > > Why it matters: current and historical lookups may require different access paths. > > Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 21–22.

entries.text: Recall B+ tree ordered access, hash equality access, Boolean AND/OR and coordinate pairs. > [!question] Prerequisite check > What is the bitwise AND of 101010 and 110011? > [!success]- Check your answer > 100010: a position is 1 only when both input bits are 1. > > Source principle: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 8–10.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: A campus system receives frequent asset updates and supports four queries: 1. ingest updates without scattered one-record disk writes; 2. return records that are both sensor and active; 3. reject most absent IDs before searching a disk structure; 4. find map objects inside a rectangle and the version valid at time 5. No single structure is automatically best. Match each predicate to a mechanism and state what extra work or uncertainty remains.

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: A decision map flowchart TD Q{"What must the query/update do?"} Q -->|"batch writes"| L["LSM or buffer tree"] Q -->|"exact Boolean categories"| B["bitmap"] Q -->|"cheap membership rejection"| F["Bloom filter"] Q -->|"spatial range/overlap"| S["k-d / quadtree / R-tree"] Q -->|"valid-at time"| T["temporal interval index"] Figure 1 — Choose by predicate and workload Read it: start with the required operation, not a favourite data structure. Key takeaway: each branch changes the meaning of a “match” and the work still required. Provenance: teaching synthesis from Lecture3b, PDF pp. 2–22. LSM trees and buffer trees An LSM tree keeps newer ordered entries in memory ($L_0$) and merges batches into larger disk levels. With growth factor $k$, the simplified threshold relation is $T_{i+1}=kT_i$. If $T_0=100$ and $k=4$, then $T_1=400$ and $T_2=1600$ entries. Merging scans ordered inputs and produces ordered output. This reduces scattered insert work but rewrites older entries, and a lookup may search several levels. A deletion tombstone must remain until older relevant versions can no longer reappear. A buffer tree retains a search tree but stores pending updates in internal buffers. When a buffer fills, it partitions updates by child range and pushes batches downward. Queries must account for relevant buffered updates. | Structure | Batches where? | Read consequence | |---|---|---| | LSM | across memory/disk sorted levels | search/reconcile relevant levels | | buffer tree | inside internal search-tree nodes | inspect path plus pending updates | Bitmap indexes are exact set algebra All bitmaps share the same record-position order. For source bitmaps m=11010 and L1=10010, the conjunction is: 11010 & 10010 = 10010 Positions with 1 satisfy both predicates. Bitmap space grows with record count × distinct indexed values, so very high cardinality and frequent position-changing updates can weaken the basic design. Bloom filters answer “definitely not” or “possibly” Insertion sets every bit selected by the element's hash functions. Query recomputes those positions: - any zero → definitely absent; - all ones → possibly present; verify in the real structure. False positives occur when other inserted elements set all queried bits. Under the lecture's idealised approximation, after $n$ inserted values, $k$ hashes and $m$ bits: $$p\approx\left(1-e^{-kn/m}\right)^k.$$ The lecture's 10% and 1% are rounded illustrations; the reference notes derive approximately 9.52% and 0.819% under their stated model. A Bloom filter does not itself return the record and ordinarily does not support deletion without an extended design. Spatial structures prune different shapes | Structure | Partition/bound | Natural lesson | |---|---|---| | k-d tree | alternating coordinate splits | point/range pruning by axis | | quadtree | recursively equal spatial quadrants | adapts resolution by subdividing occupied regions | | R-tree | bounding rectangles over objects/groups | handles rectangles/polygons and overlap; verify exact geometry | A bounding rectangle can overlap a query even when the contained object's exact shape does not. Spatial indexes produce candidates; the final predicate may still reject false candidates. Temporal indexing The lecture separates current open-ended entries from historical closed intervals. Tutor examples use half-open intervals [start,end) because the source does not fully define endpoint inclusion. Under that declared convention, [1,5) is valid at 4 but not 5, while [5,∞) begins at 5. > [!question] Explain it yourself > Why is a Bloom “possibly present” result different from a bitmap AND result? > [!success]- Check your explanation > Bloom bits can be shared by unrelated elements, so all-one is only a candidate. Aligned bitmap AND exactly represents the indexed record positions. > > Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 8–12.

entries.title: Worked example — solve the campus questions
entries.text: 1. Writes: use an LSM or buffer tree to batch propagation. LSM inherits merge and multi-level lookup work; a buffer tree inherits pending-update visibility along the path. 2. Categories: sensor=101010 AND active=110011 gives 100010, so record positions 0 and 4 match when the leftmost bit is position 0. 3. Absent-ID rejection: use a Bloom filter. A zero bit proves absence; all ones require the real lookup. 4. Map rectangle: use k-d/quadtree for point partitioning or an R-tree for bounded objects; always test the exact spatial predicate after pruning. 5. Time 5: under the explicit half-open convention, the old [1,5) version is excluded and the new [5,∞) version is valid.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: The problem is solved by composing structures, not selecting one winner. Each mechanism answers a different predicate and carries a different residual cost: merges, buffered updates, bitmap maintenance, Bloom verification, exact geometry testing or interval-boundary handling.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source | |---|---|---|---| | LSM level | buffer-tree node buffer | sorted version level versus pending updates attached to a search-tree node | Lecture3b, pp. 4–7 | | bitmap | Bloom filter | exact aligned set representation versus probabilistic membership filter | Lecture3b, pp. 8–12 | | false positive | false negative | candidate returned for absent item versus missed present item; standard Bloom model permits only the former | Lecture3b, pp. 11–12 | | k-d tree | quadtree | data/axis split versus recursive equal-region subdivision | Lecture3b, pp. 13–17 | | R-tree bound | exact geometry | pruning rectangle versus final object predicate | Lecture3b, pp. 18–20 |

entries.title: 5-Minute Review
entries.text: - batch writes with LSM levels or node buffers; - bitmaps compute exact aligned sets; - Bloom zero means absent, all-one means verify; - spatial indexes prune regions but may return candidates; - k-d, quadtree and R-tree encode different spatial organisation; - temporal answers depend on interval semantics; - choose by predicate, update pattern and remaining work.
