entries.title: Advanced indexing
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises · Lab Advanced indexing Opening case — choose an index for each question Synthetic teaching case. A campus service stores a rapidly growing stream of asset updates, point locations, category flags, and time-stamped versions. It needs more than one access pattern. All data below are teaching inputs; no commercial DBMS is assumed. Given information - The ingestion path can hold 100 entries in its memory tree. For a simplified LSM design, disk-level size thresholds grow by factor $k=4$. - Six current records, numbered 0 through 5, have category bitmaps sensor = 101010 and active = 110011, with the leftmost bit representing record 0. - A tiny Bloom filter has 12 initially zero bits, inserted set $S=\{2,5\}$, and functions $h_1(x)=x\bmod12$, $h_2(x)=(5x+1)\bmod12$. It is deliberately small enough to inspect by hand. - Locations are A=(1,1), B=(2,6), C=(4,3), D=(6,7), E=(7,2), F=(9,5), in arbitrary map units. A range request asks for $3\le x\le8$ and $1\le y\le6$. - Asset 42 has historical version “old” valid on $[1,5)$ and current version “new” valid on $[5,\infty)$. Times are synthetic integer time units; the intervals are ==half-open==. Questions 1. Explain how LSM batching reduces scattered writes, calculate the L1 and L2 thresholds, and compare a buffer tree. What work does a query inherit? 2. Which records are both sensors and active? Distinguish this exact result from Bloom queries for 8 and 14. 3. Which locations match the rectangle? Explain how a k-d tree, quadtree, and R-tree can narrow candidates, and why a bounding-box match may still need an exact geometry check. 4. Which version of asset 42 is valid at times 4 and 5? Explain why a temporal lookup may need both current and historical indexes. Success criteria: select a mechanism from the predicate and update workload; calculate intermediate states; separate exact answers from candidates; preserve the time-boundary convention; state limitations rather than inventing benchmark numbers. | Case question | Concepts needed | |---|---| | Write cost | LSM levels, merge work, tombstones, buffered propagation | | Categories and membership | Bitmaps, Boolean operations, Bloom bits and false positives | | Location | Space partitioning, bounding regions, recursive pruning | | Valid version | Intervals, open-ended records, two-index lookup | Prerequisites: B+ tree maintenance, hashing, Boolean AND/OR/NOT, and reading coordinates. Source scope is Lecture 3b, PDF pp. 2–22; p. 23 is a reading reference. This is a chapter of mechanisms and trade-offs, not vendor configuration advice. Why random writes motivate batching When incoming keys target different B+ tree leaves, each insertion can require a different leaf-page update, even if internal levels are cached. The slide's magnetic-disk insertion-rate illustration and flash-page overwrite illustration are simplified cost arguments, not observations from this lab.[^writes] The opportunity is to accumulate several logical updates and move them together. This trades some immediate write work for later merge or propagation work. It does not make maintenance disappear. LSM trees — merge sorted batches across levels Intuition and definition A log-structured merge tree (LSM tree) maintains newer entries in a memory structure and larger sorted structures on disk. In the course model these are called $L_0,L_1,L_2,\ldots$. The memory tree is $L_0$; when full, it is merged into $L_1$, and excessive size at $L_1$ triggers a merge into $L_2$.[^lsm] lsm-levels.svg Figure 1 — LSM levels Read it: Read downward as batches move from memory into larger disk structures. Key takeaway: Write batching moves work into merging and multi-level queries; source pp. 4–6. Mechanism and worked example 1. Insert records into the ordered memory tree. 2. When its threshold is reached, scan its sorted entries together with the relevant sorted disk entries and produce a new ordered disk structure. The source describes bottom-up construction of a B+ tree while merging. 3. If that disk level exceeds its threshold, propagate the merge to the next level. 4. A query searches every relevant structure and reconciles newer entries with older ones; a match in one level is not automatically the entire current answer. Let $T_i$ be the capacity threshold in entries for level $i$ and $k$ the dimensionless growth factor. The source relation $T_{i+1}=kT_i$ gives, for synthetic $T_0=100,k=4$, $T_1=400$ and $T_2=1600$ entries. These are thresholds, not a claim that every level is simultaneously full or that one insertion writes 1600 records. Synthetic merge: an old sorted level [2,5,9] and incoming sorted batch [1,7] can be merged by repeatedly taking the smaller front entry: 1,2,5,7,9. The scans proceed sequentially. Yet old keys 2,5,9 are copied again: reduced scattered access comes with repeated data movement. Deletion, updates, and limits The source handles deletion with a special delete entry, commonly called a ==tombstone==. Lookups suppress an older record when its matching deletion is found; updates can be represented by deleting an old value and inserting a new one. During a suitable merge, the matched old record and deletion can be removed.[^lsm] Why “suitable” matters — synthetic counterexample: L2 contains A=old, and L0 contains delete A. Removing the tombstone while compacting only L0 and L1 would leave the old L2 record visible again. Safe removal must account for older relevant copies and visibility requirements. This is a correctness limitation of the source's simplified pair-removal description, not a newly confirmed DBMS rule. | Benefit in the source model | Work or limitation that remains | |---|---| | Large sequential merge operations | Existing entries can be rewritten repeatedly | | Fuller output leaves | Merges still consume space and I/O | | Lower per-insert scattered-write demand | A query may search multiple trees | | Batched flash writes | Actual erases and latency depend on the implementation | The stepped-merge variant keeps multiple trees per level, reducing how frequently all entries are merged but increasing the number of candidate trees for a query. Bloom filters can reject many irrelevant trees before an expensive lookup. The lecture gives technology names as examples; those names do not establish engine versions or a uniform storage format across all products.[^lsm] > [!question] Check your understanding > Why can fast ingestion coexist with expensive absent-key queries? Count the structures a negative lookup may otherwise need to inspect. Buffer trees — keep the search tree, delay downward movement An internal-node buffer stores pending insertions. New entries enter the root buffer; when it is full, partition its entries by child key range and move groups downward. Repeating that process eventually updates leaves. Many entries can share the cost of one downward transfer.[^buffer] buffer-tree.svg Figure 2 — Buffered propagation Read it: Group inserts by whether their keys are below or above 50. Key takeaway: Pending updates must remain visible to queries; synthetic example of p. 7. Worked example: with root separator 50 and buffered inserts 12 and 73, send 12 toward the left range and 73 toward the right. If another 80 buffered entries target the right child, they can be moved as a batch instead of issuing unrelated one-entry transfers. No numerical I/O saving is asserted without specifying page sizes, occupancies, caching, and the flush policy. Queries still follow tree ranges, but they must account for relevant pending updates in buffers; reaching an unchanged leaf while ignoring newer buffered inserts would be incorrect. Compared with the source's LSM model, a buffer tree keeps a clearer tree search path but may perform more random I/O. The source mentions applying buffering to other index families, including GiST; this is not a claim that every deployed GiST uses this exact update mechanism. Bitmap indexes — exact sets of record positions A bitmap is an array of bits. With $r$ records and an attribute value $v$, define bit $b_v[j]=1$ exactly when record number $j$ has value $v$, otherwise 0. A basic bitmap index keeps one bitmap per distinct attribute value. All bitmaps must use the same record-number order.[^bitmap] Boolean operations as set operations AND intersects predicates, OR forms their union, and NOT complements within the valid record universe. Counting set bits counts matching records without fetching each full tuple. To return the tuples, use the set-bit positions as record identifiers. bitmap-and.svg Figure 3 — Original bitmap query Read it: Align record positions and AND the two source bitmaps. Key takeaway: Only record 0 qualifies; source pp. 9–10. The original source data on PDF p. 9 is: | Record | ID | gender | income_level | |---:|---:|---|---| | 0 | 76766 | m | L1 | | 1 | 22222 | f | L2 | | 2 | 12121 | f | L1 | | 3 | 15151 | m | L4 | | 4 | 58583 | f | L3 | Thus m = 10010, f = 01101, L1 = 10100, L2 = 01000, L3 = 00001, L4 = 00010, L5 = 00000. The source's query m AND L1 gives 10000, selecting record 0, ID 76766. The column name and values are retained as original data. Space model and limitations For $d$ distinct values and $r$ records, an uncompressed one-bitmap-per-value design needs $dr$ bits, or $dr/8$ bytes if packed together without padding. For $d=5,r=1000$, this is 5000 bits = 625 bytes. If each bitmap is separately byte-aligned, use $d\lceil r/8\rceil$ instead. Headers, compression, and versioning are excluded from this academic model. Low cardinality makes the basic representation attractive; with nearly one distinct value per row, its uncompressed cost approaches $r^2$ bits. Changing record numbering requires maintaining bit alignment. The source emphasises compound conditions; a single-value bitmap can still answer a predicate, so “not particularly useful” is a workload judgement, not a logical inability. > [!warning] Complement needs a universe > With six records, NOT must flip exactly six valid positions. A programming-language integer complement may include extra high bits. Use the valid-record mask. NULLs and deleted rows also need explicit semantics in a real database; this chapter's examples have neither. Bloom filters — cheap rejection with possible false positives A Bloom filter is a probabilistic membership structure. It stores a single bit array, not one bitmap per value or one bit per record. With $m$ bits and $k$ hash functions, insert a value by setting all $k$ indexed bits to 1. To query, inspect the same positions: any zero proves absence; all ones mean possibly present, requiring an exact check if correctness needs certainty.[^bloom] bloom-bits.svg Figure 4 — Membership evidence in bits Read it: Query 8 sees a zero; query 14 shares already-set positions. Key takeaway: A Bloom positive needs verification; synthetic example. Worked construction: with $S=\{2,5\}$ and the opening functions, value 2 sets positions 2 and 11; value 5 sets positions 5 and 2. The set bits are therefore {2,5,11}. Query 8 checks {8,5} and sees zero at 8: absent. Query 14 checks {2,11} and sees two ones, even though 14 was not inserted: a ==false positive==. Why no false negatives in this model: insertion sets every position a future lookup for that same value will inspect; subsequent insertions only set bits. This depends on consistent hashing and on not clearing bits unsafely. Clearing bit 2 when deleting 5 would damage the evidence for still-present value 2. Ordinary Bloom filters therefore do not support arbitrary deletion by clearing those bits. Interpreting the lecture's probability figures Let $n$ be inserted elements, $m$ bits, and $k$ hashes per element. Under uniform independent hash placements, the probability a particular bit remains zero after $kn$ placements is $(1-1/m)^{kn}$. Approximating queried bit occupancies as independent gives: $$p_{FP}\approx\left(1-(1-1/m)^{kn}\right)^k\approx\left(1-e^{-kn/m}\right)^k.$$ This is a teaching derivation clarifying the slide estimates, not a measured guarantee. The second approximation uses the large-$m$ exponential limit. All counts and the probability are dimensionless; the storage amount $m$ is measured in bits. For the lecture's $m=10n$ and one hash, $p_{FP}\approx1-e^{-0.1}\approx0.0952$, roughly 10%. With seven hashes, $p_{FP}\approx(1-e^{-0.7})^7\approx0.00819$, roughly 0.82%, which explains the slide's rounded “1%”. For 1000 absent queries, an expected count near 8.2 is not a promise that exactly eight will be false positives. The tiny demonstration functions above are deliberately correlated and do not justify applying that independence-based estimate to the lab. Spatial indexing — prune regions, then test the predicate Spatial records may describe points, lines, polygons, or raster data. Predicates include containment and overlap; spatial and ordinary attribute conditions may be combined. A range query asks for objects within or intersecting a region, a nearest-neighbour query asks for the closest qualifying objects, and a spatial join pairs records by a spatial relationship.[^spatial] The central idea is to avoid testing every object by excluding whole regions that cannot match. The region structure differs among the three source index families. K-d trees A k-d tree recursively splits space into two parts, cycling through dimensions: x, then y in two dimensions, then x again. The source seeks roughly balanced point counts and stops splitting when a leaf has sufficiently few points. Its k-d-B extension permits multiple children per internal node.[^kd] For an x split at $x_i$, left contains $x<x_i$ and right $x\ge x_i$. A rectangular query entirely to one side needs only that child; a query spanning the split may need both. At leaves, test the actual coordinates. kd-range.svg Figure 5 — K-d range search Read it: Follow x=5, then y=4; the amber query spans both boundaries. Key takeaway: Exact tests return C,E; synthetic coordinates. Worked trace: the figure uses synthetic root split x=5 and next splits y=4. The query x in [3,8] spans x=5, so search both root children. Its y interval [1,6] spans y=4, so visit both children at that next level where present. Exact testing accepts C=(4,3) and E=(7,2), and rejects A,B,D,F. A broad query can intersect many partitions: balance alone does not mean one-path range search. Quadtrees Each quadtree node represents a rectangular region. A non-leaf divides that region into four equal-sized quadrants. Recursively split a crowded quadrant until it meets the chosen capacity; empty leaves are valid. This subdivision is geometric, not a median split chosen to balance point counts.[^quad] quadtree.svg Figure 6 — Equal geometric subdivision Read it: First split the full region into four, then split crowded SW and NE regions. Key takeaway: Partitioning follows geometric midpoints rather than point medians; synthetic example. For the same six points in [0,10]×[0,10] and capacity one, split the root at x=5,y=5. SW contains A,C and NE contains D,F, so split those two regions again at their own midpoints. NW contains B; SE contains E. All resulting occupied leaves contain one point. Treat split-boundary points as belonging to the right/top side, an explicit teaching convention. Identical or extremely close points can require a stopping/depth rule beyond a naive “split until one point” policy. R-trees An R-tree groups objects using minimum bounding rectangles. Each internal entry associates a child with a rectangle enclosing all objects beneath it. Unlike k-d/quadtree partitions, different children's bounding rectangles can overlap, so an intersection query may follow multiple paths. At each level recurse into every child whose rectangle intersects the query; inspect leaf candidates against the required predicate.[^rtree] rtree-filter.svg Figure 7 — Bounding region versus exact geometry Read it: The amber query misses the triangle even though it lies inside the triangle bounding rectangle. Key takeaway: Bounding-box intersection yields a candidate; the drawing is schematic, not the numerical coordinate example. Synthetic exact-test example: a right triangle with vertices (0,0),(4,0),(0,4) has bounding box [0,4]×[0,4]. Query rectangle [3,4]×[3,4] intersects the box, but every point of that rectangle has x+y≥6, while points in the triangle satisfy x+y≤4. It is a false candidate for triangle intersection. Bounding boxes safely reject disjoint candidates; they need not prove exact polygon overlap. The source's figure on p. 19 groups A,B,C under BB1, D,E,F under BB2, and G,H,I under BB3. Its overlapping bounding regions explain why the traversal on p. 20 can visit several children. In the worst case it may visit much of the tree. The lecture mentions R+ and R* variants and warns that usefulness declines at high dimension; their algorithms are not supplied and are not invented here. Temporal indexes — index valid intervals, including open ends Temporal data associate a record version with a validity interval. The source uses start and end, with a large end date such as 9999-12-31 for a currently valid tuple. A point-in-time query must select every version whose interval contains that time.[^temporal] Explicit teaching convention: use $[s,e)$, meaning $s\le t<e$. The slides do not fully specify endpoint inclusion. Half-open intervals avoid a double match when one version ends exactly as the next starts. If an assessment specifies another convention, use it and change the inequalities accordingly. The source proposes treating attribute $a$ as one spatial dimension and time as another. Historical records have finite time spans; current records with huge end values produce long rectangles, which can weaken pruning. Separate them: 1. Index current tuples by (a,start) in a B+ tree; for $a=v$ at time $t$, select current versions with start ≤ t. 2. Index finite historical intervals with a spatial structure such as an R-tree; test both attribute and interval membership. 3. Search both indexes and combine qualifying versions. Current membership alone does not answer every historical query. temporal-two-indexes.svg Figure 8 — Two temporal branches Read it: Check current start times and historical finite intervals, then combine results. Key takeaway: Half-open endpoint inequalities are the declared teaching convention; source structure p. 22. Source example on p. 21: CS-201 is “Intro. to C” from 1985-01-01 to 1990-01-01; “Intro. to Java” from 1990-01-01 to 2010-01-01; “Intro. to Python” from 2010-01-01 to 9999-12-31. Under the declared half-open convention, 1990-01-01 selects Java rather than both C and Java. When a current version ends, maintaining the two-index design requires moving or representing it in the historical index and adding the new current version consistently. Solve the opening case 1 — Choose a write strategy and calculate thresholds For sustained scattered inserts, LSM batching is a defensible choice: merge sorted memory batches into progressively larger structures. $T_1=4\times100=400$ entries; $T_2=4\times400=1600$. Queries inherit searches across relevant levels and version/deletion reconciliation. A buffer tree instead batches updates along the existing tree routes; it must inspect pending buffer contents correctly and may retain more random I/O. The inputs do not support a measured throughput comparison. 2 — Compute exact bitmap results and Bloom candidates Align record positions 0–5: | Operation | Result | |---|---| | sensor AND active | 101010 AND 110011 = 100010 | | Set positions | 0 and 4 | For Bloom insertion, 2 sets {2,11} and 5 sets {5,2}; only {2,5,11} are one. Query 8 reaches zero bit 8, proving absence. Query 14 sees both positions set and becomes a candidate; exact comparison with {2,5} rejects it. Bitmap membership is exact in the stated record universe; the Bloom positive is not. 3 — Answer the spatial query Test the same six coordinates against both inclusive ranges. C has 3≤4≤8 and 1≤3≤6; E has 3≤7≤8 and 1≤2≤6, so the result is C,E. A and B fail x≥3; D fails y≤6; F fails x≤8. K-d and quadtree partitions can exclude disjoint regions; an R-tree can exclude disjoint bounding rectangles. It may retain false geometry candidates, so apply the exact predicate after filtering. 4 — Answer the temporal query At t=4, historical old satisfies 1≤4<5. Current new fails start≤4 because its start is 5. At t=5, old fails 5<5, while new satisfies 5≤5<∞. Results are respectively old and new, with no duplicate boundary match. Both index branches are needed to establish the answers over time. All four opening questions now meet their success criteria. Exam-style answer and reusable method > [!summary] Match the mechanism to the source of work > LSM and buffer trees batch maintenance; bitmap indexes combine exact sets of aligned record positions; Bloom filters reject definite nonmembers; spatial indexes prune by regions; temporal indexing combines attribute and interval constraints. Every choice shifts work somewhere: merges, buffer inspection, bit maintenance, false-positive checks, multiple spatial paths, or two temporal branches. For an unfamiliar workload, identify the predicate first, then update frequency and data distribution. Define the representation and boundary conventions; calculate one concrete trace; distinguish a candidate from a result; and state where the method can degrade. Do not choose an index only from its name. Misconceptions and quick review | Mistake | Repair | |---|---| | Sequential merges mean no rewrite cost | Existing entries can be copied across repeated merges | | A flushed tombstone can always be dropped | An older unmerged version might become visible again | | Bitmap bit 7 is a hash bucket | A bitmap index position is a record number; Bloom positions are hashes | | Bloom “present” is proof | It is a candidate requiring exact membership checking | | A spatial query follows exactly one path | Overlapping regions and split-crossing queries can require several paths | | A current index answers all past-time queries | Historical finite intervals must also be searched | Redraw the eight figures from their mechanisms, recompute the bitmap result, produce a Bloom false positive, and justify the temporal endpoint inequality. Use the lab to compare candidate filtering with exhaustive exact results; technical checks do not establish study mastery. [^writes]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF p. 3. The source's rate and page-overwrite examples are illustrative, not measured here. [^lsm]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 4–6. Synthetic merges, threshold calculations, and tombstone counterexample provide pedagogical explanation of the source model. [^buffer]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF p. 7. Buffered-query correctness is explained as a consequence of pending updates, not a confirmed vendor implementation. [^bitmap]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 8–10. The five-record table and bitmap calculation are original; space arithmetic is a labelled academic model. [^bloom]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 11–12. Probability derivation is supplementary mathematical explanation of the rounded source values. [^spatial]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 13–14. [^kd]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 15–16. [^quad]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF p. 17. [^rtree]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 18–20. The synthetic triangle demonstrates the distinction between object geometry and its bounding rectangle. [^temporal]: Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF pp. 21–22. Half-open endpoints are a declared teaching assumption; the current/historical split is source-derived.

entries.title: Advanced-indexing exercises
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises · Lab Advanced-indexing exercises Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf supplies mechanisms and worked examples rather than a numbered exercise sheet. B1 and B2 reproduce its original worked data; other questions are labelled supplementary practice. Each answer follows its question in a collapsed callout. Bit strings are always read left to right as ascending record numbers. A1 — Match the question to the structure Supplementary retrieval · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Choose a suitable family for (a) batched scattered inserts, (b) several low-cardinality category predicates, (c) rejection of irrelevant LSM trees, (d) rectangle intersection, and (e) point-in-time versions. Give one limitation for each. > [!tip]- Hint > Match the kind of work: writes, exact sets, approximate membership, geometry, time. > [!success]- Solution > (a) LSM or buffer tree: merging or buffered propagation still costs work. (b) Bitmap index: requires aligned record positions and maintained bits. (c) Bloom filter: positive answers can be false positives. (d) R-tree: overlapping bounding boxes can require multiple paths and exact geometry checks. (e) Temporal index combining current and historical records: both branches may need searching and endpoint semantics must be specified. The best choice also depends on updates and distribution; no single family dominates every workload. B1 — Reconstruct the lecture bitmaps and original AND query Original course worked example · PDF pp. 9–10 · Difficulty: ★☆☆ | Record number | ID | gender | income_level | |---:|---:|---|---| | 0 | 76766 | m | L1 | | 1 | 22222 | f | L2 | | 2 | 12121 | f | L1 | | 3 | 15151 | m | L4 | | 4 | 58583 | f | L3 | Reconstruct the supplied bitmaps for m, f, and L1–L5. Reproduce the original query “males with income level L1” and give its record number, ID, and count. The wording and source field values are retained. > [!tip]- Hint > For each value, mark the rows containing it. AND bits at the same positions. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Encode. m=10010, f=01101; L1=10100, L2=01000, L3=00001, L4=00010, L5=00000. L5 is empty because none of the five records has that level. > > Step 2 — Intersect. 10010 AND 10100 = 10000. > > Step 3 — Interpret. Only ==record 0== matches: ID 76766, and the count is 1. Bits denote record numbers, not the numeric digits of the IDs. > > bitmap-and.svg > > Figure E1 — Original bitmap intersection > > Read it: Match each source row to the bit directly above its position. > > Key takeaway: Counting the one set bit is enough for the count; returning the tuple uses record 0. B2 — Read the original temporal course table Source-derived practice using original worked data · PDF pp. 21–22 · Difficulty: ★★☆ | course_id | title | dept_name | credits | start | end | |---|---|---|---:|---|---| | BIO-101 | Intro. to Biology | Biology | 4 | 1985-01-01 | 9999-12-31 | | CS-201 | Intro. to C | Comp. Sci. | 4 | 1985-01-01 | 1990-01-01 | | CS-201 | Intro. to Java | Comp. Sci. | 4 | 1990-01-01 | 2010-01-01 | | CS-201 | Intro. to Python | Comp. Sci. | 4 | 2010-01-01 | 9999-12-31 | Use the explicit teaching assumption ==[start,end)==. The source presents these records but does not specify these exact query dates or full endpoint semantics; the following questions are pedagogical applications: 1. Which CS-201 version is valid on 1989-06-01, 1990-01-01, and 2010-01-01? 2. Which records belong in the source's current-tuple index and which in its finite-interval historical index? 3. Why is searching only the current index insufficient for 1989-06-01? > [!tip]- Hint > The end is excluded. Current records have the large sentinel end date. > [!success]- Solution > 1 — Point-in-time results. 1989-06-01 lies within [1985-01-01,1990-01-01), so return Intro. to C. At 1990-01-01, C has ended and Intro. to Java begins. At 2010-01-01, Java has ended and Intro. to Python begins. Each query includes the course_id=CS-201 predicate, so BIO-101 is not returned. > > 2 — Index assignment. Current index: BIO-101 Biology and CS-201 Python, both with sentinel 9999-12-31. Historical index: CS-201 C and Java, whose end dates are finite historical boundaries. The current index can use (course_id,start); historical rectangles represent the key dimension and time interval. > > 3 — Why both branches matter. At 1989-06-01 the currently stored Python version has a later start, so it does not qualify; the matching C version is historical. A current-only lookup would incorrectly return no version. Endpoint inclusion remains a declared assumption; an instructor-specified convention takes precedence. C1 — LSM thresholds, merge work, and tombstones Supplementary guided calculation · Difficulty: ★★☆ An LSM memory level has threshold 100 entries and each subsequent level threshold is four times the preceding one. Find L1, L2, and L3 thresholds. Merge sorted incoming [1,7] with old [2,5,9]. Finally, explain the error in discarding delete A from L0 while A=old survives in an unmerged L2. > [!tip]- Hint > Thresholds multiply; merging compares front entries; a tombstone protects against older versions. > [!success]- Solution > Thresholds: L1=$4\times100=400$ entries; L2=$4\times400=1600$; L3=$4\times1600=6400$. These are capacities, not simultaneous measured occupancies. > > Merge: choose 1 before 2, then 2 before 7, then 5 before 7, then 7 before 9; append 9. Output is [1,2,5,7,9]. Existing entries 2,5,9 are copied, so sequential I/O does not imply zero rewrite work. > > Tombstone: discarding delete A without accounting for the older L2 version can resurrect A=old on a later lookup. Retain deletion evidence until relevant older versions can safely be suppressed or removed. This counterexample explains the limitation of the lecture's simplified “drop matching pairs” merge description. C2 — A Bloom filter you can draw by hand Supplementary guided construction · Difficulty: ★★☆ Start with 12 zero bits, $h_1(x)=x\bmod12$, and $h_2(x)=(5x+1)\bmod12$. Insert 2 and 5. Query 2,8,14. Then show why clearing the bits for 5 is an unsafe deletion procedure. > [!tip]- Hint > Different values can reuse a bit. Keep the exact set {2,5} separate from the filter answer. > [!success]- Solution > Insert 2: positions 2 and $(5\times2+1)\bmod12=11$. Insert 5: positions 5 and $26\bmod12=2$. Set bits are {2,5,11}. > > Query 2: positions {2,11}, both set; possibly present, and exact checking confirms membership. Query 8: positions {8,5}; bit 8 is zero, so definitely absent. Query 14: positions {2,11}; both set, but 14 is absent from {2,5}, so this is a false positive. > > To delete 5 by clearing its bits, the naive procedure clears both 5 and 2. But 2 still needs bit 2; its next query sees a zero and becomes a false negative. Ordinary Bloom-filter deletion cannot simply clear shared bits. > > bloom-bits.svg > > Figure E2 — Tiny Bloom state > > Read it: Separate exact membership from the two queried bit positions. > > Key takeaway: The no-false-negative property depends on preserving bits needed by all inserted elements. C3 — Interpret the rounded false-positive estimates Supplementary mathematical clarification of PDF p. 12 · Difficulty: ★★☆ Under the uniform independent-placement model, a Bloom filter has $m=10n$ bits. Estimate false-positive probability for $k=1$ and $k=7$ using $(1-e^{-kn/m})^k$. Interpret the expected number of positives among 1000 absent queries. Why is this not an execution result for C2's tiny filter? > [!tip]- Hint > Substitute n/m=0.1. The bit tests are approximated as independent. > [!success]- Solution > For $k=1$, $1-e^{-0.1}\approx0.0951626$, about 9.52%. Among 1000 absent queries, the model's expected count is about 95.2. For $k=7$, $(1-e^{-0.7})^7\approx0.00819372$, about 0.819%, giving an expected count about 8.19. > > The slide's 10% and 1% figures are rounded scale estimates. An expectation is not an exact observed count. C2 has a very small array and deliberately simple correlated hash functions, so the assumptions behind the estimate do not establish that filter's empirical false-positive rate. Actual finite-domain enumeration is a different measurement. D1 — Trace a spatial range and reject a false candidate Supplementary spatial diagnosis · Difficulty: ★★☆ A=(1,1), B=(2,6), C=(4,3), D=(6,7), E=(7,2), F=(9,5). Find all points in x∈[3,8], y∈[1,6]. With a k-d root split x=5 and next-level splits y=4, explain which branches the query must visit. Separately, does query rectangle [3,4]×[3,4] intersect triangle T with vertices (0,0),(4,0),(0,4), or only its bounding rectangle? > [!tip]- Hint > Check both coordinates. A range can cross a split. For the triangle use x+y≤4. > [!success]- Solution > Point result: C and E meet both ranges. A,B fail the lower x bound, D exceeds y=6, and F exceeds x=8. The query crosses x=5 and y=4, so both relevant sides must be explored at each of those splits; reaching a leaf still requires exact coordinate comparisons. > > Triangle result: T's bounding rectangle is [0,4]×[0,4], so the query intersects it. But query points have x+y≥6, while triangle points satisfy x+y≤4. There is no triangle intersection. A bounding-box filter returns a candidate; exact geometry rejects it. E1 — Compare k-d and quadtree subdivision Supplementary independent construction · Difficulty: ★★☆ Use D1's six points within [0,10]×[0,10]. A quadtree leaf holds at most one point. Assign split-boundary points to the right/top region. Draw the first root split and identify every quadrant that needs another split. Explain how this differs from choosing approximately balanced point-count splits in a k-d tree. > [!tip]- Hint > Root midpoints are (5,5). Count points in each quadrant, including F on y=5. > [!success]- Solution > Root quadrants: SW contains A,C, NW contains B, SE contains E, NE contains D,F. F=(9,5) belongs to NE under the stated boundary convention. Split SW at (2.5,2.5) and NE at (7.5,7.5); each occupied resulting leaf then contains one point, and empty leaves are allowed. > > A quadtree always divides a region into four equal geometric parts. A k-d tree splits into two, cycles dimensions, and may choose cut positions to balance point counts. Equal spatial area does not imply equal numbers of points. > > quadtree.svg > > Figure E3 — Required quadtree refinement > > Read it: SW and NE receive additional midpoint splits. > > Key takeaway: No split is needed for the one-point NW and SE quadrants. E2 — Defend the campus-service design Supplementary exam-style synthesis · Difficulty: ★★★ For the opening case in Notes, give (a) a defensible write-oriented structure and its query cost, (b) exact matching record numbers for sensor=101010 AND active=110011, (c) the roles of Bloom filtering and exact checks, and (d) the versions of asset 42 at t=4 and t=5 when old=[1,5), new=[5,∞). State one assumption that would change the method. > [!tip]- Hint > Choose from predicate semantics. Explain every result, not only the index names. > [!success]- Solution > (a) LSM batching is reasonable for sustained scattered inserts because sorted batches can be merged sequentially; queries must search relevant levels and reconcile versions/tombstones. A buffer tree is an alternative with range-directed batches and pending-buffer checks. > > (b) Position-wise AND gives 100010, selecting records 0 and 4. > > (c) A Bloom zero safely rejects an absent value under correct filter maintenance; all-one tests produce candidates, so exact membership checking is still required. R-tree bounding regions similarly prune, but exact geometry may reject surviving candidates. > > (d) At t=4, 1≤4<5 selects old. At t=5, old fails its strict end test and 5≤5<∞ selects new. Search current and historical branches as needed. > > A change from half-open to closed intervals would make both versions include t=5 unless another rule resolved the overlap. A change to bitmap record numbering would require realigning the bitmaps before AND. A range-heavy workload could favour ordered structures over hashing.

entries.title: Lab — a candidate is not yet an answer
entries.text: Course home · Notes · Exercises · Lab Lab — a candidate is not yet an answer Purpose and scope Compare exact bitmap results with Bloom and spatial candidate filtering, then verify a temporal boundary. The five-row bitmap dataset is from Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf, PDF p. 9; the other datasets are labelled synthetic constructions from this unit. The mechanisms connect to source pp. 10–12 and 15–22. This is a supplementary Python model, not a DBMS implementation or a measurement of an actual R-tree, LSM tree, or disk. Its benefit is that you can compare every filter result with an independent exhaustive predicate evaluation on a small inspectable dataset. Environment and files - Python 3 with its standard library; no third-party packages, database server, network access, or installation is required by the lab script. - filter_lab.py contains the source data, algorithms, and checks. - The recorded execution used Python 3.14.6. This is a lab execution version, not a course-specified version. Open a terminal in this unit's folder, then run: python3 Attachments/filter_lab.py The script prints JSON to standard output. It does not modify the vault or create files. It does not require an online service. Procedure 1. Read the source data and predict the bitmap AND result before execution. Notice that the displayed bit strings put record 0 on the left, while the program stores that record in integer bit 0. 2. Run the script and find bitmap. It builds masks from rows, then compares 98 AND/OR combinations with independent row predicates. A failed assertion stops the run. 3. Read bloom. It inserts {2,5}, probes all integers 0–59, compares candidate results with exact membership, and reports false positives. It also performs a deliberately incorrect bit-clearing deletion in a separate copy to demonstrate how a false negative is introduced. 4. Read spatial. The script groups points A,B,C and D,E,F under their bounding rectangles. It compares filtered answers with a full point scan for 4356 inclusive rectangles with integer endpoints from 0 through 10. This tests candidate completeness for this finite domain; it does not implement a complete R-tree. 5. Read temporal_half_open and inspect how strict end-time comparison changes the result at time 5. Results and interpretation OBSERVED — EXECUTED AND VERIFIED. The unchanged script completed with Python 3.14.6 and printed: | Check | Observed result | Interpretation | |---|---|---| | Original bitmap query | 10000; selected ID [76766] | One exact matching source record | | Bitmap comparison | 98 predicate combinations passed | Mask results agree with row-wise AND/OR predicates | | Bloom set bits | [2,5,11] | Bit positions encode membership evidence | | Query 8 | Candidate false; exact member false | Zero bit correctly rejects it | | Query 14 | Candidate true; exact member false | An actual false positive in this model | | Finite-domain Bloom enumeration | 8 false positives among 58 absent queries; no false negatives for inserted {2,5} | This deliberately simple filter does not have the slide's approximate 1% behaviour | | Naive deletion of 5 | Breaks membership evidence for 2 | Shared-bit clearing creates a false negative | | Spatial query | Candidates A–F; exact matches C,E | Candidate pruning can still retain nonmatching points | | Rectangle comparison | 4356 filtered results equal full scans | No false negatives for the checked finite rectangle set | | Triangle query | Box candidate true; exact intersection false | Bounding-box intersection does not prove polygon intersection | | Time 4 / time 5 | old / new | Half-open intervals avoid a duplicate boundary match | The eight Bloom false positives are 14,17,26,29,38,41,50,53. Their finite-domain fraction is $8/58\approx13.79\%$. This differs from the lecture's estimate because the toy filter's size, load and correlated functions are different; the lecture example assumes 10 bits per element with seven suitable hash functions. The rectangle count can be recomputed: among 11 integer coordinates, inclusive intervals allowing equal endpoints number $11+10+\cdots+1=66$. Independent x/y choices give $66^2=4356$ rectangles. A degenerate interval representing a line or point remains a valid inclusive query in this model. Practice and reflection Lab task 1 — Explain the candidate set Why can both spatial group boxes overlap the query while only C and E satisfy it? > [!tip]- Hint > A bounding rectangle encloses points but also empty space. > [!success]- Solution > The first group's bounding box spans x=1–4, y=1–6, and the second spans x=6–9, y=2–7. Both intersect query x=3–8,y=1–6, so neither group can be rejected. Testing the actual six points removes A,B,D,F. The group test is a conservative filter; exact comparisons finish the answer. Lab task 2 — Design a controlled change Without changing record numbering, change the source query from m AND L1 to f AND L1. Predict the result. Treat this variant as EXPECTED — NOT EXECUTED until you actually run your modified copy. > [!tip]- Hint > Use f=01101 and L1=10100. > [!success]- Solution > 01101 AND 10100 = 00100, selecting record 2, ID 12121. The observed-run table above records the original query only. A modified run should report its own inputs and result rather than inherit the earlier evidence. Lab task 3 — Explain the limits of verification Do 4356 passing rectangle checks prove correctness for every possible geometry, floating-point boundary, and DBMS implementation? > [!tip]- Hint > Describe exactly what was enumerated. > [!success]- Solution > No. The checks cover six fixed synthetic points, two fixed bounding groups, inclusive rectangular predicates, and integer endpoints 0–10. They do not cover arbitrary polygons, numerical robustness, disk layouts, concurrency, index update algorithms, or a specific DBMS. The finite check is strong evidence for this small model and no more. Reuse and cleanup Keep the supplied script as a reproducible baseline. For experimentation, make a separate copy outside the vault or save an explicitly named variant so that the baseline evidence remains meaningful. The baseline script creates no files, so no generated database or cache needs deletion. Study status: untested. The recorded checks verify the material and code, not your personal mastery.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A query becomes easier to reason about when you treat each intermediate result as a relation. Selection keeps qualifying rows; projection keeps named columns; set operations combine compatible relations; product pairs tuples; rename resolves names. Joins and division express common combinations. These operators explain the meaning of a query before you choose how a DBMS executes it. Goal: trace a query from its input relations to its result, explain duplicate removal, and translate “both” or “all” into the right operation. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.2,6–9,26–39.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need to distinguish a row from a column and read simple comparisons. The earlier storage and indexing units explain access paths; this unit explains which tuples the access path must eventually return. Relational algebra uses set semantics: duplicate tuples disappear and tuple order is irrelevant. SQL can use bag semantics, so do not silently assume every SQL query has this duplicate behaviour. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.6–7.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: The bank asks: “Which customers hold an account at every Brooklyn branch?” Why is finding customers at one Brooklyn branch insufficient? Keep this question in mind while learning the operators. This is the source query on Lecture4a, PDF p.39.

entries.title: 1. Describe the relation before changing it
entries.text: A schema names the attributes; an instance is the current set of tuples over that schema. An attribute has a domain of allowed values. The slides introduce atomic values and null as an unknown value; they do not establish the full SQL three-valued logic rules, so the set examples below use ordinary, known values. A superkey uniquely identifies tuples in every valid instance. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: removing any attribute destroys that guarantee. Choose one candidate key as the primary key. A foreign-key constraint links values to a referenced relation. {ID, name} may be a superkey without being a candidate key when {ID} already suffices. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.3–5.

entries.title: 2. Selection keeps rows; projection keeps columns
entries.text: Selection is $\sigma_p(r)=\{t\in r\mid p(t)\}$. Its predicate can compare attributes or constants and combine terms with AND, OR and NOT. It retains the input attributes. The source example contains (a,a,1,7), (a,b,5,7), (b,b,12,3), (b,b,23,10) over (A,B,C,D). Applying $\sigma_{A=B\land D>5}$ keeps the first and fourth tuples: the third has equal A,B but fails the second condition. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.10–11. Projection $\pi_{A_1,\ldots,A_k}(r)$ keeps only the named attributes, then removes duplicate resulting tuples. The source projection from (A,B,C) to (A,C) turns four rows into {(a,1),(b,1),(b,2)} because two input rows map to (a,1). Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.12–13. > [!question]- Try before continuing > Can projection increase the number of tuples in set relational algebra? > [!success]- Check > No. Each input tuple produces one projected tuple, and duplicates can collapse. This is a definition-based consequence of Lecture4a, PDF pp.12–13.

entries.title: 3. Combine compatible sets
entries.text: Union $r\cup s$ keeps tuples present in either input. Difference $r-s$ keeps tuples present in r and absent from s. Intersection $r\cap s$ keeps tuples in both and can be expressed as $r-(r-s)$. These operations require the same arity and compatible attribute domains; align the corresponding attributes. They combine whole tuples, not independently selected cells. Difference is directional: $r-s$ usually differs from $s-r$. For the source r={(a,1),(a,2),(b,1)} and s={(a,2),(b,3)}, union adds (b,3) once; difference is {(a,1),(b,1)}; intersection is {(a,2)}. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.14–17,27–28.

entries.title: 4. Product pairs tuples; rename makes the pairing unambiguous
entries.text: Cartesian product $r\times s$ pairs every tuple of r with every tuple of s, concatenating their attributes. With disjoint attribute names, two input tuples paired with four give eight output tuples. If names overlap, rename or qualify attributes before referring to them. The source then selects matching A=C pairs from the product. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.18–20. Rename $\rho_x(E)$ gives an expression a relation name; its extended form also names the attributes. It is particularly useful when a relation must be compared with another copy of itself. Rename changes identifiers, not the stored values. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.21. flowchart LR R[Input relation r] --> P[Pair every tuple] S[Input relation s] --> P P --> F[Keep matching pairs] F --> C[Keep requested columns] Supplementary visualisation of the composition on Lecture4a, PDF pp.18–24.

entries.title: 5. Natural join matches every common attribute
entries.text: A natural join combines tuples that agree on all common attribute names. The output includes those common attributes once, plus the attributes unique to each input. If schemas are (A,B,C,D) and (E,B,D), agreement is required on both B and D, not just one. The source defines this as a product, a matching selection, and a projection that removes duplicate common columns. A natural join can accidentally constrain an unrelated same-named attribute; inspect the schemas first. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.29–30.

entries.title: 6. Division answers an all-of question
entries.text: Let r have attributes (A,B) and let s list required B values. Then $r\div s$ keeps each candidate A whose pairing with every B in s occurs in r. In the source p.32 example, s={1,2}. Both a and b have pairings with 1 and 2; g and d do not. The answer is {a,b}. Extra pairings do not disqualify a candidate. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.31–33. The basic-operator construction is easiest to read as “candidates minus failures”: $$C=\pi_{R-S}(r),\qquad M=(C\times s)-\pi_{R-S,S}(r)$$ $$r\div s=C-\pi_{R-S}(M).$$ M contains required pairings that are missing. Project their candidate attributes, then remove those candidates. The attribute-reordering projection aligns the subtraction. Candidates are drawn from C; this avoids treating the slide's “largest relation” phrase as an unbounded search over arbitrary values. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.34–35.

entries.title: 7. Read an expression from the inside out
entries.text: For customers with Perryridge loans, first connect borrower and loan by loan_number, select branch_name=Perryridge, and project customer_name. The slides also show filtering the loan input before the product. These expressions preserve the intended answer but can lead to different amounts of intermediate work. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.24. To find the largest account balance without an aggregate operator, rename a second copy as d, find each account whose balance is less than another, project those nonmaximum balances, and subtract them from all balances. This keeps the maximum balance value, including the case where multiple accounts share it. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.25. Assignment names temporary intermediate relations, making a long expression readable. It is not a persistent table update. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.35.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Build customer/branch pairs from depositor joined with account. Separately select the Brooklyn branches and project their branch names. Divide the pairs by that required branch relation, following p.39. Joining to one Brooklyn branch only proves “at least one”; division checks every branch in the required set.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Need | Operation | Check first | | --- | --- | --- | | Qualifying tuples | Selection | Predicate refers to available attributes | | Selected attributes | Projection | Set duplicate removal | | Either / both / only in first | Union / intersection / difference | Arity and domain compatibility | | Every tuple pairing | Product | Names are unambiguous | | Matching shared values | Natural join | All common attribute names | | Every required pairing | Division | Divisor attributes belong to the dividend | Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.8–35. Physical scan/index choices belong to the next unit; these expressions establish logical results.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Explain the six basic operators from memory. Trace the source projection and explain why a row disappears. Distinguish “at both named branches” from “at all branches in a relation”. Then attempt the original query translations in Recall & practice with the notes closed.

entries.title: Sources and scope
entries.text: All 40 PDF pages of Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf were text inspected for this edition; the division formula on p.34 was also inspected visually. The slides recommend textbook chapter 2 on p.40. This edition covers the supplied lecture; it does not claim that the whole textbook chapter has been reviewed. No new past-paper claims or grades are introduced.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: A DBMS parses and translates a query, optimises a plan, then evaluates it. An algebra expression describes the logical result; a physical plan adds implementation choices. Equivalent plans can have different estimated costs. The lecture's simple disk model is $b\,t_T+s\,t_S$, where b is transfers, s is seeks, and the times use the same unit. Source: Lecture4b, PDF pp.4–11.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Use the preceding unit to identify selection and projection. Use storage and indexing to explain what a scan or index access path does. You do not need database credentials to learn the logical pipeline or calculate the supplied cost model.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Two plans return account balances below 2500. One scans the account file; the other uses a balance index. Why can equal results require different work, and what evidence is needed before calling either plan faster? This follows the source example on Lecture4b, PDF p.8.

entries.title: 1. Follow the query through three stages
entries.text: Parsing and translation: check query syntax and verify the referenced relations, then form an internal representation and an algebra expression. Optimisation: consider equivalent expressions and ways of implementing their operations. Evaluation: the execution engine follows the selected plan and returns answers. The optimiser consults statistics; the execution engine accesses data. Source: Lecture4b, PDF pp.4–7,9. flowchart LR Q[Query] --> P[Parse and translate] P --> A[Logical algebra] A --> O[Choose physical plan] S[Catalog statistics] --> O O --> E[Evaluate] D[Data] --> E E --> R[Result] Supplementary rendering of the source pipeline, PDF p.4.

entries.title: 2. Separate logical equivalence from physical strategy
entries.text: The source compares: $$\sigma_{balance<2500}(\pi_{balance}(account))$$ $$\pi_{balance}(\sigma_{balance<2500}(account)).$$ Both keep the same distinct balance values under the lecture's set model. In the first, the predicate still has its required balance attribute after projection. Moving an arbitrary selection past a projection that removes an attribute it needs is invalid. Source: Lecture4b, PDF p.8; Lecture4a, PDF pp.10–13. The same logical expression may use different algorithms. A physical evaluation plan annotates detailed strategy: for example, use an index or scan linearly and discard failing tuples. The existence of an index does not by itself prove that the chosen plan uses it or that it wins for the actual data. Source: Lecture4b, PDF pp.8–9.

entries.title: 3. Estimates depend on the database description
entries.text: The optimiser estimates using catalog information such as tuple counts, tuple sizes and relation block counts. It chooses among equivalent evaluation plans using estimated cost. An estimate is a model of expected work, not an observed runtime measurement. The lecture lists later algorithm and optimisation questions but does not supply their derivations here; join algorithms and advanced plan enumeration remain outside this unit. Source: Lecture4b, PDF p.9.

entries.title: 4. Calculate disk cost without mixing units
entries.text: The lecture lists disk access, CPU and network resources. It ignores CPU in the simplified model and warns that real systems account for it; parallel systems also need network costs. It treats read and write transfer costs equally for simplicity. $$\text{estimated disk time}=b\,t_T+s\,t_S.$$ tT is transfer time per block and tS is time per seek. With the slide's HDD values, tT=0.1 ms and tS=4 ms. Supplementary calculation: 100 transfers and 2 seeks give 100×0.1+2×4=18 ms; 20 transfers and 10 seeks give 20×0.1+10×4=42 ms. Fewer transfers can still have higher cost if seeks increase enough. Source model and constants: Lecture4b, PDF pp.10–11. The slide's SSD values are ranges: seek 20–90 µs and transfer 2–10 µs. They are source examples for 4 KB blocks, not current benchmark guarantees. Convert units before comparing: 1 ms = 1000 µs. Do not compare a value in microseconds with one in milliseconds as if their numbers had the same unit. Source: Lecture4b, PDF p.11.

entries.title: 5. What would turn a claim into evidence?
entries.text: First establish equal logical results. Then distinguish the model's estimated work from the observed execution plan and elapsed time. The supplied JDBC Task 2 measures only executeQuery; its elapsed interval is not identical to this slide's abstract disk model. Consult the separate timing practical for that task boundary. Sources: Lecture4b, PDF pp.8–11; Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf, PDF p.3.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: Both candidate plans must return the same qualifying balances. Estimate their work using data statistics and the stated model, then inspect the chosen plan if a DBMS run is available. A scan can be competitive when the index route causes costly access. This lecture gives the decision framework; it does not prove that the source's indexed option always wins.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Draw the three-stage pipeline from memory. Name two catalog statistics. Explain why logical equivalence does not require identical execution strategy. Calculate a disk estimate with consistent units, then state which resource costs were omitted. Try the calculator in Try & explore before checking the worked problems.

entries.title: Sources and scope
entries.text: All 12 PDF pages of Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf were text inspected; the cost model on p.11 was visually checked. The p.12 reading recommendation is textbook 7th edition §§15.1–15.2; the whole chapter is not claimed reviewed. No new assessment-frequency claims or DBMS-version assumptions are made.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: JDBC is the Java API used here to connect to MySQL, send SQL and read results. The two supplied programs differ by one important database action: JDBCandIndex.java attempts to create numIndex before running the same logical query. That difference does not prove the index was used or that the query became faster. The source environment details contain host, filename, schema-width and setup contradictions that must be confirmed before execution. This is a course-level practical, not a new theory unit. Task 1.1 and Task 1.2 are released; Task 2 is now released in Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf, p. 3; see the separate Released Query Timing study segment.

entries.text: > [!note] JDBC lifecycle > Plain-language meaning: load/register driver, connect, create a statement, execute SQL, process the result, then close resources. > > Why it matters: each stage has a different failure mode. > > Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex.pdf, PDF pp. 12–23. > [!note] Driver-specific connection > Plain-language meaning: the source uses MySQL Connector/J and driver class com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver. > > Why it matters: this is lab-specific configuration, not a course-wide DBMS conclusion. > > Source: Lab2, PDF pp. 5, 10, 18. > [!note] Index experiment boundary > Plain-language meaning: creating an index is not the same as observing the optimiser select it or measuring a speedup. > > Why it matters: evidence requires a plan/timing method that the supplied programs do not contain. > > Source: JDBC.java; JDBCandIndex.java.

entries.title: Exam Evidence Snapshot
entries.text: The supplied four-paper sample contains no JDBC/Lab 02 question: NOT OBSERVED IN AVAILABLE PAST-PAPER SAMPLE. This does not make the lab unimportant or excluded.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: You need basic Java classes/methods, SQL SELECT/CREATE INDEX, and the difference between compilation and runtime connectivity. > [!question] Prerequisite check > If Java code compiles without contacting a database, what has compilation not proved? > [!success]- Check your answer > It has not proved driver availability at runtime, credentials, network access, schema state, SQL success or query-plan behaviour. > > Source boundary: supplied Java files and ordinary Lab 02 validation record.

entries.title: A motivating question
entries.text: Two programs issue the same query for rows where num=7; one first creates an index on num. What evidence would justify each of these claims? 1. the index statement succeeded; 2. MySQL used the index; 3. the indexed run was faster; 4. the result set stayed logically equivalent. The supplied programs support source inspection, but not all four conclusions.

entries.title: Learn the mechanism
entries.text: Architecture and lifecycle sequenceDiagram participant J as Java program participant D as JDBC driver participant M as MySQL server J->>D: DriverManager.getConnection(...) D->>M: establish protocol connection J->>D: executeUpdate / executeQuery D->>M: send SQL M-->>D: status or rows D-->>J: update count or ResultSet J->>J: iterate rows and close resources Figure 1 — JDBC request path Read it: Java talks through the DBMS-specific JDBC driver; SQL execution happens on the server. Key takeaway: compile success and runtime database success are different evidence. Provenance: teaching construction from Lab2, PDF pp. 10–23. What the source actually configures The lab identifies MySQL, MySQL Connector/J and com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver. PDF p. 10 calls Connector/J 9.4.0 current at the time of the slide, but the server/JDK/storage-engine versions are not supplied. The Java source contains placeholders for database name, username and password; do not publish or commit real credentials. New setup handout: role and limits Database#1 Create privilege.pdf is a two-page prerequisite handout for the school phpMyAdmin interface. It says: - use http://csse-mysql.xjtlu.edu.cn; - enter the university username without the dot and preserve case; - it displays an initial course password and shows manual creation of a database named after the username; - after creation, use the SQL interface to create tables. Tutor Mode does not repeat the displayed password. Treat it as sensitive and potentially stale; use current official instructions. No university service was contacted. > [!warning] Source contradiction — database creation > Database#1 Create privilege.pdf, PDF p. 2 tells the user to create the username-named database manually. Lab2-JDBCandIndex.pdf, PDF p. 7 says there is no need to create it explicitly because it is created after login. > > Safest interpretation: these may describe different interface versions or provisioning states. Confirm current behaviour with the instructor; do not create extra schemas by guesswork. Other source discrepancies | Source A | Source B | Conflict | Safest action | |---|---|---|---| | Lab2 p. 6: host 10.7.1.127 | Lab2 p. 11: 10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME]; Java uses .127 | current server address unclear | obtain current official connection details | | Lab2 p. 11: JDBCIndex.java | supplied files: JDBC.java, JDBCandIndex.java | filename mismatch | use supplied filenames; confirm submission expectation | | SQL declares mmatch varchar(12) | supplied data include longer values | import may truncate/error by server mode | inspect actual import warnings before changing schema | | Lab2 p. 24: java.Date | p. 25 table: java.sql.Date | type wording differs | use fully qualified JDBC type from mapping table | Two programs, four distinct claims JDBC.java connects and queries Orf_Motif for the configured key/value. JDBCandIndex.java first issues a CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif(num) statement, then runs the same logical query. | Claim | Required evidence | Supplied code alone? | |---|---|---| | index statement was attempted | code inspection | yes | | index creation succeeded | runtime server response/state | no | | optimiser selected index | execution plan such as EXPLAIN | no | | indexed query was faster | controlled timing/measurement | no | | returned rows are equivalent | compare actual result sets | no runtime evidence | The dataset's static parse finds 614 supplied rows with num=7, but that is not an observed MySQL query result. Statement interfaces - Statement: fixed SQL constructed in code. - PreparedStatement: parameter placeholders for values; improves separation of SQL structure from external data and supports reuse. - CallableStatement: invokes stored procedures. The source introduces all three. It does not make every SQL identifier parameterisable; table/column/index identifiers need deliberate safe construction. > [!question] Explain it yourself > Why does creating numIndex not establish a physical B+ tree or a measured speedup? > [!success]- Check your explanation > The source does not confirm storage engine/index type, inspect an execution plan or measure comparable runs. Creation, selection and performance are separate claims. > > Source: supplied Java files; Lab2, PDF pp. 10–23.

entries.title: Worked example — evidence matrix
entries.text: Suppose a run reports successful index creation, then returns 614 rows. That would establish only the executed server state and result count for that run. To show index selection, capture a plan. To show speed, define warm/cold cache, repeated trials, identical data/server load and timing boundaries. To show logical equivalence, compare result sets with and without the index. This older explanation distinguishes static reasoning from execution. The updated ordinary Lab reference now reports a historical local run with 607 rows; see Released Query Timing for its exact boundary and limitations. This web app has not run a database experiment.

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: 1. Creation succeeded: needs an actual server response/state. 2. Index used: needs a plan. 3. Faster: needs controlled measurement. 4. Equivalent results: needs compared actual result sets. Source inspection alone proves only what statements the programs attempt.

entries.text: - JDBC driver mediates Java↔MySQL; - connect → statement → execute → result → close; - host/database provisioning details conflict and require current confirmation; - never expose credentials or contact infrastructure without authorisation; - index creation, index selection, speed and result equivalence need different evidence; - Task 2 is released; see the Released Query Timing segment.
