entries.title: Lab 2 — JDBC and Index
entries.text:
Course home · Index foundations · B+ tree theory · Lab 02 Lab 2 — JDBC and Index Lab goals By the end of the released work, you should be able to: - explain the role of ==JDBC== between a Java application and MySQL; - trace a query through DriverManager, ==MySQL Connector/J==, MySQL, and a ==ResultSet==; - map each stage of the JDBC lifecycle to the supplied Java sources; - explain the exact SQL assembled from searchKey = "num" and searchKeyValue = "7"; - distinguish the baseline query from the program that first creates numIndex; - explain why creating an index does not by itself prove that a query became faster or used that index; and - identify source inconsistencies and rerun hazards before changing an official file. Official tasks Task 1.1 — basic JDBC query Set up the environment, understand the supplied JDBC.java, and test its basic JDBC query.[^tasks] Task 1.2 — JDBC query with an index Understand and test the supplied JDBCandIndex.java, which creates an index and then runs the basic JDBC query.[^tasks] Task 2 — query execution timing Implement functionality that prints the time taken by the same query without and with an index. The measured interval must contain only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);; connection, index changes, result iteration/output, setup, and cleanup remain outside the timer.[^task2] > [!warning] Scope boundary > Task 2 measures the single executeQuery call for the Task 1 query. The local solution additionally verifies index state, logical-result equality, and the indexed execution plan; those checks are outside the measured interval. Opening practical question — what actually changes? You receive the same imported Orf_Motif data and two programs: - JDBC.java connects and runs SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7. - JDBCandIndex.java first runs CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num), then runs the same logical SELECT. Questions: What path carries the query from Java to MySQL? What is returned to Java? What changes when the index is created, and what remains unproved? Constraints: preserve the original sources; use placeholders or environment variables rather than recorded credentials; do not access university infrastructure without current authorised connection details; and do not infer a storage-engine-specific index structure without engine evidence. Success criteria: you can trace each source line, predict the SQL text, explain the result-reading loop, distinguish logical equivalence from performance evidence, and identify the checks required before a safe rerun. | Opening question | Concepts needed | |---|---| | How does Java reach MySQL? | JDBC API, DriverManager, Connector/J, Connection | | How is the query submitted and read? | Statement, executeQuery, ResultSet, rs.next() | | What does the second program add? | CREATE INDEX, object naming, repeated-run behaviour | | What can the lab prove? | Source behaviour versus execution plan and timing evidence | Architecture JDBC is the Java API used to connect Java programs to relational data. The source presents JDBC as classes and interfaces, with database providers supplying drivers.[^jdbc-definition] This lab selects the pure-Java Type 4 MySQL driver, MySQL Connector/J.[^connector] flowchart TB A["Java application"] --> B["JDBC API"] B --> C["DriverManager"] C --> D["MySQL Connector/J
Type 4 JDBC driver"] D --> E["MySQL server"] E --> F["Execute SQL"] F --> G["ResultSet for SELECT"] G --> A Figure 1 — The Lab 2 JDBC request path Read it: Follow the request downward from the Java program. For a SELECT, follow the returned ResultSet back to the application. Key takeaway: Java calls the standard JDBC interfaces; Connector/J translates that work into the MySQL protocol. The course source also shows other historical/generic driver routes, but this lab uses Connector/J.[^architecture] Environment setup Course source instructions The official slides provide two environment choices: install MySQL locally, or use the school MySQL service under current institutional access rules. They instruct students to obtain MySQL Connector/J, place the driver on the classpath or import it into the IDE, import yeast_prosite.sql, and replace the Java connection placeholders in a working file.[^mysql-setup] | Component | Source-supported requirement | Important boundary | |---|---|---| | Java | Compile and run the supplied class in its declared package | The PDF gives no JDK version | | MySQL | Local installation or the authorized school service | MySQL server version and storage engine are not stated | | Driver | MySQL Connector/J; driver class com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver | PDF p. 10 calls Connector/J 9.4.0 current; this is source-stated, not a detected installation | | Dataset | Import yeast_prosite.sql | Inspect import messages before assuming all 12,913 inserts succeeded | | Connection | Replace database, username, and password placeholders in a working copy | Never put real credentials in this vault, note, logs, or shared commands | The archived originals are here: - Official Lab 2 PDF - Official released task sheet - JDBC.java - JDBCandIndex.java - yeast_prosite.sql > [!warning] Work on a copy > Both Java files contain literal placeholders. Copy a source into the instructor-approved IDE project before adapting its package or connection parameters. Do not modify the archived original and do not paste a real password into study notes, YAML, screenshots, terminal history, or version control. Source discrepancies to check before execution 1. PDF p. 6 gives the school MySQL host as 10.7.1.127, whereas PDF p. 11 shows 10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME]. Both supplied Java files contain jdbc:mysql://10.7.1.127/[DATABASE NAME]. On 24 September 2026, a direct TCP probe from the current machine reached 10.7.1.127:3306, while 10.7.1.36:3306 did not respond within three seconds. That observation supports .127 for the current network but proves neither authentication nor universal availability.[^host-discrepancy] 2. PDF p. 11 names JDBCIndex.java, but the supplied originals are JDBC.java and JDBCandIndex.java. Use the actual supplied filenames for Tasks 1.1 and 1.2.[^preparation-name] 3. The source instructs students to modify a package name if needed. The current files declare package xjtlu.soe201.JDBC;, so an IDE project or javac -d output must respect that package. 4. The source contains institutional login guidance that may age. Follow current instructor/IT instructions. This pass performed reachability probes only; it did not submit credentials, log in, import data, or execute SQL on university infrastructure. Supplementary modern guidance This task's local compile check used JDK 17 and needed no Connector/J JAR because the driver name is loaded reflectively at runtime. That proves only that the Java syntax and standard-library references compile. Running the program requires both Connector/J and a reachable, authorized database. javac -d out Sources/JDBC.java Sources/JDBCandIndex.java This command contains no credentials and performs no network access. Runtime classpaths differ between operating systems and IDEs; follow the current lab instructions rather than copying an unverified command. Dataset — Orf_Motif The SQL source drops and recreates one table, deletes earlier rows per orf, and supplies 12,913 INSERT statements. Static parsing found 418 distinct orf values and 216 distinct acc_num values. These are source-file observations, not a claim that a remote import completed. | Column | Exact SQL type | Role in this lab | Static source observation | |---|---|---|---| | orf | varchar(12) | Printed as the second output column | No supplied NULL; maximum text length 9 | | acc_num | varchar(12) | Printed as the first output column | No supplied NULL; maximum text length 7 | | num | int(3) | Search column; the programs filter on num=7 | No supplied NULL; values 1–57; not declared unique | | pos | int(3) | Motif position | 285 supplied NULL values | | len | int(3) | Motif length | No supplied NULL; values 1–565 | | mmatch | varchar(12) | Matched sequence text | 285 supplied NULL values; source-width conflict described below | Table 1 — Compact schema for the supplied dataset Read it: Start with num, the predicate column, then follow the two printed columns acc_num and orf. The DDL contains no primary key, foreign key, NOT NULL, or engine clause. Key takeaway: num is a repeated occurrence number, not a global identifier. Static inspection finds 614 INSERT statements with num=7, spanning 252 distinct orf values. The file also contains later per-orf deletions, so insert-statement counts are not final table counts. The controlled local import described below ended with 607 rows matching num=7. Each result row prints only acc_num and orf even though SELECT * retrieves all six columns. > [!warning] Dataset import compatibility > The DDL declares mmatch varchar(12), but 771 supplied non-NULL values are longer than 12 characters; the maximum is 89. Modern MySQL strict mode treats invalid or overlong assignments as errors, while non-strict handling can adjust values and issue warnings.[^strict-mode] The SQL also begins with unconditional drop table Orf_Motif;, which can report an error if the table does not yet exist. Preserve the official SQL unchanged, inspect the import report, and ask the instructor for the intended schema rather than silently widening the archived source. JDBC lifecycle The source condenses JDBC work into six phases; the following eight-step trace separates statement creation, result acquisition, and iteration so that every supplied operation is visible.[^lifecycle] flowchart TD A["1 Import java.sql classes"] --> B["2 Load the JDBC driver"] B --> C["3 Establish Connection"] C --> D["4 Create Statement"] D --> E["5 Build and execute SQL"] E --> F["6 Obtain ResultSet"] F --> G["7 Iterate with rs.next and read columns"] G --> H["8 Close ResultSet, Statement, Connection"] Figure 2 — Lifecycle used by both supplied Java programs Read it: Each box maps to a concrete import, field, call, or cleanup line in the source table below. Key takeaway: The second program inserts one DDL operation—index creation—between statement creation and the same logical SELECT. | Stage | JDBC.java | JDBCandIndex.java | |---|---|---| | Import classes | lines 11–15 | lines 11–15 | | Load driver | line 58, Class.forName(JDBC_DRIVER) | line 67 | | Establish ==Connection== | line 60 | line 69 | | Create ==Statement== | line 65 | line 74 | | Build SQL | line 38 | lines 39 and 44 | | Execute / obtain ==ResultSet== | line 39 | index: line 40; query: line 47 | | Iterate and read | lines 48–50 | lines 57–59 | | Close resources | lines 72–74 | lines 81–83 | JDBC.java — without creating the new index Configuration fields | Name | Exact supplied meaning | |---|---| | DB_URL | JDBC URL placeholder containing host 10.7.1.127 and [DATABASE NAME] | | USER | [USERNAME] placeholder | | PASS | [PASSWORD] placeholder | | JDBC_DRIVER | com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver | | conn | JDBC Connection, initially null | | stmt | JDBC Statement, initially null | | rs | JDBC ResultSet, initially null | | sql | Current SQL string | | searchKey | Column name num | | searchKeyValue | Text 7, concatenated without quotes into the numeric predicate | Build and submit the query The source constructs: sql = "SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE " + searchKey + "=" + searchKeyValue; With the supplied constants, the exact SQL is: SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 stmt.executeQuery(sql) submits a SELECT and returns a ResultSet, matching the source tutorial's distinction between executeQuery for queries and executeUpdate for data-changing statements.[^execute] Advance and read rs.next() advances the cursor to the next row and returns whether a row is available. Inside that loop: - rs.getString("acc_num") converts the current row's acc_num value to a Java String; - rs.getString("orf") does the same for orf; and - the program prints the two values separated by a tab.[^resultset] The loop continues until rs.next() returns false. The text labels “first col” and “second col” are only console headings; the getters select by column name. > [!info] Static expectation, not a runtime observation > The unchanged SQL file contains 614 inserts whose num value is 7, and neither printed field is NULL in those source rows. A controlled local MySQL 9.4.0 import finished with 607 matching rows because the script's later DELETE statements affect the final state. A different database state or failed import can still produce a different result. JDBCandIndex.java — creating the index After making the connection and Statement, the second program constructs and executes: CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) It then constructs the same logical query: SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 stmt.execute(sql) is used for the DDL statement because the program is not expecting a query row set from CREATE INDEX. stmt.executeQuery(sql) is then used for the SELECT. Conceptually, numIndex creates an access structure keyed by num. That makes an indexed access path *available* to the optimizer. The SQL source does not declare a storage engine, and the Java source does not inspect index metadata, so this note does not assert that the physical index is a B+ tree. Use B+ tree theory for the course's ordered-tree model and hash-index theory for the contrasting equality-oriented model; neither identifies this table's actual engine. Re-running the program On a first successful run, the named index exists afterward. A later run again requests the same index name. MySQL reports a duplicate-key-name error when an index name already exists, so the program can stop at stmt.execute(sql) before reaching the SELECT.[^duplicate-index] > [!warning] Troubleshooting decision > First determine whether numIndex already exists. Do not repeatedly rerun the program and do not modify the lecturer's archived file merely to hide the failure. SUPPLEMENTARY GUIDANCE — verified MySQL syntax: SHOW INDEX FROM Orf_Motif; This lists table indexes. If the instructor explicitly asks for a reset, MySQL's documented syntax is: DROP INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif; DROP INDEX changes schema state; use it only in the intended lab database and only after confirming the index name and reset purpose.[^show-drop-index] Without new index versus with new index | Aspect | JDBC.java | JDBCandIndex.java | |---|---|---| | Schema change before query | None | Requests CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) | | Logical predicate | num=7 | num=7 | | Selected columns | * | * | | Printed columns | acc_num, orf | acc_num, orf | | Expected logical result if data are unchanged | All rows satisfying num=7 | The same rows satisfying num=7 | | Timing code | None | None | | Plan inspection | None | None | | Proof MySQL used numIndex | None | None | Same logical result ≠ proven performance improvement. The supplied programs demonstrate JDBC connectivity, SQL submission, index creation, and equivalent query structure before and after the schema change. They do not measure latency, page reads, throughput, or optimizer choice. Evidence for a general performance claim would require a controlled setup and additional observations such as repeated timings, stable data/cache conditions, and an identified server version and engine. The released Task 2 run below supplies one local executeQuery timing pair plus EXPLAIN; it does not establish a universal speedup. Statement, PreparedStatement, and CallableStatement | Interface | Course-source role | Relation to this lab | |---|---|---| | Statement | General-purpose, simple static SQL with no bind parameters | Used by both supplied programs | | PreparedStatement | Precompiled SQL that may accept runtime input parameters; recommended by the source for repeated execution | Not used in the supplied files | | CallableStatement | Calls stored procedures/functions and may use input/output parameters | Introduced in the PDF; not used in the supplied files | This comparison comes from PDF p. 26.[^statement-types] The supplied code uses Statement because it assembles a complete SQL string before submission. That works for its hard-coded teaching values. If a value came from a user or another external source, a PreparedStatement would normally separate SQL structure from parameter values. That is supplementary engineering guidance, not a rewrite of Task 1.1 or 1.2. SQL-to-Java data mapping The tutorial explains that SQL values must be mapped to Java types and gives direct, convertible, and special-class cases.[^type-mapping] | SQL type in the PDF | JDBC/Java type shown | Setter shown | |---|---|---| | VARCHAR, CHAR | java.lang.String | setString() | | NUMERIC | java.math.BigDecimal | setBigDecimal() | | INTEGER | int | setInt() | | FLOAT | float | setFloat() | | DOUBLE | double | setDouble() | | DATE | java.sql.Date | setDate() | | TIME | java.sql.Time | setTime() | | TIMESTAMP | java.sql.Timestamp | setTimestamp() | > [!note] Internal slide wording discrepancy > PDF p. 24 says SQL DATE maps to a Java Date object “defined in java.Date,” while the table on p. 25 specifies java.sql.Date. The table's fully qualified JDBC type is retained here; the inconsistency is not silently merged. Cleanup and failure limits Both programs explicitly close ResultSet, Statement, and Connection in that order, matching PDF p. 23.[^cleanup] This cleanup is reached only if earlier operations complete. Because the source uses throws and has no finally block or try-with-resources, an exception during connection, index creation, query execution, or row processing can bypass those final close calls. That limitation does not invalidate the teaching sequence, but it matters when interpreting failures. A compile pass is not a runtime pass, and a runtime exception is not evidence about query performance. Supplementary engineering notes These notes support safe interpretation; they are not lecturer-required modifications. Keep credentials out of source control The official examples use string constants for clarity. In a real project, secrets should come from an approved runtime configuration or secret store rather than committed Java or Markdown. This lab note intentionally contains placeholders only. Prefer bounded resource lifetime Modern Java often uses try-with-resources so each JDBC object closes even when an exception occurs. Do not replace the official source during Task 1.1/1.2; first understand the explicit lifecycle the lecturer supplied. Use parameters for external values For an externally supplied numeric value, use a parameter marker and PreparedStatement rather than concatenating raw input. The current fixed 7 is a teaching constant, not an invitation to concatenate untrusted text. Treat import warnings as evidence After importing the SQL in an authorized environment, inspect errors and warnings, confirm the table definition actually created, and verify row counts before attributing a missing or shortened value to JDBC. The mmatch width conflict makes this especially important. Released-task procedure and checkpoints Task 1.1 procedure 1. Preserve the archived JDBC.java; place a working copy in the instructor-approved project. 2. Confirm the package path and that Connector/J is on the runtime classpath. 3. Import the SQL only into the intended authorized lab database; inspect the import report. 4. Replace placeholders in the working copy without recording real credentials in this vault or logs. 5. Before execution, predict the exact SQL and explain each lifecycle line. 6. Run only in the authorized environment. Record observed output separately from this source-derived expectation. 7. Close or terminate the client cleanly and remove any insecure working credential copy according to instructor policy. Task 1.2 procedure 1. Confirm whether numIndex already exists before running. 2. Trace the DDL and the subsequent SELECT in JDBCandIndex.java. 3. Run in the authorized lab environment only. 4. Check that the logical rows correspond to the Task 1.1 predicate; do not infer a speedup from similar output. 5. Use the released Task 2 procedure below for the timing comparison. Task 2 procedure 1. Remove numIndex outside the timer, then verify that no index exists on Orf_Motif(num). 2. Start System.nanoTime(), call stmt.executeQuery(sql), and stop the timer immediately after the call returns. 3. Iterate the first ResultSet only after its timer has stopped. 4. Create numIndex outside the timer and verify that it exists. 5. Time only the same stmt.executeQuery(sql) call again, then iterate afterward. 6. Compare the two logical result multisets and require them to match. 7. Run EXPLAIN after the indexed timer has stopped and require key=numIndex. long startNanos = System.nanoTime(); ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(SELECT_SQL); long elapsedNanos = System.nanoTime() - startNanos; Connection establishment, statement creation, index removal/creation, result iteration/output, comparison, plan inspection, and cleanup are all outside this interval.[^task2] Completed reference solution for Tasks 1.1, 1.2, and 2 The runnable solution is Lab2Solution.java, with exact commands in Solution README. The five files under Sources/ remain byte-for-byte unchanged. The solution keeps the source SQL statements, reads connection details from environment variables, closes JDBC resources with try-with-resources, measures only executeQuery, compares both result sets without assuming row order, and verifies the indexed query plan. Run it safely Compile with JDK 17 and MySQL Connector/J. Set the three environment variables only in the shell used for the lab; do not paste a real password into this note or commit it to source control. export LAB_DB_URL='jdbc:mysql://HOST:3306/DATABASE' export LAB_DB_USER='USERNAME' read -s LAB_DB_PASSWORD && export LAB_DB_PASSWORD CONNECTOR_JAR='Solution/lib/mysql-connector-j-9.4.0.jar' BUILD_DIR="$(mktemp -d)" javac -Xlint:all -cp "$CONNECTOR_JAR" -d "$BUILD_DIR" \ 'Solution/Lab2Solution.java' java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution baseline java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution indexed java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution timing unset LAB_DB_PASSWORD Use baseline before the index exists for Task 1.1. Use indexed for Task 1.2; it creates numIndex only when metadata shows that it is absent. On a fresh isolated lab database, mode both runs the controlled before/after sequence and refuses to proceed if numIndex already exists. The timing mode implements Task 2; it deliberately removes and recreates numIndex, so run it only in the intended lab database. Observed local result — 24 September 2026 The reference solution was compiled with JDK 17.0.18 and Connector/J 9.4.0. It was first validated against an ephemeral local MySQL 9.4.0 server, then independently revalidated against an isolated local MySQL 8.0.46 server. Both runs imported the exact archived yeast_prosite.sql bytes with non-strict SQL mode so its declared varchar(12) width did not abort the overlong supplied values, and both produced the results below. This is local validation, not evidence about the school server. | Check | Observed result | |---|---| | Import messages | Expected first-line error: DROP TABLE Orf_Motif found no table in the fresh database; import continued | | Final table rows | 12,791 | | Task 1.1 query | 607 rows for SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 | | Task 1.2 query | 607 rows; same (acc_num, orf) multiset as Task 1.1 | | Created index | numIndex on num; MySQL reported index method BTREE in this local environment | | Indexed plan | type=ref, possible_keys=numIndex, key=numIndex, estimated rows=607 | | Task 2 time without index | 8.723 ms (8,723,125 ns) | | Task 2 time with index | 2.083 ms (2,083,375 ns) | | Task 2 logical comparison | 607 rows in each run; equal order-independent (acc_num, orf) multisets | > [!success]- Interpretation > Task 1.1: the program connects through Connector/J, submits the source query, iterates its ResultSet, and reads acc_num and orf. The controlled local run observed 607 final matches. > > Task 1.2: the solution created numIndex, submitted the same logical query, and observed the same 607 logical rows. The local EXPLAIN row named numIndex in both isolated validations, so index use is observed for those local MySQL runs. > > Task 2: the timer surrounded only executeQuery. The observed local run measured 8.723 ms without an index and 2.083 ms with numIndex; both returned the same 607 logical rows, and EXPLAIN selected numIndex. > > Limit: one local observation does not establish a universal speedup or the behaviour of the university server. Cache state, server load, data size, engine, statistics, and repeated-trial methodology can change timings. The local server used non-strict mode, and the school's authenticated import outcome and plan remain untested. Supplementary practice Exercise 1 — reconstruct the two SQL statements Without looking back, write the exact query produced by both programs and the additional DDL produced by JDBCandIndex.java. > [!tip]- Hint > Substitute searchKey and searchKeyValue into the concatenated strings. > [!success]- Solution > Both programs produce SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7. The second also produces CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) before that query. The first changes no schema; the second requests a persistent named index. Exercise 2 — classify four claims Classify each claim as supported, unsupported, or requires runtime evidence: 1. The supplied query filters on num. 2. MySQL used numIndex for the second program. 3. Both programs print acc_num and orf. 4. The indexed query is faster by a specific percentage. > [!tip]- Hint > Separate source-code facts from optimizer and timing observations. > [!success]- Solution > 1 is supported by both Java sources. 2 requires runtime plan evidence; the completed local Task 2 run supplied that evidence with key=numIndex. 3 is supported by the two getString calls. 4 requires an explicit local timing observation and must not be generalized beyond its test conditions. Exercise 3 — diagnose the second run The first run creates numIndex; the second run stops before printing rows. Give the most direct source-grounded hypothesis and a safe first check. > [!tip]- Hint > Identify the first schema-changing statement and remember that the index remains after the program exits. > [!success]- Solution > The second CREATE INDEX numIndex ... can fail because that index name already exists. First inspect indexes with SHOW INDEX FROM Orf_Motif;. Do not drop anything until the instructor's reset intent and the target database are confirmed. Resolve the opening practical question Decision: both programs use the same JDBC request path and the same logical SELECT; the second program adds one persistent schema operation before the query. Justification: Class.forName selects Connector/J, DriverManager.getConnection produces the Connection, createStatement produces the Statement, and executeQuery returns a ResultSet. The row loop advances with rs.next() and prints acc_num plus orf. Operation: the baseline assembles SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7. The second assembles CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num), executes it, and then assembles the same SELECT. Result: if both runs use the same successfully imported data, their logical result sets should match. The controlled local run observed 607 final rows in each mode and an order-independent match. The source contains 614 candidate inserts with num=7, but later deletions reduce the local final table result; another database state still requires its own observation. Interpretation: index creation makes a new access path available. The supplied Task 1 programs contain no plan inspection or timing, while the completed Task 2 solution measures only executeQuery and separately verifies key=numIndex. Its observed local difference is evidence for that run, not a universal performance guarantee. Quick review - Can you draw Java → JDBC → Connector/J → MySQL → ResultSet from memory? - Can you identify the exact lines that create Connection, Statement, and ResultSet? - Can you explain why num=7 can return many rows? - Can you separate a compile check, JDBC runtime check, database connectivity check, and performance experiment? - Can you explain the duplicate-index rerun failure and the mmatch import risk? - Can you identify the exact three Task 2 timing lines and explain why iteration is excluded? Study status: untested. Source review, compilation, and successful local execution validate the implementation, not your personal mastery or remote university-server behaviour. entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Run the same Task 1 query with and without an index and print the time spent in only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);. Connection setup, creating an index and consuming results belong outside the timed interval. Compare logical results and inspect the index state separately. Source: tasks PDF pp.1–3 and the updated reference lab's Released Task 2 section.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: Complete the preceding JDBC setup practical. Use an isolated, intended lab database with valid configuration. These web activities explain the task and do not connect to the university database or execute Java. Required university server and JDK versions remain unconfirmed by the task sheet.

entries.title: 1. Keep the query fixed
entries.text: Both Task 1 source programs select SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7. The indexed version makes an index on num available before submitting that query. Do not compare different predicates, tables, or result interpretations and call that an index experiment. Source: tasks PDF pp.1–2; official JDBC.java and JDBCandIndex.java.

entries.title: 2. Place the timer around exactly one call
entries.text: The updated reference solution uses: long startNanos = System.nanoTime(); ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(SELECT_SQL); long elapsedNanos = System.nanoTime() - startNanos; Convert nanoseconds to milliseconds by dividing by 1_000_000.0. Keep the while (resultSet.next()) loop after the timer. The task defines its interval as the API call; The driver can retrieve and buffer rows during executeQuery; moving the iteration loop afterward does not isolate server execution from transfer time. Supplementary technical reference: [Connector/J implementation notes]( ResultSet section, checked 2026-10-07. Streaming configurations can change that boundary. Source: tasks PDF p.3; reference 03 Lab.md, Released Task 2 timing lines.

entries.title: 3. Record index state and the chosen plan
entries.text: An index existing, an optimiser choosing it, and an elapsed time are three different observations. Record the intended before/after index state and inspect a plan separately. The local reference solution records numIndex; do not recreate a named index blindly on every rerun. A duplicate-index error can stop the intended experiment before the SELECT. Source: official JDBCandIndex.java, index creation; updated reference lab's execution procedure.

entries.title: 4. Establish equal results
entries.text: Consume both result sets outside the timer and compare them without assuming row order. Keep duplicates when comparing multisets rather than changing query semantics. The reference run compared (acc_num, orf) multisets with 607 rows in each run. This is recorded local evidence, not a promised row count for every import. Source: updated reference lab's Task 2 logical comparison.

entries.title: 5. Explain a measurement honestly
entries.text: The existing reference records one local pair, 8.723 ms and 2.083 ms. It supports a difference in that controlled run. Cache state, load, statistics, data size and configuration can change the result. These values are not newly measured by this web import and do not establish a universal speedup or university-server behaviour. Source: updated reference lab's observed local execution and limits.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Point to the exact three timer lines. Identify the operations excluded from the interval. Explain how you would show equal logical results and actual plan selection, then name one condition that could change the timings. Use the local cost activity to separate a theoretical estimate from an actual JDBC interval.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: An index can reduce transferred blocks yet increase expensive seeks. Suppose a file occupies 400 blocks and an unclustered index matches 100 scattered records. With index height 4, transfer time 0.1 ms and seek time 4 ms, a full scan costs 44 ms, while the lecture's pessimistic secondary-index model costs 426.4 ms. The access path matters more than the mere existence of an index. This supplementary calculation uses Lecture5a pp.5,10 and the disk model from Unit 06. This edition integrates the verified 12 October archive: Lecture5a, 23 pages, dated 10 October 2026. It is a new web lesson, not a claim that the file was first released this week. Week 6 optimisation sources are visible on Learning Mall but remain pending acquisition. Prerequisites: Unit 01 storage, Units 02–04 indexes, Unit 05 algebra and Unit 06 cost units.

entries.title: Select an Access Path With Explicit Assumptions
entries.text: Let b_r be file blocks, h the lecture's number of index-node accesses, b the consecutive matching data blocks and k the matching records. For cold accesses, retain transfers B and seeks S separately, then compute $T=B t_T+S t_S$. | Access path | Transfers B | Seeks S | Conditions | |---|---:|---:|---| | Linear scan | $b_r$ | 1 | Contiguous relation; test every record | | Successful equality scan on a key, average | $b_r/2$ | 1 | Source average model; absence may need full scan | | Binary search | $\lceil\log_2 b_r\rceil$ plus matching blocks | Same search count, then retrieval | File physically ordered on equality attribute | | Candidate-key B+ lookup | $h+1$ | $h+1$ | One matching data record | | Clustered non-key equality | $h+b$ | $h+1$ | Matching records contiguous | | Unclustered non-key equality, pessimistic | $h+k$ | $h+k$ | Each matching record may be on another block | The deck calls the clustered non-key case a primary index. Keep its physical locality assumption explicit rather than assuming every primary-key definition implies clustering. Cached index pages, repeated data blocks and storage hardware can change actual costs. These estimates are not measured runtimes. Source: Lecture5a pp.4–10.

entries.title: Handle Ranges and Boolean Conditions Completely
entries.text: For a clustered lower range, seek to the first qualifying key then read the following blocks sequentially. For a prefix range ending at an upper bound, a scan from the start may avoid unnecessary index seeks. An unclustered range can fetch many scattered blocks, so compare against a full scan. For an AND, one selective indexed condition may generate candidates; test the remaining conditions on every candidate. A suitable composite index is another possibility. For an OR, union the candidate pointers from every disjunct and remove duplicate pointers before retrieval. If any branch lacks a complete access path, its matches still need finding, often by scanning. Lecture5a p.13 loosely says some indexes may be available; using only indexed branches would silently lose valid OR results. Negation requires the complement relative to the relation, not simply returning the positive matches. Source: Lecture5a pp.11–14; the completeness qualification is local reasoning about the stated predicate.

entries.title: Project Columns and Remove Duplicates
entries.text: Relational projection drops unwanted attributes and eliminates duplicate resulting tuples. Sorting the projected tuples makes duplicates adjacent; hashing sends equal tuples to the same group. SQL SELECT without DISTINCT may preserve duplicates, so do not transfer set-algebra semantics automatically to SQL. An index orders references logically; following a secondary index is not equivalent to physically sorting the data and may cause an I/O per tuple. Source: Lecture5a pp.15–16; algebra/SQL distinction retained from Unit 05.

entries.title: Create Runs Before Merging
entries.text: For b blocks and M memory frames, read up to M blocks, sort them in memory and write each sorted run. Initially there are $N=\lceil b/M\rceil$ runs. A merge reserves input buffers for participating runs and an output buffer. With one frame per buffer, merge at most M−1 runs; with b_b frames per buffer, fan-in is $F=\lfloor M/b_b\rfloor-1$. Require F≥2 before using logarithmic multipass formulas. More buffering improves sequential I/O but reduces fan-in and may add a pass. Source: Lecture5a pp.17–21. For the supplied b=12, M=3 example, runs shrink 4→2→1 in two merge passes. The initial groups of three are sorted separately, then paired and finally merged. The repeated key a has payloads 19 and 14: the figure sorts by key, with equal-key ordering not specified as a stable-sort requirement. Source: Lecture5a p.20; Lab4 Q3 p.5.

entries.title: Count Transfers and Seeks With One Output Convention
entries.text: For b>M and $P=\lceil\log_F\lceil b/M\rceil\rceil$, the source omits the final output write: $$B=b(2P+1),\qquad S=2\lceil b/M\rceil+\lceil b/b_b\rceil(2P-1).$$ Initial run generation reads and writes 2b blocks; each intermediate merge reads and writes 2b; the final merge reads b. If the final sorted file must be stored, add b writes and $\lceil b/b_b\rceil$ seeks. For b=12, M=3, b_b=1, P=2 gives 60 transfers and 44 seeks when streamed; storing the final file gives 72 and 56. An in-memory input is a separate case; do not apply a negative-pass term mechanically. Source: Lecture5a pp.21–22.

entries.title: Return to the Access-Path Decision
entries.text: For the opening example, scan: $400(0.1)+1(4)=44$ ms. Unclustered index: $104(0.1+4)=426.4$ ms. A clustered lookup retrieving eight consecutive blocks would instead cost $12(0.1)+5(4)=21.2$ ms. The final comparison requires selectivity, locality, available ordering, memory and a consistent output policy. These are supplementary examples with stated parameters, not new measured results. Lecture5a pp.1–2 introduce scope; pp.3–16 cover selection/projection; pp.17–22 cover sorting and its example; p.23 recommends reading, which is not imported here. No new assessment corpus, exam probabilities or official marks are inferred.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: The smaller relation is not always the cheapest outer input, and the fewest transferred blocks do not always yield the shortest time. In Lecture5b's example, indexed nested loops uses 25,100 transfers but also 25,100 seeks; block nested loops uses 40,100 transfers and only 200 seeks. At 0.1 ms per transfer and 4 ms per seek, the estimated times are 102,910 ms and 4,810 ms. This local arithmetic explains the source's comparison without claiming a database benchmark. Source: Lecture5b, 25 pages, verified against the 12 October acquisition manifest. Keep this physical evaluation unit separate from later query optimisation, whose current Week 6 files have not yet been acquired. Prerequisites: selection costs and external sorting in Unit 07, join semantics in Unit 05.

entries.title: Define the Result Before Choosing the Algorithm
entries.text: A natural join matches all shared attribute names and returns one copy of those shared columns. It is not a Cartesian product without conditions, nor a join on a guessed single attribute when several names are shared. The physical strategy must preserve the same result. Source: Lecture5b pp.3–4. The lecture uses customer:10,000 records/400 blocks and depositor:5,000 records/100 blocks. Lab4 instead uses much larger relations. Do not carry the lecture's cardinalities into the tutorial. Default lecture estimates are pessimistic unless memory availability says otherwise. Source: Lecture5b pp.5–8; Lab4 p.2.

entries.title: Compare Tuple and Block Nested Loops
entries.text: For outer r, inner s, and little memory, tuple nested loops transfers $B=b_r+n_r b_s$ with $S=b_r+n_r$ seeks. Each outer tuple triggers another inner scan. The two source orientations give depositor outer:2,000,100 transfers/5,100 seeks; customer outer:1,000,400/10,400. Their time ordering depends on the transfer/seek weights. Block nested loops reuses each outer block for every tuple pair with an inner block. The source's one-outer-block model costs $B=b_r+b_r b_s$, $S=2b_r$. Depositor outer costs40,100/200; customer outer40,400/800. These are the source model, not a formula for an arbitrary multi-block outer buffer. If the smaller relation fits completely as the retained inner input, the source simplifies to $b_r+b_s$ transfers and2 seeks. Source: Lecture5b pp.6–10.

entries.title: Probe the Inner Index Without Hiding Retrieval Cost
entries.text: Indexed nested loops applies to equality/natural joins when the inner join attribute has a suitable index. For each outer tuple, probe the index and fetch all matching inner records. With one matching key record and h index accesses, $B=b_r+n_r(h+1)$ and the deck uses the same count for seeks. In its depositor/customer example, h=4 yields25,100/25,100. For a non-key clustered lookup, transfer and seek costs differ: per probe, h+b transfers but h+1 seeks, where b is matching data blocks. Estimate b from supplied statistics or state the assumption; “one lookup” does not mean “one block”. Real caching and repeated keys can reduce actual work; do not silently add that benefit to the cold source model. Source: Lecture5b pp.11–13; Lecture5a pp.7–10.

entries.title: Merge Sorted Inputs and Account for Sorting
entries.text: Sort both inputs on the join attributes if necessary, then advance pointers, retaining matching equal-key groups. The stated merge scan costs $b_r+b_s$ transfers and $\lceil b_r/b_b\rceil+\lceil b_s/b_b\rceil$ seeks, assuming each equal-key group fits in memory. Duplicate keys require producing every matching pair. The source's one-pass scan estimate can fail when groups do not fit. Keep output conventions explicit: materialising sorted files adds their final writes before a later join reads them. If final merges stream directly into the join, do not charge an additional full input scan for the same reads. Buffer feasibility still has to hold for both inputs. Source: Lecture5b pp.14–16; Lecture5a p.21. The accounting clarification prevents incompatible formulas being combined.

entries.title: Partition With One Hash and Probe With Another
entries.text: Partition both relations using the same hash of join attributes so equal keys land in corresponding partitions. Keep the smaller build partition in memory, build a hash table using a different hash function, then scan the corresponding probe partition and emit all actual key matches. A hash collision alone is not equality. Cross-partition comparisons are unnecessary; the probe partition need not fit entirely in memory. The source handles equality/natural joins, not arbitrary inequalities. Source: Lecture5b pp.17–20. Choose enough partitions for build partitions to fit; allow room for skew, buffers and the in-memory table. A fudge factor is a planning allowance, not a proof that every partition fits. A one-pass partition stage with n_h output buffers of b_b blocks plus an input buffer of b_b blocks requires at least $(n_h+1)b_b$ frames. This direct buffer count is needed when using the tutorial's assumptions.

entries.title: Read the Hash-Join Cost as a Conditional Model
entries.text: The supplied estimate is $B=3(b_r+b_s)+4n_h$ and $S=2(\lceil b_r/b_b\rceil+\lceil b_s/b_b\rceil)+2n_h$. The correction budgets writing and rereading partially filled partition blocks. For b_r=400,b_s=100,n_h=5,b_b=3, B=1,520 and S=346. The simple three-times base counts partition-read, partition-write and join-read; output-result writing is omitted. If the whole build fits and partitioning is unnecessary, the deck gives one scan of both inputs and2 seeks. Source: Lecture5b pp.21–22. The lecture's example assigns a20-block build partition to20 memory blocks; an implementation also needs buffers and hash-table overhead. Treat its arithmetic as an idealised cost model, not proof that all allocations fit simultaneously. Skew or recursive partitioning changes the cost.

entries.title: Aggregate and Implement Set Operations
entries.text: Sorting or hashing groups equal keys for COUNT,MIN,MAX,SUM and AVG. Partial AVG must retain both sum and count: an unweighted average of group averages is generally wrong. For set union, keep distinct tuples from either side; for intersection, keep tuples present in both; for r−s, remove s tuples from the r set. Corresponding hash partitions must use a compatible first hash and then check actual tuple equality. Preserve the distinction between set semantics and SQL bag variants such as UNION ALL. Source: Lecture5b pp.23–24; SQL distinction retained from Unit 05.

entries.title: Return to the Weighted Comparison
entries.text: The opening indexed join costs $25100(0.1+4)=102910$ ms. Block nested loops costs $40100(0.1)+200(4)=4810$ ms. Hash join costs $1520(0.1)+346(4)=1536$ ms under the source's idealised assumptions. These are conditional estimates; include sorting, partition overflows, output policy and actual statistics before choosing a plan. The required question is “cheapest under which model?”, not “which algorithm is always best?”. Coverage: Lecture5b pp.1–2 introduce scope; pp.3–22 cover joins and worked comparisons; pp.23–24 cover aggregation and set operations; p.25 recommends reading. Lab4 Q1–Q6 are worked separately in the tutorial clinic. No new official marking scheme, measured runtime or exam-frequency evidence is claimed.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: This clinic maps every Lab4-Tutorial question and subquestion to local worked reasoning. It uses the verified eight-page PDF from the12 October archive, not a newly downloaded answer key. The live answer-key resource42127 is visible but has not been acquired; these solutions are not represented as official answers. The main risks are mixing tuple/block counts, forgetting seeks, assuming unspecified selectivity and combining incompatible output conventions.

entries.title: Q1: Indexed Versus Repeated Scans
entries.text: Lab4 p.2 gives customer:1,000,000 records/8,000 blocks and depositor:500,000/1,000. With depositor outer and the lecture height bound for n=100 pointers, h=4 and a key lookup needs h+1=5 accesses. Indexed nested loops gives2,501,000 transfers and seeks, hence10,254,100ms with0.1ms transfer/4ms seek. Tuple nested loops gives4,000,001,000 transfers and501,000 seeks, costing402,004,100ms. One-outer-block BNL gives8,001,000 transfers/2,000 seeks, costing808,100ms. Under these cold source assumptions, BNL wins among those three algorithms. No memory-fit or caching benefit is assumed.

entries.title: Q2: Identify Missing and Conflicting Assumptions
entries.text: Lab4 pp.3–4 gives customer:5,000 tuples/500 blocks and transaction:80,000/7,000. It describes transaction as sorted by its key, yet also supposes a sparse primary index on customer_Number, which is not its stated key transaction_ID. A sparse clustered access plan needs physical ordering consistent with the indexed customer_Number; this must be clarified rather than silently inferred. Conditionally assume that ordering, use N=7 and the lecture minimum-occupancy height bound h=7. For customer outer, BNL transfers3,500,500 blocks and makes1,000 seeks, costing354,050ms. Let b be the matching transaction blocks per customer lookup. Clustered INL costs $B=500+5000(7+b)$ and $S=500+5000(7+1)=40500$, hence $T=165550+500b$ ms. A uniform packed estimate of16 matches/customer and80,000/7,000 tuples/block suggests b≈2, giving166,550ms; it is an explicit estimate, not an exact conclusion from total counts. Index height is an upper-bound convention, not a measured shape. Confirm ordering and match distribution before presenting a definitive plan comparison.

entries.title: Q3: The Twelve-Block External Sort
entries.text: Lab4 p.5 and Lecture5a pp.20–22 give b=12,M=3,b_b=1. Initial runs:4; fan-in:2; run counts4→2→1; merge passes:2. With the source's final-output-write omission, B=60,S=44. If the output must be stored, add12 transfers/12 seeks, giving72/56. Both conventions describe the same run structure; do not change the number of passes to adjust for output writing.

entries.title: Q4: Declare Where the Sorted Results Go
entries.text: Lab4 p.6 gives customer8,000 blocks,depositor1,000,M=100,b_b=5, initially unsorted. Fan-in19, initial runs80/10 and merge passes2/1. Fully materialised sorting costs48,000/4,000 transfers and6,560/420 seeks respectively. A subsequent merge scan adds9,000 transfers and1,800 seeks: total61,000 transfers/8,780 seeks, omitting join-result writing. The source sort formula omits final sorted writes. Applying it gives40,000+3,000 transfers and4,960+220 seeks for the sorts. Blindly adding a later separate merge scan gives52,000/6,980, but omits the writes needed to make those sorted files persistent. If final merges are genuinely fused into the join, their read costs already include consuming the inputs: the ideal transfer subtotal is43,000, not52,000. Recheck simultaneous buffer allocation and equal-key-group capacity before claiming such a fused execution is feasible. The question leaves this policy unstated; local solutions expose the alternatives instead of claiming one unqualified official total.

entries.title: Q5: Conditional Hash Cost and Buffer Feasibility
entries.text: Lab4 p.7 supplies50 partitions and b_b=20, and asks to count partially filled blocks. Substitution into Lecture5b p.21 gives $B=3(8000+1000)+4(50)=27200$ and $S=2(400+50)+2(50)=1000$. Estimated time with the Q4 weights is6,720ms. This is conditional arithmetic under the stated one-pass premise. If “information from Q4” includes M=100, the proposed simultaneous allocation requires(50+1)×20=1,020 frames, contradicting that memory budget. Even the source's one-pass assertion does not resolve the allocation conflict. State that inconsistency; revise memory, buffers, partition count or pass structure before treating6,720ms as an executable plan estimate. No DBMS run is claimed.

entries.title: Q6: Materialise Before the Subsequent Merge Join
entries.text: Lab4 p.8 gives b_r=5,b_s=3,M=3,b_b=1 and explicitly requires final sorted results to be written. (a) r makes2 initial runs; s fits in memory and needs no external runs (one sorted in-memory sequence). (b) r needs1 merge pass; s needs0. (c) Materialised r costs2×5×(1+1)=20 transfers. Reading, in-memory sorting and writing s costs3+3=6, even though external merge sort is unnecessary. (d) The subsequent merge scan reads5+3=8 blocks under the source's group-fit condition. (e) Total34 transfers, excluding join-result writes. Calling the in-memory sort “free” would omit its explicitly requested disk input/output.

The historical original source archives, ordinary vault notes and learner progress are preserved.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Synthetic opening case. Two operators form a legal plan. The producer costs 500 block transfers and produces a 40-block intermediate relation. The consumer costs 200 transfers, including reading those 40 blocks. Their formulas exclude output writes. Can you compare a materialised boundary with a permitted pipeline without counting a read twice? Your goal is to identify the algorithm, the boundary between operators and the cost convention before adding numbers. Prerequisites: Unit 05 relational algebra and Units 06–08 physical evaluation. This lesson covers Lecture6a PDF pp.3–12, with identity/outcomes on pp.1–2. Algebraic rewrite rules on pp.13–29, Lecture6b and Lab5 remain separate pending teaching work. No database timing or official assessment result is claimed.

entries.title: Separate a Logical Expression From Its Evaluation Plan
entries.text: A relational expression specifies the required result. An evaluation plan also chooses an algorithm for each operation and coordinates their execution. The same logical expression can therefore have different physical plans. For example, a selection result may be stored before its parent consumes it, or passed directly along a legal pipeline. Equivalent results do not imply identical disk work. Source: Lecture6a pp.3–4,9,11–12. For each edge in the expression tree, ask: what does the child produce, what does the parent require, and must the intermediate result be stored? Do not assume that changing an edge permits changing predicates or discarding tuples.

entries.title: Store an Intermediate Result or Pass Tuples On
entries.text: Materialisation completes an intermediate operation, writes its result as a temporary relation, then lets a later operation consume it. In the lecture's example, selection feeds a join and the join feeds projection. Materialisation is generally applicable in the supplied evaluation model, but temporary storage adds work. Pipelining lets a parent consume tuples while its child is producing them, avoiding a temporary disk relation where permitted. Source: Lecture6a pp.4–7. flowchart LR A[Selection] -->|materialised boundary| T[Temporary disk relation] T --> B[Parent operator] C[Selection] -->|permitted pipeline| D[Parent operator] Figure 1 — Alternative boundaries, not different query results. Read it from left to right: the upper path stores an intermediate relation; the lower path passes tuples to its consumer. Key takeaway: removing a temporary file requires a legal execution arrangement. This teaching diagram abstracts the source tree on PDF p.5; it is not an extra official exercise.

entries.title: Count Writes Without Counting Reads Twice
entries.text: The lecture's operator formulas omit output writes. For materialised evaluation, add the intermediate writes to the sum of operator costs; the consuming operator's cost may already include the corresponding reads. Final query-output writes remain excluded unless explicitly requested. Source: Lecture6a p.6, with the streaming contrast on p.7. Return to the opening case. First identify the ledger: | Item | Materialised | Pipelined | |---|---:|---:| | Producer work | 500 | 500 | | Consumer work other than the intermediate read | 160 | 160 | | Read intermediate relation from disk | 40 | 0 | | Write intermediate relation to disk | 40 | 0 | | Total block transfers | 740 | 660 | Materialised cost is $500+200+40=740$. The 200 already contains the 40-block read: adding another 40 for reading would incorrectly give 780. Under the synthetic assumption that all other work is unchanged and streaming is legal, pipelined cost is $500+(200-40)=660$. The saving is 80 transfers, one intermediate write and one intermediate read. These are transfer counts, not milliseconds; seeks and CPU are not modelled. If the two algorithms change, recompute their costs instead of mechanically subtracting 80.

entries.title: Explain Push, Pull and Blocking Phases
entries.text: A producer-driven (push) pipeline sends tuples to the parent through a buffer. When that buffer is full, the child waits for space. A demand-driven (pull) pipeline starts with a request for the next output tuple; each operator requests tuples from its children as needed and retains state between requests. A pipeline therefore does not mean that no memory or state is needed. Source: Lecture6a p.8. Pipelining is not possible across every phase. External sorting may need preliminary processing of the whole input; a hash join has a preliminary build phase. This prevents a claim that every operator can immediately stream its final result from its first input tuple. It does not establish that every phase of every such algorithm must always materialise its output. Source: Lecture6a p.7; the phase distinction is a local clarification of that stated limitation.

entries.title: Apply the Course Convention Before Comparing Plans
entries.text: Lecture6a p.10 gives a specific convention: an edge labelled pipeline permits pipelining; an unlabelled edge is assumed not to permit it. For joins, unless explicitly stated otherwise, the source singles out the nested-loop family for its pipelining treatment. Preserve these annotations in course exercises rather than replacing them with assumptions about an arbitrary DBMS. This is a course modelling rule, not a universal statement that all other join implementations can never pipeline. Use this method: identify the logical result; choose the stated operator algorithms; inspect every boundary; separate intermediate reads and writes; calculate costs in one unit; then check which cost components and final-output policy are excluded. A cost-based optimiser chooses using estimates, so the estimated winner is not guaranteed to be the fastest measured execution. Source: Lecture6a pp.9–12. The opening example establishes a conditional 80-transfer saving, not an unconditional claim that pipelining is always faster.

entries.title: What is the blocking factor for unspanned fixed records?
entries.text: $\lfloor\text{block size}/\text{record size}\rfloor$: the number of complete records that fit in one block.

entries.title: Why is the final block count rounded upward?
entries.text: Any remaining record needs a real block even when that block is not full.

entries.title: What makes an index primary in this course?
entries.text: Its search-key order matches the physical sequential order of the data file.

entries.title: What does a dense index represent, and how are duplicate search-key values handled?
entries.text: Every search-key value in the data file has an index entry. Duplicate values must lead to all their matching records, for example via a run or pointer list. One entry per record is a particular layout, not the only dense layout.

entries.title: What invariant makes a sparse primary index usable?
entries.text: Ordered data lets a representative entry select the block/range containing the target.

entries.title: What is an index entry's basic size here?
entries.text: Search-key bytes plus pointer bytes, unless the source explicitly supplies additional overhead.

entries.title: What are the HDD read-time phases?
entries.text: Seek time, rotational waiting and transfer time.

entries.title: Why can one page fetch serve several rows?
entries.text: Several rows may share the fetched page, which remains available while buffered.

entries.title: One 300-byte student and its five 200-byte module records must stay together. What group size must the block-capacity calculation use, and why?
entries.text: One 300-byte student record together with its five 200-byte module records: a 1300-byte group.

entries.title: Why does a small index not prove a cheap query?
entries.text: Qualifying records may still occupy many scattered data pages; cache and clustering are unspecified.

entries.title: What does B+ tree order mean in this course?
entries.text: The maximum number of child pointers in an internal node.

entries.title: How many keys can an order-$n$ leaf hold at most?
entries.text: $n-1$ search-key entries.

entries.title: In a B+ tree lookup, where is key membership confirmed?
entries.text: At the reached leaf, not at an internal separator.

entries.title: In this course’s B+ tree convention, which child range is chosen when the search key equals a separator?
entries.text: Route to the right-hand range beginning at that separator.

entries.title: After splitting a B+ tree leaf, which key is copied into the parent?
entries.text: The first key of the new right leaf is copied into the parent.

entries.title: After splitting a B+ tree internal node, which separator is promoted?
entries.text: The middle separator moves to the parent and is removed from the split children.

entries.title: What repair preference does the lecture use after underflow?
entries.text: Merge first when an eligible sibling combination fits; otherwise redistribute.

entries.title: When does deletion reduce the height of a B+ tree?
entries.text: When an internal root is left with one child and that child replaces it.

entries.title: Why are leaves linked?
entries.text: To continue ordered range scans without returning to the root for each next key.

entries.title: What must every root-to-leaf path share?
entries.text: The same depth; this is the tree's height-balance invariant.

entries.title: What does a hash function return for lookup?
entries.text: A candidate bucket address; actual keys must still be compared.

entries.title: What handles a full static bucket?
entries.text: One or more linked overflow pages under the source model.

entries.title: In this course’s extendable hashing, what does global depth measure?
entries.text: The number of high-order hash bits currently read by the directory.

entries.title: What does a bucket’s local depth measure in extendable hashing?
entries.text: The number of prefix bits that distinguish one physical bucket.

entries.title: How many directory entries exist at global depth $i$?
entries.text: $2^i$ pointer entries.

entries.title: At global depth $i$, how many directory entries point to one bucket of local depth $i_j$?
entries.text: $2^{i-i_j}$ directory pointers.

entries.title: When can a full extendable-hash bucket split without doubling the directory?
entries.text: When its local depth is less than the global depth.

entries.title: Why preserve leading zeros?
entries.text: High-order prefix routing depends on the fixed-width bit positions.

entries.title: When can buddy buckets coalesce?
entries.text: Equal local depth, correct buddy prefixes, and combined entries fitting one bucket.

entries.title: Why is hashing poor for ordered range scans?
entries.text: Bucket addresses do not preserve adjacent search-key order.

entries.title: What does an LSM tree batch?
entries.text: Ordered updates, merging memory batches into larger sorted disk levels.

entries.title: What must an LSM lookup reconcile?
entries.text: Relevant versions and tombstones across every searched level.

entries.title: What does a buffer-tree internal buffer hold?
entries.text: Pending updates waiting to be partitioned and pushed toward child ranges.

entries.title: What record-position invariant must hold before combining two bitmap indexes?
entries.text: The same record-position order.

entries.title: If any queried Bloom-filter bit is zero, what can you conclude under the standard insertion-only model?
entries.text: The queried element is definitely absent under the filter model.

entries.title: If all queried Bloom-filter bits are one, what can you conclude and what must happen next?
entries.text: Only possible membership; the real structure must verify it.

entries.title: How does a k-d tree divide space?
entries.text: By recursive coordinate splits, typically alternating dimensions.

entries.title: How does a quadtree divide two-dimensional space?
entries.text: Recursively into four equal spatial quadrants.

entries.title: What does an R-tree internal entry bound?
entries.text: A minimum bounding rectangle covering objects or child regions.

entries.title: Why can temporal endpoint assumptions change an answer?
entries.text: A version at the boundary may be included or excluded depending on interval convention.

entries.title: What does selection change?
entries.text: Selection keeps tuples satisfying a predicate; it preserves the attribute schema.

entries.title: What does projection change?
entries.text: Projection keeps named attributes. In set relational algebra identical result tuples collapse to one.

entries.title: What is union compatibility?
entries.text: Equal arity and compatible corresponding attribute domains; align names/order before a set operation.

entries.title: Is difference commutative?
entries.text: No. r−s keeps tuples in r absent from s; s−r asks the opposite question.

entries.title: How large is a Cartesian product?
entries.text: Every left tuple pairs with every right tuple: |r×s|=|r|·|s|. Rename ambiguous attribute names.

entries.title: What does natural join match?
entries.text: Equality of all attributes with common names, then one copy of each common attribute remains.

entries.title: Why rename a relation?
entries.text: To name an intermediate result or distinguish copies of the same relation and their attributes.

entries.title: For relations r(X,Y) and s(Y), what does division r ÷ s return, and where do candidate X values come from?
entries.text: Return X tuples from πX(r) that occur in r paired with every Y tuple in s. Extra Y pairings are allowed; if s is empty, every candidate in πX(r) qualifies.

entries.title: For r(X,Y) and s(Y), how does candidates minus failures implement division?
entries.text: Start T=πX(r). Missing pairs are (T×s)−r. Project their X values and subtract those failed candidates from T.

entries.title: How can difference find a maximum?
entries.text: Rename a second copy, find values smaller than some other value, and subtract those nonmaximum values from all values. Ties remain.

entries.title: How do borrower and depositor answer both versus either?
entries.text: Intersect projected customer names for both; union them for either.

entries.title: Does algebra projection equal ordinary SQL SELECT?
entries.text: Not necessarily: this lecture uses sets; SQL without DISTINCT can preserve duplicates and has additional NULL behavior.

entries.title: What are the three query-processing stages, and which stage runs the chosen plan?
entries.text: Parsing/translation, optimization, and evaluation. Evaluation executes the chosen plan.

entries.title: Does equivalent algebra imply equal cost?
entries.text: No. Equivalent results can be computed by different algorithms and access paths with different costs.

entries.title: What does a query plan add?
entries.text: Concrete algorithms and evaluation choices for algebra operations.

entries.title: What information helps cost estimates?
entries.text: Catalog statistics such as relation size, tuple size and distinct values; estimates may differ from measured execution.

entries.title: State the lecture’s estimated disk-time formula and define its counts and time units.
entries.text: b·tT+s·tS, where b counts transferred blocks and s counts seeks; both time parameters must use compatible units.

entries.title: Why can fewer transferred blocks still be slower?
entries.text: A plan may save transfers while adding expensive seeks. Compare both terms.

entries.title: What is omitted from the simplified comparison?
entries.text: The lecture focuses on disk access and typically ignores CPU and network in the model. Real elapsed time has additional factors.

entries.title: What is 1 millisecond in microseconds?
entries.text: 1000 microseconds. Convert units before adding time terms.

entries.title: What does JDBC stand for?
entries.text: Java Database Connectivity.

entries.title: Which driver class does the source use?
entries.text: com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver.

entries.title: Which method executes a query returning rows?
entries.text: executeQuery, returning a ResultSet.

entries.title: Which method is suitable for CREATE INDEX?
entries.text: executeUpdate, because the statement changes schema state rather than returning query rows.

entries.title: What does ResultSet.next() do?
entries.text: Advances the cursor to the next row and reports whether one exists.

entries.title: What proves index selection?
entries.text: An observed execution plan or equivalent server evidence, not index creation alone.

entries.title: What proves a speedup?
entries.text: Controlled measurements under comparable data, cache, server and timing conditions.

entries.title: What exact Java call does released Lab 02 Task 2 ask you to time?
entries.text: The newer task sheet releases timing only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); before and after indexing. See the Released Query Timing segment.

entries.title: What disagreement between the two JDBC setup documents needs confirmation?
entries.text: The privilege handout requires manual database creation, while Lab2 says provisioning is automatic.

entries.title: Does the static count of 614 parsed source records establish the number returned by MySQL for num=7?
entries.text: No. It is a static count from parsing supplied SQL, not an observed SELECT result. The recorded local run returned 607 rows for num=7; that historical count is also environment-specific, not a promised result for a future import.

entries.title: Which operation does released Task 2 time?
entries.text: Only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); with timestamps immediately before and after that call.

entries.title: Where must the result-iteration loop be placed, and does that exclude all row transfer from executeQuery timing?
entries.text: Place the application’s ResultSet.next() loop and printing after the ending timestamp. The driver may already retrieve and buffer rows inside executeQuery, so this does not exclude all data transfer from the measured call.

entries.title: How are nanoseconds converted to milliseconds?
entries.text: Subtract nanoTime timestamps and divide by 1_000_000.0.

entries.title: Which query stays constant?
entries.text: SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7, for both index states.

entries.title: Why compare multisets rather than row order?
entries.text: Without ORDER BY row order is not guaranteed; repeated keys/rows still require counts, so plain set equality can hide duplicates.

entries.title: Do historical faster timings prove indexing always wins?
entries.text: No. The recorded local result is a single environment observation with its own plan/data/cache/driver boundary.

entries.title: Why can fewer transfers still mean a slower plan?
entries.text: Seek time may dominate: compare B×tT+S×tS using the same time unit.

entries.title: What enables binary search on a file?
entries.text: Physical ordering on the selection attribute, not merely the existence of some index.

entries.title: What changes between clustered and unclustered equality retrieval?
entries.text: Clustered matches occupy consecutive blocks; scattered matches can require an I/O and seek for each record.

entries.title: What must an OR access plan cover?
entries.text: Every disjunct, including unindexed branches, and duplicate candidate pointers must not cause duplicate set results.

entries.title: Why can projection be expensive?
entries.text: Removing duplicate projected tuples requires grouping, often by sorting or hashing.

entries.title: How many initial runs and which merge fan-in?
entries.text: $N=\lceil b/M\rceil$ and $F=\lfloor M/b_b\rfloor-1$, with F at least two for multipass merging.

entries.title: What does the external-sort cost formula omit?
entries.text: The final sorted-output write; add it when a persistent sorted file is required.

entries.title: What must a natural join compare?
entries.text: Every shared attribute name, then return one copy of each shared column.

entries.title: What distinguishes tuple from block nested loops?
entries.text: The former rescans the inner input per outer tuple; the latter reuses an outer block for all its tuple comparisons.

entries.title: Which input needs an index for indexed nested loops?
entries.text: The inner relation needs an index on the equality join attribute.

entries.title: Why must merge-join costs include an ordering policy?
entries.text: Unsorted inputs need sorting; final-write and reread costs depend on materialisation versus streaming.

entries.title: Must the whole probe partition fit in memory?
entries.text: No: retain the build partition and stream the probe partition, subject to buffers and skew.

entries.title: Why is a hash collision insufficient for a join result?
entries.text: Equal keys hash together, but different keys can collide; check actual equality before emitting.

entries.title: What state supports correct partial AVG?
entries.text: Sum and count; combine their sums, then divide total sum by total count.

entries.title: What dataset belongs to Lab4 Q1?
entries.text: Customer1,000,000 records/8,000 blocks; depositor500,000 records/1,000 blocks.

entries.title: What makes Q2 numerically underdetermined?
entries.text: Physical ordering and per-key matching-block distribution are not fully established by the totals.

entries.title: How many merge passes sort12 blocks with3 frames?
entries.text: Two:4 initial runs become2 then1 with fan-in2.

entries.title: Why is an in-memory sort not necessarily free in Q6?
entries.text: The question requires sorted data written to disk, so include reading and writing those3 blocks.

entries.title: What inconsistency must Q5 report?
entries.text: The inherited M=100 cannot hold51 buffers of20 frames each; the one-pass premise needs clarification.

entries.title: What does an evaluation plan add to a logical expression?
entries.text: Algorithms for individual operations and a strategy for coordinating their execution.

entries.title: What does materialisation store?
entries.text: An intermediate result as a temporary relation for later operations to consume.

entries.title: Which cost must be added to the lecture's operator sums?
entries.text: Intermediate-result writes; check whether their reads are already included in the consuming operators.

entries.title: What happens when a push buffer is full?
entries.text: The producer waits until the consumer creates space.

entries.title: What must a pull operator retain between requests?
entries.text: State indicating where to resume when the next tuple is requested.

entries.title: What does an unlabelled plan edge mean in this lecture?
entries.text: Pipelining is assumed unavailable on that edge under the course convention.
