entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf
entries.text: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 1
entries.text: Database Development and Design (SOE201) Lecture 5a: Query Evaluation Part 1 Dr. Wei Wang AIAT

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 2
entries.text: Learning Outcomes n Algorithms for Evaluating Selection n Algorithms for Evaluating Projection n Algorithms for External Sorting 10/10/26 2

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 3
entries.text: Selection Operator n Notation: s p(r) n p is selection predicate n Defined by: sp(r) = {t | t Î r and p(t)} in which p is a formula of propositional calculus of terms connected by: Ù (and), Ú (or), ¬ (not) Each term is of form: <attribute> op [<attribute> or <constant>] where op can be one of: =, ¹, >, ³. <. £ n Selection example: s branch-name=‘Perryridge’ (account) 10/10/26 3

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 4
entries.text: Evaluation of Selection n File scan – search algorithms that scan files and retrieve records that fulfill selection condition. n Blocks of relation are stored contiguously n Also called linear scan n Index scan – search algorithms that use index n Selection condition must be on search key of index n By default, use B+-tree index 10/10/26 4

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 5
entries.text: Algorithm for Selection (File Scan: Linear Search) n Scan each block and test all records to see whether they satisfy selection condition. n Cost estimate = br block transfers + 1 seek n br denotes number of blocks containing records from relation r n If selection is on key attribute, can stop on finding record (Linear Search, Equality on Key) n Average cost = (br /2) block transfers + 1 seek n Linear search can be always applied, regardless of: n Selection condition n Ordering of records in file, or n Availability of indices 10/10/26 5

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 6
entries.text: Algorithms for Selection (File Scan: Binary Search) n Applicable only if selection is equality comparison on attribute on which file is ordered. n Cost estimate (number of block transfers and seeks): n Cost of locating first tuple by binary search on blocks n élog2(br)ù block transfers and élog2(br)ù seeks n In time: élog2(br)ù * (tT + tS) n If there are multiple records satisfying selection n Add transfer cost of number of blocks containing records that satisfy selection condition n If br is not too big, then most likely binary search doesn’t pay. n Note that tT is several (say, 40) times smaller than tS n Two algorithms needs to be wisely chosen for specific query at hands. 10/10/26 6

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 7
entries.text: Selection Using Indices (Primary Index on Candidate Key, Equality) n Cost to retrieve single record that satisfies corresponding equality condition n (hi + 1) block transfers, and (hi + 1) seeks n hi is height of B+-tree index n In time: (hi + 1) * (tT + tS) n Recall that height of B+-tree index is at most élogén/2ù(K)ù, where n is number of pointers per node and K is number of unique search keys. n E.g. for relation with 1,000,000 (1 million) different search keys, and with 100 index entries per node, hi = 4 n Unless relation is really small, this algorithms always “pays” when indexes are available. 10/10/26 7

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 8
entries.text: Selection Using Indices (Primary Index on Non-key, Equality) n Retrieve possibly multiple records. n Records are on consecutive blocks n Cost: n (hi + b) block transfers and (hi +1) seeks n b is number of blocks containing matching records n Once first record in found, rest can be read sequentially n In time n (hi + b) * tT + (hi +1) * tS , or n hi * (tT + tS) + tS + tT * b 10/10/26 8

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 9
entries.text: Selection Using Indices (Equality on Candidate Key, Secondary Index) n Retrieve single record as search- key is candidate key n (hi + 1) block transfers and (hi + 1) seeks n In time: (hi + 1) * (tT + tS) 10/10/26 9

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 10
entries.text: Selection Using Indices (Equality on Non-key, Secondary Index) n Retrieve multiple records if search- key is not candidate key n Each of n matching records may reside on different block n Cost: n (hi + n) block transfers and (hi + n) seeks n Can be very expensive if n is big. n Note n multiplies time for seek. 10/10/26 10

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 11
entries.text: Comparative Selection sA£V (r) or sA ³ V(r) n Using linear scan or binary search just as before. n Using primary index, comparison n For sA ³ V(r), use index to find first tuple ³ v and scan relation sequentially from there n For sA£V (r) just scan relation sequentially till first tuple > v; n Using index would be useless, and require extra seeks on index file. n Using secondary index, comparison n For sA ³ V(r) use index to find first index entry ³ v and scan index sequentially from there, to find pointers to records. n For sA£V (r) just scan leaf pages of index to find pointers to records, till first entry > v n In either case, retrieving records n Requires I/O for each record (lot) n Linear file scan may be much cheaper 10/10/26 11

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 12
entries.text: Conjunctive Selection sq1Ù q2Ù. . . Ù qn(r) n Using one index n First select qi and previous algorithms that results in least cost for sqi (r). n Then test other conditions on tuples after fetching them into memory buffer. n Choice of first condition is crucial. n One must use estimates to know which one is best. n Using multiple-key index n Use appropriate composite (multiple-key) index if available. 10/10/26 12

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 13
entries.text: Disjunctive Selection sq1Ú q2 Ú. . . Ú qn (r) n Use linear scan. n Or, use index scan if some conditions have available indices. n Use corresponding index for each condition, and take union of all obtained sets of record pointers. n Then fetch records from file 10/10/26 13

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 14
entries.text: Selection With Negation: s¬q(r) n Use linear scan n If index is applicable to q n Find satisfying records using index n s¬q(r) is simply set of tuples in r that are not in sq(r) 10/10/26 14

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 15
entries.text: Evaluating Projection n Projection drops columns not in selected attribute list. n Expensive part is removing duplicates. n Duplicate elimination can be implemented via hashing or sorting. n On sorting, duplicates will come adjacent to each other, duplicates can be deleted. n Hashing is similar; duplicates will go into same bucket. 10/10/26 15

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 16
entries.text: Sorting n Sorting algorithms are important in query processing at least for two reasons: n Query itself may require sorting (order by clause) n Some algorithms for other operations, like merge join, set operations and aggregation, require that relations are previously sorted and duplicates removed. n To sort relation: n May build index on relation, and then use index to read relation in sorted order. n This only sorts relation logically, not physically n May lead to one disk block access for each tuple. n For relations that fit in memory, sorting algorithms like quicksort, selection and insertion sort, can be used. 10/10/26 16

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 17
entries.text: External Sort-Merge n For relations that don’t fit in memory, need special algorithms, e.g. external sort-merge. n Take into account block transfers and seeks. n Let M denote memory size: number of disk blocks whose contents can be buffered in main memory. n First thing to do is to create sorted runs. Let i be 0 initially. Repeat following till end of relation: (a) Read M blocks of relation into memory; (b) Sort in-memory blocks; (c) Write sorted data to run file Ri ; (d) Increment i. Let final value of i be N (that is, there are N run files) n Next step: merge sorted runs 10/10/26 17

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 18
entries.text: External Sort-Merge cont’d Merge sorted runs (N-way merge): assume N < M. 1. Use N blocks of memory to buffer input runs (1 for each of N run files), and 1 block to buffer output. Read first block of each run into memory. 2. Repeat 1. Select first record in sort order (i.e. smallest) among all buffer pages 2. Write record to output buffer. If output buffer is full write it to disk. 3. Delete record from its input buffer page. 4. If buffer page becomes empty then read next block (if any) of run into buffer. 3. Until all input buffer pages are empty 10/10/26 18

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 19
entries.text: External Sort-Merge (Cont.) n If N ³ M, several merge passes are required. n In each pass, contiguous groups of M - 1 runs are merged. n One pass reduces number of runs by factor of M -1 (and creates runs longer by same factor). n For example, if M=11, and there are 90 runs, one pass reduces number of runs to 9, each 10 times size of initial runs n Repeated passes are performed till all runs have been merged into one. 10/10/26 19

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 20
entries.text: Example: External Sorting Using Sort-Merge Suppose that relation has 12 blocks; one tuple fits in one block; memory holds at most three blocks. 10/10/26 20

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 21
entries.text: Cost Analysis n Assume relation in br blocks, memory size M, number of run file ébr/M ù. n Buffer size bb (read bb blocks from each run and bb blocks for output writing; before it was assumed bb =1). n Cost of Block Transfer n Each time can merge ⌊(M-bb)/bb⌋ runs, i.e. ⌊(M/bb⌋-1; n So, total number of merge passes required: élog⌊M/bb⌋–1 ébr/M ùù. n Block transfers for initial run creation as well as in each pass is 2br (read/write all br blocks). n Thus total number of block transfers (For final pass, we don’t count write cost): 2br + 2br élog⌊M/bb⌋–1 ébr/M ùù - br = br ( 2 élog⌊M/bb⌋–1 ébr/M ùù + 1) n Cost of seeks n During run generation: one seek to read each run and one seek to write each run 2 ébr / Mù n During merge phase: need 2 ébr / bbù seeks for each merge pass n Total number of seeks: 2 ébr / Mù + 2 ébr / bbù élog⌊M/bb⌋-1 ébr/M ùù - ébr / bbù = 2 ébr / Mù + ébr / bbù (2 élog⌊M/bb⌋-1 ébr/M ùù -1) 10/10/26 21

entries.title: Lecture5a - Query Evaluation 1.pdf · p. 22

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 1
entries.text: Database Development and Design (SOE201) Lecture 5b: Query Evaluation Part 2 Dr. Wei Wang AIAT

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 2
entries.text: Learning Outcomes n Algorithms for Evaluating Join n Nested Loop Join n Block Nested Loop Join n Indexed Nested Loop Join n Merge Join n Hash Join n Algorithms for Evaluating Aggregation n Algorithms for Evaluating Set Operations

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 3
entries.text: Natural-Join Operator Notation: r s n Let r and s be relations on schemas R and S respectively. Then, r s is relation on schema R È S obtained as follows: n Consider each pair of tuples tr from r and ts from s. n If tr and ts have same value on each of attributes in R Ç S, add tuple t to result, where n t has same value as tr on r n t has same value as ts on s n Example: R = (A, B, C, D) S = (E, B, D) n Result schema = (A, B, C, D, E) n r s is defined as: Õr.A, r.B, r.C, r.D, s.E (sr.B = s.B Ù r.D = s.D (r x s))

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 4
entries.text: Join Operation n Several different algorithms to implement joins exist n Nested-loop join n Block nested-loop join n Indexed nested-loop join n Merge-join n Hash-join n Choice is based on cost estimate.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 5
entries.text: Banking Example § Examples in rest slides use following information: § Number of records of customer: 10,000 § Number of blocks of customer: 400 § Number of records of depositor: 5,000 § Number of blocks of depositor: 100

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 6
entries.text: Nested-Loop Join n Simple join algorithm that can be used independently of everything. n To compute theta join: r q s for each tuple tr in r do begin for each tuple ts in s do begin test pair (tr,ts) to see if they satisfy join condition q if they do, add tr • ts to the result; end end n r is called outer relation and s inner relation of join. n Quite expensive in general, since it requires to examine every pair of tuples in two relations.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 7
entries.text: Nested-Loop Join cont’d n In worst case, if there is enough memory only to hold one block of each relation. n By default, worse scenarios are always considered unless explicitly stated. n Let nr be number of tuples in relation r, br and bs be number of blocks of r and s. Estimated cost is: n nr * bs + br block transfers, and n nr + br seeks n If smaller relation fits entirely in memory, use it as inner relation. n Reduces cost to br + bs block transfers and 2 seeks n In general (but not always), it is better to have smaller relation as outer relation if none fits in memory.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 8
entries.text: Nested-Loop Join Cost - Example n Assuming worst case memory availability, cost estimate is n with depositor as outer relation: n 5,000 * 400 + 100 = 2,000,100 block transfers, n 5,000 + 100 = 5,100 seeks n with customer as outer relation n 10,000 * 100 + 400 = 1,000,400 block transfers, n 10,000 + 400 = 10,400 seeks n If smaller relation (depositor) fits entirely in memory, cost estimate will be 500 block transfers and 2 seeks

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 9
entries.text: Block Nested-Loop Join n Variant of nested-loop join in which every block of inner relation is paired with every block of outer relation. for each block Br of r do begin for each block Bs of s do begin for each tuple tr in Br do begin for each tuple ts in Bs do begin Check if (tr,ts) satisfy join condition; if they do, add tr • ts to result; end end end end

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 10
entries.text: Block Nested-Loop Join Cost n Worst case estimate: n br * bs + br block transfers, and n 2 * br seeks n Each block in inner relation s is read once for each block in outer relation (instead of once for each tuple in outer relation). n If smaller relation fits into memory, cost is: br + bs block transfers and 2 seeks.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 11
entries.text: Indexed Nested-Loop Join n Index lookups can replace file scans if n Join is equi-join or natural join, and n Index is available on inner relation’s join attribute n To compute join For each tuple tr in outer relation r use index on inner relation s to look up tuples that satisfy join condition with tuple tr if they do, add tr • ts to result; n In some cases, it pays to construct index just to compute join.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 12
entries.text: Indexed Nested-Loop Join – cont’d n Worst case: buffer has space for only one page of r. n Cost of join: br + nr * c block transfers and br + nr * c seeks n Where c is cost of traversing index and fetching all matching s tuples for one tuple in r, e.g. hi +1 using B+-tree. n c can be estimated as cost of single selection on s using join condition n If indices are available on join attributes of both r and s, use relation with fewer tuples as outer relation.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 13
entries.text: Example of Indexed Nested- Loop Join Costs n Compute depositor customer using indexed nested loop join, with depositor as outer relation. n Suppose customer have primary B+-tree index on join attribute customer-name (also key in this case), with n=20. n customer has 10,000 tuples, height of B+-tree is at most 4, and one more access is needed to find actual data n Relation depositor has 5,000 tuples n Nested loop join: 2,000,100 block transfers and 5,100 seeks n Block nested loops join: 400*100 + 100 = 40,100 block transfers and 2 * 100 = 200 seeks n Indexed nested loops join: 100 + 5,000 * (4+1) = 25,100 block transfers and seeks. n Number of block transfers is less than that for block nested loop n But number of seeks is much larger n In this case, using Indexed Nested Loop Join doesn’t pay

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 14
entries.text: Merge-Join n Merge join needs two steps: n Sort both relations on join attribute, if not already sorted; n Join step is similar to merge stage of external sort-merge. n Merge-join algorithm n Initialise two pointers, pr and ps, pointing to r and s n While not done n pr and ps move through relations. n Group of tuples of inner relation s with same value on join attributes is read into set Ss . n Do join on tuple pointed to by pr and tuples in Ss n End while

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 16
entries.text: Merge-Join cont’d n Only for equi-joins and natural joins n Each block needs to be read only once n Assuming that all tuples for any given value of join attributes fit in memory n Thus, cost of merge join is: br + bs block transfers + ébr / bbù + ébs / bbù seeks n Plus cost of sorting if relations are unsorted. n bb is number of blocks allocated in memory for each relation n It makes sense to allocate multiple buffer blocks to each relation, provided extra memory is available.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 17
entries.text: Hash-Join n Only applicable for equi-joins and natural joins. n Hash function h is used to partition tuples of both relations n h maps JoinAttrs values to patitions {0, 1, ..., n}, where JoinAttrs denotes common attributes of r and s. n r0, r1, . . ., rn denote partitions of r tuples n Each tuple tr Î r is put in partition ri where i = h(tr [JoinAttrs]). n s0, s1. . ., sn denotes partitions of s tuples n Each tuple ts Îs is put in partition si, where i = h(ts [JoinAttrs]). n General idea: n Partition relations according to above n Perform join on each partitions ri and si n No need to compute join between different partitions n If value is hashed to i, r tuple having that value is in ri and s tuple having that value is in si.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 19
entries.text: Hash-Join Algorithm 1. Partition relation s using hashing function h. When partitioning relation, some blocks of memory (bb) are reserved for input buffer and output buffer for each partition; 2. Partition r similarly; 3. For each partition i: (a) Load si into memory and build in-memory hash index using join attribute. This hash index uses different hash function than earlier h for partitioning. (b) Read tuples in ri from disk. For each tuple tr, locate each matching tuple ts in si using in-memory hash index. Output concatenation of their attributes. Relation s is called build input and r is called probe input.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 20
entries.text: Hash-Join Algorithm cont’d n Number of partitions n for hash function h is chosen such that each si should fit in memory. n Typically n is chosen as ébs/Mù * f, where f is “fudge factor”, typically around 1.2, to avoid overflows n Probe relation partitions ri need not fit in memory

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 21
entries.text: Cost of Hash-Join n Cost of hash join: n 3(br + bs) + 4 * nh block transfers n Or, 2(br + bs) + 2 * nh + (br + bs) + 2 * nh n 2( ébr / bbù + ébs / bbù) + 2 * nh seeks n Each of nh partitions could have partially filled block that has to be written and read back n Build and probe phases require only one seek for each of nh partitions of each relation, since each partition can be read sequentially. n If entire build input can be kept in main memory (then no partitioning is required), cost estimate goes down to br + bs and 2 seeks.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 22
entries.text: Cost of Hash-Join Example n Assume that memory size is 20 blocks, bdepositor= 100 and bcustomer = 400. n Assume relation depositor is used as build input. Partition it into five partitions, each of size 20 blocks. n Similarly, partition customer into five partitions, each of size 80. n Assuming bb=3 blocks are allocated for input buffer and output buffer n Therefore total cost: 3(100 + 400) + 4*5= 1，520 block transfers + 2( é100/3ù + é400/3ù) + 2*5 = 346 seeks n Compare to previous algorithms: n Block nested loop: 40,100 block transfers and 200 seeks; n Index nested loop: 25,100 block transfers and 25,100 seeks.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 23
entries.text: Aggregation n Aggregation can be implemented similarly to duplicate elimination. n Sorting or hashing can be used to bring tuples into same group together, and then aggregate functions can be applied on each group. n Optimisation: combine tuples in same group during run generation and intermediate merges, by computing partial aggregate values n For count, min, max, sum: keep aggregate values on tuples found so far in group. n For avg, keep sum and count, and divide sum by count.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 24
entries.text: Set Operations n Set operations (È, Ç and -): can either use variant of merge- join after sorting, or variant of hash-join. n Set operations using hashing: n Partition both relations using same hash function n Process each partition i as follows. n Using different hashing function, build in-memory hash index on ri. n Process si as follows ! rÈs n Add tuples in si to hash index if they are not in. n At end, add tuples in hash index to result. ! rÇs n Output tuples in si to result if they are already in hash index ! r–s n For each tuple in si, if it is in hash index, delete it from index. n At end, add remaining tuples in hash index to result.

entries.title: Lecture5b - Query Evaluation 2.pdf · p. 25
entries.text: End of Lecture n Reading n Textbook Chapters 15.5 and 15.6 10/10/26 25

entries.text: Database Development and Design (SOE201) Lecture 6a: Introduction to Query Optimisation 1 Dr. Wei Wang AIAT

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 2
entries.text: Learning Outcomes n Introduction to Query Optimisation n Materialisation and Pipelining n Equivalence Rules n Transformation of Relational Expressions n Generation of Equivalent Expressions

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 3
entries.text: Evaluation of Expressions n So far we have seen algorithms for individual operators n These have then to be combined to evaluate complex expressions with multiple operations.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 4
entries.text: Evaluation of Expressions – cont’d n Alternatives for evaluating expression tree n Materialisation: generate results for expression whose inputs are relations or relations that are already computed. Temporary relations must be materialised (stored) on disk. n Pipelining: pass on tuples to parent operators even as operation is being executed (no need to store temporary results onto disk).

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 5
entries.text: Materialisation n Materialised evaluation: Use intermediate results materialised into temporary relations to evaluate next-level operations. n e.g. compute and store selection (treat it as new relation), then compute join with customer and store result, and finally compute projections on customer-name.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 6
entries.text: Materialisation cont’d n Materialised evaluation is always applicable. n May require considerable storage space: cost of writing results to disk and reading them back can be quite high n Cost formulas learned so far ignore cost of writing final results to disk, so n Overall cost = Sum of costs of individual operators + cost of writing intermediate results to disk

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 7
entries.text: Pipelining n Pipelined evaluation: evaluate several operations simultaneously, passing results of one operation on to next. n e.g. in previous expression tree, don’t store result of selection n instead, pass tuples directly to join. n Similarly, don’t store result of join, pass tuples directly to projection. n Cheaper than materialisation: no need to store temporary relation to disk. n However, pipelining may not always be possible, e.g. external merge-sort and hash-join where preliminary phase is required over whole relations.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 8
entries.text: Pipelining – cont’d n Pipelines can be executed in two ways: demand driven and producer driven n Producer-driven (or eager or push) n Operators produce tuples eagerly and pass to parents n Buffer maintained between operators, child puts tuples in buffer, parent removes tuples from buffer n If buffer is full, child waits till there is space in buffer, and then generates more tuples n Demand driven (or lazy, or pull) n System repeatedly requests next tuple from top level operator n Each operation requests next tuple from child operations as required, in order to output its next tuple n In between calls, operation has to maintain “state” so it knows what to return next.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 9
entries.text: Evaluation Plan n Evaluation plan defines exactly what algorithm is used for each operation, and how execution of operations is coordinated.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 10
entries.text: Notes on Using Pipelining n If edge in evaluation tree is labelled with pipeline, then pipelining can be used. n For join operations, unless stated explicitly, only nested-loop-family join can always use pipelining. n If edge in evaluation tree is NOT labelled with pipelining, then it is assumed that pipelining cannot be used. n Annotations will be made explicit. 10/17/26 10

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 11
entries.text: Cost-based Query Optimisation n Cost difference between evaluation plans for given query can be enormous n E.g. seconds vs. days in some cases n Cost-based query optimisation n Find logically equivalent expressions of given expression n Estimate cost of all plans, e.g. n Choose algorithms to use for executing operator n Choose specific indices to use n Select detailed strategy with ”least” cost (optimised plan)

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 12
entries.text: Cost-based Query Optimisation – cont’d n Estimation of plan cost based on: n Statistical information about relations, e.g. number of tuples, number of distinct values for attribute n Statistical estimation for intermediate results to compute cost of complex expressions n Cost formulae for algorithms, computed using statistics n Since cost is estimate, selected plan is not necessarily least-costly plan; n However, as long as estimates are good, chosen plan will not be much more costly than least-costly one.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 13
entries.text: Equivalent expressions n Alternative ways of evaluating given query n Equivalent expressions n Different algorithms for each operation

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 14
entries.text: Transformation of Relational Expressions n Two relational algebra expressions are said to be equivalent if they generate same set of tuples on every legal database instance n Note: order of tuples is irrelevant n In SQL, inputs and outputs are multisets of tuples n Two expressions in multiset version of relational algebra are said to be equivalent if the two expressions generate same multiset of tuples on every legal database instance. n Equivalence rule says that expressions of two forms are equivalent if n Can replace expression of first form by second, or vice versa

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 15
entries.text: Equivalence Rules n Rule 1: Conjunctive selection operations can be deconstructed into sequence of individual selections. s q Ùq ( E ) = s q (s q ( E )) 1 2 1 2 n Rule 2: Selection operations are commutative. s q (s q ( E )) = s q (s q ( E )) 1 2 2 1 n Rule 3: Only last one in sequence of projection operations is needed, others can be omitted. P L1 (P L2 (! (P Ln ( E )) !)) = P L1 ( E ) n Rule 4: Selections can be combined with Cartesian products and theta joins. n (a). sq(E1 X E2) = E1 q E2 n (b). sq1(E1 q2 E2) = E1 q1Ù q2 E2

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 16
entries.text: Equivalence Rules cont’d n Rule 5: Theta-join operations (and natural joins) are commutative. E1 q E2 = E2 q E1 n Rule 6. n (a) Natural join operations are associative: ( E1 E2 ) E3 = E 1 ( E2 E3 ) n (b) Theta joins are associative in following manner: (E1 q1 E2) q2Ù q3 E3 = E1 q1Ù q3 (E2 q2 E3) where q2 involves attributes from only E2 and E3

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 17
entries.text: Equivalence Rules cont’d n Rule 7. Selection operation distributes over theta join operation under following two conditions: n (a) When q0 involves only attributes of one of expressions (E1) being joined. sq0(E1 q E2) = (sq0(E1)) q E2 n (b) When q1 involves only attributes of E1 and q2 involves only attributes of E2. sq1Ùq2 (E1 q E2) = (sq1(E1)) q (sq2 (E2))

entries.text: Pictorial Depiction of Equivalence Rules

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 19
entries.text: Equivalence Rules cont’d n Rule 8. Projection operation distributes over theta join operation as follows: n (a) Let L1 and L2 be attributes from E1 and E2, if q involves only attributes from L1 È L2: ÕL1 ÈL2 ( E1 q E2 ) = (ÕL1 ( E1 )) q (ÕL2 ( E2 )) n (b) Consider join E1 q E2. n let L1 and L2 be sets of attributes from E1 and E2, respectively. n let L3 be attributes of E1 that are involved in join condition q, but are not in L1 È L2, and n let L4 be attributes of E2 that are involved in join condition q, but are not in L1 È L2. Õ L È L ( E1 1 2 q E2 ) = Õ L1 È L2 ((Õ L1 È L3 ( E1 )) q( Õ L È L ( E2 ))) 2 4

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 20
entries.text: Equivalence Rules cont’d n Rule 9. Set union and intersection are commutative (set difference is not commutative) E1 È E2 = E2 È E1 E1 Ç E2 = E2 Ç E1 n Rule 10. Set union and intersection are associative (set difference is not associative). (E1 È E2) È E3 = E1 È (E2 È E3) (E1 Ç E2) Ç E3 = E1 Ç (E2 Ç E3) n Rule 11. Selection operation distributes over È, Ç and –. sq (E1 È E2) = sq (E1) È sq(E2) sq (E1 Ç E2) = sq (E1) Ç sq(E2) sq (E1 – E2) = sq (E1) – sq(E2) n Rule 12. Projection operation distributes over union PL(E1 È E2) = (PL(E1)) È (PL(E2))

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 22
entries.text: Example: Pushing Selections n Query: Find names of all customers who have account at some branches located in Brooklyn. Pcustomer_name(sbranch_city = “Brooklyn”(branch (account depositor))) n Transformation using rule 7a (distribute selection). Pcustomer_name((sbranch_city =“Brooklyn” (branch)) (account depositor)) n Performing selection as early as possible reduces sizes of relations to be joined.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 23
entries.text: Example: Multiple Transformations n Query: Find names of all customers with account at Brooklyn branch whose account balance is over $1000. Pcustomer_name((sbranch_city = “Brooklyn” Ù balance > 1000 (branch (account depositor))) n Transformation using join associatively (Rules 6a and 7a): Pcustomer_name((sbranch_city = “Brooklyn” Ù balance > 1000 (branch account)) depositor) n Then, apply “perform selections early” (Rule 7b) sbranch_city = “Brooklyn” (branch) sbalance > 1000 (account) n Thus, sequence of transformations can be useful.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 24
entries.text: Multiple Transformations cont’d

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 25
entries.text: Transformation Example: Pushing Projections Pcustomer_name((sbranch_city = “Brooklyn” (branch) account) depositor) n When compute (sbranch_city = “Brooklyn” (branch) account ) we obtain relation whose schema is: (branch_name, branch_city, assets, account_number, balance) n Push projections using equivalence rules 8b; eliminate unneeded attributes from intermediate results to get: Pcustomer_name ((Paccount_number ( (sbranch_city = “Brooklyn” (branch) account )) depositor )) (HINT: L1 is null, L2 is customer_name; L3=L4=account_number) n Performing projection as early as possible reduces sizes of tuples to be joined.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6a - Query Optimisation 1.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 26
entries.text: Join Ordering Example n For relations r1, r2, and r3, (r1 r2) r3 = r1 (r2 r3 ) (Join Associativity) n If r2 r3 is quite large and r1 r2 is small, may choose (r1 r2) r3 to compute and store smaller temporary relation.

entries.text: Estimation of Size of Selection n sA=v(r) n nr / V(A,r) : number of records that satisfy selection n Equality condition on key attribute: size estimate = 1 if it exists n sA£v (r) (case of sA ³ v (r) is symmetric) n Let c denote estimated number of tuples satisfying condition. n Let min(A,r) and max(A,r) denote lowest and highest values for attribute A. n If min(A,r) and max(A,r) are available in catalog n c = 0 if v < min(A,r) v - min( A, r ) n c = nr . max( A, r ) - min( A, r ) n If histograms available, can refine above estimate n In absence of statistical information c is assumed to be nr/ 2.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 5
entries.text: Estimation of Size of Joins n Cartesian product r x s contains nr .ns tuples; each tuple occupies sr + ss bytes. n If R Ç S = Æ (same as Cartesian product), then r s is same as r x s. n If R Ç S is key for R, then tuple of s will join with at most one tuple from r n Therefore, number of tuples in r s is no greater than number of tuples in s. n If R Ç S is foreign key in S referencing R, then number of tuples in r s is exactly same as number of tuples in s. n Case for R Ç S being foreign key referencing S is symmetric.

entries.text: Banking Example § Number of records of customer: 10,000 § Number of blocks of customer: 400 § Number of records of depositor: 5,000 § Number of blocks of depositor: 100 § Example query: “depositor customer”, customer_name in depositor is foreign key (referencing customer), hence, result has exactly ndepositor tuples, which is 5,000.

entries.text: Estimation of Size of Joins cont’d n If R Ç S = {A} is not key for R or S. If assume that every tuple t in R produces tuples in R S, number of tuples in R S is estimated to be: nr * ns V ( A, s ) If reverse is true, estimate obtained will be: nr * ns V ( A, r ) Lower of these two estimates is probably more accurate.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 8
entries.text: Join Operation: Running Example n Running example n compute size estimates for “depositor customer” without using information about foreign keys. n Catalog information: n n = 10,000; f customer = 25, which implies that b customer customer =10,000/25 = 400. n n = 5000; f depositor = 50, which implies that b depositor depositor = 5,000/50 = 100. n V(customer_name, depositor) = 2,500 n Implies that, on average, each customer has two accounts. n V(customer_name, customer) = 10,000 (primary key) n Two estimates are: nr * ns n V ( A, s ) = 5,000 * 10,000/2,500 = 20,000 nr * ns n V ( A, r ) = 5,000 * 10,000/10,000 = 5,000 n Choose lower estimate, which in this case, is same as earlier estimate using foreign keys (customer_name in depositor is foreign key on customer, so size is 5,000).

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 9
entries.text: Size Estimation for Other Operations n Projection: estimated size of ÕA(r) =V(A,r) n Set operations n For unions/intersections of selections on same relation: rewrite and use size estimate for selections. Let si denote size of sqi (r). n Conjunction: n Disjunction: nr * ( ) n For operations on different relations: n estimated size of r È s = size of r + size of s. n estimated size of r Ç s = minimum size of r and size of s. n estimated size of r – s = r. n All three estimates may be quite inaccurate, but provide upper bounds on sizes.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 10
entries.text: Estimation of Number of Distinct Values in Selection n If q forces A to take specified value:V (A,sq (r)) = 1, e.g. A = 3 n If q forces A to take on one of specified set of values:V(A,sq (r)) = number of specified values, e.g. (A = 1 V A = 3 V A = 4 ) n If selection condition q is of form: A op v (op is >, <, etc); s is selectivity of selection. V(A,sq (r)) = V(A,r) * s n In all other cases: use approximate estimate of min(V(A,r), nsq (r) )

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 11
entries.text: Estimation of Number of Distinct Values in Join n If all attributes in A are from r, then estimated V(A, r s) = min (V(A,r), n r s) n If A contains attributes A1 from r and A2 from s, then estimated V(A, r s) = min(V(A1,r)*V(A2 – A1,s), V(A1 – A2,r)*V(A2,s), nr s)

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 12
entries.text: Cost-Based Join Order Optimisation n Consider finding best join-order for r1 r2 . . . rn n There are (2(n – 1))!/(n – 1)! different join orders for above expression. n With n = 3, number is 12 n With n = 5, number is 1,680 n With n = 10, number is greater than 17 billion! n No need to generate all join orders. n Using dynamic programming, least-cost join order for any subset of {r1, r2, . . . rn } is computed only once and stored for future use.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 15
entries.text: Dynamic Programming in Join Order Optimisation n To find best plan (join tree) for set of n relations: n Consider all possible plans of form: S1 (S – S1), where S1 is any non-empty subset of S. n Recursively compute cost for joining subsets of S to find cost of each plan. Choose cheapest of alternatives. n Base case for recursion: single relation access plan n e.g. find best selection strategy for particular relation Ri n When plan for any subset is computed, store and reuse it when required again, instead of re- computing it.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 16
entries.text: Join Order Optimisation Algorithm // initialise bestplan[S].cost to ∞ procedure findbestplan(S) if (bestplan[S].cost ¹ ¥) return bestplan[S] // else bestplan[S] has not been computed earlier, compute it now if (S contains only one relation) set bestplan[S].plan and bestplan[S].cost based on best way of accessing S /* Using selections on S, e.g. indices on S */ else for each non-empty subset S1 of S such that S1 ¹ S P1= findbestplan(S1) P2= findbestplan(S - S1) A = best algorithm for joining results of P1 and P2 cost = P1.cost + P2.cost + cost of A if cost < bestplan[S].cost bestplan[S].cost = cost bestplan[S].plan = “execute P1.plan; execute P2.plan; join results of P1 and P2 using A” return bestplan[S]

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 17
entries.text: Cost of Join Order Optimisation n With dynamic programming, time complexity of optimisation with bushy trees is O(3n). n With n = 10, this number is 59,000 instead of 176 billion! n Space complexity is O(2n) as number of subsets of S is 2n n Although both numbers still increase rapidly with n, commonly occurring joins usually have less than 10 relations, and can be handled easily.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 18
entries.text: Choice of Evaluation Plans n Must consider interaction of evaluation techniques when choosing evaluation plans n Choosing cheapest algorithm for each operator independently may not yield best overall algorithm n Merge-join may be costlier than hash-join, but may provide sorted output which reduces cost for outer level aggregation. n Nested-loop family joins may provide opportunity for pipelining n Practical query optimisers incorporate elements of following two broad approaches: n Search all plans and choose best in cost-based fashion. n Use heuristics.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 19
entries.text: Cost-Based Optimisation with Equivalence Rules n General-purpose cost-based optimiser based on equivalence rules n Easy to extend optimiser with new rules to handle different query constructs n But procedure to enumerate all equivalent expressions is very expensive n Many optimisers follow approach based on n Heuristic transformations to handle constructs other than joins n Applying cost-based join order selection algorithm to subexpressions involving only joins and selections n To make the approach work efficiently requires following: n Space-efficient representation of expressions n Efficient techniques for detecting duplicate derivations of same expression n Dynamic programming based on memoisation n Avoid generating all possible equivalent plans 10/17/26 19

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 20
entries.text: Heuristic Optimisation n Cost-based optimisation is expensive, even with dynamic programming. n Systems may use heuristics to reduce number of choices that must be made in cost-based fashion. n Heuristic optimisation transforms query-tree by using set of rules that typically (but not in all cases) improve execution performance: n Perform selection early (reduces number of tuples) n Perform projection early (reduces number of attributes) n Perform most restrictive selection and join operations (i.e. with smallest result size) before other similar operations. n Some systems use only heuristics, others combine heuristics with partial cost-based optimisation.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 21
entries.text: Other heuristics: Left Deep Join Trees n In left-deep join tree, right-hand-side input for each join is relation, not result of intermediate join.

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 22
entries.text: Cost of Left Deep Join Optimisation n To find best left-deep join tree for set of n relations: n Consider n alternatives with one relation as right-hand side input and other relations as left-hand side input. n Modify dynamic programming optimisation algorithm: n Replace “for each non-empty subset S1 of S such that S1 ¹ S” n By: for each relation r in S, let S1 = S – r. n If only left-deep trees are considered, time complexity of finding best join order is O(n!), with dynamic programming this can be reduced to O(n 2n) n Space complexity remains at O(2n) n Cost-based optimisation is expensive, but worthwhile for queries on large datasets (typical queries have small n, generally < 10)

entries.title: Week 6 · Lecture6b - Query Optimisation 2.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 23
entries.text: Structure of Query Optimisers n Many optimisers considers only left-deep join orders. n Plus heuristics to push selections and projections down query tree n Reduces optimisation complexity and generates plans amenable to pipelined evaluation. n Even with use of heuristics, cost-based query optimisation imposes substantial overhead. n But worth for expensive queries n Optimisers often use simple heuristics for very cheap queries, and perform exhaustive enumeration for more expensive queries

entries.title: Software Engineering I — Tutor Mode
entries.text: Software Engineering I — Tutor Mode SOE203 · Companion edition. The standard notes remain your reference. How to use this companion Orient with In 60 Seconds and Concept Preview → learn the mechanism → close references and attempt recall/practice → open a hint if needed → compare reasoning → record a demonstrated gap → revisit the explanation → try transfer. Preview cards orient you; recall cards test retrieval. Reading a solution is not evidence of mastery, and no fixed review interval is claimed optimal. Six complete historical question sections are available inside ExamsSoftware1.pdf: five coded CPT203 papers and one XJTLU-branded set with no visible code/date. XJTLU's catalogue identifies CPT203 as Software Engineering I, but the local material says SOE203; the code equivalence is unconfirmed. Use the corpus as adjacent-code historical evidence, not proof of the current format. No official marking scheme is supplied. All study status starts untested. Optional chat conventions include /teach, /quiz, /grade, /weak, /cram; they do not run automatically. Resume from the tutor state, preserving prior attempts and source versions. Standard course index · Source scope and unresolved issues Unit 01 — Introduction and Professional Responsibility - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference Unit 02 — Software Processes - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference Unit 03 — Empirical Development and Scrum - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference - Original practical lab Unit 04 — Requirements Engineering and SRS - Tutor Notes - Recall and Practice - Standard reference - Original practical lab If You Are Short on Time > [!warning] Evidence boundary > The six question sections are fully visible, but cover pages are missing, one set is undated, the local course code differs, and no marking scheme is present. This is a study-priority guide based on the supplied historical assessment sample, not a forecast of the next exam. Open the complete paper inventory, marks and limitations Priority 1 — High Exam Relevance Follow prerequisites first, then use the observed history: 1. Process models and justified selection — observed in 6/6 question sections, 112 known marks across process/agile allocations. Learn the decision method in Unit 02 · 5-Minute Review, then attempt Unit 02 · Problem T1. 2. Requirements engineering and specification — observed in 6/6, 68 known marks, plus use-case modelling in 2/6 for 30 marks. Review Unit 04 · Definitions and distinctions, then attempt Unit 04 · Problem E1. 3. Agile decision reasoning — observed in 5/6, 55 shared marks; only one set directly tests Scrum mechanics. Review Unit 03 · 5-Minute Review, then attempt Unit 03 · Problem E1. The mark groups above are not additive: agile allocations overlap the broad process total. Priority 2 — Medium Exam Relevance - Fundamental lifecycle activities — observed once for 8 marks, shared with Unit 02. Use Unit 01 · 5-Minute Review and Card 11. - Specific Scrum mechanics — directly observed once for 6 marks even though broader agile reasoning recurs. Keep acceptance criteria, accountabilities and evidence loops precise; do not turn general agile frequency into a claim about velocity, poker or every Scrum event. Priority 3 — Remaining Source-Supported Material Do not drop the rest of the course. Professional responsibility, specification ownership, the four introductory quality attributes, change/evolution, detailed Scrum roles/events, estimation/forecast limits, EARS, interaction analysis, traceability and controlled change remain source-supported even where they were not observed—or were observed less often—in this historical sample. The papers also repeatedly contain design principles, testing/JUnit, risk/quality management, and UML class/state/activity/sequence diagrams. These are recorded as NOT IN MATERIALS for the currently supplied corpus. They are gaps, not permission to invent unsupported Tutor units. If You Have Only 30 Minutes This is a suggested schedule, not a measured learning guarantee: - 5 minutes — foundation: retrieve the four lifecycle activities and the difference between a process and a model from Unit 01 Card 11 and Unit 02 Card 01. - 8 minutes — process choice: read Unit 02 review and outline Problem T1 before opening its hint. - 7 minutes — agile reasoning: distinguish empirical learning from a model name, then outline Unit 03 Problem E1. - 8 minutes — requirements: review user/system and functional/quality distinctions, then outline Unit 04 Problem E1. - 2 minutes — closed-book recall: speak one justification, one limitation and one missing-evidence question for each of the previous two answers. Sacrifices: this route omits most worked examples, full exercise navigation, detailed Scrum events/forecasting, use-case drawing practice, EARS variants, traceability/change-control practice, professional ethics and all unsupported historical-paper gaps. It is not full coverage. Production and study status All four companion units are ready for self-study: eight primary notes, 53 recall cards and 23 local practice problems. The navigation covers all 68 original tasks and their subparts through the unchanged reference exercises/labs. All study status remains untested. Source and structural review passed for the original Tutor edition; the assessment update was separately checked against all 29 page images and the affected Markdown. Native Obsidian viewing and A4 export remain untested. The preserved source disagreements matter when interpreting examples; Unit 03 locally corrects the standard reference's chart panel count. Historical CPT203 question evidence is available with the code/cover/scheme limitations above; the current SOE203 format and official marking criteria remain unconfirmed. entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: Software engineering begins when other people must depend on software over time. A working program is one part of that commitment. You need to identify the whole product, establish who controls its requirements, judge four different quality attributes, manage change, and communicate honestly about evidence and risk. These ideas connect: ownership determines whose needs matter; quality makes those needs discussable; lifecycle work produces evidence; professional responsibility governs the claims you make. After studying, you should be able to explain why a demonstration is insufficient, distinguish generic from customized products, diagnose a quality weakness, and justify a release decision within practical constraints. No programming background is required. Source: S15 PDF pp.4–8,17–28,35–41 (full filenames in the cards and references below).

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: > [!info] The professional product > Concept: The professional product. > > Plain-language meaning: People need configuration and understandable documentation as well as executable behavior. > > Why it matters: A program can work for its author yet fail the people receiving it. > > Connects to: quality and lifecycle evidence. > > Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF pp.4–8,14–15. > [!info] Specification ownership > Concept: Specification ownership. > > Plain-language meaning: The person paying or using a product does not always control its future requirements. > > Why it matters: Ownership changes how scope decisions are negotiated. > > Connects to: generic and customized products. > > Source: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF p.2, Q3. > [!info] Four quality lenses > Concept: Four quality lenses. > > Plain-language meaning: Changeability, trust, resource use and user fit answer different questions. > > Why it matters: One good attribute cannot establish the others. > > Connects to: maintainability; dependability/security; efficiency; acceptability. > > Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p.17, source table. > [!info] Change and responsibility > Concept: Change and responsibility. > > Plain-language meaning: Software does not physically wear out; changed logic and assumptions can introduce faults. > > Why it matters: Engineering must support useful evolution while making honest claims about its risks. > > Connects to: modularity, validation and professional duties. > > Source: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF pp.21–23,35–38.

entries.title: Before You Start
entries.text: A requirement says what is needed from a system; a constraint limits acceptable solutions, such as a budget. A stakeholder is someone with a relevant interest in the system. Here these are working meanings needed to understand the lecture's requirements/customer discussion; Unit 04 develops the requirements methods. A program expresses instructions, while configuration supplies environment-specific information needed to operate it. [^product] > [!question] Quick prerequisite check > Does a demonstration establish that somebody else can install and maintain the program? > [!success]- Answer > No. It shows behavior in the demonstrated environment, while installation, configuration and maintainable knowledge require their own evidence. Source: S15 PDF pp.6,14–15.

entries.title: The motivating question — A release under pressure
entries.text: Synthetic case. A university commissions a room-display service. It runs quickly on its author's laptop. Only that author knows the configuration. Staff cannot correct a room without asking the author. No one checked unauthorized changes. Management says the demonstration looks good and the budget is nearly spent. A room-allocation policy may change after release. Your task: Explain what is missing, who decides scope, what the demonstration proves, how to handle future change, and what to say about release. A successful answer covers the complete product and all four qualities, identifies missing evidence, and proposes a feasible next decision without inventing a numerical target or promising zero defects. | Question | Knowledge needed | |---|---| | What is being delivered? | Program versus professional system | | Who decides a scope change? | Specification ownership | | What evidence is missing? | Four quality attributes | | Why can tomorrow's change break today's behavior? | Dependencies and deterioration | | What may the team honestly promise? | Constraints and responsibility |

entries.title: 1. Why does a working program still need engineering?
entries.text: > [!note] Supplementary historical example — operating conditions matter > A 1992 U.S. GAO report describes a Patriot tracking calculation whose time inaccuracy increased with continuous operation; its Appendix II lists approximately 0.34 seconds of inaccuracy after 100 hours. The teaching connection is that a short successful demonstration cannot establish behavior over a much longer operating period. This case does not prove that every failure has the same cause or that one design method prevents all failures. > > Primary source: [GAO/IMTEC-92-26]( Appendix II, printed p.15. Supplementary context, outside the course lecture. Intuition. A recipe that only its author can follow is not yet a dependable service for a kitchen. Similarly, a program that runs for its author is not the whole product another person needs. The analogy concerns supporting knowledge, not a claim that software follows physical wear mechanisms. Precise idea. The source describes a software system as software components plus configuration, system documentation and user documentation. Software engineering concerns all aspects of software production, including supporting management, within organizational and financial constraints. Computer science emphasizes theory and fundamentals; software engineering emphasizes practical development and delivery. Neither distinction makes theory irrelevant to engineering. [^product] Work through the release claim. First identify the users' task: staff must display and correct rooms. Then identify what has been delivered: one successful execution. Next identify what someone else needs: usable configuration, instructions and system knowledge, plus evidence about intended behavior. The gap between those lists explains why documentation, estimation and relevant discussion are engineering work, even when they add no executable feature. The lecture's Java screenshot includes this output statement: System.out.print("Hello World!"); This snippet illustrates an output statement; it does not install or validate a complete system. The lecture's Java screenshot illustrates a program; it does not establish a required language/version. Its System.out.print("Hello World!") call is explained in the standard reference. No code is executed in this companion. [^product] | Question | Evidence from a successful demonstration | Evidence still needed for delivery | |---|---|---| | Does the behavior work? | The demonstrated input and environment | Agreed behavior under relevant conditions and failure cases | | Can others operate it? | The author can run this setup | Reproducible configuration and instructions, checked by intended users | | Can it change? | The current version runs | Understandable system knowledge and checks when requirements change | | Can a team support it? | One author knows the implementation | Shared information and an achievable agreement about responsibility and effort | A program can already have excellent structure and tests. The distinction here is the scope of the evidence, not a claim that individual programming is necessarily fragile or unprofessional. Source principles: S15 PDF pp.6–9,14–15; the comparison is supplementary teaching reasoning. Worked decision. Reserve effort for documented configuration and a user check before calling the service ready. The justification is not “documentation is always good”; it is that the next user cannot reproduce the demonstrated behavior without the author's private knowledge. If the budget cannot cover the agreed delivery, negotiate scope or schedule instead of redefining an incomplete demonstration as completion. > [!question] Explain it yourself > Why can estimating work and writing user instructions count as engineering, although neither changes the program’s output? > [!success]- Check your explanation > Engineering covers all aspects of production under constraints. Estimation supports an achievable commitment; instructions help intended users operate the delivered system. Source: S15 PDF pp.7–9.

entries.title: 2. Who owns the specification?
entries.text: Problem first. The university pays a supplier, but can it insist on any future feature? Payment alone does not answer the question. For a generic product, the developer controls the specification for a wider market. For a customized product, a particular customer commissions the system and controls its specification through agreement with the developer. This is a distinction about product boundary and authority, not free versus paid software. [^ownership] Visible worked comparison. Suppose the university buys a general image editor. Its users can request an interface change, but an individual customer normally cannot dictate the supplier's roadmap. Now suppose the university commissions its own room service. Its agreed requirements determine the custom product, and later changes must be negotiated with the supplier because they may affect effort and schedule. A generic component can sit inside that customized service; classify the level you are discussing. Return to the case: “commissions” makes customized development the supported interpretation. The university decides desired scope through agreement; the developer must explain implementation consequences. Neither party can make an added feature consume no resources by calling it a small change.

entries.title: 3. How do the four quality attributes guide action?
entries.text: Problem first. The screen responds quickly. Is the product therefore good? The source's four attributes make this question precise. [^quality] | Attribute | Ask this question | Case evidence and limit | |---|---|---| | Maintainability | Can it evolve as needs change? | Knowledge held by one author makes future changes difficult | | Dependability and security | Can users trust behavior and protection against damage or misuse? | Unauthorized changes were not checked; do not claim protection passed | | Efficiency | Does it use time, memory and processing resources appropriately? | A quick demonstration is limited evidence for that demonstrated workload | | Acceptability | Can intended users understand and use it in their environment? | Staff need the author's help for their normal task | How to reason step by step: name the observed fact; connect it to an attribute's meaning; state what the fact does and does not prove; choose evidence addressing the gap. A fast but wrong room display can be responsive and still undependable. An accurate display that staff cannot operate can be unacceptable. These are pedagogical counterexamples to the inference “one strength means total quality.” Worked plan. Have a second person reproduce the setup and explain a change, check permitted and unauthorized operations, agree a representative workload before measuring performance, and ask intended staff to complete their task. These are proposed evidence-gathering actions, not reported successful tests. The source supplies no performance target for this invented service, so do not silently invent one. The lecturer groups dependability and security together as one of four attributes. Lab Q1 asks for four additional attributes but lists five suggestions; any appropriate four should be explained. Usability, for example, overlaps with acceptability rather than becoming a fifth essential row. [^quality]

entries.title: 4. Why does software deteriorate if it does not wear out?
entries.text: Intuition. Changing a shared assumption can disturb code that still looks untouched. Logical relationships matter even when there is no physical material to erode. The source's curves show an idealized fall in failure rate as faults are fixed, then a schematic “actual” curve with spikes after changes. They illustrate possible new errors and interacting changes, not measured probabilities or a law that every change must fail. [^change] change-and-failure.svg Figure 1 — Following change into possible failure risk Read it: Follow the changed need through modification and possible side effects, then the controls used to reduce them. An arrow is a possible causal link, not a guaranteed failure. Key takeaway: Control dependencies and evidence around change; waiting alone does not wear out code. Provenance: Reused unchanged teaching SVG from the standard edition, based on S15 PDF pp.21–23; informal causal diagram, not UML. Worked change. A new allocation rule alters which room is displayed. First clarify the actual rule with stakeholders to avoid implementing the wrong change. Next identify the responsible part of the software and affected interactions. Make the change in a maintainable structure; then recheck the new behavior and behavior that used to work. Keep supporting information current so later engineers can understand the result. This operationalizes the source's requirements work, modularity, maintainability and comprehensive testing. [^change] Limit. Refusing all changes may preserve old behavior while making the product useless. Testing reduces uncertainty; it cannot establish the absence of every possible fault. Likewise, maintaining an existing system often preserves valuable knowledge, but the lab's strong preference for maintenance does not prove replacement is never justified. [^challenges]

entries.title: 5. How do lifecycle and responsibility change the release decision?
entries.text: Problem first. Management counts visible code as progress and asks the team to say “ready.” What work and obligations does that claim hide? The four fundamental activities are specification, design and implementation, validation, and evolution. They establish needs, construct a solution, check it against needs, and change it over time. They are activities, not a rule that each happens only once. Estimation, coordination and documentation support them. [^process] The long delivery time and high cost discussed in Lab Q2 follow from skilled work across these activities and the rework caused by dependencies. Rare inputs and environments help explain why not every fault is found before delivery. Embedded institutional knowledge helps explain maintenance effort. Intangibility and incomplete integration make “90% done” harder to verify than a count of physical objects. Each explanation connects a mechanism to a consequence instead of merely calling software complex. [^challenges] Application context changes the balance: stand-alone applications, interactive transaction systems, embedded control, batch processing, entertainment, simulation and data collection do not have identical constraints. The lecture's aircraft versus e-commerce contrast emphasizes criticality versus evolving requirements. Its web discussion emphasizes reuse, browser constraints and learning through increments for diverse users. AJAX and cloud-pricing remarks are historical source examples, not required technologies or current market claims. [^process] Professional responsibility extends to the effects of requirements, plans, tests and manuals as well as programs. The source names confidentiality, competence, intellectual property rights and computer misuse. In the case, competence includes representing what was checked honestly; confidentiality means entrusted information is not a convenient public debugging artifact. Client satisfaction does not cancel these obligations. [^ethics] Visible worked argument. “The client likes it, therefore release is responsible” has an unsupported step: satisfaction does not show that unauthorized modification was checked. A defensible response reports the successful demonstration and its limits, identifies the unfinished checks, and negotiates a release decision that respects scope, budget and affected users. Certification can support evidence of a minimum professional standard, but it cannot substitute for this product-specific reasoning. [^ethics]

entries.title: Return to the motivating question
entries.text: 1. Deliver the whole system: make configuration, instructions and maintainable knowledge part of the deliverable, because other people must operate it. 2. Agree scope with the commissioning university: treat the service as customized; discuss the costs of later policy changes. 3. Separate four quality conclusions: maintainability and acceptability show concrete weaknesses; efficiency has narrow demonstration evidence; dependability/security still lacks the stated check. 4. Prepare for evolution: clarify the room rule, contain side effects through maintainable responsibilities, and test changes and affected existing behavior. 5. Communicate the release boundary: report evidence and unknowns, then negotiate scope or schedule within budget. Do not claim unperformed validation passed. This closes every case question without prescribing an unsupported architecture, performance threshold or zero-defect guarantee.

entries.title: Definitions and distinctions
entries.text: | Pair | Decisive distinction | Source | |---|---|---| | Program / software system | Instructions versus the wider delivered components and supporting information | S15 pp.5–6 | | Generic / customized | Developer versus commissioning customer specification control | S12 p.2 Q3 | | Efficiency / acceptability | Resource use versus fit for intended users | S15 p.17 | | Deterioration / physical wear | Change-induced logical risk versus material degradation | S15 pp.21–23 | | Certification / product evidence | Minimum professional standard versus behavior of this particular system | S12 p.3 Q5 |

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Full Understanding Return to sections 1–5 and the case decisions. The standard reference expands application examples, the Java illustration and all original questions; use it when a distinction remains unclear. 5-Minute Review Identify the complete product and intended users. Establish who controls the specification. Use all four quality attributes separately. Explain change-induced risk through dependencies, then connect requirements work, maintainability and testing to risk reduction. Choose lifecycle emphasis for the actual application. State evidence, unknowns, constraints and consequences before recommending release. 60-Second Recall - Program versus system - Specification owner - Four quality attributes - One strength versus whole quality - Change without physical wear - Four lifecycle activities - Honest release evidence [^product]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF pp.4–9,14–15,43; Java screenshot at p.14 is illustrative and was not executed. [^ownership]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF pp.18–19; Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF p.2 Q3. [^quality]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p.17, visually inspected table; Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF p.1 Q1. [^change]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF pp.21–23; Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF pp.2–3 Q4. [^challenges]: Week 1-Lab-Introduction-ExampleAnswers.pdf, PDF pp.1–2 Q2; Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF p.20. [^process]: Week1-Lecture-Introduction.pdf, PDF pp.24–33.
