entries.title: Software Processes
entries.text: Software Processes Course index · Notes · Exercises Learning goals Choose and justify a process using requirement stability, failure consequences, feedback opportunities and reusable components. Explain how the same four fundamental activities appear in different models. Interpret process diagrams and distinguish evidence of progress from a model's promises. Prerequisite: Unit 01's product, quality and lifecycle concepts. Opening case — Choose a process before choosing a slogan Source-based case: Lab Q1 asks about four systems: an anti-lock braking controller; a virtual-reality system for studying software maintenance; a replacement university accounting system; and an interactive journey planner seeking the lowest environmental impact. The source provides no budgets, technologies or detailed requirements. Task: Recommend a process basis for each, explain the decisive condition, and state what you would need to confirm before applying the recommendation. Do not assume one process fits all four. Success criteria: Each recommendation connects a property of the system to a process mechanism, states a trade-off and avoids claiming a model alone guarantees quality. Detailed designs of braking or accounting systems are outside this unit. What We Need to Learn | Decision | Concepts needed | |---|---| | What exactly are we selecting? | Actual process versus simplified model | | When is early agreement valuable? | Waterfall, deliverables, review and rework | | When is early user feedback valuable? | Incremental development and interleaved activities | | When can existing software shape requirements? | Reuse and two requirements activities | | What work remains in every model? | Specification, design/implementation, validation, evolution and supporting work | 1. A process is work; a model is an abstraction A software process is the actual related activities, methods and practices used to develop and maintain a product. It can involve new code, changes to existing systems, or configuring and integrating existing software. A software process model is a simplified representation of that process. It helps explain the overall organization without describing every local task.[^model] > [!note] Model selection is a reasoned approximation > The model tells us how work is organized; the actual process must still specify people, products, reviews, tools and local constraints. A model's name cannot establish that the work was done well. A ==critical system== is one whose failure can produce significant human, economic or environmental loss. Safety-critical is an important case, but criticality is broader than physical safety. Novelty and change are different dimensions: a system can be highly critical and also poorly understood. This is why models can be combined rather than selected by a single industry label.[^model] The source lists wider families—linear/sequential, iterative/incremental, agile, prototyping, component-based, formal methods, hybrid, RAD and lean—on p. 8. Names such as V-Model, Spiral, Kanban, XP, CBD, DSDM and DevOps are orientation examples there, not fully taught methods. The detailed comparison in this unit covers the three models actually developed in the lecture.[^model] 2. Waterfall — make phase commitments visible The waterfall model represents principal activities as distinct phases with outputs and approval points. A phase produces an artifact that the next phase uses: requirements guide design, design guides implementation, and the integrated implementation is checked before operational use. A deliverable is an output to be supplied; a milestone marks a significant point in the plan.[^waterfall] waterfall-phases.svg Figure 1 — Principal waterfall phases Read it: Move down the main progression. Unit testing is already present during implementation. Rework can return to earlier phases, as the original diagram's feedback arrows and pp. 19–21 explain. Key takeaway: The model emphasizes stage outputs and review, not a factual claim that real projects never revisit earlier decisions. Provenance: Teaching redraw of the principal sequence in Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 15–21; informal process diagram. What flows between the phases | Phase | Work and output | Why the next phase needs it | |---|---|---| | Requirements | Elicit services and constraints; agree a requirements document | Designers need to know the problem to solve | | Design | Specify architecture, interfaces and component and data design | Implementers need a coherent solution structure | | Implementation and unit testing | Produce code, documentation and unit checks | Integration needs functioning parts with understood behavior | | Integration and system testing | Combine parts, execute tests, record results | Operational acceptance needs evidence about the whole | | Operation and maintenance | Deploy, configure, train, support, correct and improve | The product must remain useful after delivery | Source: PDF pp. 16–17. The table explains purpose; it is not a complete mandated document template. Why revisiting an earlier phase is costly Suppose a requirement changes after design approval. The change may invalidate design decisions, implementation and test expectations. The team must update affected artifacts and repeat their review/approval. The cost is therefore change propagation plus reapproval, not merely editing a sentence. Lab Q4 asks why revisits should be limited.[^waterfall] Trade-off. Documentation gives managers visible evidence of completed work, preserves decisions, supports traceability and allows resource planning by phase. These benefits depend on the documents being accurate and on early assumptions being sufficiently stable. Prematurely freezing a mistaken requirement can produce a well-documented system that disappoints users. The lecture's strengths include structure, planning, documentation, control, resource allocation, milestones and controlled change. Its limitations include rigidity, delayed whole-system feedback, uncertain risks remaining unresolved, limited working-product feedback, administrative effort, uneven resource use and delayed benefits. A signed document is evidence of an agreement; it is not automatically evidence of a useful working system.[^comparison] > [!warning] Reconcile the lecture's “late testing” wording > PDF p. 25 says testing occurs late, but pp. 16–17 include unit testing during implementation and pp. 62–63 show reviews and early test planning. The usable interpretation is that major integration/acceptance evidence can arrive late in a simple sequential delivery. It is incorrect to infer that every check must wait until all code is finished. Likewise, p. 24 praises controlled-change risk management while p. 25 says the model does not inherently include risk-management activities. Review gates may help control changes, but an explicit risk-identification and mitigation process still has to be supplied. These claims describe different things and should not be memorized as “waterfall has no risks”. 3. Incremental development — learn through working versions An increment adds useful functionality to the existing product. Incremental development builds an initial version, exposes it to user comment and evolves it through further versions. Specification, development and validation are ==interleaved==: discovering a problem while implementing or checking can change what should be specified next.[^incremental] Mechanism. Begin with an outline of overall needs. Choose a useful subset, clarify it sufficiently, build and validate it with the current system, and obtain feedback. Use what was learned to decide the next subset. This bounds some commitments and brings selected evidence forward. It does not remove the need for architecture, planning, documentation or checking. Worked example — the source's flower shop PDF p. 33 proposes basic product listing and user registration first. The team designs, builds, unit-tests, integrates and deploys that increment, then gathers feedback. It next plans shopping-cart and checkout functionality; later versions add payment, order tracking and reviews. Interpretation. A first increment need not deliver the complete eventual business benefit. Product listing can be evaluated early, but it does not yet allow a complete purchase. This limitation should be explicit to stakeholders. If feedback reveals that product selection needs a different organization, the team can adapt before every later feature is built. Counterexample. A change to a shared definition of “product” may affect both the old listing and the new cart. PDF p. 32's statement that “only the current increment” needs changing is therefore an optimistic local-change case, not a universal property. PDF pp. 36–37 themselves warn about dependencies and cross-increment effects. Benefits need enabling conditions Earlier useful functionality provides earlier feedback and possibly earlier value. Smaller planning horizons may improve estimates. Frequent integration can reveal problems earlier. Teams may work in parallel when dependencies and coordination permit it. None of these benefits follows just by naming a release “increment 1”.[^incremental] Costs include integrating new and old work, coordinating dependencies, supporting released increments while creating new ones, allocating varied skills, controlling scope changes, maintaining stakeholder involvement, and managing the incomplete functionality of early versions. Quality needs continuous effort across versions; smaller batches do not make faulty work correct by themselves. Incremental is not identical to agile. Incremental describes how functionality grows. The course's Appendix 3 describes agile as a broader emphasis on adaptation, collaboration, short cycles and frequent feedback. A team can pre-plan increments extensively. Scrum, introduced next, adds a particular empirical framework.[^appendix] 4. Reuse — negotiate fit before integration Reuse-oriented engineering centers development on available components and systems. The source distinguishes remotely invoked web services, packaged collections of objects integrated with a framework, and configurable stand-alone systems. Its .NET and J2EE mentions are examples of frameworks, not selected tools or confirmed versions for this course.[^reuse] reuse-and-requirements.svg Figure 2 — Why requirements are revisited during reuse Read it: Broad requirements guide component analysis; candidate capabilities then inform requirements modification. Continue through design with reuse, development/integration and validation. Key takeaway: Requirements work occurs twice because the information available changes after candidate components are examined. Provenance: Teaching redraw of Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF p. 47, preserving stage order and terminology; informal process flow. Worked example — replacing a university system Before evaluating a reusable accounting package, identify the services needed and its relationships with existing university systems. Without those needs, “this package looks impressive” is not a reason to select it. After evaluating candidates, compare their actual capabilities with the needs. Negotiate acceptable adjustments and identify required additions before designing integration. This is why Lab Q3 requires two separate requirements activities, rather than choosing components once and forcing users to accept all their limitations.[^lab] Trade-off. Reuse can reduce new development effort, cost and risk, and accelerate delivery. It can also force compromises that undermine users' real needs and place component evolution under another supplier's control. Reusing a part does not prove it fits the new whole; system validation remains necessary. 5. Compare mechanisms, not slogans The lecture develops fifteen comparison dimensions on pp. 38–40. They can be applied as three sets of questions rather than memorized as an unconditional ranking: | Dimension | What to ask before deciding | |---|---| | Requirement stability; adaptability; user-centered work; market change | How much is known, and how will feedback alter priorities? | | Early functionality; time to market; maintenance/enhancement | Can a partial delivery be useful, and how often must the product evolve? | | Size/complexity; risk; integration | Can work be decomposed safely, and when do we need evidence about the whole? | | Stakeholder involvement; documentation/audits; regulatory constraints | Who can review work, what evidence is needed, and how stable are the constraints? | | Resource availability; parallel work | Which skills are available and which dependencies prevent independent work? | Under the lecture's assumptions, stable and well-understood requirements favor early agreement and phase planning; uncertain interactive behavior favors increments and feedback. Reusable capabilities introduce an additional selection-and-fit problem. The models are not mutually exclusive.[^comparison] The lecture illustrates these tendencies with avionics, medical devices, banking, government and infrastructure on the planning/documentation side, and e-commerce, social/mobile apps, healthcare management and educational software on the evolving-requirements side. These are classroom examples of rationale, not verified descriptions of named companies' internal processes or rules prescribing one method to an entire industry. Size alone is insufficient: a small uncertain project can need feedback, and a large project can need both formal agreements and incremental work. 6. The activities inside every model Specification — decide what should be built Requirements engineering identifies required services and constraints. The lecture's workflow includes a feasibility study, elicitation and analysis, specification, and validation. Feasibility asks whether a proposed system is practicable; elicitation discovers needs; analysis clarifies and reconciles them; specification records them; validation checks that they represent stakeholder needs. The source diagram associates these with a feasibility report, system models, user/system requirements and an agreed requirements document. Feedback means this is not one irreversible pass.[^activities] Customers and end users need understandable high-level requirements; developers need more detailed system requirements. A wrong early requirement can misdirect both design and implementation, so detecting it only after coding can mean rebuilding the wrong solution rather than repairing a small programming defect. Design and implementation — turn requirements into an executable system Design defines structure, data, interfaces and sometimes algorithms. PDF p. 57 shows platform information, requirements specification and data description as inputs, with architecture, interface, component and database specifications as outputs. Designers add detail iteratively and revise earlier decisions.[^activities] Architectural design chooses the principal components and relationships. Interface design specifies how components interact; ambiguity here can make independently correct parts fail together. Component design describes operation, which may be a functional description, changes to reused software or a detailed model. Database design specifies relevant data structures and representations. This last activity is independently present in this course source; no particular DBMS, indexing topic or other course's examples are imported. Implementation includes coding, reviews, unit tests, integration and build management. A build assembles the executable product from its parts. The level and representation of design detail varies: critical work may need explicit precise documents; model-driven work may use diagrams; an agile team's design knowledge may also be expressed in code. Less separate paperwork does not mean no design. Validation — obtain evidence at the right level The lecture treats verification and validation broadly as showing conformity to specification and alignment with customer expectations. Testing executes the system with selected data; inspections and reviews examine artifacts without needing that execution. They can occur throughout development.[^validation] | Source testing stage | Purpose | Synthetic example | |---|---|---| | Development/component testing | Check parts during development | A journey-cost component calculates an expected result for controlled input | | System testing | Check the integrated whole and component interactions | The route displayed uses the same cost that the selection component ranked | | Acceptance testing | Check operational suitability using customer-supplied data and needs | Intended users evaluate their real journey-planning cases | PDF p. 65 describes development testing in the narrow component-testing sense. Do not infer that all testing performed by developers must be isolated: Appendix 1 also includes integration. A source diagram on p. 63 links requirements to acceptance-test plans, system specification to system-integration plans, and system design to subsystem-integration plans. Planning a test and executing it are different events. A test case specifies inputs, expected results and conditions. Execution records actual results. Defect tracking preserves findings. Regression testing reruns prior tests after changes to look for newly introduced failures. Acceptance criteria state the conditions expected by stakeholders. None of these activities justifies a claim that every possible defect has been excluded. Appendix p. 71's phrase “free of defects” is treated as an objective, not something ordinary testing guarantees.[^appendix] Evolution — maintain usefulness after delivery The source distinguishes corrective maintenance (fix defects), adaptive maintenance (respond to environment changes), perfective maintenance (improve performance, usability or maintainability), and preventive maintenance (reduce future problems). Release coordination and user support accompany those changes. Evolution continues engineering work rather than constituting a separate, intellectually trivial activity.[^appendix] Supporting activities — make the work repeatable and visible Project management plans, schedules, manages risk, and monitors/control progress. Configuration management keeps track of artifact versions, coordinates changes and builds. Deployment includes release, installation/configuration and user support/training. Documentation supports both users and maintainers. Process improvement assesses how the team works and introduces changes to improve it. These responsibilities support every model; they should not disappear because a diagram omits them.[^appendix] Solve the opening case | System | Decision and source rationale | Consequence, limitation and confirmation needed | |---|---|---| | Anti-lock braking | The lab recommends a plan-driven/waterfall basis with careful upfront analysis because failure can endanger people | Requires precise needs and rigorous evidence. Confirm constraints and required assurance; choosing waterfall alone does not establish safety | | Virtual reality for maintenance research | Incremental development, perhaps with UI prototyping, because the system is novel and needs will emerge | Early versions support learning; confirm users and evaluation goals. Prototype feedback does not establish final-product quality | | Replacement university accounting | Reuse-oriented development because many needs are established and integration with existing systems matters | Evaluate candidates against real needs, then renegotiate fit. Confirm that suitable reusable software exists | | Low-impact journey planner | Incremental development because the interface and requirements benefit from real user experience | Evaluate useful behavior early and revise priorities. Confirm environmental-impact assumptions and whether partial releases are useful | These reproduce the supplied suggestions while exposing assumptions. The accounting answer is not proved simply by the word “university”; it depends on component availability and fit. Likewise, hard real-time or safety constraints do not make every incremental development activity impossible; they can make partial deployment and late architectural change inappropriate. The distinction between developing in parts and releasing an operationally incomplete system is crucial.[^lab] Success check: All four recommendations connect a source property to a process mechanism, state a limitation and identify missing information. None substitutes a product label for assurance or a detailed design. Exam-style answer and reusable method Example answer: Incremental development is useful when business requirements evolve because early versions expose assumptions to users and reduce the amount of work committed before feedback. Its benefits depend on useful decomposition and continued integration; dependencies and scope growth can still cause overruns. Plan-driven agreements may be preferable for stable interfaces and evidence obligations, while reuse requires requirements to be reconciled with available capabilities. For any process-choice answer: identify what is known and uncertain; identify failure consequences; test whether useful increments are possible; examine reuse; select a model or combination; explain one mechanism, one consequence and one limitation. Then state how the four activities and supporting work will be performed. This is a decision procedure, not a scoring formula that can replace missing project information. Common mistakes and quick review - “Waterfall never revisits a stage”: pp. 19–21 explicitly describe feedback and rework. - “Incremental means no planning”: increment selection, dependencies and integration require planning. - “A reusable component removes requirements work”: it creates a second fit/negotiation activity. - “Testing happens only at the end”: distinguish unit work, early test planning and later whole-system execution. - “All real-time systems are safety-critical”: the source lab's explanation is a common scenario, not a definition of real-time behavior. > [!summary] Review checkpoint > Name the three studied models and the mechanism behind each. Explain why a requirements change can require reapproval. Give one condition that defeats the benefit of early increments. Explain why tests at component, system and customer levels answer different questions. [^model]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 3–13. [^waterfall]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 14–22; Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q4. [^comparison]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 23–26 and 38–45. [^incremental]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 27–37, including the diagram on p. 28 and flower-shop case on p. 33. [^reuse]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 46–49, including the process diagram on p. 47. [^activities]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 50–61, especially diagrams on pp. 54 and 57. [^validation]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 62–66, especially the test-plan diagram on p. 63. [^appendix]: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF pp. 67 and 70–74. Page 69 is course grouping administration; p. 75 links an unviewed introductory video. [^lab]: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF pp. 1–2, Q1–Q5; explanations above identify where a suggested answer relies on an assumption.

entries.title: Software Processes — Exercises
entries.text: Software Processes — Exercises Course index · Notes · Exercises Original Lab 2 tasks have local solutions. A process suggestion must be justified from the problem, and alternatives require explicit assumptions. Exercise L1 — Choose a model for four systems ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 1, Q1(a–d). Suggest and justify a process model for each: a. Anti-lock braking control in a car. b. A virtual-reality system to study software maintenance. c. A university accounting system replacing an existing system. d. An interactive travel planner helping users find journeys with the lowest environmental impact. > [!tip]- Hint > Use criticality, uncertainty, feedback and reusable capabilities as distinct decision dimensions. > [!success]- Solution > a — Braking. The suggested answer chooses plan-driven/waterfall development with careful upfront requirements analysis, possibly formal transformations, because incorrect behavior can threaten safety. This is a process basis, not sufficient safety evidence. > > b — Research VR. Choose incremental development, perhaps with UI prototyping: novelty and user interaction make evolving requirements likely, so early feedback can change what is built next. > > c — Accounting replacement. Choose reuse-oriented development under the source assumption that established needs can be met by available software and integrated with systems such as research-grant management. Confirm component fit; a familiar domain does not prove a particular package meets every need. > > d — Journey planning. Choose incremental development because user experience with the interactive interface will refine requirements. Deliver meaningful functionality and use feedback without ignoring cross-increment dependencies. > > Interpretation. Each answer is conditional. A justified hybrid can be defensible, but must explain how it preserves necessary evidence and manages the named uncertainty. Exercise L2 — Business change and real-time constraints ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 1, Q2. Explain why incremental development is the most effective approach for business software systems. Why is it less appropriate for real-time systems engineering? > [!tip]- Hint > Explain the source’s assumed business environment; distinguish hardware constraints, criticality, development and deployment. > [!success]- Solution > Step 1 — Business rationale. Business goals and processes change; early useful increments let users clarify needs before the whole system is committed. Interleaved specification/development/validation can reduce rework. > > Step 2 — Real-time case in the source. Hardware coupling, whole-system timing constraints and costly physical changes can make it difficult to deploy an incomplete increment. Where failures are safety-critical, additional upfront analysis and planned evidence are needed. > > Step 3 — Limit the generalization. “Real-time” concerns timing constraints and does not by itself imply safety-criticality. Internal iterative development may remain possible even when incomplete operational deployment is unacceptable. Thus incremental development is a strong business-system choice under change/feedback assumptions, not a theorem that excludes every other process. Exercise L3 — Two requirements activities in reuse ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q3. Why is it essential to have two separate requirements-engineering activities in the reuse-based process? > [!tip]- Hint > What can you know before component analysis, and what do you learn only after it? > [!success]- Solution > Before selection: understand the needed functions and broad constraints well enough to evaluate candidate systems/components. > > After selection: compare actual capabilities with business needs; identify needed changes/additions and negotiate acceptable requirements modifications. > > Reason: available software constrains the feasible solution. Skipping the first activity makes selection directionless; skipping the second risks pretending the selected component meets needs it does not meet. The source p. 47 sequence places component analysis between specification and modification. Exercise L4 — Why waterfall revisits are costly ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q4. A waterfall engineer may revisit the previous stage for refinement. Explain in your own words why the number of revisits should be limited. > [!tip]- Hint > Trace a modified requirement through approved artifacts rather than simply saying iteration is slow. > [!success]- Solution > Each completed stage has documented outputs that have been reviewed and approved. Revisiting changes those outputs and can invalidate dependent design, implementation and test work, requiring further updates and reapproval. Repeated cycles consume time and budget. Therefore the team should reduce avoidable revisits through careful work and controlled decisions. This is not a reason to knowingly preserve a critical defect: compare the cost of correcting it with the consequence of leaving it unresolved. Exercise L5 — Why requirements matter early ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week 2-Lab- Software Process-Example-Answer.pdf, PDF p. 2, Q5. Explain why requirements engineering is a critical stage in the software process. > [!tip]- Hint > Distinguish building the wrong thing from coding the intended thing incorrectly. > [!success]- Solution > Requirements guide design and implementation. If a requirement misstates the needed service or constraint, later work may correctly implement the wrong solution. Repair then needs reconsideration of the requirement and its dependent artifacts. Early elicitation, analysis and validation reduce this risk. The source’s “inevitably” emphasizes propagation risk; a later review can still catch a mistake before it reaches operational software. Exercise P11 — What a process model includes ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF p. 11, embedded question. What will be included in software process models? > [!tip]- Hint > Think at the framework level: what activities, relationships and outputs help explain the process? > [!success]- Solution > A model represents principal activities/phases and their organization, including sequence, overlap and feedback where relevant. It can show the outputs or deliverables connecting activities, such as requirements feeding design. The actual process adds local roles, detailed practices and constraints. The three lecture diagrams illustrate different organizations rather than every detail of a project. Exercise P75 — What is agile ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Week2-Lecture-Software Processes-r.pdf, PDF p. 75, introductory prompt; context p. 74. Give the brief, informal meaning of agile introduced at the end of the lecture. > [!tip]- Hint > Use Appendix 3; do not assume that merely delivering numbered releases defines the whole approach. > [!success]- Solution > In the lecture’s introduction, agile emphasizes adapting to change, close customer collaboration and frequent feedback while delivering small functional increments in short cycles. Incremental development is one important feature, but by itself does not establish the broader philosophy or a specific framework. Scrum is developed in the next supplied teaching materials; the linked video was not viewed. Exercise S1 — Read the test-planning evidence SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Provenance: Synthetic practice using the concepts taught in Notes. A manager says: “The model places system testing after implementation, so we should wait until then to plan acceptance tests.” Use the source diagram on PDF p. 63 to identify the error. > [!tip]- Hint > Distinguish the information used to define a test from the executable product needed to run it. > [!success]- Solution > Requirements can inform the acceptance-test plan before code exists; system specification can inform system-integration plans, and system design can inform subsystem-integration plans. Execution must wait for the relevant product, but planning expected evidence need not. The manager confuses ordering of test execution with ordering of test design. Exercise S2 — Diagnose a reuse shortcut SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Provenance: Synthetic practice using the concepts taught in Notes. A team chooses a component first, then deletes every requirement the component cannot satisfy. Explain why this is not an adequate reuse-oriented process. > [!tip]- Hint > Use both requirements activities and the need to preserve real business value. > [!success]- Solution > Candidate analysis is useful only relative to broad needs. After selection, requirements may be negotiated, but deleting every mismatch can produce a system that fails essential business needs. Identify which requirements are negotiable, which require additions and which make the candidate unsuitable; then validate the integrated whole. Reuse reduces new code but does not erase responsibility for fit.

entries.title: In 60 Seconds
entries.text: When requirements and technical assumptions are uncertain, progress depends on learning from evidence. Scrum connects three pillars—transparency, inspection and adaptation—to accountabilities, events and artifacts. Acceptance criteria describe what an item must do; Definition of Done establishes the shared quality threshold. Relative estimates support discussion, and observed Done work supports a conditional forecast. You should be able to locate who owns a decision, explain why “almost done” cannot count as Done, resolve divergent estimates by uncovering assumptions, and calculate a forecast with units and limitations. The Campus Express activity is a UI-refinement exercise; its proposed estimates are not measured team performance. Source: S07 pp.4–46, S09 pp.1–15, S03 pp.1–4 and S14 Q1–Q7.

entries.title: Concept Preview
entries.text: > [!info] Empirical learning > Concept: Empirical learning. > > Plain-language meaning: Make the work visible, compare it with a goal, and adjust using what you learn. > > Why it matters: A plan based on uncertain assumptions needs an evidence-driven way to change. > > Connects to: defined control and the cone of uncertainty. > > Source: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, PDF pp.1–3,6. > [!info] Scrum decisions > Concept: Scrum decisions. > > Plain-language meaning: Product value, implementation and team effectiveness have distinct accountabilities. > > Why it matters: Meetings help only when evidence reaches someone able to act. > > Connects to: Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Master. > > Source: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, PDF pp.7–10. > [!info] Acceptance and Done > Concept: Acceptance and Done. > > Plain-language meaning: An item’s behavior and the product’s shared quality threshold answer different questions. > > Why it matters: A correct-looking screen may still lack review or usable integration. > > Connects to: acceptance criteria, Increment and velocity. > > Source: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet.pdf, PDF p.1, Definition of Done. > [!info] Sizing and forecasting > Concept: Sizing and forecasting. > > Plain-language meaning: Compare work to a shared baseline; forecast using comparable completed work. > > Why it matters: Numbers do not remove unknown scope, and points are not hours. > > Connects to: planning poker, mean velocity and conditional forecasts. > > Source: SE Methodologies Scrum - Reading Material.pdf, PDF pp.12–14.
