entries.title: Requirements Engineering — Exercises and Worked Solutions
entries.text: Requirements Engineering — Exercises and Worked Solutions Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab These are the original End-of-Chapter Review Questions from Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, in their original order. Q27–Q28 form the practical in Lab; Q29 preserves the additional E-003 question in the reading's “Apply What You've Learned” box. Repeated in-chapter questions remain explicitly mapped. All solutions are reasoned model answers; proposed policies/thresholds are labelled. Exercise Q1 — Process timing ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q1. What distinguishes the timing of Requirements Engineering in a Waterfall model compared to an Agile model? > [!tip]- Hint > Compare where the baseline is created and how later detail changes. > [!success]- Solution > In the course’s Waterfall model, RE is concentrated upfront and a validated SRS is baselined before system design. In Agile, backlog items and acceptance criteria are refined continuously, with feedback informing later work. Both need stakeholders and validation; cadence and governance differ. Internal iterations during the upfront RE phase do not turn the whole lifecycle into Agile. Exercise Q2 — Cost of late correction ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q2. Why is an omitted or ambiguous requirement in Waterfall significantly more expensive to fix during testing than during upfront specification? > [!tip]- Hint > Follow a mistaken requirement through downstream artifacts. > [!success]- Solution > An omitted or ambiguous statement can shape architecture, code, interfaces, test expectations and user procedures. Discovering the error in testing may require revising and rechecking all of those dependencies. During specification, fewer downstream commitments exist, so clarification often costs less. This explains the risk without assuming every late correction has an identical or exponential cost. Exercise Q3 — Elicitation versus analysis ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q3. What is Requirements Elicitation, and how does it differ from Requirements Analysis & Classification? > [!tip]- Hint > Separate raw evidence from the interpretation of that evidence. > [!success]- Solution > Elicitation discovers and records stakeholder needs, domain constraints and observations with attribution. Analysis organizes levels and viewpoints, clarifies statements, classifies them and detects conflicts. An interview quote remains raw evidence even when it sounds like a requirement. When analysis discovers a missing fact, return to elicitation; preserve the quote rather than silently replacing it with the analyst’s interpretation. Exercise Q4 — Technique and evidence ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q4. Name three Elicitation techniques and, for each, describe how its findings should be documented. > [!tip]- Hint > Match the evidence to a durable artifact. > [!success]- Solution > Three valid choices: Interview: capture dated notes attributed to the stakeholder, preserving wording and unresolved questions. Workshop/JAD: keep minutes, speaker-attributed raw requests and actions. Observation/shadowing: record time-stamped field notes and the current workflow, distinguishing observed facts from inferred needs. Add each relevant statement to the Elicitation Register with source/date/status. Surveys with tabulated results, document analysis with citations and prototypes with annotated feedback are also source-supported alternatives. Exercise Q5 — Elicitation deliverables ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q5. List the deliverables that come out of the Elicitation phase. Why is none of them yet a finalized User or System Requirement? > [!tip]- Hint > Include supporting evidence and models, not just the register. > [!success]- Solution > The outputs are the Elicitation Register, draft use-case diagram, draft use-case descriptions, stakeholder/viewpoint list, draft domain glossary and supporting interview notes, workshop minutes, observations, prototypes/feedback. They preserve a broad initial understanding. They have not yet been fully organized, classified, conflict-checked, refined and validated, so they are not finalized authorized UR/SR statements. “Draft” does not mean useless: it makes uncertain content reviewable. Exercise Q6 — Use-case maturity ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q6. Explain why a Use Case Description can reasonably be written in both Stage 1 (Elicitation) and Stage 3 (Specification). What changes between the two versions? > [!tip]- Hint > A document can keep its identity while increasing precision. > [!success]- Solution > In Stage 1, the description captures the stakeholder’s interaction in accessible language, often emphasizing the main success path so the user can correct misunderstandings. In Stage 3, the same use case is refined after analysis: actor, pre/postconditions, alternate and error flows, terms and requirement links become precise. It is incorporated into the SRS and validated before sign-off. The stage changes its maturity and purpose, not necessarily its identifier. Exercise Q7 — Approval before a quick swap ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q7. Rewrite the raw statement "the system should let students swap rooms quickly, but only if a lecturer approves it first" as one or more EARS-pattern requirements. Which pattern(s) did you use, and why? > [!tip]- Hint > Preserve this question’s student requester and lecturer approver: they differ from the main lecturer/admin case. Do not invent the meaning of quickly. > [!success]- Solution > First clarify whether swap means room-allocation change or only request submission, who the lecturer approver is, and which measurable deadline applies. Preserve the question’s roles. One proposed decomposition is: WHEN a student submits a room-swap request, the system shall record it as pending lecturer approval (event-driven); IF lecturer approval has not been recorded, THEN the system shall prevent the requested allocation change (unwanted behavior); WHEN the authorized lecturer approves an eligible request, the system shall apply the approved room change (event-driven). These separate request, authorization and effect. “Quickly” still requires a performance requirement with agreed timing endpoints, threshold and conditions; no number is given, so mark that target UNCONFIRMED and do not baseline it. These are proposed clarifications, not permission to replace the main case’s Ms. Lee sign-off rule. Exercise Q8 — User versus system ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q8. Explain the difference between a User Requirement and a System Requirement. Why must User Requirements be organized before System Requirements are written? > [!tip]- Hint > Ask who must understand the statement and what precision they need. > [!success]- Solution > A UR explains a stakeholder’s service/goal in accessible terms; an SR refines exact behavior and constraints for developers/testers. UR-1 allows mobile weekly timetable viewing; the source SR-1.1 specifies a triggering event, calendar display and a 3.0-second/4G target. Organizing the user need first lets stakeholders validate the problem before engineers optimize a technical solution. Otherwise precise APIs or schemas can implement the wrong goal. SRs need precision, not arbitrary implementation prescriptions. Exercise Q9 — Viewpoints versus levels ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q9. What is Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA), and how does it differ from sorting requirements by abstraction level? > [!tip]- Hint > Viewpoint and abstraction are separate axes. > [!success]- Solution > VOA checks Interactor, Indirect and Domain perspectives so direct interviewees do not crowd out other needs or constraints. Sorting by abstraction instead separates high-level user intent from detailed system commitments. A domain policy can generate both a user-level constraint and a precise system rule. The same requirement can therefore have a viewpoint tag and an abstraction-level tag; neither classification substitutes for the other. Exercise Q10 — Reset password securely ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q10. Using FURPS+, classify the following statement into its Functional and Non-Functional parts: "The system shall let a user reset their password securely within 10 seconds." > [!tip]- Hint > Separate the operation, its time budget and the vague security promise. > [!success]- Solution > Functional part: let a user reset a password, tagged Functionality. Performance part: finish the defined reset operation within 10 seconds, tagged Performance; specify when timing starts/stops and under what load/network, including whether human/email delays count. Security part: “securely” is not testable; elicit identity-verification, authorization and other applicable controls rather than guessing them. Security behavior can be tagged Functionality/security and/or constraints as appropriate to the course catalog. Do not mistake the FURPS+ label F for a different kind of statement that excludes FRs: the slides and reading differ on that convention. The original sentence must be split and clarified before acceptance tests are authoritative. Exercise Q11 — Interaction grid ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q11. Build a small Matrix-Based Interaction Analysis grid for three requirements of your choosing, and explain how you would resolve any conflict you find. > [!tip]- Hint > Select three explicit commitments; score each unordered pair once and explain every nonzero score. > [!success]- Solution > Example choices (proposed): A — an authenticated student can view a weekly timetable; B — the full timetable renders within 3.0 seconds over the agreed 4G test conditions; C — schedule traffic uses the agreed encryption control. > > | Pair grid | A | B | C | > |---|---:|---:|---:| > | A | — | +1 | 0 | > | B | +1 | — | −1 | > | C | 0 | −1 | — | > > A/B is marked compatible because usable schedule viewing is supported by responsiveness. A/C is neutral for this narrow interaction assessment. B/C is a potential resource conflict, following the source’s example: extra processing/handshake work may consume part of the time budget. It is not proof both cannot be met. Establish a representative workload, estimate or prototype timing, and consider a design that satisfies both. If commitments are incompatible, have authorized stakeholders revise a target, scope or budget and record the rationale; do not silently weaken mandatory security. The values are qualitative judgments, not probabilities or arithmetic utilities. Exercise Q12 — Measurable usability ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q12. Rewrite the following as a measurable Non-Functional Requirement: "The system shall have a friendly interface." > [!tip]- Hint > Replace friendly with an observable user task, a threshold and conditions. > [!success]- Solution > One proposed NFR: In a usability test with ten representative first-time lecturers, at least nine shall complete the specified room-swap request workflow in under three minutes without external help. Metric: task completion time and success count; thresholds: <3 minutes and ≥9/10; conditions: first-time representative users, defined workflow and no help. Nine of ten is a proposed acceptance threshold, not a supplied course fact; obtain stakeholder agreement. Record device, start/end events and recruitment criteria. Other justified measurable proposals are valid. Exercise Q13 — The measurable-NFR ingredients ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q13. List the three ingredients every measurable NFR needs. Why does "the system shall respond quickly" fail the Measurability Checklist? > [!tip]- Hint > A number alone is not enough if its unit or environment is missing. > [!success]- Solution > The three ingredients are the metric, a threshold with unit, and the conditions under which it applies. “Respond quickly” does not define how to measure the response, how quick is acceptable or the workload/environment. A tester cannot reproducibly decide pass/fail. Clarify the response endpoints, agree a threshold such as the case’s 3.0 seconds only where that case applies, and specify conditions rather than guessing a universal value. Exercise Q14 — SRS organization ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q14. Name the standard sections of an SRS document. Where would a use case diagram belong, and where would the Requirements Traceability Matrix belong? > [!tip]- Hint > Follow the course’s five major SRS sections and its subdivisions of section 3. > [!success]- Solution > The standard taught here is: 1 Introduction; 2 Overall Description; 3 Specific Requirements, divided into 3.1 FRs, 3.2 External Interfaces, 3.3 NFRs, 3.4 Use Cases/Models; 4 Appendices; 5 Approval/Sign-off. A use-case diagram belongs in 3.4, connected to finalized descriptions. The RTM belongs in 4 Appendices. Glossary, assumptions, dictionary and revision history support interpretation and control. This is the course template, not a claim every organization must use the same headings. Exercise Q15 — Group the catalog ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q15. Explain how Functional Requirements should be grouped within an SRS, and how Non-Functional Requirements should be grouped. Why not just list all requirements in one flat table? > [!tip]- Hint > Think about how a reviewer searches for behavior and how cross-cutting qualities interact. > [!success]- Solution > Group FRs by feature/module, such as scheduling, room swaps and notifications. Group NFRs by quality/constraint category, such as performance, usability, reliability or supportability. Use stable IDs and cross-references so an NFR can constrain several FRs without being duplicated inconsistently. A flat undifferentiated table makes feature coverage, related quality constraints and ownership harder to review as the catalog grows. Keep the RTM as the connecting view across groups. Exercise Q16 — Check versus technique ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q16. Distinguish a validation check (Section 4.7.1) from a validation technique (Section 4.7.2). Give one example of each. > [!tip]- Hint > One names a property; the other names an activity that gathers evidence about it. > [!success]- Solution > A validation check asks whether a property holds—for example, consistency asks whether FIFO priority and urgent precedence contradict. A technique is how we investigate—for example, a walkthrough places both requirements before Dr. Li and Ms. Lee and explores the same-room scenario. Reviews, prototypes and test-case generation are techniques; validity, consistency, completeness, realism and verifiability are checks. One technique can support several checks. Exercise Q17 — Derive a test ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q17. Which validation technique would you use to check whether a requirement is Verifiable? Walk through how you would apply it to a requirement of your choice. > [!tip]- Hint > Try to derive a reproducible test from the wording alone. > [!success]- Solution > Use test-case generation. Choose SR-2.1: if room capacity is below enrollment, reject the swap. Set capacity 30 and enrollment 45; submit as a lecturer meeting the use case’s preconditions; expect rejection and the specified warning. Add an equality case to ensure the capacity rule itself does not reject when capacity = enrollment, while retaining other applicable checks. If the requirement only said “a suitably sized room,” the input relation and expected decision would be undefined, revealing a verifiability defect. Designing this test does not mean it has been run. Exercise Q18 — Combine techniques ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q18. Explain why combining multiple validation techniques (e.g., a review and test-case generation) catches more defects than relying on just one. > [!tip]- Hint > Different techniques expose different classes of missing evidence. > [!success]- Solution > A review can notice contradictory approval policies or missing stakeholder scope even if each statement has a test. Test-case generation exposes ambiguous timing, inputs and expected outcomes. A UI prototype can reveal that a mandatory reason field or practical workflow is missing despite a plausible written description. Combining them therefore tests complementary assumptions and reduces blind spots. It costs more effort and still cannot prove absence of every defect; use the findings to revise the SRS and recheck affected areas. Exercise Q19 — Forward and backward tracing ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q19. Differentiate between Forward Traceability and Backward Traceability. How does backward traceability prevent "Gold Plating"? > [!tip]- Hint > Trace forward to find omissions; trace backward to find unsupported additions. > [!success]- Solution > Forward traceability follows a requirement into design, implementation and tests so an approved need is not omitted. Backward traceability starts with a module/code/test artifact and asks which approved requirement or justified derived constraint requires it. An extra feature with no justification is a gold-plating candidate: remove it from scope or take it through authorization rather than quietly expanding delivery. Necessary infrastructure can be justified through architecture/derived constraints; an unexplained row is a review finding, not an automatic deletion order. Exercise Q20 — Informal changes ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q20. Why is it dangerous to accept requirement changes informally via email or verbal communication during late-stage Waterfall implementation? > [!tip]- Hint > A message may record a request without authorizing a changed baseline. > [!success]- Solution > An informal acceptance can leave the SRS, code, tests and budget describing different products. Dependencies, regression work and schedule impact may be missed, producing scope creep and disputes about what was agreed. Capture the email or conversation as ECR input, assess impacts through the RTM, obtain the authorized decision and update the baseline plus affected artifacts. The communication medium is not inherently wrong; bypassing the agreed decision and version-control process is the problem. Exercise Q21 — RTM impact analysis ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q21. Explain, step by step, the role of the RTM during an Impact Analysis triggered by a new Engineering Change Request (ECR). > [!tip]- Hint > Start with changed requirements; follow every outgoing relationship and then check shared dependencies. > [!success]- Solution > 1. Record the ECR and identify the requirement IDs/versions it would change. 2. Query the RTM for dependent UR/SR/catalog entries, modules, code/API references and tests. 3. Inspect connected interfaces and shared constraints to find effects beyond the first row; the RTM is an index, not a substitute for engineering analysis. 4. Estimate implementation, data/interface changes, retesting, effort, cost and milestone impact. 5. Give this evidence to the CCB. 6. If approved, revise the SRS baseline, RTM, implementation/test plans and schedule/budget; retain history. If rejected, log the rationale and keep the baseline. In the case, NFR2 affects SR-1.1, GetScheduleService.java and TC-API-204; encryption evidence and timing checks must be updated, not merely the catalog sentence. Exercise Q22 — Already-booked room ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q22. Write an Unwanted Behavior EARS requirement for the case study: a lecturer attempts to request a room that is already booked at that time. > [!tip]- Hint > State an unwanted condition and an observable response; keep the earlier rejection variant distinct from the later waitlist revision. > [!success]- Solution > Following the main chapter’s rejection variant: IF a lecturer requests a room already booked for the requested time, THEN the system shall reject the swap request and refresh the available-room list. This uses Unwanted Behavior (IF/THEN), identifies the conflicting time and defines the response. It is a proposed formulation of the original rule. The supplement later replaces flat rejection with a waitlist and approved urgent precedence; a final combined specification must resolve that change explicitly rather than implementing both without conditions. Exercise Q23 — Performance and encryption ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q23. Given the conflict between NFR1 (loading time < 3s) and a High-Security Encryption requirement, explain how an engineering team should resolve this during RE Analysis. > [!tip]- Hint > A conflict score identifies a negotiation and evidence task, not permission to weaken a control. > [!success]- Solution > Mark the potential conflict symmetrically: > > | | NFR1 load <3s | High-security encryption | > |---|---:|---:| > | NFR1 load <3s | — | −1 | > | High-security encryption | −1 | — | > > Clarify the exact encryption obligation, data path and performance measurement. Measure or prototype a representative workload to establish whether overhead actually threatens the budget. Explore an implementation that meets both; if not feasible, assess scope, resources or an authorized target change and record the decision/owner. Do not silently reduce a mandatory security level. At original v1.0 in this source story, encryption was a future risk, not a committed NFR2; the later ECR makes it binding in the scenario. Document that status difference. The main text also alternates “<3s” and “within 3.0s”; settle the equality boundary before final testing. Exercise Q24 — Trace the room-swap need ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q24. Trace UR-2 (the room-swap requirement) through every phase checkpoint in this chapter, from its Elicitation Register entry to its RTM row. > [!tip]- Hint > Preserve E-003 as a condition even though it has no independent UR number. > [!success]- Solution > Feasibility: the case is allowed to proceed on its technology/budget/integration assumptions. Elicitation: Dr. Li’s E-002 records the urgent-swap problem; E-003 records Ms. Lee’s sign-off; UC-04 captures the interaction. Analysis: E-002 becomes UR-2, tagged Functionality with performance expectations; E-003 is attached as a constraint. Specification: SR-2.1 refines capacity rejection, and UC-04 supplies the pending-review workflow; FR2 triggers an administrator alert. SR-2.1 alone does not fully implement every part of UR-2. Validation: TC-UNIT-402 is derived for the capacity rule; prototype/walkthrough checks expose missing reason and approval/queue issues. RTM: UR-2 → SwapModule → TC-UI-105; SR-2.1 → CapacityChk (CapacityChecker/RoomValidationUtil.java in fuller reading) → TC-UNIT-402. Changes use ECR/CCB control. The source’s Passed labels are example statuses, not results from this task. Exercise Q25 — Transfer to an everyday app ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q25. Pick any everyday app on your phone. Write one User Requirement and derive one corresponding System Requirement from it, using EARS syntax. > [!tip]- Hint > Choose one familiar user outcome, then derive one observable system behavior. > [!success]- Solution > Chosen everyday app type: an alarm app (illustrative example, no actual phone inspection). UR-A1: A user can set an alarm to be alerted at a chosen time. Proposed SR-A1.1: WHEN the device clock reaches the enabled alarm’s saved trigger time, the alarm application shall present the configured alert. This is event-driven EARS. It refines a trigger and observable response without prescribing an internal scheduler. Clarify time zones, missed alarms, device power/permission conditions and timing tolerance before treating it as complete. Many other apps are valid if the derived SR preserves the user goal. Exercise Q26 — Spiral versus upfront ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★☆☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q26. Explain, in your own words, why the Spiral View (progressive refinement) does not contradict the idea that Waterfall RE happens 'upfront.' > [!tip]- Hint > Distinguish the lifecycle phase boundary from activities inside that phase. > [!success]- Solution > “Upfront” describes the placement of RE before the course’s downstream design/implementation stages. The spiral describes repeated learning within RE: business needs are elicited/specified/validated, then user needs, then detailed system requirements. Validation can send a draft back for clarification before a baseline is approved. Internal iterations are compatible with an upfront phase gate; they do not mean the team has completed separate agile product Sprints. Later baseline changes still use the course’s change-control process. Practical review questions Q27 and Q28 are preserved with adjacent hints and full solutions in Library Book Reservation — SRS Lab. Exercise Q29 — Where E-003 goes ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, §4.9, Apply What You've Learned, third prompt. E-003 (“room swaps should never bypass my sign-off”) never receives its own UR or SR ID anywhere in this chapter. Using the ID legend in the Glossary, explain where its content actually ends up in the SRS instead, and why it does not need an ID of its own. > [!tip]- Hint > No separate UR does not mean no traceable constraint. Ask whether alerting someone actually enforces their approval. > [!success]- Solution > The course attaches E-003 as a business constraint on UR-2 and the UC-04 approval workflow rather than creating a separate user goal. E-003 already has a raw-evidence ID, so preserve that reference in the parent requirement, description and test coverage. Its intended content is that allocation changes remain subject to Ms. Lee’s approval; FR2’s notification supports the workflow but alone does not enforce it. A separate UR/SR ID is not required by the source’s chosen organization if the condition is precise, independently checkable and traceable through the parent. Supplementary engineering note: giving an approval constraint its own stable ID may improve reviewability in a real catalog; neither choice permits omitting it. The supplied excerpt’s enforcement details remain incomplete.

entries.title: Library Book Reservation — SRS Lab
entries.text: Library Book Reservation — SRS Lab Course index · Notes · Exercises · Lab Objective and setup Produce a small requirements traceability matrix and a one-page SRS outline using the course's own applied review tasks. Original source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions Q27–Q28; method from §§4.6.1 and 4.8.1. These are document-design tasks; no implementation or particular tool/version is required. Use Notes and a Markdown editor. Keep this exercise's Library Book Reservation scope separate from the university timetable and Campus Express examples. The source specifies no reservation policies, users, database or API. State assumptions before designing a trace: assumptions below are illustrative proposals, not lecturer requirements. No code, running library system or test results were provided. Expected output: Exactly five RTM requirement rows with meaningful links and honest status, plus an SRS outline containing headings only. The outline should fit one A4 page under normal document settings; native A4 pagination is not verified here. An implementation, actual executed tests and stakeholder approval are outside this document task. Actual execution: Document examples authored and structurally checked; no software behavior was executed. Exercise Q27 — Five-row library reservation RTM ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q27. Design a 5-row Requirements Traceability Matrix for a simple 'Library Book Reservation' feature. > [!tip]- Hint > Choose a small set of explicit, compatible requirements. Give each a stable ID, justified design responsibility and a test with an observable outcome. Planned tests must not be labelled Passed. > [!success]- Solution > Proposed scope/assumptions: An authenticated library member may reserve an available copy, review their active reservations and cancel a reservation. Concurrent attempts must not allocate the same copy twice. The timing target below is a proposal needing approval; borrowing, fines, waitlists and expiry are outside this small example. > > Requirement definitions (proposed, not official policy): > > - FR-L1: WHEN an authenticated member requests an available copy, the reservation system shall create an active reservation for that member and mark that copy reserved. > - FR-L2: IF the requested copy has become unavailable before reservation commitment, THEN the system shall reject the attempt without creating a reservation and inform the requester. > - FR-L3: WHEN a member opens My Reservations, the system shall display that member’s active reservations. > - FR-L4: WHEN a member cancels their active reservation before collection, the system shall cancel it and return the copy to availability. > - NFR-L1: Under an agreed test workload of up to 50 concurrent members, at least 95% of reservation-create responses shall be returned within 2 seconds of request receipt during a 10-minute measurement window. The dataset and arrival pattern must be agreed before execution. > > Exactly five RTM rows. The requirement/purpose column records justification; design components and test IDs are proposed artifacts, not existing code. > > All five requirements are at System level. FR-L1–FR-L4 are draft requirements with planned tests; NFR-L1 is a proposed target and has not been run. > > | Requirement and purpose | Design | Test and evidence | > |---|---|---| > | FR-L1: Reserve an available copy | Reservation service | TC-L1: one valid request creates the linked reservation and changes copy state | > | FR-L2: Exclusive allocation; constrains FR-L1 | Reservation commit | TC-L2: concurrent requests for one copy yield at most one committed reservation; loser is informed | > | FR-L3: Review own reservations | Member reservations view | TC-L3: fixture with two members displays only requester’s active reservations | > | FR-L4: Cancel an uncollected reservation | Cancellation service | TC-L4: valid cancellation changes reservation and copy availability consistently | > | NFR-L1: Timely response; constrains FR-L1 and FR-L2 | Reservation request path | TC-L5: record latency distribution under agreed workload; ≥95% ≤2s | > > Why this is traceable: Start at a requirement to find the design/test obligation, or start at a component/test to find its purpose. FR-L2 supplies the concurrency condition that “available” in FR-L1 alone fails to settle. A test ID is useful only with its procedure/results and version; the table provides planned outcomes without fabricating execution. Other coherent five-row catalogs are valid if assumptions and coverage are explicit. Exercise Q28 — One-page library SRS outline ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE · Difficulty: ★★☆ Source: Requirements Engineering - Reading Material.docx, End-of-Chapter Review Questions, Q28. Draft a one-page SRS outline (section headings only) for the 'Library Book Reservation' feature, following the structure in Section 4.6.1. > [!tip]- Hint > Use the course’s five major sections, keeping specific requirements in 3.1–3.4 and the RTM in an appendix. Submit headings only, not a second full catalog. > [!success]- Solution > The following is the headings-only proposed outline. It retains the course template and groups the small feature catalog coherently. Printed one-page fit depends on native export settings; no export is claimed. > > 1. Introduction > - 1.1 Purpose > - 1.2 Scope of Library Book Reservation > - 1.3 Definitions, Acronyms and Glossary > - 1.4 References and Document Overview > 2. Overall Description > - 2.1 Product Perspective > - 2.2 Product Functions > - 2.3 User Characteristics > - 2.4 Constraints > - 2.5 Assumptions and Dependencies > 3. Specific Requirements > - 3.1 Functional Requirements > - 3.1.1 Create and Protect Reservations > - 3.1.2 View and Cancel Reservations > - 3.2 External Interface Requirements > - 3.3 Non-Functional Requirements by Quality/Constraint Category > - 3.4 Use Case Specifications and Supporting Models > 4. Appendices > - 4.1 Data Dictionary > - 4.2 Requirements Traceability Matrix > - 4.3 Interaction Analysis Grid > - 4.4 Revision History > 5. Approval and Sign-off Review and troubleshooting Check that the RTM has five requirement rows, every test has an expected outcome, and every status reflects actual evidence. If a requirement cannot produce a clear test, refine the condition rather than marking it verified. If your outline becomes several pages, remove explanatory paragraphs—the original question asks for headings only. Keep proposed design responsibilities free of unsupported framework/version assumptions. A five-row matrix is a learning example, not a complete real library specification. Missing institutional policies remain questions for elicitation. No external stakeholder interview, approval, implementation or test execution took place.

entries.title: In 60 seconds
entries.text: A model deliberately hides detail to answer a particular question. Context shows the boundary; use cases show external roles and their goals; sequence diagrams show ordered messages for one scenario. First decide who needs the model and what decision it supports. Source: lecture PDF pp. 4–7.

entries.title: Before you start
entries.text: Recall functional requirements from Unit 04. You need to distinguish an external actor from an internal object, a goal from an implementation step, and a condition from a sequence. This unit develops context/use-case/sequence topics only. Class, activity and state-machine diagrams appear in the agenda but have no teaching section in this supplied deck; they remain pending.

entries.title: 1. Choose a perspective and precision
entries.text: | Perspective | Question | Model | |---|---|---| | External | What lies outside? | Context | | Interaction | Who interacts, or in what order? | Use case / sequence | | Structural | What data structure exists? | Class (pending here) | | Behavioural | How does behavior evolve? | Activity / state machine (pending here) | An existing-system model clarifies current behavior for requirements discussions. A planned-system model communicates a proposed design. Model-driven tooling needs correct, complete specifications for what it generates; a discussion sketch can omit more detail. Accuracy expectations depend on purpose. Source: lecture PDF pp. 5–7.

entries.title: 2. Context is a boundary decision
entries.text: A context diagram shows surrounding systems and connections, not internal design or message order. Choosing the boundary affects responsibility and stakeholder interests. Supplementary boundary sketch derived from the courier tutorial: flowchart LR Customer --> Delivery[Parcel Delivery Management System] Delivery --> PayLink[External PayLink] Delivery --> SMS[External SMS gateway] Finance[Corporate invoicing software: outside scope] The Finance system is outside this project; the prompt does not require an integration to it. A box in this context sketch is not a UML use-case oval. Source: lecture PDF p. 9; Week 5 Tutorial.docx, Question 2.

entries.title: 3. Actors and goals
entries.text: A use-case diagram gives a high-level functional view: named system rectangle, actors outside, goal ovals inside, plain actor associations. An actor is a role, not a particular person; it can be a person, external system, device or timer. Primary actors pursue goals, supporting actors provide services, and offstage stakeholders have interests without directly using the system. Source: lecture PDF pp. 11–12. For the hotel exercise: Guest associates with Search Available Rooms, Book a Room, View Booking Details, Make Payment and Cancel Reservation. Hotel Receptionist associates with Check In Guest, Check Out Guest and Generate Occupancy Reports. The statement does not establish mandatory include links between these goals. Do not add policy because a booking app usually has it. Source: Week 5 - UML Lecture Exercise.docx, Hotel Reservation System.

entries.title: 4. Include, extend and generalization
entries.text: Include points from the base task to required reused behavior. Extend points from conditional additional behavior to its base use case, with its condition stated. Generalization points from specialized actor/use case to its general parent. Source: lecture PDF pp. 13–14; courier tutorial. Airline examples: Book Flight includes Make Payment; Apply Promo Code extends Book Flight [code supplied]; Request Special Assistance extends Check-In Online [assistance requested]. The exercise describes authentication as a prerequisite for every other passenger goal. Its wording can be represented as a precondition; if the teaching exercise expects an included authentication use case, state that abstraction rather than assuming a fresh login occurs within each action. The visually reviewed airline diagram in ANSWER.docx omits authentication despite that prerequisite in the worksheet. Keep the prerequisite visible in your explanation; this discrepancy does not prove that authentication is unnecessary. The diagram confirms the payment/include and promo/assistance/extend directions. > [!question]- Predict the arrow > A returned library book is overdue. Which use case extends which, and does every return require login? > [!success]- Check > Charge Overdue Fine extends Return Book [past due date], with the arrow toward Return Book. The prompt explicitly says return does not require login. Source: Week 5 Tutorial.docx, Question 1.

entries.title: 5. Requirements become scenarios
entries.text: The lecture traces banking requirements to goals and numbered flows. The newly verified Use-case Description.pdf supplies Fund Transfer and OBS-01…OBS-17. Deck references to OBS-18…OBS-20 exceed this PDF’s scope; do not invent those requirements. A full description names the use case and primary actor; preconditions; numbered main flow; alternates/exceptions branching from numbered steps; and postconditions. In Transfer Funds: choose accounts/amount, validate, show confirmation, confirm, post debit/credit/reference, then receipt/log. Insufficient funds and invalid account stop validation; cancellation discards; a posting fault rolls back. Source: lecture PDF pp. 15–22.

entries.title: 6. Read a sequence diagram
entries.text: Time runs downward on participants' lifelines. A synchronous message calls and waits; a dashed return carries its response. Activation bars show executing/waiting periods. Keep abstraction levels consistent. alt chooses guarded alternatives, opt performs one guarded optional block, loop repeats. Source: lecture PDF pp. 24–28. Supplementary textual reconstruction of the supplied login scenario (PDF pp. 29–30; lecture exercise Login): sequenceDiagram actor User participant Browser participant Auth as Authentication server User->>Browser: Submit credentials Browser->>Auth: Verify credentials activate Auth Auth->>Auth: Check stored records Auth-->>Browser: Authentication result deactivate Auth alt valid Browser-->>User: Welcome else invalid Browser-->>User: Error end Both branches are outcomes, not two messages that always run. The diagram is explanatory, not a prescribed implementation protocol.

entries.title: 7. Compose guarded interactions
entries.text: Checkout uses an opt [payment succeeded] for inventory update and order confirmation in the deck. The supplied ANSWER.docx checkout image uses alt [PaymentSuccessful] / [PaymentFailed] instead: the success branch updates stock and confirms the order; the failure branch sends Order Failed to the customer. These are two source variants. Neither supplies a refund or retry policy. Transfer Funds nests an outer alt for invalid/valid inputs, an opt for confirmation within valid, then an alt for posting success/fault. Sources: lecture PDF pp. 31–35; ANSWER.docx checkout image. For the vehicle-renewal tutorial, a missing record or unpaid fines must terminate before payment. For QuickMed, each failed check terminates the request; stock checks repeat for each medication; home delivery is optional. A declined payment is explicitly out of scope. These are fictional software scenarios, not clinical advice. Full adjacent worked reasoning is in Recall & practice.

entries.title: Review and source boundary
entries.text: Explain why a context diagram cannot substitute for a sequence diagram. Draw arrows for mandatory payment and optional insurance. Trace an early rejection without later successful messages. Then attempt all eight supplied Week 5 exercise/tutorial tasks in Recall & practice. The original source documents remain available from Source library. All five answer images were visually inspected and remain preserved in the original DOCX. Differences between worksheet, deck and answer image are stated above. The new local reasoning and Mermaid reconstructions are independently derived teaching aids; they are not claimed as lecturer-issued solutions. Class/activity/state teaching chapters remain outside this supplied deck; the banking-description PDF is now verified and available.

entries.title: Week 5 supplied figures — Compare the models
entries.text: These are byte-identical images extracted from the preserved lecture-exercise answer DOCX. They are supplied answer figures, not new local reconstructions or an official exam marking scheme. Hotel reservation Supplied hotel use-case diagram Read the boundary and Guest/Receptionist associations. The answer names the cancellation oval “Cancel Booking”, whereas the exercise uses “Cancel Reservation”; preserve that naming variant. No include/extend links are shown. Source: ANSWER.docx, Hotel Reservation System image. Airline booking Supplied airline use-case diagram Book Flight includes Make Payment; promo and special-assistance extensions point toward their base goals. The source omits the worksheet’s authentication prerequisite; the diagram does not remove that requirement. Source: ANSWER.docx, Air Ticket Booking System image. Login at two abstraction levels Supplied login overview sequence Supplied detailed login sequence Both use alternative success/failure responses. The second makes server verification explicit as a self-message. Different detail is not an extra execution result; do not run both alternative outcomes as one trace. Source: ANSWER.docx, Login images 1 and 2. Checkout Supplied checkout sequence The successful branch updates inventory before confirming; the failed-payment branch reports Order Failed. This supplied alt differs from the lecture’s success-only opt. Neither adds a refund or retry policy. Source: ANSWER.docx, Online Shopping Checkout image.

entries.title: Banking example — Retry, confirmation and source disagreement
entries.text: The three-page banking example is now available. Read the complete flow and OBS requirement map. It supplies seventeen requirements, not the twenty mentioned in some deck references. Insufficient funds and an invalid/unlinked destination do not post a transfer; the use-case description returns to step 3 to edit details. The earlier Practice 9 is a labelled one-attempt exercise: ending that attempt is different from ending the whole interactive use case. Cancellation discards the request and returns to Transaction Summary. Posting faults roll back partial effects, keep a support reference, report failure and return to the summary. Visible source conflict: the p.1 postcondition says “Origin a/c credited, destination a/c debited”. OBS-11 on p.2 explicitly says debit source and credit destination. The reconstruction below follows the explicit OBS-11 requirement and flags the conflicting postcondition for confirmation; it does not silently amend the original PDF. Supplementary sequence reconstruction, grounded in p.1 and OBS-07…OBS-14. It adds a retry loop to express the documented return to step 3; it is not a lecturer-issued diagram or implementation proof. sequenceDiagram actor Customer participant Bank as Online Banking System loop Enter or revise details until valid Customer->>Bank: Source, destination, amount Bank->>Bank: Validate balance and linked destination (OBS-07) alt insufficient funds Bank-->>Customer: Insufficient funds, return to step 3 (OBS-08) else invalid destination Bank-->>Customer: Invalid account, return to step 3 (OBS-09) else valid Bank-->>Customer: Confirmation summary (OBS-10) end end alt customer cancels Bank->>Bank: Discard request (OBS-14) Bank-->>Customer: Transaction Summary else customer confirms Customer->>Bank: Confirm transfer (OBS-11) Bank->>Bank: Debit source, credit destination, reference alt posting fault Bank->>Bank: Roll back partial effects, keep support reference (OBS-12) Bank-->>Customer: Transfer failed, Transaction Summary else posted successfully Bank->>Bank: Record history in both accounts (OBS-13) Bank-->>Customer: Transfer receipt end end The same PDF has a three-consecutive-invalid-login lock (OBS-04) and a ten-minute inactivity logout (OBS-17). These are this banking scenario’s rules; do not replace them with the different Week 4 answer example’s more-than-five-failures/window/lock-duration rule. No lock duration is specified here.

entries.title: Your route through this tutorial
entries.text: Work through all fourteen tasks in Recall & practice. Each has an adjacent hint and complete explanation. First attempt from memory, then compare the supplied answer, its scope and unresolved criteria. Both earlier question-only files and the new answer DOCX files are preserved in Source library.

entries.title: 1. Classical Waterfall and evolving requirements
entries.text: The worksheet compares an upfront approved requirements baseline with incremental Agile elaboration. Waterfall aims to reduce expensive downstream misunderstandings. Agile still performs requirements work and validation repeatedly. Avoid the absolute claim that Agile has no upfront work or Waterfall can never revisit a decision. Source: Tutorial Q1; Unit 04 notes.

entries.title: 2. Feasibility needs several kinds of evidence
entries.text: The parking budget addresses only one aspect. Check technical feasibility, operational fit, time/staff capacity and relevant constraints. When answering elicitation questions, connect the challenge to a concrete technique: observation for tacit practice, prototypes for unclear interaction needs, or workshops for conflicts. Source: Tutorial Q2–3.

entries.title: 3. Convert a wish into testable behavior
entries.text: Flight alerts, unusual withdrawals, approaching drivers and unlocked doors each need a trigger, defined conditions, response and acceptance criteria. User requirements express stakeholder goals; system requirements elaborate behavior. Terms such as instantly, exactly and unusual remain unresolved until criteria are agreed. The new sheets supply example values: flight 30 seconds, bank 3× average/10 seconds, driver updates every 5 seconds, and geofence/door notification within 30 seconds. Treat them as values in these supplied examples, not universal requirements; the sources leave some measurement and sensor semantics open. Source: Tutorial Q4; Additional Q1–3.

entries.title: 4. Separate functions and quality expectations
entries.text: Search, filtering, workout sync and offline downloading describe functions. Supplied targets are search 2 seconds/95%, workout sync completion 2 seconds, product filtering 1.5 seconds/95%, and download initiation with visible progress within 1 second. Completion and initiation are distinct events; normal load still needs definition. FURPS Performance covers those timing concerns; security is grouped under Functionality in the supplied course framework; concurrent-save integrity concerns Reliability. FURPS categories do not replace functional/quality analysis. Source: Tutorial Q5; Additional Q4–8.

entries.title: 5. Reason about interactions
entries.text: The 500 ms signed-answer problem is a possible resource/latency conflict. Mark the interaction, explain a concrete mechanism, propose a design and identify what needs testing. The supplied Q6 answer proposes acknowledging receipt before signing completes, then asynchronous signing/audit. Preserve that proposal while distinguishing receipt from signed acceptance and requiring explicit failure/recovery semantics; it cannot silently weaken the original requirement. Source: Tutorial Q6.

entries.title: Review
entries.text: Explain one requirement without using vague speed or accuracy language. Identify at least one criterion still requiring stakeholder agreement. Compare your complete fourteen attempts with the local worked reasoning, then revisit the cards marked for review. Supplied example thresholds are now visible; they are not measured results, official exam marks or predictions.

entries.title: Week 4 supplied answers — Boundaries worth checking
entries.text: Main answer sheet: six unchanged questions with new answers. Additional answer sheet: eight unchanged questions with new answers. Their numbers are answer-example requirements; the original question text did not prescribe them. - Main Q4: the answer reacts to departure-time changes, not only delays; it combines an Interactor need with a Domain data trigger. - Main Q6: a −1 matrix entry indicates a likely conflict, not measured impossibility. Its asynchronous-signing trade-off needs explicit acknowledgement semantics. - Additional Q6: one second applies to starting the download with progress, not finishing an entire episode. - Additional Q7: “more than 5” consecutive failures within 10 minutes triggers a 30-minute lock plus identity re-verification; preserve the strict boundary and the supplied Functionality label. - Additional Q8: Reliability is the source category; preserving all edits is an acceptance property, not proof that a merge algorithm has been implemented. Use the fourteen original practice identities to revisit saved answers. Existing ratings and written attempts remain your records; revised source explanations do not reset them or establish new mastery.

entries.title: Requirements Engineering — Revised Reading
entries.text: Requirements Engineering — Revised Reading Text transcription of Requirements Engineering - Reading Material (2).docx, SHA-256 bd94b39059dddef4a70da2f5e28e168c21edc9d236f252c53068ae974ae297d6. Paragraphs and all 55 tables are retained; nested tables are labelled and printed below their parent table. Word layout is not reproduced. The figure is available in the original DOCX. Version warning: the revised file retains a contents/review label for §4.9, but removes the actual §4.9 case-study summary and its three “Apply What You’ve Learned” prompts. End-of-chapter questions remain. The web preserves earlier practice as historical material rather than deleting saved answers. Source examples and Passed/sign-off stories are teaching scenarios, not actual executions or approvals. SOFTWARE ENGINEERING Chapter 4 Requirements Engineering Eliciting, Analyzing, Specifying, and Validating What a System Must Do | Course Roadmap This is the fourth chapter in the course sequence: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Software Engineering Chapter 2 — The Software Process Chapter 3 — Introduction to Agile Methodologies Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering (this chapter) Chapter 3 was the only chapter where we studied Agile software development. Starting with this chapter, and continuing through system design, implementation, and testing, the course works within the traditional Waterfall Model so that you experience both major process paradigms. | | --- | Reading Material & Study Guide Contents Learning Objectives 4.1 Where This Chapter Fits: From Agile Back to Waterfall 4.1.1 A Recap of the Waterfall Process 4.2 The Requirements Engineering Roadmap 4.2.1 The RE Activities and Their Deliverables 4.2.2 The Spiral View: Progressive Refinement 4.3 Phase 0: Feasibility Study 4.4 Phase 1: Requirements Elicitation 4.4.1 What Is Requirements Elicitation? 4.4.2 Where Do Requirements Come From? 4.4.3 Elicitation Techniques & How to Document Them 4.4.4 Common Elicitation Challenges & How to Resolve Them 4.4.5 Output of the Elicitation Phase 4.5 Phase 2: Requirements Analysis & Classification 4.5.1 Formalizing Raw Statements with EARS Syntax 4.5.2 Organizing Requirements: Abstraction Levels & Viewpoints 4.5.3 Challenge: Functional vs. Non-Functional Requirements Get Blended 4.5.4 Challenge: Hidden Architectural Conflicts 4.6 Phase 3: Requirements Specification 4.6.1 The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) Document 4.6.2 Governance & Key Challenges 4.6.3 Functional & Non-Functional Requirements in Depth 4.7 Phase 4: Requirements Validation 4.7.1 The Five Validation Checks 4.7.2 Requirements Validation Techniques 4.7.3 Worked Examples of Requirements Validation 4.8 Requirements Traceability & Change Control 4.8.1 Requirements Traceability 4.8.2 Change Control Governance 4.9 Case Study: The Complete Picture Key Takeaways Glossary of Key Terms End-of-Chapter Review Questions Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter, you should be able to: - Explain why Requirements Engineering (RE) is performed upfront in the Waterfall model and contrast this with the Agile approach from Chapter 3. - Describe the five RE phases — Feasibility Study, Elicitation, Analysis & Classification, Specification, and Validation — and the deliverable each one produces. - Explain what Requirements Elicitation is, where its raw material comes from, how to document it, and what it hands off to Analysis. - Distinguish between User Requirements and System Requirements, and explain why jumping straight to System Requirements is a common novice mistake. - Write unambiguous requirements using the EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) patterns. - Classify requirements using FURPS+ and detect conflicts using an interaction analysis grid. - Write functional and non-functional requirements — including measurable, testable non-functional requirements. - Explain the structure of a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) and how use cases, tables, and UML diagrams fit into it. - Apply requirements validation techniques — reviews, prototyping, test-case generation, and walkthroughs — individually or in combination. - Explain Requirements Traceability, build a simple Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM), and describe the Change Control Board (CCB) process. - Apply all of the above to a running case study — a University Timetabling System — that develops phase by phase across the chapter. 4.1 Where This Chapter Fits: From Agile Back to Waterfall In Chapter 3, we studied Agile methodology: iterative development, flexible scope, continuous customer feedback, and requirements that evolve sprint by sprint. | Important Note for the Rest of the Course Chapter 3 was the only chapter that used Agile. From this chapter onward — Requirements Engineering, System Design, Implementation, and Testing — the course operates inside the traditional Waterfall Model. Keep this in mind: many of the practices in this chapter (heavy documentation, formal sign-off, change control boards) exist because of the Waterfall model's plan-driven nature, not because they are universally "the right way" to do RE. | | --- | The Waterfall Model | 1. Requirements | 2. System Design | 3. Implementation | 4. Testing | | --- | --- | --- | --- | The Waterfall model is a sequential, plan-driven process: each phase must be completed, reviewed, and formally approved before the next phase begins. There is no built-in mechanism to revisit an earlier phase once it is signed off — which is exactly why the RE phase you are about to learn is so rigorous. 4.1.1 A Recap of the Waterfall Process You first met the Waterfall model back in Chapter 2 (The Software Process). Before going further into Requirements Engineering, it's worth recapping what actually defines Waterfall — because almost every practice in this chapter exists because of these traits. Three Core Characteristics - Sequential & Phase-Gated. Work flows in one direction, phase by phase. Each phase ends with a formal review and sign-off — a "gate" — before the next phase may begin. - Plan-Driven & Documented. Upfront planning replaces continuous conversation. Formal documents (like the SRS) are the primary way information crosses from one phase — and one team — to the next. - Rigid & Predictable. Scope, budget, and schedule are fixed early, which makes the project easy to track — but expensive to change once a phase is baselined. What Happens in Each Phase? Seeing the whole pipeline helps explain why Requirements carries so much weight: everything downstream is built directly on top of it. | Phase | What Happens | Key Deliverable | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. Requirements (this chapter) | Discover, analyze, specify, and validate what the system must do and the constraints it must satisfy. | Baselined SRS | | 2. System Design | Translate the SRS into software architecture, data models, and interface designs. | Design Specification | | 3. Implementation | Developers write and unit-test code that satisfies the design — and, ultimately, the original requirements. | Working Modules | | 4. Testing | Integrate all modules and verify / validate the complete system against the original requirements. | Verified System | Advantages and Disadvantages Like any process model, Waterfall is a set of trade-offs, not a free lunch: | Advantages | Disadvantages | | --- | --- | | Clear milestones and a strong audit trail — easy for stakeholders to track progress. Predictable budget and schedule, fixed early in the project. Well suited to fixed-scope, safety-critical, or heavily regulated projects. Formal documentation eases handoff between teams and over staff turnover. | Little room for change once a phase is baselined — scope changes are slow and costly. Stakeholders don't see working software until very late in the project. Requirements errors found during Testing are the most expensive of all to fix. High risk of building the wrong thing if early requirements are misunderstood. | | Why This Matters for This Chapter The biggest disadvantage above — costly late-stage fixes — is exactly what a rigorous Requirements phase exists to prevent. That single idea is the thread running through everything in the rest of this chapter. | | --- | Waterfall RE vs. Agile RE Requirement Engineering in Waterfall happens upfront, in its entirety. Engineers must elicit, analyze, specify, and validate as close to 100% of the requirements as possible before any architecture, database design, or code is written. Agile, in contrast, treats requirements as something that emerges continuously. The table below contrasts the two directly. | Dimension | Waterfall Requirements Engineering | Agile Requirements Engineering | | --- | --- | --- | | Timing & Cadence | Completed entirely in one dedicated upfront phase. | Continuous, in short iterations across the whole project. | | Documentation | Heavy, formal Software Requirements Specification (SRS). | Lightweight backlog items, user stories, acceptance criteria. | | Scope Change | Rigid — changes require a formal change-control procedure. | Flexible — the backlog is continuously reprioritized. | | Sign-off Target | Stakeholders sign off before system architecture begins. | Refined continuously with the product owner, sprint by sprint. | 4.2 The Requirements Engineering Roadmap Requirements define what a system should do, plus the constraints it must operate under. Requirements Engineering (RE) is the process of discovering, analyzing, documenting, and validating those needs. Rather than a single rigid pipeline, RE is best understood as an interlocking roadmap of five phases, each producing a specific deliverable, layered on top of a spiral of progressive refinement. 4.2.1 The RE Activities and Their Deliverables The roadmap breaks into five phases — this chapter dedicates one numbered section to each (4.3 through 4.7): | 1. Feasibility Phase 0 | 2. Elicitation Phase 1 | 3. Analysis Phase 2 | 4. Specification Phase 3 | 5. Validation Phase 4 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | These five phases are not strictly linear — Validation regularly sends work back to Elicitation or Analysis when gaps are found, and Specification draws directly on the requirements Analysis has organized. | Phase | What It Does | Deliverable | | --- | --- | --- | | 0. Feasibility Study | Evaluates technical, financial, and operational viability. | Feasibility Report | | 1. Elicitation | Gathers raw stakeholder needs and domain constraints — no organizing yet. | Elicitation Register (raw requirements, draft use cases) | | 2. Analysis & Classification | Organizes, classifies, and resolves conflicts in the raw material from Elicitation. | Organized User & System Requirements | | 3. Specification | Translates organized requirements into the formal, unambiguous SRS. | Draft Software Requirements Specification (SRS) | | 4. Validation | Checks correctness, completeness, and consistency; loops back if gaps are found. | Baselined (signed-off) SRS | 4.2.2 The Spiral View: Progressive Refinement While Waterfall requires the whole requirements phase to finish before design starts, the internal work of engineering those requirements is itself iterative. Think of it as three concentric loops, each one repeating the same four activities — Elicitation, Analysis, Specification, and Validation — but at a deeper level of detail. Each loop's validated output becomes the input the next loop refines. Skipping straight to the System loop without validating the Business and User loops first is one of the most common — and costly — mistakes in Waterfall RE. | | --- | 4.3 Phase 0: Feasibility Study Before spending time and money on requirements elicitation, an organization runs a Feasibility Study to determine whether the proposed system is even worth pursuing. Core Objectives - Determine whether the system contributes to the organization's overall objectives. - Evaluate whether the system can be built with current technology, within budget and schedule. - Assess whether the system can be integrated effectively with existing operational infrastructure and legacy systems. Key Input Sources Executive summaries, business mandates, high-level user expectations, legacy system architecture documentation, and technology market benchmarks. The Feasibility Report: Three Possible Outcomes | Outcome | Meaning | | --- | --- | | 1. Proceed | The project is technically and financially viable — move directly into Elicitation. | | 2. Scope Down | The project is only viable if specific high-cost or high-risk requirements are removed. | | 3. Cancel Project | The project is technically unfeasible, financially unviable, or misaligned with corporate goals. | | Case Study Checkpoint — Feasibility A university's IT Steering Committee commissions a Feasibility Study for a proposed Timetabling System. Current technology (a standard web/mobile stack) can meet the need, the budget covers a small development team for two semesters, and the system can integrate with the existing student records database. Outcome: Proceed. The Feasibility Report clears the project to move into Phase 1 — Elicitation, where we meet the people who will actually use the system. | | --- | 4.4 Phase 1: Requirements Elicitation 4.4.1 What Is Requirements Elicitation? Requirements Elicitation is the process of discovering and capturing the needs, wants, and constraints of stakeholders and the problem domain. It answers one question only: "What do stakeholders want and need?" It deliberately does not yet ask "How do these fit together?" or "Do these conflict?" — that is Phase 2's job. Elicitation is fundamentally a human, social activity — talking to people, watching them work, and reading what already exists — rather than a desk exercise. The raw material it produces is often messy, contradictory, and incomplete, and that is expected: it gets organized in Analysis, not here. | Elicitation vs. Analysis — Don't Blend Them Elicitation (Phase 1): Gather raw statements from stakeholders, as close to their own words as possible. Capture everything; judge nothing yet. Analysis & Classification (Phase 2): Take that raw material and organize it — sort User vs. System requirements, classify with FURPS+, and detect conflicts (Section 4.5). | | --- | 4.4.2 Where Do Requirements Come From? Requirements originate from a web of stakeholders and domain sources. Below are the four most common sources, each with a realistic example. | Source | Focus | Concrete Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Operational Managers | Workflow throughput, resource allocation, auditing, staff performance oversight. | "The system shall generate a weekly summary report detailing total room allocation requests, approval turnaround times, and unutilized room slots grouped by department." | | Corporate Policies | Business constraints, financial rules, brand guidelines, organizational hierarchy. | "All purchases or resource allocations exceeding $5,000 must undergo a multi-level approval sequence, requiring digital signatures from both the Department Head and Financial Controller." | | Physical Environment | Hardware limits, ambient conditions, physical locations, network access, sensor limits. | "The handheld barcode scanner software must maintain screen readability in direct sunlight up to 100,000 lux and operate continuously between -20°C and 50°C." | | Data Privacy Laws & Regulators | Statutory compliance (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS). | "The system shall automatically purge all personal identification records, activity logs, and personal email addresses exactly 30 days after account termination, in accordance with GDPR Article 17 ('Right to Erasure')." | 4.4.3 Elicitation Techniques & How to Document Them Different sources call for different techniques — and each technique has a natural way to document what it uncovers. The table below pairs them. | Technique | What It Captures | How to Document It | | --- | --- | --- | | Interviews | Deep, individual insight from a specific stakeholder (e.g., Ms. Lee, the Facility Administrator). | Interview notes attributed to the stakeholder, with date — kept close to their own wording. | | Workshops / JAD Sessions | Consensus and trade-offs across multiple stakeholders in one room. | Workshop minutes, plus a running requirements log of every raw statement raised. | | Observation & Shadowing | Tacit knowledge — habits users perform automatically and forget to mention. | Field notes and simple "as-is" workflow diagrams of what was observed. | | Questionnaires / Surveys | Broad input from a large stakeholder population. | Tabulated survey results, summarized by question. | | Document Analysis | Existing policies, forms, and legacy manuals that already encode a rule. | Extracted requirement statements, each citing its source document. | | Prototyping (Low-Fidelity) | Reactions to a concrete UI idea, before code is written. | Annotated wireframes plus a log of stakeholder feedback per screen. | The Elicitation Register Across every technique above, the single most useful artifact is an Elicitation Register — a running table that captures each raw statement exactly as it was gathered, before any analysis: | Field | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Informal ID | A temporary tag (e.g., E-014) so the statement can be referenced before it earns a formal UR/SR ID in Phase 2 or 3. | | Raw Statement | The stakeholder's need, captured as close to their own words as possible. | | Source | Who said it, and through which technique (interview, workshop, observation, document, survey). | | Date | When it was captured — useful when requirements evolve or contradict each other over time. | | Status | Draft, by default. (Only Phase 2 promotes an entry to "Organized" or "Classified.") | Example — Elicitation Register (excerpt, University Timetabling System) | ID | Raw Statement | Source | Date | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | E-001 | "I want to see my class schedule on my phone, not just on the desktop portal." | Sarah (Student), interview | 3 Feb | Draft | | E-002 | "When I need to swap a room urgently, right now I have to email the admin and hope she sees it in time." | Dr. Li (Lecturer), workshop | 5 Feb | Draft | | E-003 | "Room swaps should never bypass my sign-off — I'm accountable for room conflicts." | Ms. Lee (Facility Administrator), interview | 6 Feb | Draft | These three entries recur throughout this chapter as a running case study: E-001 and E-002 are picked up in Phase 2 (Section 4.5) and organized into User Requirements, while E-003 becomes a business constraint attached to E-002's requirement rather than a standalone entry. Use Case Diagrams: A First Map of Actors and Use Cases Before writing a detailed description of any one interaction, it helps to see the whole system at a glance. A Use Case Diagram groups system functions visually by user role ("Actors") and by system boundary — a lightweight sketch of who does what, drawn directly from the raw Elicitation Register and stakeholder list above. It requires no analysis yet: it is simply a map of the raw material, not a judgment about it. Each oval on the diagram — each candidate use case — becomes a natural target for a full Use Case Description below. The diagram scopes which interactions exist; the description spells out how one of them actually plays out, step by step. Use Case Descriptions: A Documentation Technique for Elicitation A Use Case Description bridges a high-level user goal and a concrete interaction, in structured narrative form. It is one of the most useful ways to document what Elicitation uncovers, because stakeholders can read it back and immediately confirm — or correct — the team's understanding. Template - Use Case ID & Name — unique identifier and descriptive action name. - Primary Actor — the specific user role initiating the action. - Pre-conditions — system state that MUST be true before the use case can execute. - Post-conditions (Success Guarantee) — state of the system after successful execution. - Main Success Scenario (Happy Path) — the step-by-step numbered interaction flow. - Extensions / Alternate Flows — branching paths for optional choices or errors. Worked Example — UC-04: Request Urgent Timetable Room Swap | Field | Description | | --- | --- | | Primary Actor | University Lecturer | | Pre-conditions | 1. Lecturer is authenticated. 2. Lecturer has an assigned lecture session within the next 48 hours. | | Post-conditions | 1. Swap request record created with status PENDING\_ADMIN\_REVIEW. 2. Notification email queued for the Facility Administrator. 3. Room slot temporarily flagged as SWAP\_REQUESTED. | | Main Success Scenario | 1. Lecturer opens "My Schedule" and selects a class session. 2. System displays class details and available alternative rooms. 3. Lecturer selects a target room and enters a mandatory reason. 4. Lecturer submits the request. 5. System validates room capacity and equipment against class size. 6. System logs the request and returns a confirmation tracking ID (REQ-XXXX). | | Extensions | 5a. Target room capacity is smaller than enrollment: 1. System warns: "Selected room capacity (30) is smaller than enrollment (45)." 2. System prompts the Lecturer to pick another room or request a capacity override. 5b. Target room is concurrently requested by another lecturer: 1. System flags the concurrency conflict. 2. System rejects the submission and refreshes the available room list. | | Frequently Asked: Should Use Case Descriptions Be Written in Stage 1 or Stage 3? Both — but for different purposes, at different levels of finish: Stage 1 (Elicitation): drafted informally, in the stakeholder's own language, focused on the happy path. Its job is to confirm the team correctly understood one specific interaction — nothing more. Stage 3 (Specification): the same use case is revisited, finalized, and formalized — every extension and alternate flow is fully specified, pre/post-conditions are made precise, and it becomes part of the baselined SRS (Section 4.6.1). We introduce the template here, in Elicitation, because that is when you first capture it. Just remember: the version that ends up in the SRS has already been through Analysis and Validation, and is far more precise than the draft above. | | --- | 4.4.4 Common Elicitation Challenges & How to Resolve Them | Challenge | Resolution Strategy | | --- | --- | | 1. "Tacit Knowledge" — users rely on subconscious habits and forget to explain core steps. | Process Ethnography & Shadowing — engineers observe users performing daily tasks in real time. | | 2.
