Its deliverables are deliberately raw: | Deliverable | Description | | --- | --- | | Elicitation Register | The running log of raw, informally-tagged requirement statements described above. | | Draft Use Case Diagram | A lightweight actor/system-boundary sketch scoping which interactions exist — not yet analyzed. | | Draft Use Case Descriptions | Happy-path-only narratives confirming the team's understanding of key interactions (e.g., UC-04). | | Stakeholder & Viewpoint List | Who was consulted, and which Viewpoint they represent (formalized as VOA in Phase 2, Section 4.5.2). | | Domain Glossary (Draft) | A first pass at shared terminology, to be refined as Analysis proceeds. | | Supporting Artifacts | Interview notes, workshop minutes, field observations, low-fidelity prototypes and feedback. | Nothing above is yet classified as a User Requirement or System Requirement, prioritized, or checked for conflicts — that transformation is exactly what Phase 2, Analysis & Classification, does next. | Case Study Checkpoint — Elicitation The team runs interviews and a workshop with three stakeholders: Sarah (a Student), Dr. Li (a Lecturer), and Ms. Lee (the Facility Administrator). The Elicitation Register fills up with entries like: E-001 (Sarah, interview): "I want to see my class schedule on my phone, not just on the desktop portal." E-002 (Dr. Li, workshop): "When I need to swap a room urgently, right now I have to email the admin and hope she sees it in time." E-003 (Ms. Lee, interview): "Room swaps should never bypass my sign-off — I'm accountable for room conflicts." A draft Use Case Description (UC-04, above) is written from E-002 to confirm the room-swap workflow with Dr. Li. These raw, unorganized entries — plus the domain glossary and stakeholder list — move to Phase 2 for analysis. | | --- | 4.5 Phase 2: Requirements Analysis & Classification Elicitation (Phase 1) produces a raw, unorganized pile of stakeholder requests. Analysis & Classification turns that pile into a coherent, structured framework. Skip this step and three things go wrong: - Developers treat all requests as a flat list, missing architectural dependencies. - Conflicts between requirements stay hidden until code integration, causing massive rework. - Non-functional attributes get ignored during architecture design, causing performance bottlenecks after release. 4.5.1 Formalizing Raw Statements with EARS Syntax Before the raw Elicitation Register can be organized, classified, or checked for conflicts, its entries need to be rewritten in a single, unambiguous sentence format. A stakeholder's raw words — "the system should swap rooms quickly" — cannot be sorted, tagged with FURPS+, or scored in a conflict matrix, because two readers could disagree about what it actually commits the system to. EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) fixes this by giving every requirement one of five sentence templates. Everything Analysis does later in this section — the User/System split, FURPS+ tagging, and the Interaction Analysis grid — assumes the statement it's working with is already in EARS form. | Pattern | Template | When to Use | | --- | --- | --- | | Ubiquitous | The \ shall \ . | Always true, no trigger or condition | | Event-Driven | WHEN \ , the \ shall \ . | A specific event fires it | | State-Driven | WHILE \ , the \ shall \ . | Only during a state | | Option-Driven | WHERE \ , the \ shall \ . | Optional feature/configuration | | Unwanted Behavior | IF \ , THEN the \ shall \ . | Error or exception handling | Pattern 1 — Ubiquitous Template: The \ shall \ . - The system shall display all date and time values in UTC format. - The system shall log all user authentication attempts in an immutable audit table. Patterns 2 & 3 — Event-Driven and State-Driven Event-Driven template: WHEN \ , the \ shall \ . - WHEN a lecturer submits a room swap request, the system shall email the facility administrator within 5 seconds. State-Driven template: WHILE \ , the \ shall \ . - WHILE database sync is in progress, the system shall disable the manual data import button. Patterns 4 & 5 — Option-Driven and Unwanted Behavior Option-Driven template: WHERE \ , the \ shall \ . - WHERE biometric hardware is present, the app shall allow fingerprint authentication. Unwanted Behavior template: IF \ , THEN the \ shall \ . - IF an invalid password is entered 3 times, THEN the system shall lock the account for 15 minutes. | Why This Comes Before Organizing and Classifying A requirement written in EARS syntax carries its own trigger, condition, and response as separate, identifiable parts. That structure is exactly what the rest of Analysis needs: it's what lets a requirement be tagged cleanly under FURPS+, and it's what lets a conflict-detection grid compare two requirements' conditions against each other in Section 4.5.4. Formalizing first means every later step in Analysis — and every ID like UR-1 or NFR1 you'll see for the rest of this chapter — already refers to a precise, testable sentence, not a raw stakeholder quote. | | --- | 4.5.2 Organizing Requirements: Abstraction Levels & Viewpoints The next task of Analysis is to take the now-formalized requirements and sort them — by level of detail, and by whose perspective they represent. Two structured mechanisms do this. 1. Requirement Abstraction Levels: User vs. System | | User Requirements | System Requirements | | --- | --- | --- | | Written for | Stakeholders (non-technical) | Developers and testers | | Style | Natural language, simple tables, intuitive diagrams | Structured, technical, precise | | Answers | What services does the user need? What are the business goals? | What exact functions, API endpoints, data structures, and operational constraints must exist? | | Avoid the "Rabbit Hole" Trap Novice engineers often dive into low-level System Requirements — database schemas, API protocols, caching strategies — before they fully understand the high-level User Requirements. Focusing on technical mechanisms too early causes teams to build a complex, well-engineered system that solves the wrong problem. Rule of thumb: you cannot specify how a system should work until you fully understand what problem the user is trying to solve. | | --- | Why this distinction matters. User Requirements keep the SRS in language every stakeholder can read and validate for themselves — Sarah or Dr. Li can confirm "yes, that's what I meant" without needing to understand databases or APIs. System Requirements give developers and testers the precision to actually build and test against. Blur the two together and one of two failure modes follows: either stakeholders can't confirm you understood them correctly, because the document is too technical for them to sign off on, or developers are left guessing at intent, because the document never got precise enough to build from. That second failure mode is exactly how the "rabbit hole" trap above happens. 2. Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA) Purpose: VOA groups requirements by the perspective they come from, so that no stakeholder's needs get overlooked simply because they never spoke up in an interview: - Interactor Viewpoints — people who directly use the UI. - Indirect Viewpoints — stakeholders who never touch the system but rely on its outputs (e.g., auditors, executives). - Domain Viewpoints — environmental and technical constraints imposed by the domain itself. Why we need it. Elicitation techniques like interviews and workshops naturally capture the people in the room — usually Interactor viewpoints. VOA forces the analyst to also ask: who is affected but wasn't interviewed (an Indirect stakeholder, like an auditor who needs a compliance report), and what constraints exist regardless of what anyone says (a Domain constraint, like a data-protection law or an existing legacy database schema)? Without deliberately checking all three, a system requirements engineer only ever hears from — and designs for — the loudest voices in the elicitation sessions. 4.5.3 Challenge: Functional vs. Non-Functional Requirements Get Blended A Functional Requirement (FR) describes a specific behavior the system must perform — an input, output, or action. A Non-Functional Requirement (NFR) describes a quality attribute or constraint on how well the system performs — speed, security, usability, and the like. In practice, stakeholders rarely separate the two on their own. Stakeholders often blend a performance constraint directly into a feature description — e.g., "The system shall print invoices instantly." Is "instantly" a feature or a performance target? Both, tangled together. | Resolution — the FURPS+ Framework FURPS+ is a checklist for separating operational behavior (Functional) from quality constraints (Non-Functional): Functionality — features, capabilities, security Usability — human factors, aesthetics, consistency, documentation Reliability — availability, accuracy, recoverability, failure rate Performance — speed, throughput, efficiency, response time Supportability — testability, maintainability, configurability + — Design, Implementation, Interface, and Physical constraints Under FURPS+, "The system shall print invoices instantly" splits into a Functional requirement ("the system shall support printing invoices") plus a Performance requirement ("the invoice print job shall complete within 2 seconds of submission"). | | --- | | FAQ — Is the "F" in FURPS+ the Same as a Functional Requirement? No — and the distinction matters. The F in FURPS+ ("Functionality") is a category label: a bucket you tag a requirement with, covering features, capabilities, and security behaviors in general. An FR (Functional Requirement) is a single, specific, EARS-formatted statement — e.g., "WHEN a lecturer submits a room swap request, the system shall email the facility administrator within 5 seconds." Every FR you write gets tagged Functionality under FURPS+, but the FURPS+ label itself is not a requirement — it's a classification. So why does an otherwise Non-Functional-oriented checklist include an F category at all? FURPS+ was designed as a complete classification scheme — one place to tag every requirement you write, not just the non-functional ones. Leaving Functionality out would force you to track FRs in one system and NFRs in another. Including F means a single FURPS+ tag on any requirement tells you at a glance which of the six categories it belongs to, whether that requirement turns out to be functional or non-functional in nature. | | --- | 4.5.4 Challenge: Hidden Architectural Conflicts An architectural conflict occurs when satisfying one requirement makes it harder — or impossible — to satisfy another, because both press on the same underlying resource or design decision (processing time, memory, bandwidth, or a single code path). Two requirements can each be individually clear and individually testable, and still conflict once combined. Satisfying one requirement can directly impair another — for example, real-time responsiveness versus heavy encryption overhead. These conflicts are easy to miss when requirements are reviewed one at a time. | Resolution — Matrix-Based Interaction Analysis Build a grid that scores every pair of requirements: +1 = Compatible, 0 = Neutral, −1 = Conflict. This surfaces trade-off points before architecture design begins. | | --- | | | FR1: Mobile Display | NFR1: Load \< 3s | NFR2: High Encryption | FR2: Instant Swap | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | FR1: Mobile Display | — | +1 | 0 | 0 | | NFR1: Load \< 3s | +1 | — | −1 (Conflict) | 0 | | NFR2: High Encryption | 0 | −1 (Conflict) | — | 0 | | FR2: Instant Swap | 0 | 0 | 0 | — | Reading this grid: NFR1 ("load under 3 seconds") and NFR2 ("high encryption") conflict, because strong encryption adds processing overhead that works against a tight load-time budget. This tells the architecture team, before a single line of code is written, that they need an explicit trade-off decision — e.g., asynchronous decryption, caching, or a relaxed encryption tier for this specific data path. Note: labels like "NFR1: Load \< 3s" are shorthand tags for full EARS-formatted statements written in Section 4.5.1 (e.g., NFR1 is the Ubiquitous statement "The mobile application shall load timetables within 3.0 seconds over a 4G connection"). The grid only works because each requirement is already precise enough to compare — that precision is what EARS syntax guarantees. 4.6 Phase 3: Requirements Specification Once requirements are analyzed, engineers translate them into technical System Requirements, documented inside the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). Three ideas define what "Specification" actually means as a phase: - From User to System. Every User Requirement approved in Phase 2 is rewritten as one or more precise, technical System Requirements — the UR-1 → SR-1.1 pattern you'll see worked through below. - One Document, Every Artifact. Every FR, NFR, use case, and diagram this chapter has produced is assembled into a single governed deliverable — the SRS — rather than staying scattered across interview notes and whiteboard photos. - Governed, Not Casual. The SRS isn't just written and shipped — it passes through a formal Steering Committee sign-off, discussed in Section 4.6.2, before it becomes the baselined contract between the development organization and the client. 4.6.1 The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) Document Every artifact this chapter has built — User Requirements, System Requirements, EARS statements, use cases, the interaction grid — is ultimately assembled into one document: the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). Once validated, this document becomes the formal, baselined contract between the development organization and the client — Section 4.8 revisits that role in the context of traceability and change control. Here, we look at what actually goes inside it. Standard SRS Structure | Section | Contents | | --- | --- | | 1. Introduction | Purpose, scope, definitions/acronyms/glossary, references, document overview. | | 2. Overall Description | Product perspective, summary of product functions, user characteristics, constraints, assumptions & dependencies. | | 3.1 Functional Requirements | Every FR, in EARS syntax, organized by feature/module — not one giant flat list. | | 3.2 External Interface Requirements | UI, hardware, software, and communication interface requirements. | | 3.3 Non-Functional Requirements | Every NFR, organized by FURPS+ category, written to be measurable (Section 4.6.3). | | 3.4 Use Case Specifications & Models | Use case diagrams and finalized use case descriptions; UML diagrams where they add clarity. | | 4. Appendices | Data dictionary, Requirements Traceability Matrix (Section 4.8.1), interaction analysis grid, revision history. | | 5. Approval / Sign-off | Signatures from the Joint Steering Committee (Section 4.6.2), marking the document baselined. | Should the SRS Include Use Cases, Tables, and UML? Yes to all three — used deliberately, not decoratively: - Use Case Diagrams & Descriptions — yes, in Section 3.4. They show actor-system interactions at a glance and give the finalized version of the drafts written during Elicitation (Section 4.4.3). - Tables — yes, extensively: the FR list, the NFR list, the RTM, the interaction/conflict grid, and the glossary are all naturally tabular, and tables make a large requirement set scannable and comparable. - UML Diagrams — yes, where they clarify something text alone cannot: a Class Diagram for the domain data model, a Sequence Diagram for a complex multi-step interaction (like the UC-04 room-swap flow), or a State Diagram for a State-Driven (WHILE...) requirement. Not every requirement needs a diagram — reserve them for genuinely complex behavior; a diagram for every trivial requirement adds noise, not clarity. How to Include All Functional and Non-Functional Requirements A large project can easily produce hundreds of requirements. The SRS stays usable only with a consistent organizing scheme: - Unique, stable IDs. Every requirement keeps a prefix indicating its type and module — e.g., UR-2, SR-2.1, FR-SCHED-01, NFR-PERF-01 — matching the ID scheme already used in the RTM (Section 4.8.1). See the ID legend in the Glossary for how all these prefixes relate to one another. - Group FRs by feature/module. A subsection per module (e.g., Scheduling, Room Swap, Notifications) — not one undifferentiated list — so a reviewer can find everything about one feature in one place. - Group NFRs by FURPS+ category. A dedicated subsection per quality attribute (Performance, Usability, Reliability, Security, Supportability, Constraints), so each is reviewed as a coherent set. - Cross-reference everything. Every FR should state which Use Case it realizes; every NFR should state which FR(s) or module it constrains. - One consistent sentence template. Every requirement uses an EARS pattern (Section 4.5.1), so the whole catalog reads uniformly regardless of who wrote which section. - Maintain the RTM as the master cross-reference. The Requirements Traceability Matrix (Section 4.8.1) is what ultimately proves nothing was left out or left orphaned. What Else Should the Document Include? Beyond the requirement catalog itself, a complete SRS typically also carries: - A Data Dictionary. Precise definitions of every data entity and field referenced by the requirements (e.g., what exactly is a "class session"?). - A Revision History. Every baseline version (v1.0, v1.1...) with the date and Change Control Board decision that produced it (Section 4.8.2). - Assumptions & Dependencies. External factors the requirements rely on — e.g., "assumes the university's existing student database remains available." - A Glossary. The domain terminology agreed during Elicitation (Section 4.4.3), finalized. 4.6.2 Governance & Key Challenges Moving from analyzed user needs to a formal specification requires sign-off from a Joint Steering Committee: | Role | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Lead System Architect & Business Analyst | Verifies technical feasibility and conceptual completeness. | | Client Representative / Project Sponsor | Confirms high-level user requirements accurately represent business objectives. | | Project Manager | Confirms specified scope matches contractual budget and timeline. | Beyond governance, two challenges recur while writing the specification itself: - Natural Language Ambiguity ("Requirement Smells"). Words like "fast," "user-friendly," "secure," or "robust" mean different things to different readers. This is exactly what EARS syntax (Section 4.5.1) exists to prevent — every requirement that reaches Specification should already be in one of the five EARS patterns. - Over-Specification (Implementation Bias). Accidentally prescribing implementation details (e.g., naming a specific SQL table) instead of describing external system behavior. 4.6.3 Functional & Non-Functional Requirements in Depth Building on the FR/NFR distinction introduced in Section 4.5.3, this section goes deeper: concrete categories, and — most importantly — how to write an NFR so it can actually be tested. Functional Requirements (FR) define a specific behavior the system must perform — a concrete input, output, or action. They answer "what does the system do?" and are written using the EARS patterns you learned in Section 4.5.1. | Category | Example Functional Requirement | | --- | --- | | Data Management | WHEN a student updates their profile address, the system shall update the central student information database. | | User Management | The system shall allow an administrator to deactivate a lecturer account. | | Reporting | The system shall generate a weekly room-utilization report grouped by department. | | Integration | WHEN a new semester is created in the timetabling system, the system shall synchronize course codes with the university's ERP system. | Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) define a quality attribute or constraint on how well the system performs its functions — not what it does. FURPS+ (Section 4.5.3) gives the categories; the challenge is writing them so they can actually be tested. Writing Measurable Non-Functional Requirements An NFR is only useful if a tester can look at it and say Pass or Fail with no argument. That requires three ingredients in the sentence itself: | The Measurable-NFR Template The \ shall \ within/under \ when/under \ . Metric — what is being measured (time, throughput, error rate, uptime %, concurrent users, MTBF...). Threshold — a specific number with a unit. "Fast" is not a threshold; "2 seconds" is. Condition — the context under which the threshold applies (load level, network type, hardware, percentile of requests). | | --- | Applying that template to common vague requirements: | Vague (Unmeasurable) | Rewritten (Measurable) | | --- | --- | | "The system shall be fast." | "The system shall return search results within 2 seconds for 95% of queries under normal load (≤100 concurrent users)." | | "The system shall be user-friendly." | "A first-time user shall complete the room-swap workflow in under 3 minutes without external help, measured via usability testing with 10 representative users." | | "The system shall be secure." | "The system shall encrypt all data at rest using AES-256 and require multi-factor authentication for all administrator accounts." | | "The system shall be reliable." | "The system shall maintain 99.9% uptime measured monthly, excluding scheduled maintenance windows." | | "The system shall be scalable." | "The system shall support up to 10,000 concurrent users with less than 5% degradation in response time." | | Measurability Checklist Before finalizing any NFR, confirm: Does it contain a number? Does that number have a unit (seconds, %, requests/sec, concurrent users)? Does it state the condition under which the number applies? Could a tester write a Pass/Fail test case from this sentence alone? That last question is exactly the Verifiability validation check from Section 4.7 — writing measurable NFRs here is what makes that check pass later. | | --- | | Case Study Checkpoint — Specification From User Requirement to System Requirement Nested table in row 1, column 1 (below) The same pattern repeats for every User Requirement, not just UR-1. Dr. Li's UR-2 goes through the identical transformation: Nested table in row 1, column 1 (below) The Timetabling System's draft functional and non-functional requirements, in EARS syntax, ready for Section 3.1/3.3 of the SRS: Nested table in row 1, column 1 (below) Where's NFR2? The Interaction Analysis Grid (Section 4.5.4) only flagged encryption as a future risk against NFR1 — it was never a committed requirement at baseline time, so it does not appear in this table. NFR2 is written out in full only once it is actually triggered, six months later, by a formal Engineering Change Request — see the worked example in the Traceability & Change Control checkpoint (Section 4.8.2). These entries, together with UC-04 (finalized) and the interaction grid from Phase 2, are exactly what Section 4.6.1's SRS structure asks for in Sections 3.1, 3.3, and 3.4. Next, Phase 4 must validate all of it before it can be baselined. | | --- | Nested table in row 1, column 1 | Step | Requirement | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Phase 1 (Elicitation) | UR-1: "The system shall allow students to view their weekly timetable on mobile devices." | Drafted from Sarah's raw statement (E-001). Focuses strictly on operational need — no database schema, no network protocol. | | Phase 3 (Specification) | SR-1.1: "WHEN a student logs into the mobile app, the system shall fetch and render the current week's schedule array in calendar format within 3.0 seconds over a 4G network connection." | Derived after UR-1 was organized in Phase 2 and approved by the Steering Committee. Gives developers and QA concrete, testable parameters. | Nested table in row 1, column 1 | Step | Requirement | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Phase 1 (Elicitation) | UR-2: "The system shall allow lecturers to request an urgent swap to another available room for a scheduled class session." | Drafted from Dr. Li's raw statement (E-002). E-003 ("swaps should never bypass my sign-off") attaches as a business constraint on UR-2, rather than becoming its own requirement. | | Phase 3 (Specification) | SR-2.1: "IF the requested room's capacity is less than the class's enrollment, THEN the system shall reject the swap and prompt the lecturer to select another room." | Ties to UC-04's extension 5a. Turns the vague "available room" idea into a testable rejection condition a developer can implement directly. | Nested table in row 1, column 1 | ID | EARS Type | Requirement | | --- | --- | --- | | FR1 | Ubiquitous | The system shall display weekly class schedules in a calendar view. | | FR2 | Event-Driven | WHEN a room change request is submitted by a lecturer, the system shall send an alert notification to the administrator. | | FR3 | State-Driven | WHILE the database synchronization is in progress, the system shall display a visual loading indicator. | | FR4 | Option-Driven | WHERE text-to-speech accessibility is enabled, the system shall read out room schedule details upon selection. | | FR5 | Unwanted Behavior | IF an invalid university ID is entered during authentication, THEN the system shall display an "Invalid Credentials" error message. | | NFR1 | Ubiquitous | The mobile application shall load timetables within 3.0 seconds over a 4G connection. | 4.7 Phase 4: Requirements Validation 4.7.1 The Five Validation Checks Validation checks whether the specified requirements correctly reflect what stakeholders actually expect. There are five check types, each catching a different class of defect. | Check Type | What It Catches | Concrete Example | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. Validity | Features that don't align with real operational needs. | Confirming room swap requests actually require administrative sign-off per university policy, avoiding unnecessary automated overrides. | | 2. Consistency | Requirements that contradict each other. | Catching that FR-2 says "All requests are automatically approved" while NFR-4 says "All allocations require manual admin confirmation." | | 3. Completeness | Scenarios that were simply forgotten. | Noticing the spec never defines the account-recovery workflow for a user who loses their two-factor device. | | 4. Realism | Requirements that are physically or financially impossible. | Proving that 50,000 requests/sec is unachievable under a $10,000 cloud infrastructure budget. | | 5. Verifiability | Requirements that can't be objectively tested. | Rewriting "System shall render UI quickly" into "System shall render the home screen in under 1.5 seconds" so it has a clear Pass/Fail test. | 4.7.2 Requirements Validation Techniques The five checks above describe what to look for. The techniques below describe how a team actually goes looking for it. None of these techniques is exclusive — a mature RE process routinely combines several on the same SRS draft. | Technique | How It Works | Checks It's Best At | | --- | --- | --- | | Requirements Reviews / Inspections | A panel (peers, domain experts, QA) walks through the SRS against a checklist, formally (e.g., a Fagan inspection) or informally. | Consistency, Completeness, Validity | | Prototyping | Build a throwaway or evolutionary prototype (UI mockup or working proof-of-concept) and have stakeholders interact with it. | Validity, Completeness — especially for UI-heavy requirements | | Test-Case Generation | For each requirement, attempt to write a concrete Pass/Fail test case. If you can't, the requirement fails. | Verifiability | | Walkthroughs | An informal, step-by-step presentation of requirements or use cases to stakeholders, to confirm shared understanding. | Validity, Completeness | | Model / Consistency Checking | Cross-check the System Models (use case diagrams, data-flow diagrams, state charts) against each other and against the text. | Consistency | | Traceability Analysis | Use the RTM (Section 4.8.1) to find orphan requirements (no design/test) or orphan code (no requirement). | Completeness, Consistency | | Combine, Don't Choose Just One A single technique rarely catches every defect type. A common, effective combination: run a formal review and attempt test-case generation on the same SRS draft, while running prototyping in parallel for any UI-heavy features. Section 4.7.3 below applies several of these techniques to the same case study. | | --- | 4.7.3 Worked Examples of Requirements Validation Each example below applies one technique from Section 4.7.2 to a requirement you've already seen in this chapter. Example 1 — Test-Case Generation (from SR-2.1) Requirement: "IF target room capacity is less than enrollment, THEN the system shall reject the swap." - Given a room with capacity 30 and a class enrollment of 45, - When the lecturer submits the swap request, - Then the system rejects the request and displays a capacity warning. This is exactly Test Case TC-UNIT-402 in the RTM (Section 4.8.1) — the requirement was verifiable enough to generate a test directly from its wording. Example 2 — Requirements Review (catching an unmeasurable NFR) A reviewer checks a draft requirement against the Measurability Checklist (Section 4.6.3): "The mobile app shall load timetables quickly." It fails — no number, no unit, no condition. The review sends it back rewritten as NFR1: "The mobile application shall load timetables within 3.0 seconds over a 4G connection." Example 3 — Prototyping (confirming UC-04 with a real stakeholder) The team builds a low-fidelity mockup of the Room Swap screen and walks Dr. Li through it. He confirms the flow matches UC-04's main success scenario, but points out the mockup is missing the mandatory "reason for swap" field — a completeness gap the prototype catches before a single line of production code is written. Example 4 — Walkthrough (confirming validity with Ms. Lee) The team presents the finalized FR1–FR5 / NFR1 table (Section 4.6.1) to Ms. Lee. She confirms FR2's administrator alert matches her expectations, closing the loop on E-003 from the original Elicitation Register — every requirement she cares about is present and correctly understood. | Case Study Checkpoint — Validation Running the techniques above over the Timetabling System's draft SRS finds no remaining Verifiability failures (every FR/NFR can be tested), no Consistency conflicts beyond the already-logged NFR1/NFR2 trade-off (Section 4.5.4, to be resolved during System Design), and one Completeness gap (the missing "reason for swap" field, now added to UC-04). With these closed, the SRS is ready for baselining — see the RTM in Section 4.8.1. | | --- | 4.8 Requirements Traceability & Change Control In a Waterfall project, the Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is the formal binding contract between the development organization and the paying client. Once the SRS passes Validation, it becomes baselined — the project scope is frozen. Because System Architecture, Database Design, Implementation, Unit Testing, and User Acceptance Testing are all built directly from these requirements, an unmanaged change can wreck the timeline, blow the budget, and introduce bugs. Two disciplines manage this risk: Requirements Traceability and Change Control Governance. 4.8.1 Requirements Traceability Traceability is the continuous ability to track a requirement forward and backward through the entire development lifecycle. | Type | Direction | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | Bidirectional | Both ways | Connects user requirements down to system specs, architecture, code, and tests — and back again. | | Forward (Requirements → Implementation) | Requirement → Code/Test | Ensures every requirement is designed, coded, and tested. Prevents "omitted scope" errors. | | Backward (Implementation → Requirements) | Code/Test → Requirement | Ensures every piece of code maps back to an authorized requirement. Prevents "Gold Plating." | | What Is "Gold Plating"? Gold Plating is a dangerous engineering habit where developers build unrequested features or unnecessary technical complexity — "while I'm in here, I'll also add...". It inflates cost and schedule without adding contracted value, and backward traceability is the main defense against it: if a piece of code doesn't map to a requirement ID, it shouldn't exist. | | --- | The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) The RTM is the administrative tool that maintains traceability across every phase of the Waterfall lifecycle. The table below is our case study's own RTM — it directly traces the UR-1/SR-1.1 and UR-2/SR-2.1 pairs from the Specification checkpoint (Section 4.6.1) through to their test cases: | Req ID | Description | Level | Design Module | Code / API | Test Case | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | UR-1 | User can view weekly class schedule on mobile. | User | TimetableUI | ScheduleView.tsx | TC-UI-101 | Approved | | SR-1.1 | WHEN schedule tab opened, fetch JSON in \<2.0s over 4G. | System | ScheduleController | GetScheduleService.java, /api/v1/schedules | TC-API-204 | Passed | | UR-2 | Lecturer can request an urgent room swap. | User | SwapModule | RoomSwapForm.tsx | TC-UI-105 | Approved | | SR-2.1 | IF target room capacity \< enrollment, THEN reject swap. | System | CapacityChecker | RoomValidationUtil.java | TC-UNIT-402 | Passed | Why the RTM Matters - Impact Analysis — when a change is proposed, engineers consult the RTM to see which design modules, schemas, and test cases are affected. - Gap Analysis — finds orphan requirements (no assigned design module) or orphan code (no originating requirement). - Test Coverage Verification — QA confirms 100% of requirements have a corresponding test before release. 4.8.2 Change Control Governance Even with careful upfront planning, real-world conditions change: laws update, priorities shift, hardware limits appear. Instead of allowing uncontrolled changes — the primary cause of Scope Creep — Waterfall mandates a formal Change Control Process. The Change Control Board (CCB) The CCB is the official decision-making body that reviews, approves, or rejects proposed changes to a baselined requirement document. | Member | Evaluates | | --- | --- | | Project Sponsor / Client Executive | Business necessity and approves financial cost additions. | | Project Manager | Impact on schedule, milestones, and staffing. | | Lead System Architect | Technical feasibility, refactoring complexity, architectural side effects. | | Quality Assurance (QA) Manager | Re-testing effort, regression suite adjustments, validation risk. | Change Request Lifecycle — Step by Step | 1. Change Request Stakeholder identifies a need | 2. Impact & Cost Analysis Architect & PM assess impact | 3. CCB Review Business/Tech/Finance/PM vote | | --- | --- | --- | | If Approved | If Rejected | | --- | --- | | 1. Update the SRS baseline (e.g., v1.0 → v1.1). 2. Update the RTM and code. 3. Adjust budget and schedule. 4. Re-sign the contract. | 1. Document the rationale in the CCB Log. 2. Retain the existing baseline. | - Submission of an Engineering Change Request (ECR): a formal document logging the request ID, submitter, description, and justification. - Impact Assessment: leadership uses the RTM to estimate files to modify, database migrations required, work-hours needed, and impact on milestones. - CCB Deliberation: the board weighs business benefit against cost, schedule delay, and technical risk. - Formal Decision & Baseline Revision: rejected changes are archived with justification; approved changes trigger a new SRS version, updated RTM entries, and revised schedule/budget. | Check Your Understanding Differentiate between Forward Traceability and Backward Traceability. How does backward traceability prevent "Gold Plating"? Why is it dangerous to accept requirement changes informally via email or verbal communication during late-stage Waterfall implementation? Explain, step by step, the role of the RTM during an Impact Analysis triggered by a new Engineering Change Request (ECR). | | --- | | Case Study Checkpoint — Traceability & Change Control Six months after baselining, a new data-privacy regulation requires all schedule data in transit to be encrypted end-to-end. A Facility IT lead submits an ECR. The team consults the RTM above: the change touches SR-1.1 and its code artifact GetScheduleService.java, and its test case TC-API-204 will need updating. This is exactly the load-time-versus-encryption trade-off the Interaction Analysis Grid flagged back in Section 4.5.4 as a future risk, not yet a committed requirement. The ECR is what finally turns that anticipated risk into a real, written requirement: NFR2 — "The system shall encrypt all schedule and swap-request data in transit using TLS 1.3, and at rest using AES-256." The CCB approves it — the SRS is re-baselined as v1.1, and the RTM rows for both SR-1.1 and the newly-added NFR2 are updated to point at the revised code and a new test case. This is the same Change Control process described above, now applied to the exact requirements this chapter has followed from Elicitation through Validation. | | --- | Key Takeaways - In Waterfall, Requirements Engineering is an upfront, plan-driven phase that must be completed, baselined, and validated before design begins. - RE breaks into five phases — Feasibility, Elicitation, Analysis & Classification, Specification, and Validation. Elicitation gathers raw material without judging it; Analysis is where organizing and classifying happens. - The Spiral View of RE shows how requirements are progressively refined across Business, User, and System layers through iterative loops of Elicitation, Specification, and Validation. - The Feasibility Study is Phase 0: it produces a Feasibility Report to judge technical, financial, and operational viability before elicitation begins. - Requirements originate from human stakeholders, corporate policies, physical environmental conditions, and statutory privacy regulations — captured in an Elicitation Register and documented with techniques like interviews, workshops, and use case descriptions. - User Requirements must be elicited first — jumping into low-level System Requirements too early causes over-engineering and misaligned software. - Functional Requirements govern component implementation, while Non-Functional Requirements act as architectural drivers — and every NFR should be written measurably (a metric, a threshold, and a condition). - The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes FRs by module and NFRs by FURPS+ category, and deliberately includes use cases, tables, and UML diagrams where they add clarity. - Transitioning from User to System specifications requires formal approval from a Joint Steering Committee. - EARS syntax (Ubiquitous, Event-Driven, State-Driven, Option-Driven, Unwanted Behavior) eliminates ambiguity in System Requirements. - The five Validation Checks — Validity, Consistency, Completeness, Realism, Verifiability — describe what to look for; techniques like reviews, prototyping, test-case generation, and walkthroughs describe how to find it, and are usually combined. - Requirements Traceability (via the RTM) and a formal Change Control Board prevent unmanaged scope creep and protect architectural control after baselining. - Across the whole chapter, one case study requirement (a student's mobile timetable) was followed continuously from a raw Elicitation statement to a baselined, traceable, change-controlled System Requirement. Glossary of Key Terms Telling the ID Codes Apart This chapter's case study uses a chain of short ID codes — E-xxx, UC-xx, UR-x, SR-x.x, FRx/NFRx, TC-xxx — to trace one requirement across every phase. Used consistently, they're a fast way to know exactly which phase produced a given statement and how precise it is. Here's how to tell them apart: | Prefix | Meaning | Assigned During | Example | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | E-xxx | A raw statement from Elicitation, exactly as a stakeholder said it — not yet analyzed. | Phase 1 (Elicitation) | E-002 | | UC-xx | A use case: a named actor-system interaction, drafted informally then finalized. | Drafted Phase 1, finalized Phase 3 | UC-04 | | UR-x | A User Requirement: one or more E-xxx statements organized into a natural-language need. | Phase 2 (Analysis & Classification) | UR-2 | | SR-x.x | A System Requirement: a precise, EARS-formatted, testable statement derived from a UR. The decimal ties it to its parent — SR-2.1 belongs to UR-2. | Phase 3 (Specification) | SR-2.1 | | FRx / NFRx | An entry in the SRS's formal requirement catalog. Numbered sequentially — the number does not encode a parent UR the way SR-x.x does. | Phase 3 (Specification) | NFR2 | | TC-xxx | A Test Case: a concrete procedure used to verify one requirement, referenced from the RTM. | Phase 4 (Validation) | TC-API-204 | | Reading the Numbering Two different numbering habits are at work here, and mixing them up is the most common source of confusion. SR-x.x deliberately encodes its parent UR in the decimal — SR-1.1 and SR-1.2 both belong to UR-1, while SR-2.1 belongs to UR-2 — so you can tell lineage from the ID alone. FRx and NFRx, by contrast, number sequentially through the SRS's requirement catalog and carry no parent encoding at all; FR3 and NFR1 don't tell you which UR they trace back to on their own — that link only exists in the RTM (Section 4.8.1). When in doubt: a dot in the middle of an ID means "traces to one specific UR"; no dot means "look it up in the RTM instead." | | --- | | Term | Definition | | --- | --- | | Baseline | A formally approved version of the requirements (or SRS) that freezes project scope; further changes require formal change control. | | CCB (Change Control Board) | The decision-making body that reviews, approves, or rejects proposed changes to a baselined requirement document. | | EARS | Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax — five sentence templates (Ubiquitous, Event-Driven, State-Driven, Option-Driven, Unwanted Behavior) used to write unambiguous requirements. | | ECR (Engineering Change Request) | The formal document used to submit a proposed change to a baselined requirement. | | Elicitation Register | The running log of raw, informally-tagged requirement statements produced during Requirements Elicitation, before any analysis or classification. | | Feasibility Study | Phase 0 of RE; evaluates whether a proposed system is technically, financially, and operationally viable. | | Functional Requirement (FR) | A requirement defining a specific behavior, input, output, or action the system must perform — answers "what does the system do?" | | FURPS+ | A classification framework for requirements: Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability, plus Design/Implementation/Interface/Physical constraints. | | Gold Plating | Building unrequested features or unnecessary complexity beyond what was specified — prevented by backward traceability. | | Measurable NFR | A non-functional requirement written with a metric, a quantified threshold, and the condition under which it applies, so it yields a clear Pass/Fail test. | | Non-Functional Requirement (NFR) | A requirement describing a quality attribute or constraint (e.g., performance, security) rather than a specific behavior. | | Requirements Analysis & Classification | Phase 2 of RE; organizes and classifies the raw material produced by Elicitation, and detects conflicts between requirements. | | Requirements Elicitation | Phase 1 of RE; the process of discovering and capturing stakeholder needs and domain constraints, without yet organizing or judging them. | | Requirements Validation Technique | A concrete method (review/inspection, prototyping, test-case generation, walkthrough, model checking, traceability analysis) used to perform the five validation checks. | | RTM (Requirements Traceability Matrix) | A table cross-referencing each requirement to its design module, code artifact, test case, and status across the project lifecycle. | | Scope Creep | Uncontrolled expansion of project scope without corresponding adjustments to budget, schedule, or resources. | | SRS (Software Requirements Specification) | The formal, baselined document containing all validated user and system requirements, organized into sections (introduction, overall description, specific requirements, appendices); acts as the binding contract between developer and client. | | System Requirement | A detailed, technical requirement written for developers and testers, specifying exact system functions and constraints. | | Traceability (Forward / Backward) | The ability to trace a requirement forward into design/code/tests, or trace code/tests backward to their originating requirement. | | Use Case Description | A structured template capturing an actor, pre/post-conditions, main success scenario, and alternate flows for a system interaction; drafted informally during Elicitation and finalized during Specification. | | User Requirement | A high-level, natural-language statement of what a stakeholder needs from the system, without implementation detail. | | Validation (Requirements) | The process of checking that specified requirements are valid, consistent, complete, realistic, and verifiable. | | Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA) | A technique for categorizing requirements by perspective: Interactor, Indirect, or Domain viewpoints. | End-of-Chapter Review Questions Use these to check your understanding before moving to Chapter 5. Try to answer without looking back at the chapter first. Section 4.1 — Process Foundations - What distinguishes the timing of Requirements Engineering in a Waterfall model compared to an Agile model? - Why is an omitted or ambiguous requirement in Waterfall significantly more expensive to fix during testing than during upfront specification? Section 4.4 — Requirements Elicitation - What is Requirements Elicitation, and how does it differ from Requirements Analysis & Classification? - Name three Elicitation techniques and, for each, describe how its findings should be documented. - List the deliverables that come out of the Elicitation phase. Why is none of them yet a finalized User or System Requirement? - Explain why a Use Case Description can reasonably be written in both Stage 1 (Elicitation) and Stage 3 (Specification). What changes between the two versions? Section 4.5 — Requirements Analysis & Classification - Rewrite the raw statement "the system should let students swap rooms quickly, but only if a lecturer approves it first" as one or more EARS-pattern requirements. Which pattern(s) did you use, and why? - Explain the difference between a User Requirement and a System Requirement. Why must User Requirements be organized before System Requirements are written? - What is Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA), and how does it differ from sorting requirements by abstraction level? - Using FURPS+, classify the following statement into its Functional and Non-Functional parts: "The system shall let a user reset their password securely within 10 seconds." - Build a small Matrix-Based Interaction Analysis grid for three requirements of your choosing, and explain how you would resolve any conflict you find. Section 4.6 — Specification & the SRS - Rewrite the following as a measurable Non-Functional Requirement: "The system shall have a friendly interface." - List the three ingredients every measurable NFR needs. Why does "the system shall respond quickly" fail the Measurability Checklist? - Name the standard sections of an SRS document. Where would a use case diagram belong, and where would the Requirements Traceability Matrix belong? - Explain how Functional Requirements should be grouped within an SRS, and how Non-Functional Requirements should be grouped. Why not just list all requirements in one flat table? Section 4.7 — Requirements Validation - Distinguish a validation check (Section 4.7.1) from a validation technique (Section 4.7.2). Give one example of each. - Which validation technique would you use to check whether a requirement is Verifiable? Walk through how you would apply it to a requirement of your choice. - Explain why combining multiple validation techniques (e.g., a review and test-case generation) catches more defects than relying on just one. Section 4.8 — Traceability & Change Control - Differentiate between Forward Traceability and Backward Traceability. How does backward traceability prevent "Gold Plating"? - Why is it dangerous to accept requirement changes informally via email or verbal communication during late-stage Waterfall implementation? - Explain, step by step, the role of the RTM during an Impact Analysis triggered by a new Engineering Change Request (ECR). Section 4.9 — Case Study Application - Write an Unwanted Behavior EARS requirement for the case study: a lecturer attempts to request a room that is already booked at that time. - Given the conflict between NFR1 (loading time \< 3s) and a High-Security Encryption requirement, explain how an engineering team should resolve this during RE Analysis. - Trace UR-2 (the room-swap requirement) through every phase checkpoint in this chapter, from its Elicitation Register entry to its RTM row. Applied / Synthesis Questions - Pick any everyday app on your phone. Write one User Requirement and derive one corresponding System Requirement from it, using EARS syntax. - Explain, in your own words, why the Spiral View (progressive refinement) does not contradict the idea that Waterfall RE happens 'upfront.' - Design a 5-row Requirements Traceability Matrix for a simple 'Library Book Reservation' feature. - Draft a one-page SRS outline (section headings only) for the 'Library Book Reservation' feature, following the structure in Section 4.6.1.

entries.text: Online Banking — Supplied Week 5 Example Source: Use-case Description.pdf, all three pages; SHA-256 f60f96b56628613187da82ebdac2169aab9ebca8d14f1ae99b848674345664d5. This is a faithful study summary; open the original for exact wording. Requirements are fictional teaching inputs, not actual banking behavior or execution evidence. Fund Transfer description (PDF p.1) Primary actor: Customer. Precondition: customer logged in. 1. Select Transfer Funds (OBS-06). 2. Display eligible accounts (OBS-06). 3. Select source, destination and amount (OBS-07). 4. Validate amount and destination (OBS-07). 5. Show confirmation (OBS-10). 6. Customer confirms (OBS-11). 7. Debit, credit and generate reference (OBS-11). 8. Display receipt and record transaction (OBS-13). Alternates: insufficient funds (OBS-08) and invalid destination (OBS-09) at step 4 display their messages and return to step 3. Cancellation (OBS-14) at step 6 discards the request and returns to Transaction Summary. A posting fault (OBS-12) at step 7 rolls back, keeps a support reference, reports failure and returns to Transaction Summary. Postcondition conflict: p.1 prints origin credited/destination debited; OBS-11 p.2 explicitly requires source debited/destination credited. Both are preserved as a discrepancy. The web reconstruction follows OBS-11 pending confirmation. Requirements map (PDF pp.2–3) | ID | Source pattern | Faithful study summary | | --- | --- | --- | | OBS-01 | Ubiquitous | Authenticate with customer ID and password before account functions. | | OBS-02 | Event-driven | Valid credentials → Account Summary. | | OBS-03 | Unwanted behaviour | Invalid credentials → error and no account access. | | OBS-04 | Unwanted behaviour | Three successive invalid logins → lock account and direct customer to contact bank. | | OBS-05 | Event-driven | Authenticated View Account Balance → current selected balance. | | OBS-06 | Event-driven | Authenticated Transfer Funds → eligible accounts. | | OBS-07 | Event-driven | Entered source/destination/amount → validate available balance and valid linked destination. | | OBS-08 | Unwanted behaviour | Amount exceeds balance → insufficient-funds message, no transfer. | | OBS-09 | Unwanted behaviour | Invalid/unlinked destination → invalid-account message, no transfer. | | OBS-10 | Event-driven | Valid details → confirmation summary of accounts and amount. | | OBS-11 | Event-driven | Confirmed validated transfer → debit source, credit destination, reference. | | OBS-12 | Unwanted behaviour | Posting fault → rollback partial debit/credit, failure message, keep support reference. | | OBS-13 | Event-driven | Successful posting → receipt and history in both accounts. | | OBS-14 | State-driven | During confirmation screen → allow cancellation instead of confirmation. | | OBS-15 | Event-driven | Authenticated Pay Bills entry → validate and schedule payment. | | OBS-16 | Event-driven | Logout selection → terminate authenticated session. | | OBS-17 | Complex | Authenticated session and ten minutes inactivity → automatic logout. | OBS-01…OBS-11 are on p.2; OBS-12…OBS-17 on p.3. The PDF does not supply OBS-18…OBS-20 despite deck references. It does not specify an account-lock duration or bill-payment exception flow. entries.title: What makes a software system broader than a program?
entries.text: It includes software components, configuration, system documentation and user documentation, not only executable instructions.

entries.title: What is the scope of software engineering?
entries.text: All aspects of software production, including supporting management, within organizational and financial constraints.

entries.title: Who controls a generic product’s specification?
entries.text: The product developer controls it for a wider market.

entries.title: Who controls a customized product’s specification?
entries.text: The commissioning customer controls it through agreement with the developer.

entries.title: Which software quality attribute concerns adapting a system when requirements change?
entries.text: Maintainability: the software can evolve as customer and business needs change.

entries.title: Which grouped quality attribute concerns reliability, safety and protection from misuse?
entries.text: Dependability and security cover reliability, safety and protection against malicious access or damage.

entries.title: Which quality attribute concerns response time, processing time and memory use?
entries.text: Efficiency concerns appropriate response time, processing time, memory and other resource use.

entries.title: Which quality concerns fit for intended users?
entries.text: Acceptability concerns understandability, usability and compatibility with the systems intended users employ.

entries.title: Why can changing software raise failure risk?
entries.text: A modification can introduce faults or disturb interactions, even when the software does not physically wear out.

entries.title: Why can a code-complete claim misrepresent progress?
entries.text: Integration and defect correction may remain, with an uncertain amount of work before useful checked behavior exists.

entries.title: What are the four fundamental lifecycle activities?
entries.text: Specification; design and implementation; validation; evolution.

entries.title: What can professional certification indicate, and what does it fail to guarantee about a particular software product?
entries.text: It can provide evidence of meeting a defined professional standard. It does not guarantee continuing competence or the correctness of every product; product-specific evidence remains necessary.

entries.title: What is a software process model?
entries.text: A simplified representation of a software process and the organization of its activities.

entries.title: What makes a system critical?
entries.text: Failure can cause significant human, economic or environmental loss.

entries.title: Why can an approved requirement be costly to change?
entries.text: Its dependent design, implementation, tests and documents may need revision and reapproval.

entries.title: Which checks occur during Waterfall implementation?
entries.text: Unit testing, alongside coding and code reviews; not every check waits for the final integrated system.

entries.title: What does an increment add?
entries.text: Useful functionality to an existing version; it need not provide the complete final workflow.

entries.title: In incremental development, what does interleaving specification, development and validation mean?
entries.text: Specification, development and validation inform each other during work instead of being entirely separate one-time phases.

entries.title: What can undermine independent increments?
entries.text: Shared dependencies can make a change affect earlier increments and require coordination and integration checks.

entries.title: Why are requirements revisited after component analysis?
entries.text: Candidate capabilities reveal mismatches requiring negotiated changes or additions to meet real needs.

entries.title: How can choosing a reused component reduce a development team’s control over future changes?
entries.text: Control over component evolution, because the supplier decides new component versions.

entries.title: What is system testing concerned with?
entries.text: The integrated system, including unexpected interactions and interface problems between components.

entries.title: What is regression testing?
entries.text: Rerunning earlier tests after changes to look for newly introduced failures.

entries.title: What distinguishes test planning from execution?
entries.text: Planning specifies intended inputs, conditions and expected evidence; execution runs checks and records actual results.

entries.title: What does empirical control use to guide decisions?
entries.text: Observed evidence and adaptation when important aspects of the work or context remain uncertain.

entries.title: What does transparency enable?
entries.text: A shared understanding of actual work and quality so inspection uses trustworthy evidence.

entries.title: What does inspection compare?
entries.text: Artifacts and progress against goals or standards to detect meaningful deviations.

entries.title: What does adaptation do?
entries.text: Changes the work or process in response to what inspection reveals.

entries.title: What is the Product Owner accountable for?
entries.text: Maximizing product value and effective, understandable, ordered backlog management.

entries.title: What is the Developers’ delivery responsibility?
entries.text: Plan and perform the work needed for a usable Increment meeting the Definition of Done.

entries.title: How can a Scrum Master become a taskmaster?
entries.text: By assigning every task and replacing Developers’ self-management with status reporting.

entries.title: What separates Review from Retrospective?
entries.text: Review inspects product outcomes and context with stakeholders; Retrospective improves how the team works.

entries.title: What do acceptance criteria describe?
entries.text: The particular behavior or conditions required of an individual backlog item.

entries.title: What does a 90%-finished item contribute if DoD is unmet?
entries.text: Zero Done story points for that Sprint; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

entries.title: Why ask high and low poker voters to explain?
entries.text: Their estimates may include different scope, effort, risks or assumptions that must be clarified before agreement.

entries.title: When does this activity require splitting a large item?
entries.text: At 13 points or higher under the explicit Step 3 instruction; page 1’s >13 wording differs.

entries.title: How is mean velocity calculated?
entries.text: Add comparable Done points across observed Sprints and divide by the number of Sprints.

entries.title: In the course’s Scrum chart (slide 46), what does each vertical axis measure, and can either be read as story-point velocity?
entries.text: Remaining effort in hours on the left; remaining and completed task counts on the right. Neither axis measures Done story points, so neither directly gives story-point velocity.

entries.title: What separates elicitation from analysis?
entries.text: Elicitation preserves attributed needs and constraints; analysis interprets, organizes, classifies and compares them.

entries.title: Why organize user needs before detailed system rules?
entries.text: Stakeholders must confirm the intended outcome before developers optimize or specify a technical solution.

entries.title: What question does viewpoint analysis ask?
entries.text: Whose direct, indirect or domain perspective must this requirement represent?

entries.title: When is the ubiquitous EARS pattern appropriate?
entries.text: When the obligation has no trigger or condition: the system shall perform the stated response.

entries.title: In an event-driven EARS requirement, what does WHEN introduce?
entries.text: An event that triggers the specified system response.

entries.title: In a state-driven EARS requirement, what does WHILE introduce?
entries.text: A continuing state during which the specified obligation applies.

entries.title: In the course’s option-driven EARS template, what does WHERE introduce?
entries.text: An included feature or configuration option, rather than merely an incoming runtime event.

entries.title: What does IF…THEN express in unwanted-behavior EARS?
entries.text: The unwanted condition and the required response when it occurs.

entries.title: What separates an FR from a FURPS+ category label?
entries.text: An FR states a behavior; a category classifies requirements and is not itself a testable statement.

entries.title: Which three ingredients make a quality target measurable?
entries.text: A defined metric, a threshold with unit, and the conditions under which it applies.

entries.title: In the course’s requirements interaction matrix, what does a score of −1 establish?
entries.text: A potential conflict needing explanation and evidence; it does not prove the requirements are jointly impossible.

entries.title: What separates a validation check from a technique?
entries.text: A check names the property examined; a technique gathers evidence about that property.

entries.title: What makes an SRS version a baseline?
entries.text: Authorized approval of that version, after which revisions follow the agreed change-control process.

entries.title: What does backward traceability investigate?
entries.text: Which authorized requirement or justified derived constraint explains a design, code or test artifact.

entries.title: How does a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) help evaluate a proposed change?
entries.text: Locate affected requirements, design/code and tests so impact analysis can inform the authorized change decision.

entries.title: Why omit detail in a model?
entries.text: To make one aspect discussable and support a defined audience and decision.

entries.title: What does a context diagram establish?
entries.text: The system boundary and external systems; not internal design, use-case order or a scenario timeline.

entries.title: What is an actor?
entries.text: An external role interacting at the boundary, potentially a person, system, device or timer.

entries.title: In a UML use-case diagram, which way does an «include» arrow point?
entries.text: From the base use case to the mandatory included behavior.

entries.title: In a UML use-case diagram, which way does an «extend» arrow point?
entries.text: From conditional additional behavior to the base use case, with its extension condition stated.

entries.title: What does a sequence diagram describe?
entries.text: Participants exchanging ordered messages for one scenario; time runs downward.

entries.title: What distinguishes alt and opt?
entries.text: alt has guarded alternatives; opt has a single guarded optional block without an explicit else.

entries.title: What does a loop fragment represent in a UML sequence diagram?
entries.text: A guarded repetition of enclosed messages.

entries.title: What does a complete use-case description include?
entries.text: Actor/goal, preconditions, main flow, numbered alternates/exceptions and postconditions.

entries.title: Why stop messages after an early rejection?
entries.text: Later success actions require preconditions that the rejected branch did not establish.

entries.title: Why does a user requirement need elaboration?
entries.text: Stakeholder goals must be translated into observable behavior, triggers, conditions and agreed acceptance criteria.

entries.title: Is a budget alone a feasibility argument?
entries.text: No. Technical capability, operational fit, schedule and constraints must also be assessed.

entries.title: Does Agile avoid requirements work?
entries.text: No. It revisits requirements incrementally; classical Waterfall invests earlier to reduce costly downstream misunderstanding.

entries.title: Is an unmeasured quality adjective testable?
entries.text: No. Define an agreed measure, conditions and threshold; do not silently invent official values.

entries.title: What do interactor, indirect and domain viewpoints mean?
entries.text: Interactor uses/interfaces directly; indirect has interests without direct use; domain contributes rules or constraints from the application domain.

entries.title: How do functional and FURPS classifications differ?
entries.text: Functional versus quality separates behavior from its constraints; FURPS categories group concerns and are not a one-to-one synonym for that separation.
