entries.text: 4.5.3 FR & NFR IN DEPTH Writing Measurable Non-Functional Requirements Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) define a quality attribute — not what the system does, but how well. An NFR is only useful if a tester can look at it and say Pass or Fail with no argument. Example: When a student opens the class schedule page over a 4G connection, the system shall display the schedule within 3 seconds The <system> shall <behavior> within/under <threshold + unit> when/under <condition>. Metric Threshold Condition What is being measured (time, A specific number with a unit. The context under which the throughput, error rate, uptime %, “Fast” is not a threshold; “2 threshold applies (load level, concurrent users). seconds” is. network type, hardware). entries.text: 4.5.3 CHALLENGE: FR VS. NFR BLENDING Resolution — the FURPS+ Framework Stakeholders rarely separate the two on their own. Engineers are expected to identify FR apart from NFR. — FURPS+ gives six categories to sort them into: F Functionality U Usability R Reliability Features, capabilities, Human factors, Availability, accuracy, security aesthetics, docs recoverability P Performance S Supportability + Constraints Speed, throughput, Testability, maintainability Design, Implementation, response time Interface, Physical Example: “The system shall print invoices instantly” splits into a Functional req. (support printing) + a Performance req. (completes within 2 seconds). Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 42

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 47
entries.text: 4.5.3 FREQUENTLY ASKED Is the “F” in FURPS+ the Same as a Functional Requirement (FR)? No —It is not a true Functional Requirement. ”F” in FURPS+ (Functionality) is a category — feature set, security scope, audit and compliance controls — used to group and review related requirements together. It is a label, not a testable sentence. FR (Functional Requirement) is one individual, EARS-formatted, testable statement (Section 4.6.3) Why put an F in an NFR-style framework? They describe a quality of a function, not the function itself. But got grouped under "F" because they don't fit neatly under Usability, Reliability, Performance, or Supportability either. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 43

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 48
entries.text: THE SIMPLE TEST One Question Separates Them Can I remove this requirement and the system still does the same task, just less safely, traceably, or controllably? NO — THE TASK DISAPPEARS YES — THE TASK STILL WORKS → It’s a true FR → It sits under “F” Write it as an EARS statement and attach it Document it once as a cross-cutting review item, directly to the feature's acceptance criteria. referenced by every feature it touches. Example: “The system shall allow a user to cancel Example: “All trading actions require MFA” or a pending order before execution.” “every trade generates an immutable audit log entry.” FURPS+ Quick Reference — FR vs. “F” 3

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 49
entries.text: SIDE-BY-SIDE · TRADING SYSTEM EXAMPLES FR or “F”? A Working Example Requirement Type Why The system shall allow a user to place a limit order FR Removing it deletes a feature. specifying price and quantity. The system shall allow a user to cancel a pending order FR A discrete, testable action. before execution. Order placement still works — just The system shall encrypt all API traffic using TLS 1.2+. “F” insecurely — without it. The system shall log every trade with timestamp, user ID, Adds traceability; doesn’t change what “F” and order details. the trade does. Rule of thumb: if the rule is core business logic tied to one feature, write it as an FR inside that feature. If it’s a cross- cutting policy applied across many features, document it once under “F.” FURPS+ Quick Reference — FR vs. “F” 4

entries.text: 4.5.4 CHALLENGE: HIDDEN CONFLICTS Resolution — Matrix-Based Interaction Analysis An architectural conflict occurs when satisfying one requirement makes another harder to satisfy (e.g., real-time speed vs. heavy encryption). Score every pair: +1 Compatible, 0 Neutral, −1 Conflict. FR1: Mobile NFR1: Load < 3s NFR2: Encryption FR2: Swap FR1: Mobile — +1 0 0 NFR1: Load < 3s +1 — −1 (Conflict) 0 NFR2: Encryption 0 −1 (Conflict) — 0 FR2: Swap 0 0 0 — Reading it: NFR1 and NFR2 conflict — encryption overhead works against the load-time budget, an explicit trade-off is needed before any code is written. Note: tags like “NFR1” are shorthand for the full EARS statement written in Section 4.5.1 — the grid only works because each requirement is already precise enough to compare. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 44

entries.text: 4.6.0 WHAT IS SPECIFICATION? From Organized Requirements to a Baselined SRS Requirements Specification takes the organized, classified requirements from Phase 2 and writes them into one authoritative, contractually-binding document: the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). Once the Joint Steering Committee signs it, the SRS becomes the baseline every later phase is measured against. From User to System One Document, Every Artifact Governed, Not Casual Every User Requirement (UR) is EARS-formatted FRs, measurable A dedicated sign-off process and refined into one or more precise NFRs, use cases, and UML two recurring failure modes — System Requirements (SR) — see diagrams are all assembled into ambiguity and over-specification the worked UR → SR examples the standard SRS structure, next. — are guarded against before ahead. baselining. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 47

entries.text: 4.6.1 THE SRS DOCUMENT Standard SRS Structure Every artifact this chapter has built — requirements, EARS statements, use cases, the interaction grid — is ultimately assembled into one document: the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). Section Contents 1. Introduction Purpose, scope, definitions/glossary, references, document overview. 2. Overall Description Product perspective, product functions summary, user characteristics, constraints. 3.1 FR (EARS syntax) · 3.2 External Interfaces · 3.3 NFR (FURPS+, measurable) · 3.4 Use 3. Specific Requirements Cases & UML. Data dictionary, Requirements Traceability Matrix, interaction analysis grid, revision 4. Appendices history. 5. Approval / Sign-off Signatures from the Joint Steering Committee, marking the document baselined. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 48

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 65
entries.text: 4.8.1 TRACEABILITY Forward, Backward, and Bidirectional Type Direction Purpose Connects user requirements down to specs, code, and tests — Bidirectional Both ways and back. Every requirement is designed, coded, tested. Prevents “omitted Forward Requirement → Code/Test scope.” Every piece of code maps to an authorized requirement. Prevents Backward Code/Test → Requirement “Gold Plating.” What is “Gold Plating”? Building unrequested features or unnecessary complexity — “while I'm in here, I'll also add…” It inflates cost and schedule without adding contracted value. Backward traceability is the main defense: if code doesn't map to a requirement ID, it shouldn't exist. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 65

THE CCB EVALUATES EVERY CHANGE FROM FOUR ANGLES Lead System Project Sponsor Project Manager QA Manager Architect Business necessity; Impact on schedule, Technical feasibility, Re-testing effort, approves financial cost milestones, staffing. refactoring complexity. regression risk. additions. entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 71
entries.text: CASE STUDY CHECKPOINT Traceability & Change Control: A Real ECR Six months after baselining, a new data-privacy regulation requires all schedule data in transit to be encrypted end-to-end — the risk the Interaction Grid had only flagged as “future” back in Analysis. A Facility IT lead submits an ECR. The ECR writes the anticipated risk into a real requirement for the first time: NFR2 — “The system shall encrypt all schedule and swap-request data in transit using TLS 1.3, and at rest using AES-256.” The team consults the RTM: the change touches SR-1.1 and its test case TC-API-204 will need updating, since encryption overhead affects the 3.0s load-time budget — precisely the NFR1-vs-NFR2 trade-off logged during Analysis. The CCB approves it — the SRS is re-baselined as v1.1, and the RTM rows for SR-1.1 and the new NFR2 are updated. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 71

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 72
entries.text: QUICK REFERENCE Telling the ID Codes Apart Several ID prefixes appear side by side in this chapter — here's how to tell them apart: Prefix Meaning Assigned During Example E-xxx Raw statement from Elicitation, unanalyzed. Phase 1 (Elicitation) E-002 UC-xx Use Case: an actor–system interaction. Phase 1 → Phase 3 UC-04 UR-x User Requirement — organized, for stakeholders. Phase 2 (Analysis) UR-2 SR-x.x System Requirement — technical, from one UR. Phase 3 (Specification) SR-2.1 FRx / NFRx Functional / Non-Functional Requirement (SRS's list). Phase 3 (Specification) FR1, NFR1 TC-xxx Test Case — verifies one requirement (in the RTM). Phase 4 (Validation) TC-API-204 Reading the numbering. SR-2.1 means “the 1st System Requirement derived from UR-2” — the decimal ties it to its parent UR. FR/NFR numbers, by contrast, just count sequentially through the SRS's formal requirement list; they don't encode a parent ID. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 73

FURPS+, and includes use cases, tables, and UML. ● Elicitation captures raw needs; Analysis is where ● 5 Validation Checks describe what to look for; organizing and classifying happens. techniques (reviews, prototyping, test cases) ● User Requirements come first — avoid the “rabbit describe how. hole” into System detail. ● The RTM and the CCB protect the baselined SRS from scope creep. entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 3
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS What Is a Domain Model? • A domain model is a class diagram that describes the concepts in the problem space (the real-world things, their attributes, and how they relate) without any software design decisions. • It deliberately leaves out visibility, attribute types, and full operation signatures: those are design decisions about how the software will be built, not facts about the problem domain itself. • A design class diagram is what the domain model becomes once those decisions are made -- the same classes and relationships, now carrying the visibility, types, and operation signatures the software actually needs. System Modeling with UML 33

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 4
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Domain Model vs. Design Class Diagram Same classes, same relationships -- design adds visibility, types, and operations. System Modeling with UML 34

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 5
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Class Box Notation & Four Relationships • Class box — name, attributes, operations. • Generalization — hollow triangle to the parent. • Relationships between classes: Class box • Association — a relationship, multiplicity at each end. • Aggregation — hollow diamond; parts can outlive the whole. • Composition — filled diamond; parts die Generalization with the whole. System Modeling with UML 35

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 6
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Association • Class A “uses” Class B OR Class A “knows about” Class B • The most general relationship: two classes are connected, and objects of one can reference objects of the other. Neither owns the other, and both have independent lifecycles. • Example: a Teacher and a Student. A teacher teaches many students, and a student has many teachers, but neither belongs to the other. System Modeling with UML 33

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 7
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Aggregation • Class A “has-a” Class B (weak relationship) • A whole–part relationship where the part can exist independently of the whole. The whole groups the parts, but destroying the whole doesn’t destroy the parts, and a part can be shared among several wholes. • Example: a Department and its Professors. If the department closes, the professors still exist and can join another department. System Modeling with UML 33

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 8
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Composition • Class A “own” Class B (strong relationship) • A whole–part relationship where the part cannot exist without the whole. The whole is responsible for creating and destroying its parts, and a part belongs to exactly one whole at a time. • Example: a House and its Rooms. A room doesn’t exist apart from its house, and demolishing the house destroys the rooms. System Modeling with UML 33

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 9
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Association vs. Aggregation vs. Composition Relationship In Java terms Lifecycle Association — plain line One class holds a reference to another. Independent lifecycles. The whole holds the part as a property Aggregation — hollow diamond Part can outlive the whole. field. Composition — filled diamond The whole creates and owns the part. Delete the whole, the part goes too. System Modeling with UML 38

entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Try It — Requirements for Association, Aggregation, Composition “A Client owns one Portfolio. The Portfolio object is created and assigned to the Client elsewhere in the system when the account is opened, and a Client can later be reassigned to a different Portfolio without either object being destroyed.” “A Portfolio tracks the Stocks on its watchlist. Each Stock is a security traded on an exchange; it is added to and removed from the watchlist over time, and it continues to exist -- and to be tracked by other portfolios -- even after this Portfolio stops watching it.” “A Portfolio contains Holdings, one per stock position actually owned. Each Holding is created by the Portfolio itself when a purchase is recorded, and is destroyed the moment the Portfolio is closed, because a Holding has no meaning apart from the Portfolio it belongs to.” • Client — Portfolio: a reference held elsewhere, independent lifecycles → association. • Portfolio ◇ Stock: the part outlives the whole → aggregation. • Portfolio ◆ Holding: the part cannot outlive the whole → composition. System Modeling with UML 39

entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Association, Aggregation, Composition — in Java public class Client { private Portfolio portfolio; // ASSOCIATION: reference held, not created here public Client(Portfolio portfolio) { this.portfolio = portfolio; } } public class Portfolio { private List<Stock> watchlist = new ArrayList<>(); // AGGREGATION private List<Holding> holdings = new ArrayList<>(); // COMPOSITION public void addToWatchlist(Stock stock) { watchlist.add(stock); // Stock supplied from outside -- not created here } public void buy(Stock stock, int shares, double price) { Holding h = new Holding(stock, shares, price); // created HERE holdings.add(h); // lives and dies with this Portfolio } public void close() { holdings.clear(); // every Holding is destroyed with the Portfolio } } A reference passed into the constructor (association) vs. an object built with ‘new’ inside the owner and cleared with it (composition). entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Identifying Classes and Attributes: A Practical Method Nous-verb Analysis • Filter nouns into classes, attributes, or discards • Noun-verb analysis: nouns → candidate classes/attributes; verbs → candidate operations. • Keep as a class if it has its own identity, its own data, and its own behavior or relationships. • Make it an attribute if it’s a simple value describing something else. • Discard if it’s redundant, vague, outside the system’s scope, or refers to the system itself. • Merge synonyms: if the text says both “member” and “patron,” pick one. • Naming: singular CamelCase nouns, pronounceable, never starting with a digit. System Modeling with UML 44

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 18
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Identifying Relationship and Operations: A Practical Method Nous-verb Analysis • Turn verbs into associations or operations • Verbs that connect two nouns usually become associations: a member borrows a book, a member pays a fine. • Verbs describing something a class does usually become operations in a design class diagram: register(member), addBook(book), returnBook(). • “Has,” “contains,” “consists of” often signal aggregation or composition. • Constraints in the text become multiplicities: “up to five books at a time” gives Member 1 — 0..5 active Loan. • In a pure domain model, you’d keep the associations and skip the operations, since operations belong to the design phase System Modeling with UML 44

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 Lecture.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 19
entries.text: CLASS DIAGRAMS Nous-verb Analysis: Strengths and limitations The technique’s strength is that it’s mechanical and easy to start: it gives you a first-pass list quickly and keeps you grounded in the requirements’ vocabulary. Its weakness is that natural language is imprecise: • The same concept may appear under different words. • Important concepts may be implied but never named. • Grammar can mislead: “a payment” is a noun, but “to pay” is a verb for the same idea. System Modeling with UML 44

entries.text: What Is an Activity Diagram? • An activity diagram models the flow of control through a process or workflow -- the sequence of actions, decisions, and parallel paths needed to get something done -- independent of which class or object performs each step. • Purpose: capture a business process or a use case's internal logic during requirements analysis, document a workflow that spans multiple actors or systems, and spot missing decision branches or parallel work early -- before any code is written. • Unlike a state machine diagram, which tracks how one object's state changes over its lifetime, an activity diagram tracks the steps of a process, which may span many objects and even many systems. • Common uses: documenting a business workflow (e.g., order fulfillment), a use case description, or an algorithm with conditional or parallel steps.

entries.text: Behavioral Model – State Machine Diagram • State machine diagram models the finite set of states an object or system Automated Stock Trading Bot can occupy, the events that cause it to move between those states, and the conditions and actions attached to those moves. • At any instant the object is in exactly one state, and its response to an event depends on which state it’s currently in. • Its purpose is to describe how something behaves over its lifetime rather than how it’s structured.

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 - State Machine Diagram.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 3
entries.text: Behavioral Model – State Machine Diagram • How a state machine diagram helps you? • It clarifies requirements by forcing you to enumerate every state and decide, for each event, what should happen. • It exposes invalid behavior. Any transition not drawn is, by definition, not allowed. • It guides implementation and testing. The diagram maps almost directly to code, and each arrow becomes a test case. • It communicates behavior compactly. Developers, testers, and domain experts can all read the same picture.

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 - State Machine Diagram.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 4
entries.text: Use Case Description • Scenarios in use case description represent sequence of activities that involves actors and the system • The actor and the system exchange information in the sequence of activities • It is one of the good source to identify • States • Events • Conditions • Actions

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 - State Machine Diagram.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 5
entries.text: Identifying States • States appear in preconditions and postconditions in status words and adjectives (“pending,” “working,” “suspended”). • In the gaps between steps where the system has done its part and is waiting for an actor, an external system, or time to do something. • Looks from the above two points for candidate states.

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 - State Machine Diagram.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 6
entries.text: Identifying Events • Events are whatever ends a wait: - • an actor’s action • a message from another system • time passing (“after 30 days,” “at market close”) • The trigger at the top of a use case is also an event • The conditions that start alternative flows are usually events too.

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 - State Machine Diagram.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 7
entries.text: Identifying Conditions • Conditions show up as “if,” “only if,” “provided that,” validation rules, and business-rule references. • In alternative flows, watch for whether the branch is caused by something happening (an event) or by something being true (a guard)

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 - State Machine Diagram.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 8
entries.text: Identifying Actions • Actions are the system’s responses: verbs like “records,” “sends,” “notifies,” “reserves,” “calculates.” • Once you’ve found them, decide where each belongs. • If it happens whenever the object enters or leaves a state, make it an entry or exit hook • if it’s tied to one specific move, put it on that transition.

entries.title: Week 6 · Week 6 - State Machine Diagram.pdf (teaching edition pending) · p. 9
entries.text: Working Example • Scenario: borrowing a book from a library. The object being modeled is a single copy of a book. • Precondition: member is registered and the book is on the shelf. • Main flow: 1. Member asks to borrow the book. 2. System checks that the member has fewer than 5 books on loan. 3. System records the loan and sets a due date 14 days ahead. 4. Member returns the book by the due date. 5. System records the return and the book goes back on the shelf. • Alternative flows: 2a. Member already has 5 books: system refuses the loan. 4a. Member renews before the due date: if nobody has reserved the book, system extends the due date by 14 days. 4b. Due date passes without a return: system emails the member a reminder. 4c. Member returns an overdue book: system charges a late fine. 4d. Book is 30 days overdue: system marks it lost and bills the member for a replacement. 4e. A lost book turns up: system waives the replacement bill. • Business rule: a librarian may withdraw a damaged book from circulation while it’s on the shelf. • Postcondition (success): the loan is closed, the book is Available on the shelf, and the member’s loan count is reduced by one.

entries.title: CS enrichment: Repair the inner grandchild
entries.text: Insert 30, 10, 20 into an empty AVL tree. The root is 30; its left child is 10, whose right child is 20. Heights count edges. Which repair preserves the BST order and restores balance? The inner grandchild must first become the outer child. Rotate left at 10, then right at 30: root 20 has children 10 and 30. Only rotate left at 30 Trap: rotating away from the heavy subtree cannot repair this shape. Swap keys 10 and 30 without changing links Trap: balance is structural; swapping keys can break sorted traversal. Left rotation at 10, then right rotation at 30 Correct: this is the left-right case, not the left-left case. Only rotate right at 30 Trap: using the left-left repair for an inner insertion leaves a different imbalance.

entries.title: CS enrichment: Height bounds do not benchmark a workload
entries.text: A service uses an AVL tree. Another team proposes a red-black tree for a mixed lookup/insert/delete workload. No benchmarks have been collected. What conclusion is defensible? Both maintain logarithmic height. Different balance invariants affect constants and update work; the faster implementation depends on workload and memory behavior. A height bound alone does not establish wall-clock speed. Red-black trees have O(1) worst-case search Trap: weaker balance is still logarithmic, not constant depth. AVL always wins because it is more tightly balanced Trap: smaller height does not account for maintenance and implementation costs. AVL deletion requires at most one repair at one ancestor Trap: deletion can propagate height changes toward the root. Both have O(log n) search; benchmark update and lookup costs Correct: asymptotic guarantees do not select a universally fastest implementation.

entries.title: CS enrichment: A finalized vertex becomes cheaper
entries.text: Directed edges: s→a costs 2, s→b costs 5, b→a costs −4. There are no other edges. Dijkstra permanently settles a before b. Which diagnosis is correct? The path s→b→a costs 1, but a was settled with distance 2. A negative edge invalidates the usual finalization argument even without a negative cycle. Bellman-Ford supports negative weights when no reachable negative cycle prevents finite shortest paths. It is safe because there is no negative cycle Trap: absence of negative cycles is insufficient for standard Dijkstra. Add 4 to every edge and use the same shortest path Trap: paths with different edge counts receive different total offsets. The shortest distance to a is 2 because its direct edge is smallest Trap: local edge choice is not a proof of shortest path optimality. Dijkstra can finalize the wrong distance; use a suitable negative-weight algorithm Correct: a later route improves an already settled vertex.

entries.title: CS enrichment: The representation is part of the bound
entries.text: Nonnegative graph. Version A uses adjacency lists and a binary heap. Version B scans a distance array for each minimum and uses an adjacency matrix. Which standard bound fits these implementations? List traversal touches O(E) edges; heap operations contribute logarithmic overhead, yielding O((V+E) log V). Array minimum scans and matrix rows produce O(V²) in the standard dense implementation. Both: O(E log E), regardless of representation Trap: matrix scans can visit entries for absent edges. A: O(V); B: O(E) Trap: neither bound accounts for selecting the next minimum. A: O(V²); B: O(log V) Trap: the heap bound is assigned to the matrix implementation, and logarithmic total work cannot even read this graph. A: O((V+E) log V); B: O(V²) Correct: the priority queue and adjacency representation both matter.

entries.title: CS enrichment: Density is not a 0/1 proof
entries.text: Capacity 50. Items (weight,value): (10,60), (20,100), (30,120). A density-greedy algorithm takes the first two. Items cannot be split. Which result and justification are valid? The chosen value is 160; taking the weight-20 and weight-30 items yields 220. Density selection works for fractional knapsack because exchanging fractions is allowed; indivisible items remove that argument. Greedy gets 160; the optimum is 220 Correct: this small counterexample disproves universal optimality of density-greedy for 0/1 knapsack. Greedy is optimal at 160 because density is highest Trap: importing the fractional greedy-choice argument into the indivisible problem. Take all three for 280 Trap: the weights sum to 60 and violate the capacity constraint. Take half the last item to reach 220 Trap: changing the problem to fractional knapsack violates the stated rules.

entries.title: CS enrichment: A memoization key loses a decision
entries.text: A 0/1 knapsack solver solve(i, remainingCapacity) decides whether to take item i, then advances to i+1. A programmer caches only by remainingCapacity. Why can this return a wrong result? Two subproblems with the same capacity may have different remaining items. The cache must retain every state component needed to determine future choices, such as (i, capacity). Overlapping subproblems alone do not make an incomplete state valid. The key omits which items remain; include i Correct: equal capacities do not imply equal feasible choices. Memoization requires storing the full previous execution trace Trap: sufficient state, not full history, is the requirement. Dynamic programming cannot solve 0/1 knapsack Trap: the standard item/capacity recurrence is valid; its pseudo-polynomial cost is a separate issue. Always keep the largest cached value across i Trap: that value may use an item unavailable in the current subproblem.

entries.title: CS enrichment: One slow append, many cheap appends
entries.text: An initially empty dynamic array doubles capacity when full; every append writes one element. Analyze N appends with no shrinking. Which statement is correct? Copies occur at geometrically increasing capacities. Their sum is O(N), so total work is O(N) and amortized append is O(1). An individual resizing append can still cost O(N). O(1) amortized append, with O(N) worst-case resizing append Correct: a sequence bound does not remove expensive individual operations. Every append has O(1) worst-case work Trap: copying all existing elements is real work. The sequence costs O(N²) because one append is linear Trap: multiplying the maximum by every operation ignores how rarely resizes occur. Amortized means average over random inputs Trap: amortized analysis bounds an operation sequence without requiring an input probability distribution.

entries.title: CS enrichment: Nearly constant is not literally constant
entries.text: A disjoint-set forest combines union by rank with path compression over a sequence of unions and finds. What does the usual inverse-Ackermann result describe? The combined heuristics give inverse-Ackermann amortized operation cost over a sequence, often treated as nearly constant for practical sizes. It is not a literal O(1) worst-case bound for every find, and stored rank need not equal current height after compression. Rank alone proves the inverse-Ackermann result Trap: the stronger combined bound depends on compression as well as balanced linking. O(α(n)) amortized cost; individual finds need not be constant Correct: distinguish sequence behavior from a worst-case guarantee per call. Every find follows exactly one pointer Trap: compression benefits later calls; an uncompressed path can have several edges. Path compression keeps rank equal to exact current height Trap: ranks are maintained for linking decisions and are not recomputed after compression.

entries.title: CS enrichment: The subtype strengthens the contract
entries.text: Account.withdraw(x) promises to accept any 0 ≤ x ≤ balance. A FixedTermAccount subclass throws for every withdrawal before maturity, even when the base precondition holds. Which redesign respects clients of the base abstraction? The subtype imposes an extra precondition, breaking the promised behavior of Account clients. A withdrawal-capable interface can represent that capability; a fixed-term product can share storage through composition without claiming unrestricted withdrawal. Rename the subclass method and keep the same Account contract Trap: renaming cannot satisfy the behavior clients are still promised. Split withdrawal capability and share implementation through composition Correct: reuse should preserve the behavioral promise of the advertised interface. Keep inheritance because both classes have a balance field Trap: matching data fields does not establish behavioral substitutability. Catch every exception at all existing Account call sites Trap: this changes client assumptions instead of honoring the original abstraction.

entries.title: CS enrichment: A startup sequence is not one responsibility
entries.text: StartupManager validates invoices, clears image caches and sends reminders because all run at 08:00. Changes to invoice policy require editing this same class. Which judgment best describes the grouping? A shared execution time is weak evidence of functional unity. Separating domain operations and composing them in a scheduler keeps orchestration explicit. An automatic microservice split would add distributed operational costs without proving a deployment need. Temporal grouping; separate responsibilities and keep an explicit scheduler Correct: organize domain behavior around reasons to change while retaining needed orchestration. High functional cohesion because every task runs at 08:00 Trap: time of execution is confused with a shared domain responsibility. Create three network services solely to improve cohesion Trap: process distribution does not by itself improve module boundaries. Put every operation in a utility singleton to reduce coupling Trap: a shared global access point can hide dependencies rather than remove them.

entries.title: CS enrichment: An API boundary adds failure modes
entries.text: A four-person team owns a small application whose modules already have clear interfaces. There is no requirement for independent deployment or scaling. Which next step has the strongest support? Keep the module boundaries and measure actual deployment or scaling constraints before introducing remote calls. Networked services add partial failure, latency and operations; a single deployable system can still be modular. Keep a modular monolith and revisit when operational needs justify splitting Correct: distribution should solve an evidenced constraint. Microservices guarantee low coupling Trap: services can remain tightly coordinated through shared schemas and deployment assumptions. A monolith cannot have high cohesion Trap: a deployment unit is not the same as a module or responsibility. Split first; integration and monitoring can be deferred indefinitely Trap: remote boundaries introduce failures immediately, not only after the team grows.

entries.title: CS enrichment: One instance is not one request
entries.text: A singleton RequestContext stores currentUser. Requests A and B concurrently set currentUser, then compute an authorization decision. What is the central flaw? A singleton shares the same mutable request field. Interleaving can overwrite one request’s identity with another’s. Pass request-scoped immutable data into the authorization operation; safe singleton construction alone does not make all later operations safe. Singleton initialization locking prevents all later races Trap: publication of the object and synchronization of its mutable operations are different issues. Mark currentUser public so all threads agree on its value Trap: visibility modifiers do not provide request isolation. Add a second singleton to alternate requests Trap: a fixed number of shared slots cannot safely represent arbitrary concurrent requests. Shared mutable request state; pass an explicit request context Correct: lifetime and isolation must match the data.

entries.title: CS enrichment: A factory larger than its requirement
entries.text: A price calculator must choose between two stateless discount rules. There is no family of related products and no mutable lifecycle. Which design fits the stated need? An injected function or small strategy interface makes the variation explicit. Abstract Factory is intended for related product creation; adding it here introduces machinery without a demonstrated requirement. Revisit the choice if the variation grows. Duplicate the entire calculator for each discount Trap: varying one rule should not duplicate unrelated calculation behavior. Inject a discount function or strategy Correct: isolate the actual variation with a small explicit dependency. Build an Abstract Factory hierarchy for every possible future discount Trap: speculative product families increase complexity before the requirement exists. Use a singleton whose mode changes before each call Trap: global mutable selection introduces hidden ordering and concurrency dependencies.

entries.title: CS enrichment: Green mocks, broken wire format
entries.text: A service test mocks a payment client to return success. Production rejects requests because the serialized currency field uses the wrong name. All isolated tests pass. What targeted check is missing? A test that exercises the real serialization and API contract can catch a mismatch that a mock bypasses. Keep fast unit tests for local decisions; add a focused boundary test and a small end-to-end flow rather than assuming either layer alone covers everything. Retry failed production payments until a test passes Trap: retries do not repair deterministic contract errors and can repeat side effects. A real serialization/contract integration check at the payment boundary Correct: verify the behavior the mock replaced. More assertions on the same mocked success response Trap: the test still cannot observe the actual wire format. Replace every unit test with UI automation Trap: broad slow tests discard useful isolation and make failures harder to localize.

entries.title: CS enrichment: A sleep hides the synchronization condition
entries.text: A test starts a background job, sleeps 100 ms, then asserts completion. It passes locally but fails under CI load. Which repair best targets the cause? Wait on the observable completion condition with a bounded timeout, or control the scheduler/clock in an isolated test. Fixed sleep length guesses scheduling speed; unbounded waiting would hide a stuck job. Increase the sleep to ten seconds for every test Trap: longer waits remain timing guesses and slow the suite. Ignore failures after one successful retry Trap: repetition hides instability without fixing the synchronization contract. Remove the completion assertion Trap: deleting the check removes evidence that the job works. Await a completion signal with a bounded timeout Correct: synchronize on behavior instead of guessing elapsed time.

entries.title: CS enrichment: When correct matches exhaust the CPU
entries.text: Documented incident: on 2 July 2019, a Cloudflare WAF rule caused CPU exhaustion through regular-expression backtracking. Its test suite did not identify excessive CPU consumption. The following prevention choices are an original teaching exercise. Which check targets the reported gap? Functional matching examples alone do not bound resource use. Test adversarial near-matches with explicit resource budgets and review the engine’s complexity; an automata-based implementation can avoid catastrophic backtracking for supported regular expressions. Assume a syntactically valid regex has linear runtime Trap: language recognition and the chosen engine’s execution strategy are different. Increase server memory without testing regex execution Trap: the reported bottleneck was CPU exhaustion, not evidence of insufficient memory. Test adversarial near-matches with a CPU/time budget Correct: this measures the failure mode reported in the incident. Add only more normal matching examples Trap: representative happy paths can miss pathological backtracking.

entries.title: CS enrichment: A backup is useful only if it restores
entries.text: Documented incident: GitLab’s January 2017 database outage exposed unreliable backup/recovery paths. Its postmortem describes pg_dump failures and recovery from a manually created staging backup. The choices below are an original prevention exercise. Which evidence best validates the recovery contract? A backup job reporting success cannot establish recoverability. Periodically restoring into an isolated environment exercises the actual tooling, versions and stored data. Verify recovered data and alert on both backup and restore failures; keep production data safe during drills. Checking only that a backup filename exists Trap: a file can exist while containing no usable recovery data. Treating replication alone as a tested independent backup Trap: replication and recoverability are separate guarantees; destructive changes can propagate. An isolated restore drill with recovered-data assertions and failure alerts Correct: this exercises the recovery behavior rather than only the backup command interface. A mock backup client that always returns success Trap: an isolated double bypasses the recovery boundary that failed.
